question: A 25-year-old patient presents with multiple oval, slightly raised lesions on the trunk. Each lesion has a fine, thin scale attached at the periphery but detached in the centre. The patient reports mild itching. Which dermatological condition is most likely associated with it?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A scale is a flat plate or flake of stratum corneum. The silvery, easily detachable flakes described in this patient are characteristic of conditions like psoriasis.

[[figure-1]]

  • Types:
    • Collarette scale: fine, peripherally attached, centrally detached at the edge of the lesion.
    • Annular scaling: seen in porokeratosis.
    • Furfuraceous/pityriasiform: fine and loose.
    • Ichthyotic: large, polygonal.
  • Characteristic feature: Silvery scales (parakeratosis, e.g., psoriasis) reflect light at air-keratin interfaces; they can be altered by wetting.
  • It may accompany or follow many inflammatory disorders.


Crust (Option A): Dried exudate, serum, or blood on the skin surface; differs from flakes of stratum corneum.


Lichenification (Option B): Thickened skin with exaggerated markings due to chronic scratching; not a superficial flake.


Excoriation (Option D): Linear or punctate erosions caused by scratching; not a naturally formed flake of skin.


Definitions of skin lesions:

Term

Definition

Macule

Flat, non-palpable, colored spot < 1 cm

Patch

Flat, colored area > 1 cm (large macule)

Maculopapular rash

Rash containing both macules and papules

Papule

Small, raised, solid lesion < 0.5 cm

Plaque

Raised, flat-topped lesion > 1 cm (coalesced papules)

Nodule

Solid, palpable lesion in dermis/subcutis, > 0.5 cm

Tumor

Solid swelling or mass due to abnormal tissue growth

Vesicle

Small fluid-filled blister < 1 cm

Bulla

Large fluid-filled blister > 1 cm

Pustule

Small raised lesion filled with pus

Pus

Any purulent skin discharge

Petechiae

Pinpoint red/purple spots (1-2 mm) due to bleeding

Ecchymosis

Bruise > 1 cm due to bleeding under the skin

Hematoma

Localised collection of blood under the skin

Erythema

Redness due to increased blood flow or congestion

Wheal

Transient, raised, itchy lesion with redness (urticaria)

Target lesion

Round lesion with 3 zones: dusky centre, pale ring, red rim

Guttate lesions

Multiple small drop-like papules (e.g., guttate psoriasis)

Scale

Dry, thin flakes of keratin (stratum corneum)

Crust

Dried serum, blood, or exudate on the skin surface

Keratosis

Thickened area of keratinised skin

Callus

Thickened stratum corneum due to repeated friction

Lichenification

Thickened, leathery skin from chronic scratching

Atrophy

Thinning or loss of epidermis, dermis, or subcutaneous tissue

Scar

Fibrous tissue replacing lost dermis (atrophic or hypertrophic)

Fibrosis

Excessive formation of fibrous tissue

Sclerosis

Hardening or thickening of skin/subcutaneous tissue

Ulcer

Loss of epidermis and dermis with tissue loss

Erosion

Superficial loss of epidermis without scarring

Excoriation

Loss of epidermis due to scratching

Fissure

Crack or split in the skin

Sinus

Blind-ending tract opening onto skin

Fistula

Abnormal tract between two epithelial surfaces

Cyst

Closed epithelial-lined sac with fluid/semisolid material

Milium

Tiny white keratin-filled cyst

Comedo

Plug of keratin and sebum in the hair follicle

Burrow

Tiny tunnel in skin made by parasites (e.g., scabies)

Cellulitis

Infection of deep skin and subcutaneous tissue

Gangrene

Tissue death due to loss of blood supply

Poikiloderma

Combination of pigmentation, atrophy, and telangiectasia

Alopecia

Loss of hair from normally hairy areas

Aphtha

Small ulcer in the mucosa


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 4.11- 4.13.
lessonTitle: Morphology and Investigations of Skin Lesions
question: A 32-year-old patient presents with chronic, itchy plaques on the scalp and extensor surfaces of the elbows as shown. On examination, the following finding is observed. What is the dermatological finding described in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Lichenification refers to thickened, leathery skin with accentuated markings resulting from chronic rubbing or scratching, commonly seen in conditions with persistent pruritus.

Lichenification is characterised by the thickening of the Epidermis and dermis due to prolonged scratching. It is a secondary skin lesion associated with thick skin, hyperpigmentation and exaggerated skin markings. Commonly seen in Chronic eczema.


Acantholysis (Option A): Loss of cohesion between keratinocytes forming intraepidermal clefts, seen in pemphigus.


Parakeratosis (Option B): Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, seen in psoriasis or eczematous dermatitis.


Papillomatosis (Option D): Upward elongation of dermal papillae, often seen in psoriasis.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 4.11, 41.19.
lessonTitle: Morphology and Investigations of Skin Lesions
question: A middle-aged patient presents with a long history of intense pruritus. Examination reveals a thickened plaque with exaggerated skin markings and a leathery appearance at the site of repeated scratching, as shown in the image. What is this finding called?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The examination shown is the hair pull test, which is used to assess active hair shedding.
  • Approximately 50–60 hairs are gently grasped close to the scalp and pulled with steady traction.
  • A test is considered positive when more than 10% of the hairs (typically more than 5–6 hairs) are extracted.
  • A positive hair pull test in a patient with diffuse hair loss following a physiological stressor, such as a febrile illness, surgery, childbirth, or severe emotional stress, is most consistent with telogen effluvium.
  • In this condition, a large number of hair follicles prematurely enter the telogen (resting) phase, resulting in diffuse shedding approximately 2–3 months after the triggering event.
  • The condition is usually self-limiting once the underlying cause is corrected.

Alopecia areata (Option B) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by well-defined, non-scarring patches of hair loss. Although the hair pull test may be positive at the active margins of a lesion, the hallmark finding is patchy alopecia with exclamation mark hairs, rather than the diffuse shedding seen in this patient.

Androgenetic alopecia (Option C) is the most common cause of progressive patterned hair loss in both men and women. Hair loss occurs due to miniaturization of hair follicles under the influence of dihydrotestosterone (DHT). The hair pull test is usually negative, as the condition involves gradual follicular miniaturization rather than active diffuse shedding.

Trichotillomania (Option D) is a psychiatric impulse-control disorder in which patients repeatedly pull out their own hair, leading to irregular patches of hair loss with hairs of varying lengths. The hair pull test is typically negative, as the loose telogen hairs are not the primary mechanism of hair loss. The diagnosis is based on the characteristic history and examination findings.



Reference:
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8719967/
  • https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0190962216308921
question: A 28-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss for the past 3 months following a febrile illness. During examination, the manoeuvre demonstrated in the attached video is performed, and more than six hairs are easily extracted with gentle traction. This finding is most suggestive of which of the following conditions

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Dermal papilla expresses androgen receptors and 5α-reductase type 2 and controls follicle size and response to androgens.

Mechanism of Androgen Action on Hair Follicle:

  • Androgen response is follicle-specific
  • Androgen receptors are present only in dermal papilla cells
  • Follicle size depends on dermal papilla volume
  • Dermal papilla expresses 5α-reductase type 2
  • Androgens alter dermal papilla cell number & ECM
  • Dermal papilla releases:
    • Growth-promoting factors (beard hair)
    • TGF-β (in balding scalp) → inhibits hair growth

Androgens stimulate terminal hair growth in some sites but cause follicular miniaturisation and hair loss on the scalp. This paradox is determined at the level of the dermal papilla.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 89.9, 89.10
question: The primary site of androgen action, determining hair growth and pattern baldness, is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Finasteride selectively inhibits 5α-reductase type 2, the key isoform involved in androgen-dependent hair growth.

  • Testosterone → DHT via 5α-reductase
  • Isoforms:
    • Type 1: widespread in the skin
    • Type 2: androgen-target tissues (key for hair growth)
    • Type 3: role unclear
  • Finasteride inhibits type 2 → ↓ alopecia & hirsutism.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 89.9.
question: Which of the following 5α-reductase isoforms does finasteride not act upon?

correctAnswer: B. A scalp biopsy is routinely required to confirm the diagnosis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Androgenetic alopecia is a clinical diagnosis. A scalp biopsy is done only if the diagnosis is unclear or to rule out scarring alopecia.

Androgenic alopecia:

  • Pattern hair loss: Progressive, patterned scalp hair thinning due to follicular miniaturisation. (Option C)

Men

Women

Pattern of hair loss

Predominantly androgen-dependent → Androgenetic alopecia (AGA).

Women: Termed Female Pattern Hair Loss (FPHL); the androgen role is less consistent.

Male-pattern hair loss can occur in women and vice versa.

Associated conditions

Men: Possible association with coronary artery disease

Women: PCOS, hyperandrogenism (Option A), hypertension, diabetes

Trichodynia may coexist

Investigations

Men: usually not required

If hyperandrogenism is suspected:

  • Testosterone, DHEAS, androstenedione
  • Pelvic USG ± adrenal imaging
  • Scalp biopsy if diagnosis is unclear

Medical Treatment
  • Topical minoxidil (2-5%)
  • Oral finasteride 1 mg/day (5α-reductase type 2 inhibitor)
  • Dutasteride (type 1 & 2 inhibitor; more potent, more side effects)
  • Topical minoxidil - first line (Option D)
  • Antiandrogens (selected cases):
  • Spironolactone
  • Cyproterone acetate
  • Finasteride (limited evidence; teratogenic)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 89.17 - 89.23.

options.text: It is often associated with hyperandrogenism
A scalp biopsy is routinely required to confirm the diagnosis
Hair loss occurs due to follicular miniaturisation
Topical minoxidil is useful in the management

question: A 31-year-old woman presents with bitemporal recession and vertex thinning, giving a male-pattern distribution of hair loss as shown in the image. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is wrong?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Female pattern hair loss (FPHL) can occur in males and presents as central diffuse thinning with preserved frontal hairline, unlike classic male pattern baldness.

Clinical Patterns of Hair Loss:

  • Men:
    • Bitemporal recession → vertex thinning → frontal-vertex baldness
    • Classified by the Hamilton-Norwood scale
    • Occipital scalp is usually spared.

  • Women:
    • Diffuse crown thinning with preserved frontal hairline
    • “Christmas-tree” widening of the central part
    • Classified by Ludwig / Sinclair scales
    • True vertex baldness is uncommon.

Male pattern androgenetic alopecia (Option A): Typically shows bitemporal recession and vertex balding.

Telogen effluvium (Option B): Causes diffuse shedding, not patterned thinning.

Alopecia areata (Option D): Presents with well-defined patches.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 89.14-89.17.
question: A 26-year-old man presents with diffuse thinning over the central scalp with preservation of the frontal hairline. There is no bitemporal recession or vertex balding. Family history is negative. Scalp skin appears normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Alopecia areata is classically associated with nail pitting (thimble pitting) due to involvement of the nail matrix.

Nail involvement (10-15%):

  • Fine stippled (thimble) pitting - classic
  • Trachyonychia (rough nails)
  • Non-specific nail dystrophy

Alopecia Areata - Clinical Features:

  • Lesion: Smooth, well-defined bald patch; normal skin
  • Edge sign: Exclamation mark hairs
  • Course: Unpredictable; regrowth or progression
  • Severe forms:
    • Alopecia totalis - complete scalp hair loss
    • Alopecia universalis - complete body hair loss
  • Pattern: Ophiasis (occipital band)
  • Sites: Scalp, beard, eyebrows, eyelashes
  • Regrowth: Initially fine, non-pigmented
  • Pigment: White hair spared

Lichen planus (Option A): Shows longitudinal ridging and pterygium.

Psoriasis (Option C): Nail pitting is coarse and irregular with onycholysis and oil-drop sign.

Onychomycosis (Option D): Causes discolouration, subungual debris, and no pitting.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 89.31, 89.32.
question: A 22-year-old patient presents with asymptomatic patchy hair loss on the scalp. Nail examination reveals findings as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given image & features indicates Alopecia areata. Intralesional corticosteroids (e.g., triamcinolone acetonide) are the most effective first-line treatment for limited patchy alopecia areata, producing localised hair regrowth.

Alopecia Areata - Management:

  • No curative therapy
  • Spontaneous remission in ≤80% of limited patchy AA (<1 year)
  • First-Line (Limited Patchy AA):
    • Topical potent steroids (e.g. clobetasol):
      • Use ≥3 months
      • Ineffective in totalis/universalis
    • Intralesional corticosteroids (most effective):
      • Triamcinolone 5-10 mg/mL (multiple injections)
      • Side effect: transient skin atrophy
      • Not for rapidly progressive or extensive AA
    • Other options (limited benefit):
      • Minoxidil (Option A)
      • Anthralin (dithranol)
  • Second line: Oral / pulse corticosteroids - temporary benefit, high relapse (Option C)
  • Third line: Contact immunotherapy (DPCP) (Option D)
    • Best documented (≈50-60%)
    • Agent: DPCP (preferred)
    • Weekly application → mild dermatitis
    • Poor prognosis if:
      • Nail changes
      • Early onset
      • Family history
      • Totalis/universalis
  • PUVA therapy


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 89.33, 89.34.
question: A 24-year-old patient presents with a single, well-defined patch of non-scarring hair loss on the scalp as shown. What is the most effective first-line treatment for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A) 1, 3 and 5

Explanation:

Lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus erythematosus, and folliculitis decalvans cause permanent follicular destruction, leading to cicatricial alopecia.

Alopecia areata and telogen effluvium are non-scarring alopecias.

The most important conditions causing cicatricial (scarring) alopecia are:

  • Primary causes:
    • Lichen planopilaris (LPP)
    • Frontal fibrosing alopecia (FFA)
    • Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA)
    • Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE)
    • Folliculitis decalvans
    • Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp
    • Pseudopelade of Brocq
  • Secondary causes:
    • Tinea capitis (Kerion & favus)
    • Traction alopecia (advanced stage)
    • Thermal or chemical burns
    • Radiodermatitis (post-radiation therapy)
    • Scalp neoplasms (e.g., Basal Cell Carcinoma)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 89.35.
question:
Which of the following conditions are causes of cicatricial (scarring) alopecia?

  1. Lichen planopilaris
  2. Alopecia areata
  3. Discoid lupus erythematosus
  4. Telogen effluvium
  5. Folliculitis decalvans

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given image depicts tinea capitis. KOH mount of plucked hair or scalp scales demonstrates fungal hyphae/arthroconidia, making it the confirmatory diagnostic test for tinea capitis.

Tinea capitis:

  • Dermatophyte fungal infection of the scalp hair shafts (ringworm of scalp).
  • Requires stratum corneum invasion first
  • Hair invasion occurs ~ 3 weeks after inoculation
  • Spread to adjacent follicles → persistence → regression ± inflammation
  • Clinical features:
    • Partial hair loss + scaling ± inflammation
    • Broken hairs, grey patches
    • Itching variable

[[figure-1]]

  • Management:
    • First line:
      • Terbinafine (4 weeks)
      • Itraconazole (4-6 weeks)
      • Griseofulvin 10 mg/kg for 6 weeks (20 mg/kg for T. tonsurans, T. schoenleinii)
    • Adjuncts:
      • Ketoconazole/selenium sulphide shampoo (reduce spread)
      • Remove crusts (kerion)
      • Antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection

Tzanck smear (Option A): Used for herpes infections

Dermoscopy (Option B): Supportive (comma/corkscrew hairs) but not confirmatory

Slit skin smear (Option D): Used in leprosy.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.8, 32.38-32.40.
question: Which of the following is used in the diagnosis of the condition as shown in the image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Bamboo hair refers to trichorrhexis invaginata, which is a hallmark feature of Netherton syndrome, along with ichthyosis linearis circumflexa and atopy.

[[figure-1]]

Netherton syndrome:

  • Triad:
    • Trichorrhexis invaginata (bamboo hair)
    • Ichthyosis linearis circumflexa
    • Atopy (↑ IgE, eczema)
  • Hair findings:
    • Fragile, short, brittle hair
    • Sparse/absent eyebrows & eyelashes
  • Diagnosis:
    • Light microscopy of hair (gold standard)
    • Single trichorrhexis invaginata = diagnostic
    • Dermoscopy: golf-tee appearance
  • Skin features:
    • Erythema & scaling from infancy
    • Serpiginous, polycyclic plaques
  • Management:
    • No specific hair treatment
    • Avoid physical/chemical trauma

Trichothiodystrophy (Option A) is characterised by sulfur-deficient brittle hair with “tiger-tail” banding on polarised light, not bamboo hair.

[[figure-2]]

Menkes disease (Option C) shows pili torti (twisted hair) due to a copper metabolism defect.

[[figure-3]]

Trichorrhexis nodosa (Option D) involves nodes and fraying of the hair shaft, not invagination.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 89.53, 89.54.
question: The following finding is classically seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The lunula is the whitish, crescent-shaped area at the proximal portion of the nail plate, representing the distal part of the nail matrix. It is most visible on the thumb and great toe. The white colour is due to the matrix cells and obscured underlying vasculature.

Parts of nail:

  • Nail plate: firmly attached to nail bed; proximal quarter covered by proximal nail fold
  • Lunula: white distal part of matrix; most visible on thumb/great toe
  • Pink colour of nail: due to the translucent plate over the vascular nail bed
  • Cuticle: from the junction of the dorsal & ventral proximal nail fold
  • Matrix (main nail producer):
    • Dorsal-ventral proximal nail fold
    • Intermediate - germinal matrix
    • Ventral - nail bed (sterile matrix)
  • Nail bed (Option C): role in nail formation is minimal; disease may form false nail
  • Hyponychium (Option A): beneath the free nail edge
  • Onychodermal band (nail isthmus): distal attachment of nail to bed; damage → onycholysis
  • Proximal nail fold (Option D): Skin fold covering the nail’s proximal part

Important Nail Changes & Clinical Associations

  • Beau’s lines:
    • Transverse depressions → temporary matrix arrest
    • Seen in: Severe illness, chemotherapy
  • Terry’s nails:
    • White nail with distal pink band
    • Seen in: Cirrhosis, CHF, diabetes
  • Half-and-half nails (Lindsay nails):
    • Proximal white + distal brown
    • Seen in: Chronic kidney disease
  • Mees’ lines:
    • Transverse white bands → move with nail growth ❗
    • Seen in: Arsenic poisoning, systemic illness
  • Muehrcke’s lines:
    • Paired white lines → do not move
    • Seen in: Hypoalbuminemia
  • Clubbing:
    • Increased nail curvature
    • Seen in: Lung disease, cyanotic heart disease
  • Koilonychia (Spoon nails):
    • Concave nails
    • Seen in: Iron deficiency anemia
  • Nail pitting:
    • Surface depressions
    • Seen in: Psoriasis, alopecia areata
  • Oil drop sign (Salmon patch):
    • Yellow-red discolouration under nail
    • Seen in: Psoriasis

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 95.2, 95.3.
question: What is the structure marked in the given image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) is classically seen in hemochromatosis due to iron overload affecting nail structure.

  • Concave, hollow nails with reverse curvature in both transverse and longitudinal axes. Most prominent in the thumbs and great toes.
  • Common in infancy as a benign feature of the great toenail.
  • Can persist in infants with cysteine‐rich keratin deficiency (e.g., trichothiodystrophy).
  • Familial cases are usually autosomal dominant.
  • Systemic association:
    • Iron deficiency anaemia (most common)
    • Haemochromatosis
  • Dermatoses & external factors:
    • Psoriasis or dermatophyte infection → nail bed hyperkeratosis pushes nail distally
    • Mechanical/chemical trauma → nail softening (e.g., hairdressers, oil exposure, permanent wave solutions)

Iron deficiency anaemia (Option B): Can also cause koilonychia, but lab tests here indicate iron excess, not deficiency.

Trauma (Option C): May deform nails but does not typically cause concave nails.

Nail infection (Option D): Usually causes thickening, discolouration, or brittleness, not spooning.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 95.7.
question: A 55-year-old man presents with brittle, concave nails affecting his thumbs and great toes. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation. What is the most likely underlying condition associated with this nail finding?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Beau’s lines are transverse (horizontal) depressions across the nail plate caused by a temporary interruption of nail matrix growth. This arrest is most commonly due to an acute systemic illness such as severe infections (e.g., pneumonia), myocardial infarction, or drug reactions. When the cause is generalised, the condition is specifically termed Beau’s lines, reflecting a temporary nail matrix arrest.

The transverse grooves may be classified based on aetiology. Endogenous causes produce arcuate grooves that parallel the lunula, whereas exogenous causes, such as manicure-related trauma or habit-tic deformity, produce grooves that match the contour of the proximal nail fold and are often multiple, giving rise to the appearance of “washboard nails.” Localised causes include trauma, inflammation, and neurological events.

The timing of the insult can be estimated by measuring the distance of the groove from the proximal nail fold, as this reflects the time elapsed since the growth arrest. The severity of the insult correlates with the depth of the groove, while the duration of the insult is reflected by the width of the depression. Beau’s lines are often most prominent on the thumbs and great toes.

In severe cases, when the growth arrest involves the full thickness of the nail plate, the nail may shed completely, a complication known as onychomadesis.

Mees’ lines (Option A) are transverse white lines due to abnormal nail plate keratinisation (e.g., arsenic poisoning), not grooves.

[[figure-1]]

Onycholysis (Option C) refers to the separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, usually distally.

[[figure-2]]

Koilonychia (Option D) describes spoon-shaped nails, classically associated with iron deficiency or hemochromatosis.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 95.11
question: A 45-year-old man develops the following finding, as shown in the image on multiple fingernails 2 months after severe pneumonia. What is this finding called?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Yellow nail syndrome is characterised by the classic triad of yellow, slow-growing nails, lymphedema, and respiratory disease (e.g., pleural effusions, bronchiectasis).

  • Nails: Yellow, thickened, ↑ curvatures, lunula absent, cuticle lost, very slow growth
  • Classic triad:
    • Yellow nails
    • Lymphedema
    • Respiratory disease: Pleural effusions, bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis
  • Epidemiology: Adults; non-inherited
  • Pathogenesis: Lymphatic dysfunction with fibrous subungual tissue
  • Associations: Malignancy, D-penicillamine, nephrotic syndrome
  • Treatment: Variable; Vitamin E ± azoles, treat infections

Onychomycosis (Option A): Causes yellow, thickened nails but is usually associated with subungual debris and fungal elements; it does not cause lymphedema or respiratory involvement.

Lichen planus (Option B): Nail LP may cause thinning, ridging, or pterygium formation, but yellow discolouration with systemic lymphatic and respiratory features is not typical.

Psoriasis (Option D): Produces nail pitting, onycholysis, and subungual hyperkeratosis; lymphedema and pleural effusions are not features.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 95.14, 95.15.
question: A 52-year-old man presents with slowly growing, thickened, yellow nails involving most fingers and toes. Examination shows loss of cuticle and an absent lunula. He also has chronic bilateral leg swelling and a history of recurrent pleural effusions and chronic cough. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A subungual glomus tumour presents as a small bluish lesion under the nail with severe paroxysmal pain, marked cold sensitivity, and point tenderness, which are classic diagnostic features.

Glomus tumour:

  • Tumour of the glomus body (myoarterial), composed of glomus cells and vascular channels
  • Types: Solid glomus tumour, glomangioma (commonest), glomangiomyoma
  • Epidemiology: Uncommon; ↑ after 7 yrs; adults in 3rd-4th decade; no sex predilection
  • Genetics: AD inheritance (multiple lesions); glomulin gene, chr 1p21 22
  • Clinical (Solitary): Small pink/blue nodule, severe pain, cold sensitivity; subungual common

[[figure-1]]

  • Clinical (Multiple): Larger, dark blue, deep dermal, usually painless
  • Pathology: Well-circumscribed dermal tumour; SMA+, desmin−
  • Differential: Leiomyoma, eccrine spiradenoma, hemangioma
  • Treatment: Surgical excision (curative)

Eccrine spiradenoma (Option A): Painful dermal tumour, but not characteristically subungual or cold-sensitive

Pyogenic granuloma (Option C): Friable, bleeding vascular lesion without severe pain

Subungual melanoma (Option D): Pigmented lesion with nail dystrophy, usually painless initially



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 137.43-137.45.
question: A 32-year-old woman presents with severe, localised pain at the tip of her right index finger for 8 months. The pain is excruciating on exposure to cold and is triggered by minimal pressure. Examination shows a tiny bluish-red discolouration beneath the nail plate. The nail appears otherwise normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nail-patella syndrome is caused by mutations in the LMX1B gene and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, often showing vertical transmission with variable expressivity.

Nail-patella syndrome:

  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant
  • Gene: LMX1B (9q33.3)
  • Nail findings:
    • Nails: Congenital, bilateral nail dysplasia with a triangular lunula (often the only feature); fingernails, especially thumbnails, are most affected, with greater severity on the ulnar side.
    • Pattern: Changes are symmetrical, present at birth, and affect fingernails more than toenails, with severity decreasing from index to little finger.
    • Digits: Swan-neck deformity (DIP flexion, PIP hyperextension) with absent DIP creases.
  • Key skeletal features:
    • Small/absent patella
    • Elbow deformities
    • Iliac horns (pathognomonic)
  • Systemic associations:
    • Renal disease (proteinuria, HTN)
    • Open-angle glaucoma
  • Diagnosis: Clinical + X-ray pelvis (iliac horns)
  • Management: Supportive; monitor kidneys, BP, eyes

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 69.15, 69.16.
question: What is the inheritance pattern of Nail-patella syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A young adult with greasy, hyperkeratotic papules over the seborrhoeic areas (face, chest, back), involvement of flexures, and characteristic nail changes strongly points to Darier disease (keratosis follicularis).

  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant
  • Gene: ATP2A2 → encodes SERCA2 (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase)
  • Pathophysiology: Defective calcium pump → immature desmosomes & adherens junctions → loss of cell adhesion and abnormal keratinocyte differentiation
  • Histology: Acantholytic dyskeratosis
  • Clinical features:
    • Greasy papules/plaques in seborrheic areas & flexures
    • Nail abnormalities: V-shaped notches, longitudinal violaceous or white streaks

[[figure-1]]

Hailey-Hailey disease (Option A): Painful erosions at friction sites, flexural involvement, no hyperkeratotic papules, and less prominent nail changes.

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option C): Flaccid bullae and erosions, oral mucosa involvement, positive Nikolsky sign, histology shows intraepidermal acantholysis without dyskeratosis.

Seborrheic dermatitis (Option D): Erythematous, scaly patches in seborrheic areas, not associated with nail changes or acantholytic dyskeratosis.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 71.24.
question: A 22-year-old presents with greasy papules on the face, chest, and back, flexural plaques, and nail findings as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chloronychia (green nail syndrome) is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, producing green pigments in a moist environment, typically associated with onycholysis and minimal symptoms.

  • Green to green-black discolouration of the nail due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.
  • Bacterial pigments (pyocyanin, pyoverdin) stain the nail plate.
  • Occurs in a moist environment, often with onycholysis.
  • Predisposing factors:
    • Repeated water exposure (dishwashers, cleaners)
    • Nail trauma
    • Pre-existing nail disease (onychomycosis, psoriasis)
    • Occlusive gloves, artificial nails
  • Clinical features:
    • Green/green-black nail discolouration (hallmark)
    • Usually distal nail involvement & often painless
    • May have distal onycholysis ± chronic paronychia
  • Diagnosis: Clinical
  • Treatment: Keep nail dry + topical antibiotics (gentamicin); oral ciprofloxacin if severe

Onychomycosis (Option A): Usually yellow-white discolouration with subungual debris

[[figure-1]]

Subungual melanoma (Option C): Brown-black pigment, often longitudinal, may involve the nail fold

[[figure-2]]

Nail psoriasis (Option D): Pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop sign, not green discolouration

[[figure-3]]



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 95.12, 95.13.
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4298286/
question: A 38-year-old homemaker presents with discolouration of a single fingernail for 3 weeks. Examination shows findings as shown in the image below. The nail is painless. She gives a history of frequent exposure to water and detergents. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features and the polarised microscopy image are suggestive of Trichothiodystrophy.

Trichothiodystrophy is characterised by brittle hair with tiger-tail banding, due to low sulfur content in the hair shaft. Associated systemic features include short stature, photosensitivity, ichthyosis, and intellectual impairment (PIBIDS syndrome).

  • Key feature: Brittle hair with tiger-tail banding on polarised microscopy
  • Hair defects: Pili torti, trichorrhexis nodosa; hypotrichosis (scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes)
  • Nails: Dystrophic changes
  • Systemic features: Short stature, progeroid facies, microcephaly, cataracts, joint contractures, asthma
  • Subtypes:
    • Sabinas - intellectual disability, dental caries
    • Hair-brain - infertility, developmental delay
    • Tay - ichthyosis
    • PIBIDS - photosensitivity, ichthyosis, brittle hair, intellectual impairment, ↓ fertility, short stature
  • Pathogenesis: ↓ high-sulfur hair proteins
  • Genes:
    • Non-photosensitive: C7ORF11 (MPLKIP)
    • Photosensitive (NER defect): ERCC2, ERCC3, GTF2H5

Netherton syndrome (Option A): Characterised by trichorrhexis invaginata (bamboo hair) and atopic features, not tiger-tail banding.

[[figure-1]]

Menkes disease (Option C): Presents with kinky, hypopigmented hair and neurodegeneration due to copper deficiency, without tiger-tail banding.

[[figure-2]]

Trichorrhexis nodosa (Option D): A localised hair shaft defect without systemic features such as ichthyosis or developmental delay.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 68.21, 68.22.

question: A 28-year-old man complains of progressive hair thinning over the temples and crown over the past two years. There is no history of sudden hair shedding, scarring, or itching. Examination shows a receding hairline and miniaturized hairs in the affected areas. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient with a positive hair pull test and patchy hair loss has alopecia areata.

Alopecia areata is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune condition targeting the anagen hair bulb causing non-scarring hair loss. Clinical features include,

  • Localized patches of hair loss on the scalp that emerge over a few weeks. It can also affect other areas, such as the beard, eyebrows, eyelashes, and extremities.
  • Variants:
    • Alopecia Totalis: Complete hair loss from the scalp.
    • Alopecia Universalis: Complete hair loss from all over the body.
    • Ophiasis: Occipital hair loss.

[[figure-1]]

Alopecia Totalis

  • Exclamation-mark hair, with a narrower proximal end than the distal end, is commonly observed at the periphery of lesions and is a pathognomonic finding in patients with alopecia areata.
  • Pitting of nails that is superficial, geometric and regular

[[figure-2]]

Patchy hair loss

[[figure-3]]

Yellow dots and exclamation mark hair

[[figure-4]]

Pitting of nails

The pull test is positive, Very gentle traction on the unaffected hair at the margin of the patch of hair loss can remove all of the hair from the roots painlessly. It is a distinguishing feature of alopecia areata

Traction alopecia (Option A): Because of traction, there is an excess force applied to the hair follicle causing traction alopecia. On the hair pull test, it is not possible to remove the hair with a gentle tug. The patient will have a previous history of hairstyling or wearing wigs.

[[figure-5]]

Tinea capitis (Option C): Pull test, Hair may break off, but it is not removed completely. There will be other symptoms like irritation and itching.

Telogen effluvium (Option D): During stress, hair in the anagen phase prematurely converts into the telogen phase, causing hair loss. Only a fraction of the hair can be removed by gentle traction and past history is significant for stress.



Reference:

Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Section 89.10

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hair loss with increased central parting and decreased hair volume is considered to be female pattern hair loss (FPHL). It is different from female pattern baldness as there is no loss of front hairline (Option A).

[[figure-1]]

  • It is commonly seen in middle-aged women with progressive loss of terminal hair over the vertex of the scalp.
  • It presents with diffuse thinning of hair, increased hair shedding, decreased hair volume, and widening of hair partition.
  • Grade 3 FPHL is also called the ‘Fir tree / Christmas tree’ pattern.

Treatment: Topical 2% minoxidil is the first line of treatment, with or without adjuncts like spironolactone in women and finasteride in men.

question: A 28 year old female presents with concerns about hair loss and decreased hair volume, as shown below. Many members of her family also have a similar history of significant hair loss. All of the following are true about the given condition except?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presents with concerns about hair loss and hair thinning, with the family history suggesting the diagnosis of male pattern baldness in this patient.

Male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) is common in men, characterized by progressive loss of terminal hairs on the scalp, influenced by genetics and hormones. It typically begins at the temples and crown, progressing with age.

[[figure-1]]

Dihydrotestosterone (DHT), derived from testosterone, shrinks hair follicles, reducing the anagen phase and miniaturizing hair. This leads to the transformation of thick terminal hair into finer, vellus hair.

Symptoms include hair thinning and bitemporal recession of the hairline

Bitemporal recession → vertex balding → Finally left with a band of hair in the occipital region because this area is androgen-independent.

Grading: Hamilton Norwood grading

[[figure-2]]

Treatment:

  • Topical treatment: Minoxidil 5%
  • Systemic: Oral 5-alpha reductase inhibitors(finasteride, dutasteride)
  • Surgical: Hair transplantation

Alopecia areata (Option C) is an autoimmune condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, leading to sudden, round patches of hair loss. This is not consistent with the given clinical scenario.

Pseudopelade of Brocq (Option D):

  • Pseudopelade of Brocq (PPB) is a rare, idiopathic self-limiting hair disorder resulting in progressive cicatricial alopecia.
  • Footprints in snow appearance.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 89.14-86.24.

question: A 35 year old male presents with concern about hair loss and gradual thinning, as seen in the picture given below. He reports that all the male members of his family has lost their hair by 45 years, What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient with a history of autoimmune diseases and patchy hair loss as described in the question and image is suggestive of alopecia areata.

Trichoclasis is a feature of a feature of trichorrhexis nodosa, not alopecia areata.

Trichoclasis:

  • It is a transverse break in the hair shaft through a node seen in Trichorrhexis nodosa.
  • It is a hair shaft disorder where the hair shaft is excessively fragile due to the presence of nodes.
  • The end of the hair resembles a small paint brush with cortical fibers extruding through the fracture as shown in the image.
  • The proximal end of the hair shaft is normal, unlike in alopecia areata.

  • It is associated with rare genetic diseases like argininosuccinate lyase deficiency.
  • Clinical features: Sparse, brittle, and lustreless hair
  • Diagnosis is through physical examination and hair shaft microscopy
  • Treatment includes avoiding trauma to the hair and management of the medical cause.

The features of alopecia areata include

  • Ophiasis (Option A) is scalp hair loss in the occipital region, whereas sisaipho is the opposite of this variant, with scalp hair loss sparing the temporal and occipital areas.
Ophiasis Sisaipho


  • Exclamation mark hair (Option B)
  • Turning grey syndrome (Option D): It is a feature of alopecia areata where white hair are typically spared by immune cells, leading to loss of black hair with sparing of white hair
  • Nail pitting: Regular, geometric pitting of the nail bed as shown below.

Note: Psoriasis shows irregular pitting.

Treatment depends on the extent of the disease. Topical therapy for limited disease is done using intralesional steroids and contact immunotherapy whereas systemic therapy, Levamisole or Cyclosporine is used for extensive disease.



Reference:
  1. Spano F, Donovan JC. Alopecia areata: Part 1: pathogenesis, diagnosis, and prognosis. Can Fam Physician. 2015 Sep;61(9):751-5. PMID: 26371097; PMCID: PMC4569104.

question: A 30 year old woman has been complaining of patchy scalp hair loss for the past three weeks. Her past medical history is significant for vitiligo and thyroid disorders. On examination, she has a well-circumscribed area of hair loss over her occipital region, as shown below. Which among the following is not a feature of the disease described?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The boy with the above history and a characteristic Friar Tuck hair loss pattern has trichotillomania.

Trichotillomania:

  • It is a psychiatric disorder in which obsessive, recurrent pulling of one’s hair results in hair loss.
  • It is seen in adolescents or young adults, more commonly in girls.
  • Patchy hair loss with broken hair of variable lengths is seen in commonly accessible sites like the frontoparietal area of the scalp.
  • In the Friar Tuck sign or Tonsure pattern, there is uneven hair loss in a circular pattern with surrounding hairs remaining unaffected.

[[figure-1]]

  • Perifollicular hemorrhages can also be seen because of trauma to the scalp.
  • Skin biopsy shows empty hair follicles, with some forming soft twisted hairs described as trichomalacia.
  • Treatment includes cognitive behavioral therapy and antipsychotic medications like SSRI and paroxetine.
  • Trichobezoar/ Rapunzel syndrome is caused by chronic ingestion of hair; it is commonly seen in young females who may have psychological disorders, such as trichophagia and trichotillomania. Common symptoms are abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss.

Netherton syndrome (Option D) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the serine protease inhibitor. Characteristic triad includes,

  • Congenital Ichtyosiform erythroderma.
  • Trichorrhexis invaginata (Bamboo hair).
  • Atopic diathesis.

Alopecia areata (Option B) is an autoimmune condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, leading to sudden, round patches of hair loss. This is not consistent with the given clinical scenario.

Pseudopelade of Brocq (Option C) is a chronic and slowly progressive idiopathic condition with no inflammation, scaling, or erythema.

  • Smooth patches due to scarring alopecia.
  • Footprint in snow appearance-spreading patches of cicatricial alopecia.

    [[figure-2]]

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 86.17- 86.19.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presented with a history of recurrent painful, pustular lesions on the scalp which heal with scarring suggests the diagnosis of Folliculitis decalvans. A punch biopsy of the scalp and culture of extracted hair is the most appropriate investigation.

Folliculitis decalvans:

  • Folliculitis decalvans or tufted hair folliculitis is a progressive pattern of cicatricial alopecia of the scalp.
  • Its characteristic feature is the presence of multiple tufts of hair emerging from a single follicular opening also known as Doll’s hair appearance
  • The images below depict the scaring alopecia seen in Folliculitis decalvans.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • Diagnosis is based on clinical and histological findings. Ideal biopsy tissue should contain clinical signs of scarring, no follicular ostia, and active inflammation (pustules, erythema, etc.).
  • Hence, a punch biopsy that extends into the subcutaneous fat is our preferred procedure for the pathologic evaluation of FD.
  • Oral antibiotics (Tetracyclines) are the mainstay treatment.


Reference:

Goldberg J L. 2022.Folliculitis decalvans, UpToDate

question: A middle-aged woman presents with a history of recurrent painful, pustular lesions on scalp which heals with scarring. She is healthy otherwise with no history of similar lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above scenario with scalp lesions is seen in dissecting cellulitis of the scalp, which is part of the follicular occlusion tetrad. Pustular psoriasis is not part of the tetrad.

Follicular occlusion tetrad is a group of four disorders where follicular occlusion is thought to be a key pathogenic event. The components of this tetrad are:

  1. Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp
  2. Hidradenitis suppurativa (Option D)
  3. Acne conglobata (Option A)
  4. Pilonidal sinus (Option B)

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Pilonidal sinus

Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp:

  • Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp (Hoffman disease) is a type of cicatricial alopecia characterized by multiple suppurative nodular lesions over the scalp.
  • Follicular occlusion by accumulation of sebaceous and keratinous materials causes an intense neutrophilic inflammatory reaction which is exacerbated by secondary bacterial infection.
  • The patient presents with boggy, suppurative pustules and nodules that later form sinus tracts. This leads to patchy and scarring alopecia over the scalp as shown below.
  • Diagnosis is mainly clinical through history and examination.
  • Cultures are done to determine the organism causing secondary infection.

Treatment:

  • Treatment is started with oral antibiotics and/or oral isotretinoin.
  • Biologic tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitors and surgical excision are options in patients who don’t respond to earlier treatment.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 107.8 - 107.9.
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10613185/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis in this patient undergoing chemotherapy is Anagen effluvium, which refers to hair shedding during the anagen or growth stage of the hair cycle.

Hair goes through 3 stages in its life cycle. These stages are the

  • Anagen phase (growth phase): 86% of hair, 3 years.
  • Catagen phase (transition phase): 1% of hair, 3 weeks.
  • Telogen phase (falling phase): 10-13% of hair, 3 months.

[[figure-1]]

Anagen effluvium:

  • Anagen effluvium refers to hair shedding in the growth phase of the hair cycle. In this phase, the affected hairs have a cessation in their mitotic activity, causing damage to the hair shaft that results in breakage and complete hair loss if the bulb is affected.
  • The main causes of anagen effluvium are toxic or inflammatory insults from drugs, toxins, radiation, and autoimmune diseases. Infections may interrupt hair growth, resulting in a single or several bald patches.
  • Onset is rapid after 2–3 weeks after exposure to the cause.
  • It is a diffuse, non-scarring type of alopecia that is completely reversible after the stoppage of cause, with a delay of 3–6 months. It requires no particular treatment.

Catagen (Option B) is incorrect because it is the transitional phase (2–3 weeks) when hair growth slows and follicular regression begins. It is not the primary target in chemotherapy-related hair loss.

Telogen (Option C) is incorrect because telogen effluvium refers to hair shedding due to premature shift into the resting phase, typically seen after stress, fever, or childbirth, not chemotherapy. Onset is delayed (2–3 months) after the insult.

Exogen (Option D): is incorrect because this is the shedding phase of telogen hairs. It is a passive process and not directly disrupted by chemotherapy agents.



Reference:

1. Rugo H S. 2023. Alopecia related to systemic cancer therapy, UpToDate

2. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 89.6 - 86.27.
question: A 70 year old man presents with complaints of recent hair loss. He is currently undergoing chemotherapy treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Scalp examination reveals significantly decreased hair density compared to the previous visit. Which stage of his hair cycle is most likely affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presented with complaints of breathlessness, weakness, and fatigue for the past few weeks and has spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), as shown in the image, suggesting iron deficiency anemia.Koilonychia is most commonly a manifestation of chronic iron deficiency.Iron deficiency anemia is primarily a laboratory diagnosis. Low serum iron and ferritin levels plus an elevated total iron binding capacity (TIBC) are diagnostic of iron deficiency.

Other causes of koilonychia include

  • Pulmonary and thoracic causes- Bronchogenic carcinoma, suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, lung abscess, empyema), interstitial lung disease, long-standing pulmonary TB.
  • Gastrointestinal causes- Cirrhosis of the liver, UC, Crohn’s disease.
  • Cardiovascular causes- Cyanotic congenital heart disease, bacterial endocarditis, atrial myxoma, and Eisenmeger’s syndrome.


LFTs (Option A) are useful in diagnosing Terry’s nails. It's a type of leukonychia, where the proximal part is white and the distal nail appears normal and red. It is seen in alcoholic cirrhosis, T2DM, and some other autoimmune diseases.

[[figure-1]]


Serum albumin (Option B) can be useful in the diagnosis of Muehrcke's lines on nails, which are transverse, white bands that run across the nail. These are typically associated with hypoalbuminemia in nephrotic syndrome.

[[figure-2]]

Chest X-ray (Option C): Clubbing refers to increased longitudinal and transverse curvatures of the nail plate. Clubbing is commonly associated with pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases such as lung cancer, congenital heart disease, pulmonary fibrosis, asbestosis, and infective endocarditis.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 69

question: A 25 year old woman presents with complaints of the following nail lesions. Which among the following might be the most likely cause of the same?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given scenario with transverse, white bands that run parallel on the nail suggests a case of chronic arsenic poisoning. Chronic exposure to arsenic results in peripheral neuropathy, vascular insufficiency and various malignancies. Cutaneous manifestations include Mee's lines, arsenic keratosis, eczema and gangrene.

[[figure-1]]

Arsenic keratosis

[[figure-2]]

Mee's lines


Acute arsenic poisoning presents with severe nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea.

Lead (Option B):

  • Lead is a common heavy metal additive found in paints, and chronic exposure can lead to lead poisoning.
  • It presents with features of nausea, diarrhoea, weakness, tremors anaemia, headache, memory disturbances and visual defects.
  • Burton's line is a classical sign on examination. It is a bluish line present on the gums in chronic lead poisoning.

[[figure-3]]

Mercury (Option C):

  • Poisoning from mercury can occur due to inorganic sources like thermometers or organic mercury in fish (Minamata disease in Japan).
  • Mercury poisoning presents with tremors, excessive salivation, Erethism (Personality and memory disorders), and membranous glomerulopathy.

Cadmium (Option D):

Cadmium toxicity occurs commonly in people handling old metal pipes, batteries, polluted water, electric cigarettes, and areas with high air pollution. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, chest pain, flu-like symptoms, and shortness of breath. It can also lead to pneumonitis, osteoporosis, and chronic kidney disease.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 472e-2, 472e-3.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Telogen effluvium is commonly associated with systemic stress, leading to diffuse hair loss due to a disruption in the hair growth cycle, which results in increased shedding.

Telogen effluvium:

  • This is a type of diffuse hair loss triggered by systemic stress, which disrupts the normal hair growth cycle.
  • Stress causes hair follicles to prematurely enter the resting phase (Telogen) instead of the growth phase (Anagen), leading to hair shedding after about three months.
  • Chronic TE can be caused by factors like iron deficiency, thyroid disorders, crash dieting, or malnutrition. Prolonged exposure to stressors can result in long-term hair loss.

Androgenic alopecia (Option A):

  • This is a genetic condition characterized by gradual, patterned hair loss. In men, it usually results in a receding hairline and thinning at the crown.
  • In women, it often causes diffuse thinning over the crown but preserves the frontal hairline.

Alopecia areata (Option B):

  • This is an autoimmune condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, leading to sudden, round patches of hair loss.

Anagen effluvium (Option D):

  • This type of hair loss occurs during the anagen (growth) phase of the hair cycle and is often caused by exposure to toxic substances like chemotherapy agents.
  • Seen due to a disorder of the anagen phase of the hair cycle. The main causes of anagen effluvium are infection, drugs, toxins, radiation, and autoimmune disease. Infections may interrupt hair growth, resulting in a single or several bald patches.
  • Onset is rapid after 2–3 weeks after exposure to the cause.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 89.24
question: A 30 year old woman reports experiencing diffuse hair loss starting about three months after a period of significant systemic stress, including a major life event and emotional strain. She notes increased hair shedding when washing or brushing her hair. What is the most likely cause of her diffuse hair loss, given the link between systemic stress and the condition?

correctAnswer: B. Insertion of the arrector pili muscle
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The arrector pili muscle insertion marks the boundary between the upper follicle (infundibulum + isthmus, relatively permanent) and the lower follicle (suprabulbar region + hair bulb, cycling during the hair cycle).

  • The follicle is obliquely placed in the dermis
  • Arrector pili muscle: papillary dermis → mid-follicle wall
  • Sebaceous glands (± apocrine glands) open into the follicle above the arrector insertion

Regions of Hair Follicle:

  • Upper Follicle (Permanent):
    • Infundibulum:
      • From the skin surface → sebaceous duct opening
      • Epidermis-like keratinisation
    • Isthmus:
      • From sebaceous duct → arrector pili insertion
      • Trichilemmal keratinization
      • Hair follicle stem cells are located here (bulge area)
  • Lower Follicle (Cycling):
    • Suprabulbar region:
      • Outer root sheath (ORS)
      • Inner root sheath (IRS)
      • Hair shaft
    • Hair bulb:
      • Deepest part (often in subcutis)
      • Contains matrix cells and dermal papilla

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 89.3, 89.4.

options.text: Insertion of the arrector pili muscle

question: Which structure divides the permanent part of the hair follicle from the cycling part?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Most scalp follicles are actively growing (anagen) at any given time.

Hair cycle: Hair follicles undergo a cyclic pattern of growth and rest.

[[figure-1]]

  • Anagen (Growth):
    • Active hair growth determines hair length
    • Weeks (body hair) to years (scalp)
    • 80-90% of scalp follicles are in anagen
    • Mitotic activity in the hair bulb; formation of hair shaft and inner root sheath
  • Catagen (Option A) (Regression):
    • Short involution phase
    • Cell division stops, and the follicle undergoes apoptosis
    • Hair shaft forms club hair
    • The dermal papilla moves up to the arrector pili level
  • Telogen (Option B) (Rest):
    • Follicle inactive
    • Club hair is retained in the epithelial sac
  • Exogen (Option C): Active shedding of club hair
  • Kenogen (Human scalp): Latent phase after shedding before new anagen


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 89.7.
question: In a healthy adult with a normal scalp hair cycle, the majority of hair follicles are found in which phase at any given time?

correctAnswer: B. Lanugo is shed after birth
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Lanugo is prenatal hair that is normally shed in utero (8-9 months of gestation), not after birth.

Types of Hair:

  • Hair type depends on the kind of follicle and can change with age or hormonal fluctuations.
  • Lanugo: prenatal, fine, soft, unmedullated, usually unpigmented; shed in utero (~8-9 months)
  • Postnatal hair:
    • Vellus: soft, fine, unmedullated, sometimes pigmented, ≤2 cm (Option A)
    • Terminal: longer, coarse, medullated, pigmented
    • Intermediate types exist
  • Distribution:
    • Pre-puberty: terminal hair on scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes
    • Post-puberty: androgen-driven terminal hair develops from vellus in secondary sexual areas (Option C)

Animals:

  • Guard hairs: stiff, protective overcoat
  • Undercoat: fine, soft hairs
  • Vibrissae (sinus hairs): sensory, with erectile tissue (not in humans) (Option D)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 89.2.

Terminal hair develops after puberty under androgen influence

question: Which of the following is a component of SAPHO syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nodulocystic acne is a severe form of acne with deep inflammatory nodules and cysts and a high risk of scarring. Oral isotretinoin is the treatment of choice as it reduces sebaceous gland size, sebum production, follicular keratinisation, and inflammation.

  • Oral isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) is a synthetic vitamin A analogue
  • Indications: Used for severe recalcitrant acne and moderate acne unresponsive to conventional antibiotic therapy.
  • Most effective anti-acne drug; produces long-term remission in many patients after 4-6 months, dose-dependent.
  • Laboratory monitoring: Liver function tests and lipid profile should be monitored; elevations are usually mild, asymptomatic, and reversible.
  • Rare thrombocytopenia and neutropenia reported; CBC, triglycerides, cholesterol, and transaminases should be monitored.
  • Highly teratogenic → strict Pregnancy Prevention Programme (PPP) mandatory for all females of child-bearing potential.
  • Pregnancy testing: Required before starting, monthly during treatment, and 5 weeks after stopping isotretinoin.
  • Contraception: At least one (preferably two) effective contraceptive methods are advised; prescription limited to 30 days and valid for 7 days; treatment ideally starts on day 3 of the menstrual cycle.


Treatment of acne:

Grades

Lesions

Treatment

Grade I

Non-inflammatory lesions such as open (blackheads) and closed comedones (whiteheads)

Topical retinoids

(Tretinoin, Adapalene)

Grade II

Non-inflammatory lesions (comedones) + inflammatory lesions such as papules and a few pustules.

Topical retinoids + Topical antibiotics

Grade III

Multiple inflammatory papules and pustules ± nodules (moderate)

Topical retinoids + Oral antibiotics ± Benzoyl peroxide

Grade IV

Nodules + Cysts

(Most severe form)

Oral retinoids

(Isotretinoin)


Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 90.37, 90.44, 90.45.
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9180136/
question: A 20-year-old male presents with findings as shown in the image, with scarring. What is the most appropriate treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Oral isotretinoin is the treatment of choice for severe recalcitrant acne that does not respond to conventional antibiotic therapies.

  • Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid), a synthetic vitamin A analogue
  • Indications:
    • Severe acne unresponsive to conventional antibiotic therapy
    • European S3 guidelines:
      • Severe recalcitrant acne
      • Moderate acne failing standard antibiotics
  • Efficacy:
    • Most effective acne therapy available
    • Duration: ~4-6 months (dose-dependent)
    • Produces long-term remission or marked improvement
    • Relapse: More common in younger patients
  • Adverse effects:
    • Mucocutaneous (most common):
      • Cheilitis, xerosis, dry eyes, epistaxis
    • Systemic:
      • ↑ LFTs, hypertriglyceridemia
      • Myalgia, arthralgia
    • Neurological:
      • Headache
      • Pseudotumor cerebri (avoid with tetracyclines)
    • Others:
      • Photosensitivity, hair thinning
  • Teratogenicity:
    • Absolute contraindication in pregnancy
    • Causes craniofacial, cardiac, CNS defects
    • Avoid pregnancy during therapy + 1 month after

Long-term topical benzoyl peroxide (Option A): Effective for mild acne and as an adjunct to topical or oral antibiotics. It is inadequate as monotherapy for severe recalcitrant acne.

Oral doxycycline with topical retinoid (Option B): Recommended for moderate inflammatory acne. It is not appropriate once acne has failed prolonged oral antibiotic therapy, where oral isotretinoin is indicated.

Intralesional corticosteroid injections (Option D): Useful for individual large inflammatory nodules or cysts to reduce inflammation rapidly. They are not suitable as definitive treatment for severe widespread recalcitrant acne.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 90.44
question: A 19-year-old patient has severe recalcitrant acne that has failed to respond to prolonged courses of oral antibiotics and topical therapy. What is the most appropriate treatment?

correctAnswer: C. Female with severe acne unresponsive to oral isotretinoin
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Female with severe acne unresponsive to oral isotretinoin


Explanation:

Hormonal therapy is used in women with antibiotic failure, need for contraception, or when isotretinoin is contraindicated. Failure of isotretinoin indicates severe disease where hormonal therapy alone is not appropriate.


Mechanisms of Action:

  • ↓ Androgen production (ovary/adrenal)
  • Androgen receptor blockade
  • ↓ Androgen effect on sebaceous glands
  • ↑ Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) → ↓ free testosterone
  • Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs)
    • ↑ SHBG → ↓ free testosterone
    • Suppress ovulation → ↓ ovarian androgens → ↓ sebum


Indications:

  • Failure of standard antibiotic/combination therapy (Option A)
  • Need for contraception and/or menstrual regulation (Option B)
  • Isotretinoin contraindicated or unavailable (Option D)
  • Can be combined with topical therapy


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 90.43
