question: A 30-year-old patient complains of increased skin pigmentation following prolonged sun exposure. Which of the following statements regarding melanin physiology is most accurate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of hypopigmentation of the skin and hair, ocular manifestations such as nystagmus and photophobia suggest oculocutaneous albinism. It is associated with an autosomal recessive pattern.

Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by generalized hypopigmentation and ophthalmological anomalies caused by a deficiency in melanin biosynthesis with normal melanocyte count. There are seven types of OCA, all of which are associated with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

[[figure-1]]

There can be either failure of synthesis of tyrosinase enzyme or defect in tyrosinase activity.

Clinical features include hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes and ocular findings such as photophobia (which may be prominent). Iris translucency can be demonstrated by slit-lamp examination. A characteristic finding is the misrouting of the optic nerves, consisting of an excessive crossing of the fibres in the optic chiasma, which can result in strabismus and reduced stereoscopic vision.

Note: Ocular albinism has an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern.



Reference:
  1. Rook's Textbook of Dermatology - 9th Edition page no 70.7
  2. Fitzpatrick Textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, page no 1310
question: A 5-year-old child is brought to the dermatologist by concerned parents due to their child's extremely fair skin, white hair, and pale blue eyes. Upon examination, the dermatologist confirms the absence of melanin pigment in the child's skin, hair, and irises. The child also shows signs of photophobia and is noted to have nystagmus. Which of the following inheritance patterns is associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image and clinical description point towards Nevus depigmentosus, a non-progressive hypopigmented congenital skin disorder.

Key Clinical Features of Nevus Depigmentosus:

  • Present at or shortly after birth

  • Hypopigmented macules with irregular but well-defined margins

  • Distributed in a segmental or Blaschkoid pattern

  • Non-progressive and asymptomatic

  • No scaling, erythema, or associated systemic abnormalities

Vitiligo (Option B) presents with depigmented macules that may increase in size and number over time due to autoimmune destruction of melanocytes and are not restricted to dermatomal distribution.

[[figure-1]]

Nevus anemicus (Option C) typically presents as hypopigmented macules due to persistent cutaneous vasoconstriction resulting from hypersensitivity to catecholamines that become more pronounced with rubbing or trauma. It does not follow the lines of Blaschko.

[[figure-2]]

Piebaldism (Option D) is an autosomal dominant condition that presents with depigmented patches on the skin and a characteristic white forelock of hair. However, it is usually present at birth and does not follow the lines of Blaschko.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:
  1. Fitzpatrick, Richard E., et al. "Disorders of Hyperpigmentation: Melanocytes, Melanogenesis, and Pigmentary Disorders.
question: A 5-year-old boy presents with hypopigmented macules distributed along the lines of Blaschko. The lesions are asymptomatic and have been present since birth. There is no history of progression or associated symptoms. Which condition is most likely to present with this clinical manifestation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the described clinical scenario, the patient's presentation of reddish-brown macules on her hands and legs after initiating antibiotic therapy, along with a history of similar macules following the use of other medications, indicates a likely diagnosis of fixed drug eruptions.

Fixed drug eruption:

  • Well-defined slate-brown lesions recurring at the same site after drug exposure.

  • Mechanism: type IV hypersensitivity; ICAM-1 expression in keratinocytes; pigmentation from dermal macrophages.

  • Triggers: tetracyclines, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, sedatives.

  • Course: lesions may be erythematous or bullous initially, recur at same sites, sometimes new areas with re-exposure.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Page no. 88.28
question: A 30-year-old woman develops dusky red to brown patches on her arms and legs as shown in the image below after taking a specific antibiotic for sinus infections. The patches, not painful but slightly itchy, leave hyperpigmented areas after resolving. She had a similar reaction to a same medication in the past. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation is characteristic of Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE), a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by CD8+ resident memory T cells.

  • These cells persist at previously affected sites, causing lesions to recur at the same location whenever the offending drug is taken again.

Clinical features:

  • Well-defined erythematous to dusky violaceous patches or plaques
  • Mild pruritus or burning sensation
  • Recurrence at the same anatomical site after re-exposure
  • Healing with persistent slate-grey or brown post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
  • Lesions may occasionally become bullous

Common triggering drugs:

  • NSAIDs
  • Sulfonamides
  • Tetracyclines
  • Fluoroquinolones
  • Metronidazole
  • Antiepileptic drugs

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (Option B) is a residual pigmentary change following skin inflammation and does not present as recurrent lesions that reappear at the same site after drug exposure.

Lichen planus pigmentosus (Option C) presents with chronic slate-grey to brown macules without a history of recurrent drug-induced lesions at the same site.

Melasma (Option D) presents as symmetrical hyperpigmented facial patches associated with hormonal influences and sun exposure rather than recurrent medication-induced lesions.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 88.28
question: A 30-year-old woman develops dusky red to brown patches on her arms and legs after taking an antibiotic for sinusitis. The lesions are mildly pruritic, recur at the same sites with re-exposure to the medication, and heal with persistent hyperpigmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This woman with hyperpigmented patches on her cheek and a history of OCP use most likely has melasma.

Melasma: hyperpigmented facial macules with irregular margins, commonly on cheeks, forehead, and chin.

  • Causes: genetics, UV exposure, pregnancy, hormones (OCPs), cosmetics, phototoxic drugs.

  • Prevention: broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, avoid sun.

  • Treatment: topical hydroquinone, triple combination (hydroquinone + retinoid + corticosteroid), chemical peels, azelaic acid, lasers.

Lentigo (Option B) A dark brown macule from increased melanocytes, appearing in childhood, uniformly pigmented, round/oval, ≤5 mm, increasing with age..

[[figure-1]]

Freckles (Option C) are pale to dark brown macules on sun-exposed skin that darken with UV-induced melanin overproduction.

[[figure-2]]

Chloasma(Option D:) is a hypermelanosis of sun-exposed areas that occurs during pregnancy and affects 50-70% of pregnant women. It presents similar to melasma but in pregnant women. It tends to improve spontaneously postpartum, and treatment may not be necessary.



Reference:
  1. Fitzpatrick Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition
  2. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 88.10-88.13, 131.1
question: A 28-year-old female on OCP presents with hyperpigmented macules on her cheeks and forehead. On examination, the lesions appear darker than the surrounding skin and have scalloped margins. There is no associated inflammation or itching. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the clinical presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the above scenario, nevi are present at birth and are associated with hypertrichosis and rugosities. Congenital Melanocytic Nevus is the most likely diagnosis.

Congenital Melanocytic Nevi (CMN):

  • These are benign growths of melanocytes (pigment-producing cells), present at birth.
  • CMN arise from the neural crest, a temporary group of cells in embryonic development.
  • Characteristics:
    • A single lesion.
    • Exhibit hypertrichosis (increased hair growth) and rugosities (a wrinkled appearance).
  • Classification:
    • Congenital: Present at birth.
    • Acquired: Develop after birth.
  • Size and Malignant Potential:
    • Small to Medium CMN: Benign.
    • Large/Giant CMN (Bathing Trunk/Garment Nevi): Higher risk of developing melanoma (skin cancer).
  • Treatment: Surgical removal, laser therapy, or other therapies.

Mongolian spots (Option B) are typically bluish macules found in the sacral area. They tend to fade over time and are not associated with hypertrichosis.

[[figure-1]]

Nevus of Ota (Option C) a bluish/slate-gray patch affecting ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) branches of the trigeminal nerve, face, eyes, oral mucosa.

Nevus Depigmentosus (Option D) presents as a single hypopigmented (lighter) macule, typically present at birth.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 75.9-75.10
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560574/
question: A 5-month-old infant presents with a large, darkly pigmented lesion on their lower back. The lesion has been present since birth and has increased proportionally in size with the infant's growth. There is also the presence of hypertrichosis (excessive hair growth) within the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Melanocytic nevi:

  • Also called moles. They are proliferating nevus cells derived from the neural crest.
  • Acquired melanocytic nevi are nests of proliferating nevus cells and are classified into three types:
    • Junctional nevi: Present at the dermo-epidermal junction which are small and dark brown.
    • Compound nevi: Present at the dermo-epidermal junction and the dermis as these are slightly raised and lighter in color than junctional nevi.
    • Intradermal nevi: Present in the dermis are raised papules that are either skin-colored or red.
  • Treatment is usually done for cosmetic reasons, if indicative of malignancy, treatment options include electrocautery, laser treatment, and surgical excision.
  • Congenital melanocytic nevi are present at birth. Giant congenital melanocytic nevi (also called bathing trunk/garment nevi) may have malignant potential.
  • Halo nevi presents as a nevus with a halo around it which is caused by the autoimmune destruction of melanocytes surrounding the mole.



Reference:

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/benign-pigmented-skin-lesions-other-than-melanocytic-nevi-moles?
question: A 35 y/o female with a cosmetically concerning mole on her right cheek. It is a raised, skin-colored papule, approximately 4 mm in diameter. The patient reports no change in size, shape, or color of the mole, and it has been present for several years. What would be the most appropriate treatment approach for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical history and skin findings suggest a diagnosis of Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), which is associated with Café au lait macules.
  • Café au lait macules are hyperpigmented macules with smooth or serrated borders, resembling coffee stains on milk.

[[figure-1]]

Congenital or early-onset pigmented macules, light to dark brown, solitary or multiple, commonly on trunk/extremities, sometimes linked to NF-1, NF-2, or McCune-Albright syndrome.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557492/
question: A 7-year-old child presents with multiple hyperpigmented patches on the skin, as shown in the image below. These patches have been present since early childhood and are more than six in number. Which of the following skin lesions are seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presented with multiple tan to dark brown macules on her face and the dorsal aspect of her hands. These macules are 3 to 20 mm in size and have appeared after chronic sun exposure which can be diagnosed as solar lentigines

[[figure-1]]

Solar lentigines are benign pigmented skin lesions that occur in response to excessive or chronic sun exposure.

Treatment for solar lentigines is generally unnecessary unless for cosmetic purposes. Therapeutic options include lightening agents, retinoic acid, trichloroacetic acid, cryotherapy, and laser therapy. However, antibiotic therapy is not indicated for the treatment of solar lentigines.

Cryotherapy involves using extreme cold to destroy abnormal tissues such as solar lentigines. It works by freezing the affected area, leading to cellular destruction and subsequent sloughing off of the lesion.

Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) is used for chemical peels and treating conditions like solar lentigines. It induces controlled skin injury, leading to exfoliation and skin regeneration. TCA effectively removes superficial skin layers, including pigmented lesions.



Reference:

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acquired-hyperpigmentation-disorders?
question: A 45-year-old fair-skinned woman presents with multiple tan to dark brown macules on her face and the dorsal aspect of her hands. These macules are 3 to 20 mm in size and have appeared after chronic sun exposure. Which of the following therapeutic options is not indicated for the treatment of these lesions?

correctAnswer: D. The arrangement of melanosomes influences skin pigmentation.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Size of melanosomes influences their arrangement within keratinocytes, which in turn affects skin pigmentation.
  • Larger melanosomes, observed in darker skin tones, are typically dispersed individually.

Melanin Types and Production:

  • Two main types:
    • Eumelanin: Brownish-black, responsible for darker skin tones.
    • Pheomelanin: Orangish-red, found in lighter skin tones.
  • Synthesis process (Melanogenesis):

[[figure-1]]

  • Melanosomes:
    • Melanin is stored within specialized organelles called melanosomes, which are produced by melanocytes.
    • Size and Distribution:
      • Darker skin: Larger melanosomes (Option A)
      • Lighter skin: Smaller melanosomes (Option B)
    • Degradation: (Option C)
      • Varies between skin types.
      • Lighter skin: Melanosome complexes show degradative changes due to lysosomal enzymes.
      • Darker skin: Larger melanosomes can remain intact up to the stratum corneum.
  • Melanin and Skin Color:
    • Key factors: Type of melanin, Melanosome size, Melanosome distribution (dispersed vs. aggregated),
    • Skin color is NOT solely determined by the number of melanocytes.
  • Regulation of Pigmentation:
    • UV radiation
    • Hormones: Estrogens - increase pigmentation; Melanocortins - melanin production.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology 9th edition page no 88.1 -88.8

options.text: An increased number of melanocytes causes darker skin pigmentation.
Larger melanosomes are found in individuals with lighter skin tones.
The degradation rate of melanosomes is same across different skin types.
The arrangement of melanosomes influences skin pigmentation.

question: Which of the following statements accurately describes the role of melanosomes in determining skin pigmentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The correct answer is 1, 2, 4 (Amiodarone, Chloroquine, and Minocycline).

  • Paracetamol: Not associated with hyperpigmentation.
  • Triamcinolone: Corticosteroid; may cause skin atrophy or striae but not hyperpigmentation.

Drug-Induced Hyperpigmentation:

Skin hyperpigmentation caused by medications via melanin/lipofuscin accumulation, drug deposition, or post-inflammatory changes.

  • Onset: 1 week → years
  • Risk ↑ with high dose/long duration
  • Sun exposure and drug history guide diagnosis


Common Drugs & Patterns:

  • Amiodarone: Slate-grey/purple; sun-exposed areas; dose- and duration-dependent; lipofuscin + drug in macrophages.
  • Antimalarials (Chloroquine, Mepacrine): Yellowish or bluish-grey; face, extremities, nails, hard palate; melanin + drug/iron complexes.
  • Clofazimine: Violaceous-brown; lesional skin; ceroid-lipofuscin in macrophages.
  • Cytotoxic drugs (Busulfan, Doxorubicin, Cyclophosphamide, etc.): Localised/diffuse; skin, nails, mucosa, hair; mimics Addison's disease.
  • Hydantoins (Phenytoin), Barbiturates: Basal epidermal hyperpigmentation; diffuse or melasma-like.
  • Psychotropics (Chlorpromazine, Trifluoperazine, Imipramine): Blue-grey sun-exposed areas; may involve nails, cornea, conjunctiva.
  • Tetracyclines (Minocycline): Skin, nails, oral cavity, sclera; 4 patterns (acne scars, inflammation, muddy-brown, lip vermilion); partially reversible.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 88.25-88.27.
question:
Which of the following drugs are known to produce drug-induced hyperpigmentation?

  1. Amiodarone
  2. Chloroquine
  3. Paracetamol
  4. Minocycline
  5. Triamcinolone

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hyperpigmentation is associated with hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.


Conditions associated with hyperpigmentation:

  • Addison disease
  • Cushing syndrome (ACTH-dependent)
  • Nelson syndrome (post-adrenalectomy)
  • Acromegaly
  • Hyperthyroidism
  • Carcinoid syndrome
  • Lymphomas (Hodgkin > Non-Hodgkin)
  • Phaeochromocytoma
  • Systemic sclerosis
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Chronic renal failure & chronic liver disease
  • Haemochromatosis
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency & folate deficiency
  • Vitamin A deficiency
  • POEMS syndrome


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 88.17-88.25.
question:
Hyperpigmentation may be seen in which of the following conditions?

  1. Pheochromocytoma
  2. Hypothyroidism
  3. Cushing syndrome (ACTH-dependent)
  4. Haemochromatosis

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Mongolian spots are benign dermal melanocytoses that typically fade spontaneously in childhood; no treatment is required.


Mongolian spot:

  • Congenital blue-grey macular pigmentation is usually present on the sacrum of infants.
  • Age: Develops in utero (Option B), deepens in infancy, then fades.
  • Associations: Down syndrome (Option A), Hurler syndrome, GM1 gangliosidosis, mucolipidosis II, naevus of Ota.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Elongated dendritic melanocytes in mid-to-lower dermis along neurovascular bundles.
    • No fibrosis (Option D) or dermal melanophages (distinguishes from blue naevus).
  • Clinical features:
    • Diffuse, uniform blue-grey macule; round or oval; usually <10 cm.
    • Common location: lumbosacral area.
    • Can be multiple; generalised lesions may involve the buttocks, flanks, shoulders, and lower legs.
  • Course: Typically resolves in childhood.
  • Management:
    • No treatment required.
    • Persistent lesions: Q-switched laser, intense pulsed light, bleaching creams (mainly in adults).


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 132.12, 132.13.
question: A 2-week-old newborn is noted to have findings as shown in the image below. The infant is otherwise healthy. Which of the following statements about this lesion is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Giant CMN carry a significant risk of malignant transformation.


Congenital Naevi:

  • Subtypes: Small (<1.5 cm), Medium (1.5-20 cm), and Giant (>20 cm). (Option A)
  • Clinical Presentation: Present at birth, light to dark brown; flat or elevated. Texture ranges from smooth to mammillated or verrucous. Features well-defined borders and may develop coarse hair.
  • Pathology: Deeper naevus cells tend to extend deeply around skin appendages.
  • Dermoscopy: Reticular, globular, or mixed patterns. May show milia-like cysts, perifollicular pigment changes, dots/globules, and hypertrichosis (excess hair).
  • Pathogenesis: NRAS mutations; melanocyte migration/proliferation defect in utero.
  • Diagnosis: Clinical; dermatoscopy or biopsy if uncertain.
  • Management: Observation, surgical excision (staged if large) (Option D), laser/dermal techniques for cosmetic reasons.
  • Complications: Malignant melanoma (esp. large), neurocutaneous melanosis (Option B), cosmetic/psychological impact.
  • Prognosis: Good for small/medium; higher risk for large/giant lesions.


Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 132.16
  2. Giant melanocytic nevus

options.text: This lesion is classified as a giant congenital melanocytic nevus.
The patient is at increased risk of neurocutaneous melanosis.

question: A 3-month-old infant presents with a large pigmented patch covering the posterior trunk and extending to the upper thigh. The lesion has irregular borders, hypertrichosis, and some nodular areas. Neurologic examination is normal. Which of the following statements about this lesion is false?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Melasma presents as symmetrical facial hyperpigmentation, commonly during pregnancy, aggravated by UV exposure, with epidermal enhancement on Wood’s lamp examination.


Melasma:

  • Symmetric hyperpigmented macules on the face, worsened by sun exposure
  • Synonyms: Chloasma, mask of pregnancy
  • Epidemiology: F > M; age 20-40; pregnancy & OCPs; darker skin types
  • Predisposing factors:
    • UV exposure (most important)
    • Hormonal factors: pregnancy, oral contraceptives
    • Estrogen, progesterone, ↑ MSH (especially 3rd trimester)
  • Pathology: Normal melanocyte number, ↑ melanin (epidermal ± dermal)
  • Sites: Upper lip, malar area, forehead, chin
  • Types (Wood’s Lamp):
    • Epidermal: light brown, enhanced contrast
    • Dermal: grey/blue, poor contrast
    • Mixed
  • Course: Often fades postpartum; may persist
  • Investigations: None; Wood’s lamp helpful
  • Treatment: Sun protection; triple therapy (hydroquinone + retinoid + steroid); peels/lasers if needed


Chik sign (Option A): Hyperpigmentation after chikungunya infection; not pregnancy-related and differs in distribution.

[[figure-1]]

Fixed drug eruption (Option C): Presents as recurrent, well-circumscribed lesions at the same site after drug exposure, often with erythema or blistering; does not worsen with sunlight.

[[figure-2]]

Vitiligo (Option D): Causes depigmented white patches due to melanocyte loss; not brown hyperpigmentation and not influenced by sun exposure.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 88.10-88.12
question: A 32-year-old pregnant woman presents with findings as shown in the image for 6 months. The pigmentation worsens after sun exposure. Wood’s lamp shows enhanced pigmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. The lesion typically fades with reduced sun exposure
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Simple lentigo does not fade once it appears, unlike freckles.


Simple lentigo:

  • Light- to dark-brown/black macule that does not fade
  • Histology: increased melanocytes at the dermo-epidermal junction (no nesting) (Option A, C)

[[figure-1]]

  • Risk factors:
    • UV exposure is the most important environmental factor
    • Reported after topical immunotherapy: tacrolimus, SADBE, DPCP
  • Genetics: No BRAF/FGFR3/PIK3CA mutations; multiple lesions → syndromic (RAS-MAPK, mTOR)
  • Pathology: Mild ↑ melanocytes, basal hyperpigmentation, elongated rete ridges
  • Clinical features:
    • Uniformly pigmented, poorly circumscribed macules
    • Round/oval, ≤ 5 mm, pale to deep brown
    • Common in sun-exposed areas
  • D/D:
    • Freckles: Fade with sun; no ↑ melanocytes
    • Junctional naevus: Shows nests of naevus cells
    • “Jentigo” pattern: Features of lentigo + junctional naevus
  • Dermoscopy: Scalloped borders, faint irregular network
  • Management: None; photoprotection; cosmetic treatments if needed
  • Prognosis: Benign, stable (Option D)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 132.4-132.6.

options.text: It shows increased melanocytes at the dermo-epidermal junction
The lesion typically fades with reduced sun exposure
Melanocytes are increased without nest formation
It is a benign lesion that commonly appears in childhood

question: Which of the following statements regarding simple lentigo is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nevus anemicus is not a pigmentary disorder. Melanocyte number and melanin content are normal; the pale appearance results from persistent vasoconstriction, not hypopigmentation.


Nevus anemicus:

  • Congenital vascular anomaly causing a pale patch due to persistent vasoconstriction
  • Onset: Present at birth (Option A)

[[figure-1]]

  • Key Feature: Does not redden with rubbing, heat, or cold (Option D)
  • Pathogenesis: Local hypersensitivity of dermal vessels to catecholamines (Option B)
  • Diagnosis: Clinical; Wood lamp/diascopy helpful
  • Differential: Vitiligo, nevus depigmentosus, pityriasis alba
  • Associations: May be seen with NF1
  • Treatment: None required (benign)
  • Prognosis: Excellent, lifelong stability


Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 4.20
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459139/
question: Which of the following regarding nevus anemicus is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The correct diagnosis is Becker naevus.

Becker naevus typically presents in adolescent males as a unilateral hyperpigmented patch, often on the upper trunk, and may be associated with ipsilateral muscle or breast hypoplasia (Becker naevus syndrome).


Becker Naevus (Becker Melanosis):

  • Definition: Common benign hyperpigmented naevus, often hypertrichotic
  • Sex: More common in males
  • Onset: Usually peripubertal; rarely congenital
  • Site: Upper trunk most common
  • Pathology:
    • Lentiginous melanocytic hyperplasia
    • Epidermal hyperplasia
    • Smooth muscle hyperplasia
  • Classification: Does not fit neatly into standard melanocytic naevus categories
  • Associations (Becker Naevus Syndrome):
    • Ipsilateral breast hypoplasia/aplasia
    • Pectoralis major / shoulder muscle hypoplasia
    • Lipoatrophy
    • Limb growth disturbance
    • Supernumerary nipple
    • Scoliosis


Naevus of Ito (Option A): This is a blue-grey dermal melanocytosis. It lacks the brown colour and hair overgrowth of Becker naevus and does not involve underlying muscle defects.

[[figure-1]]


Congenital Melanocytic Naevus (Option C): This is present at birth and contains nests of melanocytes (naevus cells). Becker naevus is acquired in adolescence and lacks these nests.

[[figure-2]]


Nevus Spilus (Option D): This is a "speckled" lesion with dark spots on a tan background. It does not present as a large uniform patch or involve muscle hypoplasia.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 75.19, 132.15.
question: A 17-year-old boy has a unilateral hyperpigmented patch as shown in the image below, with mild ipsilateral muscle hypoplasia. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

An intradermal naevus is characterised by a flesh-coloured, dome-shaped lesion, often with hair growth, due to naevus cells being located entirely within the dermis and producing little melanin.


Acquired Melanocytic Naevi:

  • Benign melanocytic tumours (moles)
  • Start at the dermo-epidermal junction → migrate to dermis → senesce
  • Types:

[[figure-1]]

  • Junctional naevus (Option A) - melanocytes at DE junction → flat brown macule
  • Compound naevus (Option B) - junctional + dermal component → slightly raised papule
  • Intradermal naevus - dermal only → flesh-coloured dome-shaped papule

[[figure-2]]


Blue naevus (Option D): Blue-black lesion due to deep dermal melanocytes, not flesh-coloured.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 132.18-132.22.
question: A 26-year-old woman presents with a long-standing mole on her neck. On examination, the lesion looks as shown in the image. There is no surrounding pigmentation. What is the most likely type of melanocytic naevus?

correctAnswer: C. Increased melanin production with normal melanocyte number
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child is presenting with Ephelides (commonly known as freckles). The diagnosis is based on the early age of onset, the seasonal variation (darkening in summer, lightening in winter), and the characteristic "moth-eaten" border seen on dermoscopy.


Freckles (ephelides) result from UV-induced increased melanin production by melanocytes with a normal melanocyte count, leading to reversible hyperpigmented macules.


Freckles:

  • Small brown macules, ill-defined, on sun-exposed skin
  • Darken with UV, fade in winter
  • Common in children, fair skin, red hair, blue eyes
  • Pathogenesis: ↑ melanin production, normal melanocyte number (Option A)
  • Histology: Basal layer hyperpigmentation only
  • Genetics: MC1R variants
  • Differential:
    • Solar lentigines: Persistent, older age, ↑ melanocytes
    • NF1 freckling: Axilla/groin
  • Risk: ↑ melanoma risk (Option D)
  • Course: Benign (Option B), may fade with age
  • Dermoscopy: Uniform pigment, moth-eaten edge
  • Management: Reassurance + photoprotection


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 132.1-132.3.

options.text: Increased melanin production with normal melanocyte number

question: A 9-year-old fair-skinned child presents with findings as shown in the image. The lesions become darker during summer and lighten in winter. Dermoscopy shows uniform pigmentation with a moth-eaten border. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Naevus of Ito. This clinical presentation describes a classic dermal melanocytosis located in the distribution of the posterior supraclavicular and lateral cutaneous brachial nerves.


Naevus of Ito: (Naevus fusco-ceruleus acromiodeltoideus)

  • Dermal melanocytosis involving the acromioclavicular region, shoulder, upper chest, and upper back.
  • More common in Asians (especially Chinese and Japanese)
  • Less common than naevus of Ota
  • Pathology:
    • Identical to naevus of Ota
    • Dermal dendritic melanocytes are scattered among collagen bundles
  • Clinical features:
    • Unilateral blue-grey macular pigmentation
    • Distribution along the posterior supraclavicular and lateral cutaneous brachial nerves
    • Bilateral lesions uncommon
  • Complications:
    • Benign
    • Very rare malignant transformation (few reported melanoma cases)
  • Course: Persistent, similar to naevus of Ota
  • Management: Q-switched pigment-targeting lasers (treatment of choice)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 132.14, 132.15.
question: A mother brings her 8-year-old child with a long-standing, asymptomatic blue-grey patch over the right shoulder and upper chest present since early childhood, as shown in the image. There is no ocular or mucosal involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. It is distributed along the trigeminal nerve
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Naevus of Ota classically follows the V1 and V2 divisions of the trigeminal nerve.


Naevus of Ota: (Oculodermal melanocytosis, Naevus fuscoceruleus ophthalmomaxillaris)

  • Congenital bluish-brown dermal melanocytosis involving periocular skin and sclera, along V1 & V2 trigeminal distribution.

[[figure-1]]

  • Asians, females > males (Option A)
  • Present at birth/early childhood (rare pubertal onset)
  • Clinical features:
    • Blue (deep) + brown (superficial) pigmentation
    • Sites: Periorbital skin, sclera/conjunctiva, temple, forehead, malar area
    • Usually unilateral (Option B)
  • Pathology:
    • Dermal dendritic melanocytes, no epidermal involvement
    • GNAQ mutation (subset)
  • D/D: Hori naevus - acquired, bilateral, no mucosal involvement
  • Complications: Rare uveal/meningeal melanoma
  • Does not regress & Persists lifelong (unlike Mongolian spot) (Option C)
  • Management:
    • Q-switched lasers - treatment of choice
    • Cosmetic camouflage as an adjunct
    • Regular ophthalmologic follow-up is essential
    • Any new nodule → biopsy to rule out melanoma


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 132.13, 132.14.

options.text: It is more common in males
It tends to regress spontaneously with age
It is distributed along the trigeminal nerve

question: Which of the following statements regarding Naevus of Ota is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE). The clinical presentation of a recurrent lesion appearing at the same site shortly after drug ingestion is the hallmark of this condition.

Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE):

[[figure-1]]

  • Recurrent, well-defined cutaneous lesions at the same site after exposure to a drug.
  • Benign, self-limiting; post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is common.
  • Common drugs:
    • NSAIDs, Paracetamol, Co-trimoxazole, Tetracyclines
    • Others: Penicillins, Metronidazole, Carbamazepine, ACE inhibitors, food/herbals
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Delayed-type hypersensitivity via CD8+ skin-resident T cells.
    • Rechallenge → T cell activation → keratinocyte apoptosis → lesion formation.
  • Clinical features:
    • Onset: 30 min-8 h after drug exposure
    • Lesion: Round/oval, erythematous → dusky/violaceous; may be vesicular/bullous
    • Sites: Lips, genitals, palms, soles, occasionally face
    • Recurrence: Same site on re-exposure
    • Variant: GBFDE (Generalised Bullous Fixed Drug Eruption) mimics TEN, but the mucosa is usually spared
  • Investigation:
    • Oral provocation (gold standard if safe)
    • Patch test: ~50% positive at previous lesion sites
  • Management:
    • Stop offending the drug
    • Topical corticosteroids; systemic if multiple lesions
    • GBFDE: ICU/burns unit care
  • Usually self-limiting; hyperpigmentation may persist
  • GBFDE mortality ~20%


Drug-induced hyperpigmentation (Option B): Usually diffuse or patchy, develops gradually over weeks/months, not rapid and site-specific.

Acute contact dermatitis (Option C): Localised rash at the contact site, often itchy, not rapidly recurring with drug re-exposure.

Chikungunya-related hyperpigmentation (Option D): Appears days after fever, typically on the nasal dorsum, not immediately post-drug.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 118.11-118.14.
question: A 20-year-old man takes NSAIDs and, within 2 hours, develops lesions as shown. Similar lesions occurred at the same site after previous NSAID use. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The correct answer is Chikungunya fever. The patient shows the “chik sign”, which is brownish hyperpigmentation over the nasal dorsum appearing after the acute febrile phase, a hallmark of chikungunya. Severe arthralgia supports this diagnosis.

  • Chikungunya fever is a mosquito‑borne viral illness characterised by fever, severe joint pain (arthralgia), and skin symptoms.
  • The “chik sign” refers to distinctive hyperpigmentation over the nose seen in some chikungunya patients.
  • This mucocutaneous sign may appear during the disease’s recovery phase and can look similar to melasma or freckles, which makes recognition important.

Dengue fever (Option A): Fever and myalgia are common, but localised nasal hyperpigmentation is not seen.

Fixed drug eruption (Option C): Typically appears within hours of drug exposure as well-demarcated erythematous/violaceous patches that recur at the same site; in this case, the timing (1 week after fever resolution) and location (nasal dorsum) make FDE unlikely.

[[figure-1]]


Viral exanthem (Option D): Causes generalised rashes, but does not produce localised nasal pigmentation like the chik sign.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11979963/
question: A 44-year-old woman presents with fever, severe bilateral joint pain, and headache for 5 days. She was taking NSAIDs under prescription. One week after her fever subsides, she develops findings as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Skin colour is chiefly determined by the number of melanocytes
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Skin colour differences are not due to the number of melanocytes, which is relatively constant across populations. Instead, the type of melanin produced and the size, number, and distribution of melanosomes determine skin colour.

The colour of the skin depends on the amount of melanin inside melanocytes, the number and size of melanosomes, and the degree of melanin transfer to ketrtinocytes

Racial and ethnic differences in skin colour are related to the number, size, shape, distribution and degradation of melanin‐laden organelles called melanosomes. These are produced by melanocytes and are transferred to the surrounding epidermal keratinocytes.

Two types of melanin pigmentation occur in humans.

  1. Constitutive skin colour: The amount of melanin pigment that is genetically determined in the absence of sun exposure and other influences.
  2. Facultative (inducible) skin colour or ‘tan’: Results from sun exposure.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 2.1, 2.2, 88.1, 88.2.

question: Which statement regarding skin colour is incorrect?

correctAnswer: C. Granulosa cell ovarian tumours are a characteristic associated with tumours.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation-mucocutaneous lentigines (dark spots on the lips/fingers), hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps, and a positive family history-points directly to Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS).

  • Granulosa cell ovarian tumors are the most distinctive non-GI tumor associated with Peutz-Jeghers-Touraine syndrome.


Peutz-Jeghers-Touraine Syndrome (PJT):

  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant (Option D)
  • Gene: STK11 (LKB1)
  • Skin & Mucosa
    • Early-onset (Option B) lentigines on the lips
    • Buccal mucosa and digits involved
  • GI features:
    • Hamartomatous polyps (most common in the jejunum)
    • Complications: intussusception, bleeding
    • Malignant change of small-bowel polyps: rare (Option A)
  • Associated tumours:
    • Granulosa cell ovarian tumour (characteristic)
    • ↑ risk: breast, pancreas
  • Histology:

[[figure-1]]

  • GI polyps: arborising smooth muscle, frond-like epithelium
  • Acral lesions: pigment block
  • Genotype-Cancer Risk:
    • Substrate-recognition domain mutations → ↑ malignancy
    • Truncating mutations → common in breast cancer cases


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 70.14, 70.15.

options.text: Hamartomatous polyps commonly undergo malignant transformation.
Granulosa cell ovarian tumours are a characteristic associated with tumours.
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern

question: A 14-year-old girl presents with findings as shown in the image. Her father has a history of similar lesions and gastrointestinal polyps. Imaging reveals a jejunal polyp causing intermittent abdominal pain. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?

correctAnswer: C. Granulosa cell ovarian tumours are a characteristic associated tumour
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features are characteristic of Peutz-Jeghers-Touraine (PJT) syndrome, a rare autosomal dominant (Option D) lentiginosis syndrome caused by mutations in the STK11 gene.

  • It presents with early-onset lentigines (Option B) involving the lips, with associated melanocytic macules on the buccal mucosa and digits.
  • Patients develop hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps, most consistently in the jejunum, which can lead to intussusception and bleeding.
  • Malignant degeneration of the small intestinal polyps is rare (Option A).
  • Among the non-gastrointestinal tumours, granulosa cell ovarian tumours are the most characteristic association.
  • There is also an increased risk of breast and pancreatic malignancies.
  • Histologically, the gastrointestinal hamartomas show elongated, frond-like epithelium overlying an arborising network of smooth muscle bundles

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 70.14, 70.15.

options.text: Hamartomatous polyps commonly undergo malignant transformation.
Granulosa cell ovarian tumours are a characteristic associated tumour
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern

question: A 14-year-old girl presents with the mucocutaneous lesions shown in the image. Her father has a history of similar lesions and gastrointestinal polyps. Imaging reveals a jejunal hamartomatous polyp causing intermittent abdominal pain. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?

correctAnswer: C. Most of them have severe permanent neurological impairment
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child is presenting with Incontinentia Pigmenti (IP), also known as Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome. The majority (>60%) of patients with incontinentia pigmenti are neurologically normal.


Incontinentia Pigmenti (IP):

  • Rare X-linked dominant (Option B) multisystem ectodermal dysplasia
  • Usually lethal in males & affects mainly females
  • Involves skin, teeth, hair, nails, eyes, and CNS
  • Genetics & pathophysiology:
    • Caused by IKBKG (NEMO / IKK-γ) gene mutation (Option A)
    • Impaired NF-κB activation → ↑ TNF-α-induced apoptosis
    • Exon 4-10 deletion in ~85% cases
    • Inherited or de novo & affected males usually miscarried
  • Cutaneous Stages (along Blaschko lines):
    • Stage I (Vesicular): Erythematous vesicles at birth
    • Stage II (Verrucous): Hyperkeratotic, wart-like lesions (limbs)
    • Stage III (Pigmented): Swirled hyperpigmentation (fades by adolescence)
    • Stage IV (Atrophic): Hypopigmented, hairless, atrophic streaks (adolescence)
  • Extras: Peg/missing teeth, alopecia, nail dystrophy, retinal neovascularisation, ± seizures
  • >60% neurologically normal
  • Prognosis: Normal life expectancy
  • Management: Supportive; mandatory ophthalmologic follow-up (Option D)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 70.11.

options.text: It is caused by mutations in the IKBKG (NEMO) gene
Most of them have severe permanent neurological impairment

question: A newborn female presents with erythematous vesicular lesions arranged along Blaschko lines since birth. Over the next few months, the lesions become verrucous, followed later by swirled hyperpigmentation. She also has peg-shaped teeth & requires ophthalmologic follow-up. Which of the following statements about this condition is incorrect?

correctAnswer: B. It is commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant patterny
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hypomelanosis of Ito is usually sporadic, resulting from postzygotic mutations leading to mosaicism, and is not commonly inherited.


Hypomelanosis of Ito:

  • A rare neuroectodermal mosaic disorder characterised by hypopigmented skin lesions along the lines of Blaschko. (Option C)
  • Present as macular hypopigmentation
  • No skin atrophy (helps differentiate from focal dermal hypoplasia) (Option D)
  • Extracutaneous associations:
    • Neurological: intellectual disability, epilepsy
    • Ophthalmological abnormalities
    • Skeletal defects
    • Overall marked phenotypic variability
  • Genetics & pathogenesis:
    • Caused by postzygotic mutations
    • Represents cutaneous mosaicism (Option A): May be monogenic or chromosomal
    • Transmission to offspring presumed lethal, explaining sporadic occurrence
  • Current concept:
    • Not a single disease entity
    • Represents a phenotypic pattern of mosaicism manifesting as hypo- or hyperpigmentation along the Blaschko line.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 70.10

options.text: It represents a form of cutaneous mosaicism
It is commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant patterny
Skin lesions typically lack epidermal atroph

question: An 8-year-old child presents with findings as shown in the image, with a history of seizures and developmental delay. Which of the following statements about this condition is wrong?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Negative family history is not associated with worse disease outcomes and, therefore, it is not a poor prognostic factor in vitiligo.


Poor prognostic factors for vitiligo:

  • Family history of vitiligo
  • Mucosal involvement (Option B)
  • Koebner phenomenon (skin lesions at sites of trauma) (Option A)
  • Adverse clinical markers
  • Confetti-like lesions (limited evidence)
  • Longer disease duration and leukotrichia (Option C) correlated with greater body surface area involvement and poor repigmentation.


Age of onset showed inconsistent associations.

Vitiligo- prognosis
question: A patient with non-segmental vitiligo is being counselled regarding disease prognosis. Which of the following is not considered a poor prognostic factor in vitiligo?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image depicts a newborn receiving phototherapy for jaundice at the hospital.

  • Phototherapy = controlled use of non-ionising ultraviolet (UV) radiation to treat skin diseases.


PUVA therapy:

  • PUVA = Psoralen + UVA
  • Psoralen given oral/topical, followed by UVA exposure

[[figure-1]]

  • Mechanism:
    • DNA cross-linking by psoralen photoadducts
    • Inhibition of DNA replication
    • Langerhans cell depletion
    • Immunosuppression of T-lymphocyte function and migration
    • Restoration of Th17 / regulatory T-cell imbalance


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 21.1.
question:
Which of the following are the mechanisms of the treatment modality depicted in the image below:

  1. DNA cross-linking by psoralen photoadducts
  2. Inhibition of DNA replication
  3. Depletion of Langerhans cells
  4. Immunosuppressive effects on T-lymphocyte function and migration
  5. Restoration of Th17/regulatory T-cell imbalance

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

While retinoids (like tretinoin) are used for many skin conditions, such as acne, psoriasis, and photoaging, they are not a standard treatment for vitiligo.


Management of vitiligo:

  • First line:
    • Topical corticosteroids (e.g., 0.1% betamethasone, 0.05% clobetasol)
    • Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) (Option B) - mainly for face/neck
  • Second line: Phototherapy (PUVA, NB-UVB, excimer laser 308 nm) (Option A)
  • Third line:
    • Tissue grafts: punch, split-thickness, suction blister
    • Cellular grafts: cultured melanocytes/epithelial sheets (Option C)
    • Hair follicle outer root sheath cell transplantation
  • Depigmentation therapy: For extensive residual pigmentation: monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, Q-switched lasers, cryotherapy
  • Supportive:
    • Sunscreen for sun-exposed areas
    • Cosmetic camouflage


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 88.39, 88.40.
question: A 30-year-old man with stable non-segmental vitiligo seeks treatment. Which of the following is not used in the management of vitiligo?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Vitiligo is frequently associated with other autoimmune disorders due to shared genetic susceptibility and common pathways of immune-mediated destruction. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), however, is a genetic neurocutaneous syndrome and is not autoimmune in nature.


Associated conditions of vitiligo:

  • Thyroid disease: Hyperthyroidism & hypothyroidism (Option A)
  • Pernicious anemia
  • Addison’s (Option C)
  • Diabetes
  • Myasthenia gravis.
  • Alopecia areata (Option B)
  • Morphoea
  • Lichen sclerosus
  • Halo naevi
  • Malignant melanoma.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 88.35
question: A 25-year-old woman has progressive, well-defined depigmented patches over the hands and face. Which of the following is not associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Vitiligo is an acquired depigmentation disorder caused by progressive loss of melanocytes, presenting as milky-white, sharply demarcated macules.

  • Pathophysiology:
    • Autoimmune/autoinflammatory mechanism: cytotoxic T cells target melanocytes.
    • Oxidative stress: generates neoantigens triggering autoimmunity.
    • Other mechanisms: melanocyte self-destruction, defective keratinocytes, melanocytorrhagy, and neurogenic factors.
    • Genetics: polygenic; ~30% have a family history. Key genes include TYR.

Vitiligo is an acquired depigmenting disorder characterised by well-defined depigmented macules and patches due to loss of melanocytes. Lesions are usually asymptomatic, symmetrical, and commonly involve the face, hands, genitalia, and body orifices. Hair within lesions may turn white (leukotrichia), and the disease may be associated with other autoimmune disorders. True Koebner’s phenomenon is seen.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on the typical appearance of depigmented patches. Wood’s lamp examination shows milky-white fluorescence.

[[figure-1]]

Defective migration of melanocytes during embryogenesis (Option A): This describes piebaldism or Waardenburg syndrome, which are congenital.

Decreased number of melanosomes in melanocytes (Option C): Melanosome number is normal initially; melanocytes themselves are lost.

Reduced tyrosinase activity (Option D): This is seen in oculocutaneous albinism, where melanin synthesis is defective but melanocyte number is normal.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 88.34, 88.36, 88.37.

options.text: Defective migration of melanocytes during embryogenesis
Decreased number of melanosomes in melanocytes

question: Which of the following is the primary cause of the condition shown in the image below?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of pale skin, white hair, nystagmus, and specific ocular findings like foveal hypoplasia and optic nerve misrouting is diagnostic of Oculocutaneous Albinism.

Oculocutaneous albinism is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defects in melanin biosynthesis, with normal melanocyte number.

Oculocutaneous Albinism:

  • Definition: Genetic hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes due to a melanin biosynthesis defect; melanocytes are normal (Option A)
  • Inheritance: Autosomal recessive; subtypes OCA1-OCA7 (TYR, OCA2, TYRP1, SLC45A2, SLC24A5, C10orf11)
  • Clinical Features:
    • Skin & hair: pale; severity varies by subtype
    • Eyes: nystagmus, iris translucency, foveal hypoplasia, optic nerve misrouting, photophobia, reduced visual acuity
    • OCA1A: complete pigment absence; OCA1B & others: variable pigmentation
    • Increased risk of skin cancers (squamous cell carcinoma in OCA2) (Option D)
    • Normal lifespan, development, intelligence, and fertility


[[figure-1]]

  • Management:
    • Sun protection to prevent burns and skin cancer (Option C)
    • Ophthalmology referral: Corrective lenses, eye patching, or surgery for strabismus; sunglasses for photophobia


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 70.6-70.8.
question: A 3-year-old child presents with pale skin, white hair, nystagmus, photophobia, and reduced visual acuity. Ophthalmological examination shows foveal hypoplasia and optic nerve misrouting. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?

correctAnswer: B. Hypopigmentation is due to defective melanocyte trafficking
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child is presenting with Chédiak-Higashi Syndrome (CHS), a rare multisystem disorder characterised by partial oculocutaneous albinism, immunodeficiency, and unique cellular abnormalities.

[[figure-1]]

The disorder results from mutations in LYST, causing giant melanosomes in melanocytes due to defective trafficking.

Chédiak-Higashi Syndrome (CHS):

  • Inheritance: Autosomal recessive (Option A)
  • Gene: CHS1 (LYST) → defective lysosomal trafficking
  • Pathology: Giant melanosomes in melanocytes; giant inclusions in neutrophils
    • Neutrophil function is impaired, leading to recurrent infections (Option D)
  • Clinical Features:
    • Hypopigmented skin, hair, and eyes
    • Recurrent infections, neutropenia
    • Neurological symptoms (intellectual decline, tremor, cranial nerve palsies)
    • Accelerated phase: hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
  • Investigations: Giant peroxidase-positive leukocyte inclusions; hair pigment clumping
  • Management: Bone marrow transplantation (curative)
  • Phototherapy does not correct pigmentation (Option C)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 70.8, 70.9.

options.text: It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
Hypopigmentation is due to defective melanocyte trafficking
Phototherapy is the treatment of choice for pigmentation
Neutrophil function is normal in affected individuals

question: A 5-year-old boy presents with silvery hair, fair skin, and pale irides. He has a history of recurrent bacterial infections and neutropenia. Peripheral smear shows findings as shown. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

White forelock, congenital hypopigmentation, heterochromia, dystopia canthorum, and sensorineural deafness are characteristic of Waardenburg syndrome.

Waardenburg Syndrome:

  • Definition: Genetic disorder of neural crest → white forelock, hypopigmented patches, sensorineural deafness
  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant (WS1-3), autosomal recessive (WS4)
  • Genes: WS1/3 - PAX3; WS2 - MITF/SLUG; WS4 - EDNRB, EDN3, SOX10
  • Clinical Features:
    • White forelock (hallmark)
    • Hypopigmented patches (may partially repigment)
    • Heterochromia irides
    • WS1: dystopia canthorum, facial dysmorphism
    • WS3: musculoskeletal anomalies
    • WS4: Hirschsprung disease
  • Management:
    • Hearing loss: Non-progressive; manage based on severity
    • Audiogram: Usually a one-time evaluation unless indicated

Piebaldism (Option A): White forelock + hypopigmented patches, but no deafness or dystopia canthorum

Vitiligo (Option C): Acquired, progressive depigmentation; lesions appear after birth

Tuberous sclerosis (Option D): Hypopigmented “ash leaf” macules, not associated with white forelock or deafness



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 70.4, 70.5.
question: A 5-year-old has heterochromia irides, sensorineural deafness & the following skin findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. A white forelock is the characteristic clinical feature
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) White forelock is the characteristic clinical feature

Explanation:

Piebaldism is classically marked by a white forelock and stable congenital hypopigmented patches.

[[figure-1]]

Piebaldism:

  • Rare autosomal dominant pigmentary disorder (Option A)
  • Well-demarcated congenital hypopigmented macules
  • Pathophysiology:
    • KIT gene mutation → defective c-KIT tyrosine kinase receptor
    • → Failure of melanocyte migration to the skin (Option B)
    • Result: Absent melanocytes and melanin in white patches
    • Less commonly: SNAI2 mutation
  • Clinical features:
    • White forelock (most characteristic)
    • V-shaped leukoderma on mid-forehead & hypopigmented patches
    • Hands, feet, and back spared
    • Islands of hyperpigmentation within depigmented areas
    • Extent variable; sometimes only white forelock
    • Usually, no extracutaneous involvement (Option D)
    • Rare: deafness or intellectual disability (large deletions)
  • Management:
    • Sun protection (amelanotic skin burns easily)
    • Skin/epidermal grafting - effective
    • Phototherapy & topical steroids: ineffective


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 70.3, 70.4.

options.text: Caused by a defect in melanocyte production
A white forelock is the characteristic clinical feature

question: Which of the following statements regarding piebaldism is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In normal epidermis, one melanocyte supplies melanin to ~36 keratinocytes, maintaining pigmentation. This ratio is constant across skin types.

Skin colour varies due to melanosome size, number, and melanin type.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 88.3.
question: The approximate keratinocyte to melanocyte ratio in normal human epidermis is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Nevus depigmentosus is a congenital, stable, non-progressive hypopigmented macule or patch, present from early life.
  • Lesion is usually solitary, well-defined, and does not spread over time.
  • Wood’s lamp shows an off-white accentuation (less bright than vitiligo).
  • Diascopy is negative because the hypopigmentation is due to reduced melanin, not vascular changes.
  • No sensory loss or scaling is present.
  • Management is generally reassurance; no effective repigmentation treatment is required unless for cosmetic concerns.

[[figure-1]]

Vitiligo (Option A): An acquired progressive depigmentation with complete loss of melanin; Wood’s lamp shows bright chalk-white fluorescence; lesions tend to enlarge over time.

Nevus anemicus (Option C): A vascular anomaly where skin appears pale due to localized increased vasoconstriction; diascopy causes the lesion to blend with surrounding skin (positive diascopy), unlike nevus depigmentosus.

Indeterminate leprosy (Option D): Hypopigmented patch with impaired sensation and possible nerve thickening; would not be stable for years without progression, and diagnosis requires sensory loss or skin smear evidence.

This woman with hyperpigmented patches on her cheek and a history of chronic sun exposure most likely has melasma.

  • It is characterized by hyperpigmented macules with scalloped or irregular margins that are darker than the surrounding areas.
  • These patches typically appear on the face, with common locations being the cheeks, forehead, and chin.
  • It is more common in females.

  • Topical hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase, an enzyme responsible for pigment production in melanocytes, and is a common depigmenting agent.
    • Triple combination therapy of hydroquinone, retinoid, and corticosteroid is highly effective for melasma.

explanationHtml:
The presence of velvety, hyperpigmented lesions is characteristic of Acanthosis Nigricans. This condition is caused by hyperkeratosis (thickening of the skin) without an increase in melanocyte or melanin production. It commonly affects intertriginous areas (skin folds such as the neck, axillae, groins, and submammary folds) and is associated with obesity, insulin resistance, hypothyroidism, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), acromegaly, and other metabolic disturbances.

[[figure-1]]

  • Pathogenesis: The condition is linked to increased production of IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1).
  • Types:
    • Benign Acanthosis Nigricans: Associated with diabetes, obesity, or metabolic syndrome.
    • Malignant Acanthosis Nigricans: Rapid onset and linked to visceral malignancies, such as adenocarcinomas of the gastrointestinal tract.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Velvety, asymptomatic, symmetrical darkening of the skin.
    • Often begins in the neck, axillae, groins, or other intertriginous areas.
    • May lead to the development of skin tags in affected regions.
  • The presence of these lesions is a cutaneous marker for underlying metabolic abnormalities and insulin resistance.
  • Treatment involves addressing the underlying condition with lifestyle modifications and, if necessary, topical treatments like keratolytics or retinoids.

Tinea Versicolor (Option B)

  • Caused by a fungal infection (Malassezia species).
  • Presents as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented scaly macules/patches, not velvety lesions.
  • Typically has a scaly appearance, especially after sun exposure.

Seborrheic Keratosis (Option C)

  • A benign skin lesion that appears as well-demarcated, warty, or "stuck-on" plaques.
  • Common in older adults.
  • Does not have the velvety texture characteristic of Acanthosis Nigricans.

Atopic Dermatitis (Option D)

  • Also known as eczema, it appears as dry, itchy, scaly, and inflamed patches of skin.
  • Typically affects flexural surfaces (e.g., behind knees, elbows) rather than intertriginous areas.
  • Velvety hyperpigmented patches are not a feature of atopic dermatitis.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology 9th edition - page 87.2
question: A 13-year-old patient presents with the velvety lesion shown in the image below. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows depigmented patches on the arm, which are characteristic of Vitiligo.

Vitiligo:

  • Vitiligo is an acquired pigmentation disorder featuring well-defined depigmented macules on the skin.
  • Biopsies show epidermal melanocyte loss. Lesions may be localized or generalized, coalescing into large depigmented areas.
  • Wood's lamp, emitting ultraviolet A (UV-A) light, aids in diagnosis by revealing bright blue-white fluorescence with sharply demarcated borders in vitiligo lesions, particularly in individuals with pale skin.

Melasma (Option A):

  • Melasma presents as hyperpigmented (brownish) patches, often on sun-exposed areas like the face.
  • It is associated with pregnancy, oral contraceptive use, and sun exposure.

Psoriasis (Option C):

  • Psoriasis features erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales, usually on extensor surfaces like elbows and knees.
  • It does not cause depigmentation.

Dermatitis Herpetiformis (Option D):

  • This is a chronic, intensely pruritic vesicular disease associated with celiac disease.
  • It presents as grouped vesicles and papules rather than depigmented patches.

question: A 22-year-old college student presents with small, depigmented lesions which have been there for over 2 years now as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Answer: B) Segmental vitiligo

Explanation:

The presence of leukotrichia (white hair) along with depigmented patches suggests vitiligo, as leukotrichia is uncommon in congenital disorders like piebaldism or nevus depigmentosus.

Segmental vitiligo affects one side of the body and follows a dermatomal or unilateral pattern.

It occurs early in life, progresses rapidly, and then stabilises, unlike generalised vitiligo, which progresses over time.

Focal Vitiligo (Option A) is incorrect because focal vitiligo presents as small, isolated patches but does not follow a segmental/dermatomal distribution. It often progresses into generalised vitiligo, unlike segmental vitiligo, which remains localized.

Piebaldism (Option C) is incorrect because it is a congenital disorder (present from birth) due to c-KIT gene mutations. Typically associated with a white forelock (poliosis) and symmetrical patches, not segmental.

Nevus Depigmentosus (Option D) is incorrect because it is a stable hypopigmented patch present from birth. Unlike vitiligo, it does not progress or show leukotrichia.

explanationHtml:
• Wood's light assessment is a symptomatic test utilized in dermatology to assist with recognizing different skin conditions, including contagious contaminations, bacterial diseases, and color problems like vitiligo. Dermatologists are able to observe subtle changes in the skin that might not be apparent under normal lighting conditions thanks to the use of ultraviolet light to highlight fluorescent substances in the skin.
  • The patient's skin is first cleansed, and any cosmetics or lotions are removed during a Wood's lamp examination. The dermatologist applies the UV light from Wood's lamp to the patient's skin in a room that is darkened. The fluorescent substances in the skin mirror the light, making the skin seem an alternate tone, it is inspected to rely upon the condition. For instance, fungal infections can have a yellow-green appearance, while pigment disorders can have a white or blue-green appearance.

Incorrect choices:

  • Option a. Culture: Microorganisms like bacteria, viruses, and fungi can be identified and grown from a sample of tissue or bodily fluid with the help of a culture test in the laboratory. Cultures are frequently utilized in dermatology to diagnose fungal or bacterial skin infections like cellulitis, impetigo, or fungal skin infections.
  • Option c. Gram staining: A laboratory test known as "gram staining" is used to determine the kind of bacteria that is present in a sample of bodily fluid or tissue. In dermatology, it is frequently used to diagnose bacterial skin infections like folliculitis, cellulitis, and impetigo.
  • Option d. Patch test: A diagnostic test known as patch testing is used to pinpoint the substances or allergens that may be triggering allergic contact dermatitis. When the skin comes into contact with a substance that the immune system perceives as foreign and reacts against, this type of dermatitis is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The neonate has diffuse superficial flaccid blistering with skin peeling but is otherwise stable, feeding well, and shows no systemic toxicity. This favours neonatal pemphigus vulgaris.

Absence of fever, shock, or toxic appearance helps distinguish it from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS).

  • Neonatal pemphigus vulgaris occurs due to transplacental transfer of maternal IgG autoantibodies against desmogleins.
  • Neonates develop superficial flaccid bullae and erosions with a positive Nikolsky sign.
  • Absence of systemic toxicity and a maternal history of pemphigus support the diagnosis.

Neonatal pemphigus vulgaris:

  • Neonatal pemphigus is a rare, transient autoimmune blistering disorder.
  • Autoantibodies are directed against desmoglein-3 and sometimes desmoglein-1.
  • Maternal autoantibodies cross the placenta and target neonatal epidermal adhesion molecules.
  • Loss of keratinocyte adhesion causes intraepidermal blister formation (acantholysis).
  • Histology shows suprabasal intraepidermal clefting.
  • Lesions usually resolve spontaneously as maternal antibodies disappear.

Clinical features:

  • Flaccid vesicles and bullae.
  • Superficial erosions and desquamation.
  • Positive Nikolsky sign.
  • Mucosal involvement may occur.
  • The infant may otherwise appear clinically stable.

[[figure-1]]

Important DDs for neonatal vesiculobullous disorders:

  • Toxic infant with widespread tenderness → consider SSSS.
  • Trauma-induced recurrent blistering → epidermolysis bullosa.
  • Maternal autoimmune blistering disease → neonatal pemphigus.
  • Tense subepidermal bullae → bullous pemphigoid.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (Option A) is caused by exfoliative toxins of Staphylococcus aureus. Usually associated with diffuse erythema and superficial exfoliation rather than a maternal autoimmune history.

Bullous pemphigoid (Option B) is rare in neonates and presents with tense subepidermal bullae. Nikolsky's sign is usually negative.

Epidermolysis bullosa (Option C) is a genetic blistering disorder triggered by minor trauma. Does not typically produce diffuse exfoliative desquamation.



Reference:
  • https://casereports.bmj.com/content/17/9/e259305
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6074178/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario likely describes acute eczema that does not show lichenification, which is a feature of chronic eczema.


Eczema or atopic dermatitis is a chronic, pruritic, inflammatory condition of the skin. The pattern of the rash varies with age

  • Infantile phase (<2 years): The lesions are present on the face and extensor aspect of the knees and elbows consisting of erythema and discrete or confluent oedematous papules. The papules may become exudative and crusted.

  • Childhood phase (2 years to puberty): Presents as erythema, crusting, excoriation, hyper and hypopigmentation, and warty lichenification involving the elbow and knee flexures.
  • Adult phase: Similar to the childhood phase with more localized and lichenified lesions.

Based on the duration of complaints, eczema may be acute, subacute, or chronic.


Acute eczema presents with itching and dryness of the skin. Examination findings include signs of inflammation - erythema, oedema, vesicles, oozing, and crusting.

[[figure-1]]

Chronic eczema results from long-term untreated or inadequately treated eczema. Exam findings include lichenification, increased skin markings, hyperpigmentation, and thickening of the skin as shown below.

[[figure-2]]


Subacute eczema lies in between acute and chronic eczema - erythema and scaling may be seen.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The best time to visualize the results of the patch test is after 96 hours.

Patch tests are usually used to detect contact allergy of the delayed hypersensitivity type. They are usually read at 48–72 h, 96 h and again after 1 week, but can also be read at 15–30 min to detect contact urticaria. If only one patch test reading is possible, a day 4 reading has been recommended.

Indications for patch testing

  • Allergic contact dermatitis
  • Eczematous disorders failing to respond to treatment (including occupational)

The back is the most commonly used site. Before testing, the site should be free of eczema. Finn chambers or discs are used to ensure the allergen contacts the skin. The discs are applied and removed after 48 hours.

[[figure-1]]

A typical regimen is a 48 h application time, with readings taken 1 h after removal and again 48 h later (that is day 2 and day 4). A single day 2 reading is not advised as it

may lead to the labelling of some marginal irritants as allergens and positive reactions to more poorly absorbed allergens may be missed. If only one patch test reading is possible, a day 4 reading has been recommended.

The positive result might include erythema, papule, pustule, and vesicles at the site of application. It might also lead to thickening of the dermis.
