The patient presents with a mild flare of AD for which the initial management is topical steroids (ointment if lichenified; cream if scaly/oozy) along with emollients.

Management of atopic dermatitis includes

  1. Controlling environmental factors like removing triggers (example- dust), avoiding extreme temperatures, detergents, and harsh soaps.
  2. Restoring the compromised barrier: Hydration using emollients and moisturizers)

Emollients soften the skin, reduce itch, and enhance the effect of topical

corticosteroids. Persistent use of emollients when the inflammation is in

remission may reduce the time and frequency of flare-ups.

  1. Pharmacological treatment:-
  • Localized condition: Topical corticosteroids +/- antihistamines +/- antibiotics
  • For face: Calcineurin inhibitors (pimecrolimus and tacrolimus)
  • Severe disease (systemic management): Oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, and azathioprine.
  • Newer drugs :
    • Crisabole: PDE-4 inhibitor (topical).
    • Dupilumab: IL-4 receptor alpha antagonist (systemic).
    • Tofacitinib: JAK kinase inhibitors
    • Apremilast: PDE-4 inhibitor (also used in psoriasis)

  • Atopic eczema treatment algorithm:

[[figure-1]]

TCI- topical calcineurin inhibitors; TCS, topical corticosteroids.



Reference:

Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 41.26, 41.27, 41.28
question: A 14-year-old girl presents with a flare-up of her atopic dermatitis which was previously well-controlled. Examination reveals erythematous lesions over the neck. Which of the following is the initial management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient with a history of asthma and above lesions most likely has pityriasis alba (PA).


Pityriasis alba is a benign condition that predominantly affects children and adolescents and is associated with atopic asthma. The classical presentation is multiple hypopigmented, scaly, round, or oval macules and patches, predominantly over the face, upper trunk, and upper limbs. These may be associated with mild erythema or scaling. On Wood's lamp examination, lesions are nonfluorescent.


It is a self-limited condition, treatment options include emollients, low-potency topical corticosteroids, and topical calcineurin inhibitors.


Tinea versicolor (Option A): It is caused by Malasezzia species and is more common in the truncal region. It presents with hypo or hyperpigmentation in patients with oily and sweaty skin and fine scales on scratching. There may be mild pruritus and erythema with yellow to green fluorescence on Wood’s lamp. The KOH mount shows a spaghetti and meatball appearance. Treatment includes antifungal agents like topical selenium sulfide and topical ketoconazole.

[[figure-1]]

KOH mount:

[[figure-2]]

Wood's lamp:

[[figure-3]]

Indeterminate leprosy (Option B) lacks scales on examination. Indeterminate Hansen presents with a single lesion.


Vitiligo (Option C) presents with depigmented milky white patches without scaling.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 39.25
  2. http://uptodate.com/contents/acquired-hypopigmentation-disorders-other-than-vitiligo
question: A 12-year-old girl presents with multiple hypopigmented patches, as shown below. She reports a prior history of asthma. Examination reveals lesions over her face as shown below. There is mild scaling over the lesions. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given case scenario describes seborrheic dermatitis (SD), an inflammatory response to colonization by the Malassezia fungal species.

In adults and adolescents, it is characterized by yellow, greasy scales involving the face, scalp (dandruff), nasolabial folds, and retro auricular region due to the major activity of sebaceous glands here leading to increased sebum production.

[[figure-1]]


It is also seen in infants < 3 months old due to presence of maternal androgens. Involvement of the scalp and face leads to a characteristic finding called cradle cap. It is also called infantile seborrheic dermatitis.


Management includes stopping Malassezia growth using antifungals like

  • Topical creams: Azoles (Sertaconazole, Propiconazole, Luliconazole) ·
  • Azole, zinc pyrithione (ZPTO), ciclopirox olamine, and selenium sulfide-based shampoo
  • Topical corticosteroids or Topical calcineurin inhibitors + Shampoo or Azoles for dry erythema
  • Antihistamines for itching
  • Oral antifungals (itraconazole, fluconazole) for severe and unresponsive disease
  • No oil application, as sebaceous gland activity is already increased.


For contact dermatitis, it may be recommended to avoid topical creams (Option D) to remove exposure to the offending substances. In the case of SD, organic oils may be avoided as they can worsen the condition.



Reference:
  1. https://www.uptodate.com/contents/seborrheic-dermatitis-in-adolescents-and-adults
  2. Rook’s textbook for dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 107.2
question: A 55-year-old female presents with multiple red, scaly patches with greasy, yellow scales in her hair. Which of the following represents an appropriate treatment option for her?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient with a chronic hyperpigmented lesion over the medial side of the ankle and a risk factor of venous stasis (standing-security guard) most likely has varicose eczema(VE) / venous stasis dermatitis.

It is typically seen in patients with long-standing varicose veins/ venous insufficiency. Risk factors include a family history of venous disease, standing occupations (security guard), obesity, female sex, and prior deep vein thrombosis.

Chronic pooling of blood/ venous hypertension leads to circulatory changes in the dermis including dilated capillaries and increased permeability that lead to pericapillary fibrin cuffs, oedema, leucocyte accumulation, and hemosiderin deposits.

VE is characterized by erythematous, scaling patches/ plaques over a background of chronic oedema. The medial ankle is most commonly involved, and the changes may extend up to the knee. With time, due to pruritus, there may be lichenification, scaling, and even ulceration. Varicose ulcer most commonly involves gaiter area[lower 1/3rd of leg ]

[[figure-1]]

Dyshidrotic eczema (aka Pompholyx) (Option A): This is a condition associated with atopic dermatitis that presents with vesicles over the palms and fingers (classically on sides of fingers).

[[figure-2]]

Nummular eczema (Option C): This is a type of endogenous eczema characterised by sharply defined, round or coin-shaped, erythematous, and eczematous plaques. It commonly involves lower extremities. Pruritus is common, and lesions may ooze fluid.

[[figure-3]]

Asteatotic eczema (Option D): This is seen in the elderly and occurs due to decrease of lipid coating granules in epidermis. It may be more prominent in dry seasons (winter). It is characterized by cracked, dry skin called cracked porcelain or crazy paving pattern.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 39.18 - 39.20
  2. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/varicose-eczema/
question: An elderly male who works as a security guard presents with a chronic rash over his legs. Examination reveals a hyperpigmented rash with scaling over the medial aspect of both ankles, as shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient likely has exfoliative dermatitis (ED) due to inadequate treatment of his pemphigus, which can lead to high-output heart failure and not heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

Erythroderma, or exfoliative dermatitis, is a severe complication of other underlying diseases. It is characterized by diffuse erythema and scaling involving >90% of the skin surface area, which may be tender and/ or pruritic. There may be associated systemic features like lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

Complications include:

  • Bacterial infections of the skin - especially MRSA
  • Increased skin transpiration causes thermoregulation issues, dehydration, and dyselectrolytemia, which results in extensive water and protein loss. Blood shunting to the skin may lead to high-output cardiac failure in patients with pre-existing cardiac issues (not HFrEF).
  • Hypoproteinemia (oedema, muscle wasting) in those with extensive exfoliation


Reference:

Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 119.12
question: A 57-year-old male presents to you with an extensive erythematous rash that covers >90% of his body surface, as shown below. He is a known case of pemphigus foliaceous, requiring regular immunosuppressants but not adhering to medications. The skin is warm and tender to the touch. Which of the following is not a potential complication of his condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has erythroderma (exfoliative dermatitis), a severe inflammatory skin disorder involving more than 90% of the body surface area.

  • It may occur as a complication of pemphigus foliaceus.
  • Major complications result from haemodynamic and metabolic disturbances and include:
    • High-output cardiac failure due to increased cutaneous blood flow.
    • Hypothermia (Option B) due to increased skin perfusion.
    • Fluid and electrolyte imbalance due to excessive transepidermal water loss.
    • Hypoalbuminaemia (hypoproteinemia) (Option C) caused by protein loss through exfoliated scales, leading to peripheral oedema.
    • Secondary cutaneous and respiratory infections (Option A), which contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality.



Reference:

Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 39.30-39.35, 119.11, 119.12
question: A 57-year-old man with pemphigus foliaceus presents with diffuse erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area, as shown in the image. He has been non-compliant with his immunosuppressive therapy for pemphigus foliaceous. On examination, the skin is warm and tender. Which of the following is not a potential complication of this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Histamine release from mast cells
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dermatographism (dermographism or "skin writing") is the most common form of physical urticaria and is characterized by the development of linear wheals and surrounding erythema following minor mechanical trauma, such as stroking or scratching the skin.
  • The reaction is caused by degranulation of cutaneous mast cells, leading to the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators.
  • Histamine produces vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and localized edema, resulting in the characteristic wheal-and-flare response.
  • Symptoms usually appear within minutes and resolve spontaneously within 30–60 minutes.

Keratinocyte apoptosis (Option A) is the hallmark of disorders such as erythema multiforme, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, where cytotoxic T cells induce apoptosis of epidermal keratinocytes.

T-cell–mediated inflammation (Option C) is responsible for chronic inflammatory skin disorders such as allergic contact dermatitis, psoriasis, and atopic dermatitis. These conditions produce delayed inflammatory lesions rather than the rapid, transient urticarial response that occurs immediately after mechanical stimulation of the skin.

IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein (Option D) are the underlying pathogenic mechanism in pemphigus vulgaris, where antibodies target desmoglein-1 and desmoglein-3, causing loss of keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis) and flaccid intraepidermal blisters.



Reference:
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK531496/
  • https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1050294-overview
question: A 24-year-old man complains of recurrent itching and transient linear wheals over his forearms after minor scratching. The examination technique demonstrated in the attached video is performed using a blunt instrument. The skin develops an erythematous, raised linear wheal within a few minutes. This response is primarily mediated by which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical description provided, the most likely diagnosis is Eczema (specifically Atopic Dermatitis).

  • Eczema is characterised by pruritus as the predominant symptom, a chronic relapsing course, flexural involvement in children, and worsening at night & with irritants like soap.
  • Associations:
    • Children: Atopic eczema
    • Adults: Contact/hand eczema
    • Elderly: Nummular, asteatotic


Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory dermatosis in which pruritus is the cardinal symptom. The itching often precedes the appearance of skin lesions and is typically worse at night, leading to scratching, excoriations, and sleep disturbance. Symptoms are commonly aggravated by soaps, detergents, sweating, heat, and other irritants.


The clinical distribution varies with age. In children, eczema characteristically involves the flexural areas, such as the antecubital and popliteal fossae, neck, and wrists. In adults, the disease may persist or recur with prominent involvement of the hands, often overlapping with contact dermatitis. In the elderly, eczema frequently presents as nummular or asteatotic eczema, related to xerosis and environmental factors.


Pathogenetically, atopic dermatitis is associated with epidermal barrier dysfunction, often due to filaggrin deficiency, resulting in increased transepidermal water loss and enhanced penetration of allergens and irritants. This is accompanied by immune dysregulation, typically a Th2-predominant response, and is commonly associated with other atopic conditions such as asthma and allergic rhinitis.


Psoriasis (Option A): Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scales; usually on extensor surfaces, with less intense itching.



Impetigo (Option C): Acute bacterial infection with honey-colored crusts, minimal pruritus.


Tinea corporis (Option D): Annular lesions with central clearing and peripheral scaling.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 39.3, 39.5, 41.5, 41.16, 41.17.
question: A 6-year-old child presents with intense itching and recurrent skin lesions for the past 1 year. Examination shows findings as shown in the image over the flexural areas. Symptoms worsen at night and with soap use. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:


Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scales are features of psoriasis (statement 4), not eczema.


Eczema:

  • Eczema (dermatitis) is an inflammatory skin reaction pattern characterised by itching as the primary symptom (statement 1)
  • Key features:
    • Acute eczema:
      • Erythema
      • Edema
      • Vesicles (microvesiculation)
      • Oozing, crusting
    • Subacute eczema:
      • Less vesiculation
      • Scaling
      • Mild erythema
    • Chronic eczema:
      • Lichenification (thickened skin) (statement 5)
      • Hyperpigmentation
      • Excoriations (due to scratching)
    • Other important features:
      • Xerosis (dry skin)
      • Fissuring (especially hands/feet)
      • Secondary infection (impetiginisation)
    • (statement 5)
  • Histology (Hallmark): Spongiosis (epidermal oedema) is the characteristic histopathological feature of eczema (statement 2).

[[figure-1]]

  • Types:
    • Exogenous: Allergic contact, irritant contact, photoeczema
    • Endogenous: Atopic, seborrhoeic, nummular, asteatotic, hand, venous
  • Associations:
    • Children: Atopic eczema is common (statement 3)
    • Adults: Contact/hand eczema
    • Elderly: Nummular, asteatotic
  • Pathogenesis: Barrier defect + immune dysregulation (↑ with filaggrin mutation)
  • Diagnosis: Clinical
    • Patch test → hand/face/foot eczema
  • Treatment:
    • Emollients → topical steroids → calcineurin inhibitors → phototherapy/systemics


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 39.2-39.7
question:
Which of the following statements regarding eczema are correct?

  1. Pruritus is the predominant and earliest symptom
  2. Spongiosis is the histopathological hallmark
  3. Atopic eczema is common in children
  4. Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scales are typical
  5. Chronic lesions show lichenification

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Nummular dermatitis (also known as Discoid Eczema).

  • Chronic eczema with well-demarcated coin-shaped plaques
  • Epidemiology: Women - early adulthood; Men - older age
  • Pathology: Spongiotic dermatitis, lymphohistiocytic infiltrate ± eosinophils
  • Triggers: Dry skin, low humidity, contact allergens (nickel, chromate), staph colonisation, drugs (methyldopa, gold)
  • Clinical features:
    • Coin-shaped erythematous plaques
    • Vesicles → oozing/crusts → scaling
    • Intense pruritus, recurrent, symmetrical spread
  • Variants: Exudative, dry type, hand involvement
  • Differential diagnosis: Tinea corporis, psoriasis, pityriasis rosea
  • Course: Chronic, relapsing; worse in winter
  • Management:
    • Emollients + potent topical steroids
    • ± antibiotics
    • Refractory: calcineurin inhibitors, NB-UVB/PUVA, systemic therapy


Tinea corporis (Option A): Typically shows active scaly margins with central clearing but is KOH positive and less exudative.

[[figure-1]]


Psoriasis (Option B): Lesions are dry, well-defined plaques with silvery scales, usually less pruritic, and commonly involve extensor surfaces.

[[figure-2]]

Pityriasis rosea (Option D): Characterised by a herald patch followed by multiple oval lesions along cleavage lines; usually self-limiting and mildly pruritic.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 39.7-39.9.
question: A 52-year-old man presents with findings as shown in the image. The lesions are well demarcated, ooze and crust during flares, and worsen in winter. Some plaques show central clearing with peripheral scaling. KOH examination is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Hanifin and Rajka criteria, particularly the UK Working Party refinement, are the most widely used clinical diagnostic criteria for atopic dermatitis, especially in children.


UK Refinement of Hanifin & Rajka Diagnostic Criteria for Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema):

  • Mandatory criterion:
    • Pruritic skin condition (or parental report of scratching/rubbing in a child)
  • Plus ≥ 3 of the following criteria:

1. Early onset: Onset before 2 years of age (Not applied if the child is < 4 years old)

2. Typical distribution:

  • History of skin crease involvement
  • Includes cheeks in children < 10 years

3. Xerosis: History of generally dry skin

4. Atopic "list-style-type:circle" aria-level="2">Personal history of atopic disease OR first-degree family history of atopy (if child < 4 years)

5. Visible eczema:

6. Flexural dermatitis OR cheeks/forehead and outer limbs involvement in children < 4 years


Jones criteria (Option A): Used for diagnosing rheumatic fever



Rome IV criteria (Option C): Used for functional gastrointestinal disorders


ABCD rule (Option D): Used for melanoma assessment



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 41.2
question: Which of the following diagnostic criteria is commonly used for atopic dermatitis?

correctAnswer: B. Lichenification of flexures and hands
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Adult atopic eczema typically presents with chronic lichenified eczema, especially involving the flexures and hands.


Adult Atopic Eczema:

  • Adult AE is essentially similar to late childhood eczema, often persisting from earlier life.
  • Chronic lichenification is the dominant feature
  • Marked skin thickening due to long-standing scratching
  • Typical distribution:
    • Flexural areas (antecubital and popliteal fossae)
    • Hands - very common and often severe
    • Flexural inflammation may be less troublesome than in childhood

[[figure-1]]

  • Sites:
    • Face & hands (Option D)
    • Nipples (especially in adolescents and young women)
    • Lips - involvement of the vermilion and adjacent skin is common
  • Special patterns:
    • Follicular lichenified papules - frequent in Black patients and Japanese
    • Eczema on the face, upper arms and back may relate to thermal sweating or Malassezia sensitivity
    • Photosensitivity may occur in some adults
  • Hand eczema:
    • Often diffuse, chronic and lichenified
    • Strong association with occupational dermatitis
    • Previous AE and hand involvement are major risk factors

Predominant involvement of the extensors (Option A): Typical of infantile atopic eczema, which commonly affects the cheeks and extensor surfaces. Adult atopic eczema predominantly involves the flexures.

Vesiculobullous lesions limited to extensor surfaces (Option C): Not a feature of adult atopic eczema. Adult disease typically presents with chronic lichenified eczematous plaques rather than vesiculobullous lesions.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 41.19.

options.text: Vesiculobullous lesions limited to extensor surfaces
Absence of facial or hand involvement

question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of adult atopic eczema?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In infantile atopic eczema, lesions most frequently begin on the face, particularly the cheeks. As the child grows and starts crawling, involvement may extend to exposed extensor surfaces, while the napkin area is usually spared.


Infantile phase of atopic dermatitis:

  • Initial sites: Face (napkin area usually spared)
  • Later: Extensor surfaces (knees, elbows) with crawling
  • Lesions:
    • Erythema, oedematous papules
    • Exudation, crusting
  • Common: Secondary infection, lymphadenopathy
  • Triggers: Teething, infections, humidity changes


Flexural creases (Option A): Flexural involvement (antecubital and popliteal fossae) is typical of childhood atopic eczema, not the infantile phase. In infants, flexures are usually spared initially.


Extensor surfaces of knees and elbows (Option C): Extensor surfaces can be involved in infants, but they are not the first or most common initial site. Facial involvement usually precedes extensor limb lesions.


Napkin area (Option D): The napkin (diaper) area is classically spared in atopic eczema due to moisture and occlusion. Eczema in this region suggests irritant diaper dermatitis, not atopic eczema.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 41.16.

options.text: Extensor surfaces of knees and elbows

question: Which of the following is the most common first site of involvement in infantile atopic eczema?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Loss or thinning of the lateral third of the eyebrows is known as the Hertoghe sign.


Conditions Associated with Hertoghe's sign:

  • Atopic dermatitis
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Trichitillomania
  • Leprosy (especially lepromatous)
  • Alopecia areata
  • Ulerythema ophryogenes


Other ocular manifestations of Atopic dermatitis:

  • Dennie Morgan fold: A fold of skin under the lower eyelids.
  • Conjunctival irritation
  • Keratoconus: Due to a degenerative change in the cornea, which is forced outwards by the intraocular pressure, giving rise to marked visual disturbances.
  • Atopic cataract: Due to a combination of rubbing and the use of topical steroids.


Auspitz sign (Option A): Pinpoint bleeding seen in psoriasis.


Koebner phenomenon (Option C): Development of lesions at sites of trauma.


Nikolsky sign (Option D): Epidermal shearing seen in pemphigus vulgaris and related disorders.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 41.22, 41.23, 149.21
  2. https://www.jpeds.com/article/S0022-3476(20)30842-8/pdf
question: A 16-year-old boy with long-standing atopic eczema is noted to have thinning and loss of the lateral one-third of the eyebrows on examination. Loss of the lateral eyebrows in this patient represents which of the following signs?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen associated with atopic eczema, with >90% of patients showing skin colonisation.


Infections in Atopic Eczema:

  • High infection risk due to defective innate immunity
  • Staphylococcus aureus (most common)
    • Present in >90% of AE patients
    • Higher density on the lesional skin
    • Frequently produces superantigens
    • Superantigen levels correlate with disease severity

[[figure-1]]

  • Viral:
    • Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1, HSV-2)
      → Eczema herpeticum (Kaposi varicelliform eruption)
    • Human papillomavirus → warts
    • Molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus)
    • Vaccinia
    • Coxsackie A
  • Fungal: Dermatophyte and yeast infections


Role of staphylococcal superantigens:

  • More commonly expressed in AE than in non-AE skin
  • Enhance Th2 allergen responses
  • Act as potent adjuvants
  • Cause:
    • ↑ Allergen presentation (↑ HLA-II, ICAM-1)
    • ↓ Regulatory T-cell function
    • Steroid resistance
  • Contribute to severe and persistent disease.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 41.13, 41.14.
question: A 6-year-old child presents with pruritic, erythematous eczematous lesions as shown. Some lesions show crusting, suggesting secondary infection. Which of the following organisms most commonly colonises lesions in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Berloque dermatitis is a photocontact dermatitis caused by certain perfumed products that contain psoralens (e.g., bergamot oil). This condition is caused by phototoxic reactions from perfumes, leading to linear or streaky hyperpigmentation in sun-exposed areas.

  • Psoralens in perfume + ultraviolet (sunlight) exposure induce a phototoxic reaction.
  • This leads to localised hyperpigmentation along the lines in which the perfume was applied.
  • Clinical features:
    • Striking linear or streaky brown pigmentation over sun‑exposed areas where perfume was applied.
    • May show erythema and blistering in the acute phase


Melasma (Option A): Usually symmetrical facial pigmentation, not linear streaks.


Lichen planus pigmentosus (Option B): Presents as diffuse or blotchy pigmentation, often in flexural areas.


Fixed drug eruption (Option D): Round or oval, well-demarcated lesions, often recur at the same site after drug exposure, not related to perfume or sunlight.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 88.29, 88.30.
question: A 16-year-old boy presents with findings as shown in the image. He reports applying perfume daily in that area and notices the pigmentation worsens after sun exposure. There is no history of itching or inflammation. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The case describes a specific inflammatory reaction localised around a pre-existing mole, which fits the classic presentation of Meyerson's phenomenon.


Halo Dermatitis (Meyerson Phenomenon):

  • Eczematous ring around a melanocytic naevus.
  • Synonyms: Meyerson naevus, Meyerson phenomenon.
  • Epidemiology: Mainly young adults; rare.
  • Clinical: Pruritic, papulosquamous halo; resolves spontaneously; naevus unchanged.
  • Histology: Benign naevus + dermal lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltrate, acanthosis, spongiosis, parakeratosis.
  • Associations: Seborrhoeic keratoses, other raised lesions; rare progression to Sutton halo naevus.


Sutton halo nevus (Option A): Characterised by a depigmented halo, not eczematous inflammation.

[[figure-1]]


Allergic contact dermatitis (Option C): Usually related to external allergen exposure and not localised strictly to a mole.


Erythema multiforme (Option D): Presents as target lesions, often on extremities, and is not centred on a naevus.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 39.27, 39.28.
question: A 22-year-old woman presents with a pruritic, erythematous, eczematous ring surrounding a mole on her forearm. The lesion appeared spontaneously, and the mole itself has not changed in size, colour, or shape. There is no history of trauma or systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Managed by skin hydration and avoiding irritants
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation describes Asteatotic Eczema (also known as Eczema Craquelé).


Asteatotic eczema occurs in very dry skin, especially in the elderly, and management focuses on restoring hydration with emollients, humidifying the environment, and avoiding irritants.


Asteatotic eczema: (Eczéma craquelé, Winter eczema)

[[figure-1]]

  • Eczema in very dry skin, mainly in the elderly. (Option A)
  • Sites: Legs, arms, hands.
  • Appearance:
    • Dry, scaly skin with “crazy-paving” pattern, cracked fingertips (“parchment pulps”).
    • Erythematous raised borders; fissures may be hemorrhagic.
  • Triggers:
    • Low humidity, cold (Option B), ageing, trauma, soaps, and cleansers.
    • Exacerbated in winter.
  • Complications: Secondary infection; can progress to nummular dermatitis. (Option D)
  • Management:
    • Hydration: Emollients, urea-based creams, humidified environment.
    • Topical therapy: Mild corticosteroids or pimecrolimus if needed.
    • Avoid irritants, hot baths, and wool.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 39.10, 39.11.

options.text: Affects young adults and resolves spontaneously
Managed by skin hydration and avoiding irritants

question: A patient presents with intensely itchy, dry, and scaly skin on her lower legs as shown and the backs of her hands. On examination, the skin shows a characteristic “crazy-paving” pattern with fissures and slightly raised erythematous borders. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The condition described is Erythroderma (also known as exfoliative dermatitis), defined by generalised erythema and scaling affecting more than 90% of the body surface area.

Erythroderma causes hypoalbuminemia, not hyperalbuminemia.


Complications and Co-morbidities of Erythroderma:

  • Hemodynamic disturbances:
    • Increased skin blood flow → high-output cardiac failure (especially in the elderly).
    • Heat loss → hypothermia.
  • Metabolic disturbances:
    • Fluid loss through skin → proportional to basal metabolic rate.
    • Hypoalbuminemia from protein loss in exfoliated scales.
    • Peripheral oedema secondary to hypoalbuminemia.
  • Increased γ-globulins.
  • CD4+ T-lymphocytopenia (without HIV).

Treatment of Erythroderma

  • Supportive care:
    • Fluid & electrolyte balance
    • Temperature regulation (prevent hypothermia)
    • High-protein nutrition
  • Skin care:
    • Emollients, Wet wraps
    • Avoid irritants
  • Medical therapy:
    • Topical corticosteroids; Systemic steroids (selected cases)
  • Complication prevention:
    • Monitor for secondary infections (sepsis, pneumonia)

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 39.34.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema) is characterised by intensely pruritic, deep-seated “tapioca-like” vesicles, most commonly affecting the palms, fingers, and sides of the hands.

  • Therefore, itching is a prominent feature, not absent.


Pompholyx (Dyshidrotic Eczema):

  • Definition: Recurrent vesicular eczema of the palms ± soles.
  • Key lesion: Deep-seated, tense vesicles (“tapioca pudding” appearance). (Option A)
  • Sites: Palms, sides of fingers; soles (podopompholyx). (Option B)

[[figure-1]]

  • Symptoms: Intense itching, burning; later desquamation and fissures.
  • Triggers/Associations: Atopy, stress (Option D), sweating, nickel/contact allergy, fungal infection (dermatophytide).
  • Pathogenesis: Not related to sweat glands (the term dyshidrotic is a misnomer).
  • Course: Recurrent, often episodic.
  • Complications: Secondary bacterial infection, painful fissures.
  • Management (brief): Avoid triggers, emollients, potent topical corticosteroids; short courses of systemic therapy or PUVA in severe cases.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 39.11-39.18
question: Which of the following statements regarding the finding is not correct?

explanationHtml:
Answer: A) Atopic dermatitis

Explanation:

The image shows lichenified, scaly, and hyperpigmented plaques over the popliteal fossae (behind the knees).

The history of itching and involvement of flexural areas (neck, popliteal, and cubital fossae) is highly characteristic of Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema).

Atopic Dermatitis:

  • Common in children, associated with atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema).
  • Hallmark features:
    • Chronic pruritus and inflammation.
    • Flexural involvement in children and adults.
    • Lichenification due to chronic scratching.
    • Infants: More likely to have cheeks, trunk, and extensor limb involvement.
  • Exacerbating factors: Irritants, allergens, weather changes, infections.

Diagnosis:

  • Clinical diagnosis based on chronic relapsing course and typical distribution.
  • No specific lab test required.
  • Elevated IgE levels may be seen but are not diagnostic.

Management:

  1. Moisturisation (Emollients) – cornerstone of therapy.
  2. Topical corticosteroids – for flare-ups (mild to moderate strength).
  3. Antihistamines – for pruritus relief.
  4. Avoid triggers (harsh soaps, allergens, irritants).
  5. Severe cases: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (Tacrolimus), systemic immunosuppressants if needed.

Dermatitis Herpetiformis (Option B) is incorrect because it presents as intensely itchy, grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks), not flexural areas. Strongly associated with coeliac disease.

Pemphigus Vegetans (Option C) is incorrect because a rare variant of pemphigus, characterised by moist, verrucous plaques in intertriginous areas (axilla, groin), unlike the dry, lichenified lesions seen here.

Psoriasis (Option D) is incorrect because psoriasis in children often affects extensor surfaces (knees, elbows), not flexures. Lesions are well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales, unlike the ill-defined, lichenified plaques seen here.



Reference:
  1. Atopic dermatitis (eczema): Pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis - UpToDate
  2. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology. 9th ed: 41.2
question: A child presented with itchy plaques over the neck, the bilateral popliteal and cubital fossa. What could be the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Answer: B) Lichen nitidus

Explanation:

  • The image shows multiple, tiny, discrete, dome-shaped, shiny papules on the forearm.
  • The history of symptomless lesions on the forearm and shaft of the penis is characteristic of Lichen Nitidus.

Lichen Nitidus:

  • Rare chronic inflammatory disorder.
  • Presents as multiple, asymptomatic, tiny, uniform, skin-coloured to hypopigmented, dome-shaped papules.
  • Common sites:
    • Forearms
    • Dorsum of hands
    • Shaft of the penis (pathognomonic location)
    • Trunk
  • Aetiology: Unknown, but associated with atopic dermatitis, Crohn’s disease, and lichen planus.
  • Diagnosis: Clinical; biopsy if needed shows lymphocytic infiltrate in a "claw clutching a ball" pattern.

Management:

  • No treatment required if asymptomatic.
  • If symptomatic, topical steroids, emollients, or calcineurin inhibitors can be used.
  • Usually self-limiting but may persist for months to years.

Incorrect Options:

Lichen Planus (Option A) is incorrect because Lichen planus presents as violaceous, flat-topped, pruritic papules with Wickham’s striae. Usually involves flexor wrists, oral mucosa, and lower back but not commonly the shaft of the penis.

Scrofuloderma (Option C) is incorrect because it is a tuberculous skin infection that presents as cold abscesses and sinus tracts overlying lymph nodes or bones, not as discrete, shiny papules.

Scabies (Option D) is incorrect because scabies causes intensely pruritic papules, vesicles, and burrows, commonly found in finger webs, axillae, and genital areas. The absence of itching and burrows makes scabies unlikely.



Reference:

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31869173/

• The patch test is a commonly used diagnostic tool for identifying the causative allergens in allergic contact dermatitis.
  • It involves applying small amounts of suspected allergens onto adhesive patches, which are then placed on the patient's skin (usually on the back). The patches remain in place for 48-72 hours.
  • The presence of erythema, vesiculation, or induration at the site of patch application indicates a positive reaction, suggesting sensitivity to the tested allergen.

Food, environmental, drug allergies

Incorrect Options:

Radioimmunosorbent (RAST) (Option B): The RAST test is a blood test used to measure specific IgE antibodies in the serum. Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T-cells, and it does not involve IgE antibodies. Therefore, the RAST test is not appropriate for diagnosing allergic contact dermatitis.

Eosin-5′-maleimide binding test (Option C): The eosin-5′-maleimide binding test is a laboratory test used to assess the presence of hereditary spherocytosis, a congenital hemolytic anemia. It is not relevant for diagnosing allergic contact dermatitis.

Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test (Option D): It is primarily used in the diagnosis of chronic granulomatous disease, an inherited disorder characterized by defective neutrophil function. This test is not related to the diagnosis of allergic contact dermatitis.

question: A sexually active man presents with multiple painful vesicular lesions over the penile region. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above clinical scenario with imaging findings points towards the diagnosis of granuloma annulare.
  • Granuloma annulare classically presents as a chronic, asymptomatic, annular lesion with smooth, non-scaly borders. The absence of pruritus or pain and the long-standing nature of the lesion strongly support this diagnosis.
  • This condition is frequently associated with diabetes mellitus, especially in adults, and commonly involves the extremities. The annular configuration results from dermal papules arranged in a ring, while the epidermis remains normal, explaining the lack of scaling.

The key distinguishing feature is a non-scaly, skin-colored to erythematous annular plaque, which helps differentiate granuloma annulare from other annular dermatoses. The benign and often self-limiting course is characteristic.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

  • Tinea corporis (Option A): Tinea corporis presents with annular lesions having an active scaly border and central clearing. Pruritus is usually present, and scaling is a key feature, which is absent in this case.

[[figure-2]]

  • Annular lichen planus (Option C): Annular lichen planus shows violaceous, polygonal papules arranged in a ring, often associated with itching. Wickham striae may be seen on close examination, unlike the smooth surface here.

[[figure-3]]

  • Annular psoriasis (Option D): Annular psoriasis is characterized by well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales. Lesions are usually symptomatic and show scaling, which helps differentiate them from granuloma annulare.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:
  • Andrews Diseases of the Skin, Edition 13th, Page 16.
question: A woman with diabetes mellitus presents with an asymptomatic skin lesion present for the past year. On examination, there is a non-scaly, annular lesion as shown in the image. There is no itching or pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above clinical scenario points towards the diagnosis of atopic dermatitis.
  • Atopic dermatitis is characterized by chronic pruritus, xerosis, and eczematous lesions, often beginning in childhood. The presence of intense itching, especially at night, is a hallmark feature and leads to excoriations and lichenification over time.
  • A strong family history of atopy, such as asthma or allergic rhinitis, significantly supports the diagnosis. In children, the distribution commonly involves the extensor surfaces, with progression to flexural involvement in older children and adolescents.

[[figure-1]]

The key clinical features include dry skin, recurrent eczematous flares, and pruritus, forming part of the atopic triad (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis). The age of onset and chronic relapsing course are typical.

[[figure-2]]

Incorrect Options:

  • Scabies (Option A): Scabies presents with severe nocturnal pruritus but is characterized by burrows, papules, and nodules, commonly involving finger webs, wrists, and genitalia. A family history of atopy is not a feature.
  • Cradle cap (Option B): Seborrheic dermatitis in infants presents with greasy, yellowish scales on the scalp and face. It is usually non-pruritic or mildly itchy and does not cause generalized xerosis.
  • Contact dermatitis (Option C): Contact dermatitis occurs due to exposure to an external allergen or irritant and is localized to the area of contact. It lacksa chronic relapsing course and a family history of atopy.


Reference:

Andrews Diseases of the Skin, Edition 13th, Page 5.

Explanation:

In Indians and other darker-skinned populations, the most common site of melanoma is the acral areas (hands and feet).

Acral lentiginous melanoma predominates because it is unrelated to UV exposure and occurs on palms, soles, and nail beds, which explains its higher frequency in darker skin.

Incorrect Options:

Trunk (Option A): Most common in fair-skinned Western populations, not in Indians.

Genitals (Option C): Rare site; not a common location for melanoma.

Face (Option D): UV-related melanomas can occur here, but acral sites are far more common in Indians.

Explanation:

  • This patient with a known history of psoriasis and an image showing healing pustular lesions most likely has impetigo herpetifromis.
  • Impetigo herpetiformis is a rare and severe form of pustular psoriasis that typically occurs during pregnancy or postpartum.
  • It is characterized by widespread pustular eruptions with systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and electrolyte imbalances.
  • A possible fetal complication in this patient with impetigo herpetiformis during the third trimester could be low birth weight, as the condition is associated with significant maternal and fetal risks, including intrauterine growth restriction and placental insufficiency.
  • Treatment includes
    • Admit the patient
    • IV Steroids/ Cyclosporine
    • Strict monitoring with appropriate IV fluids
    • Avoiding aggravating factors

No complications (Option A): Impetigo herpetiformis usually presents with fetal complications such as low birth weight and increased perinatal mortality.


Renal Agenesis (Option B):

  • It refers to the absence of one or both kidneys at birth, often leading to severe complications such as oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, and an increased risk of urinary tract infections.
  • It is usually genetically inherited (Potter’s sequence) but could also be a complication of intake of ACE inhibitors or reno-toxic drugs during pregnancy.

Neonatal hypoglycemia (Option D):

  • It is characterized by low blood sugar levels in newborns, often due to inadequate glycogen stores or impaired glucose production.
  • It can lead to seizures, neurologic impairment, and long-term developmental issues if left untreated.
  • It is usually caused due to gestational diabetes mellitus.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Section 35

Explanation:

  • Pityriasis rosea characteristically shows collarette scaling, which is a fine rim of scale attached at the periphery of the lesion and free toward the center.
  • This follows the initial herald patch and is seen in the subsequent oval lesions distributed along cleavage lines on the trunk.

[[figure-1]]

Pityriasis rosea:

  • Acute, self-limiting papulosquamous eruption (young adults)
  • Likely viral (HHV-6/7)
  • Herald patch → 1-2 weeks later generalised eruption
  • Oval scaly lesions with collarette scale
  • Christmas-tree pattern on trunk
  • Resolves in 3-6 weeks; symptomatic treatment only

Wickham striae (Option A): Fine white reticular lines seen on papules of lichen planus, not in pityriasis rosea.

[[figure-2]]

Auspitz sign (Option B): Pinpoint bleeding after scale removal, characteristic of psoriasis.

[[figure-3]]

Nail pitting (Option D): Small depressions on the nail plate seen in psoriasis and alopecia areata, not pityriasis rosea.

[[figure-4]]

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Mucosal involvement is rare in lichen nitidus (much less common than in lichen planus).


Lichen nitidus:

  • Epidemiology: Rare; mainly children/young adults (Option A); familial cases uncommon.
  • Lesions: Pinpoint to pinhead-sized (Option D), flat or dome-shaped, shiny papules; usually asymptomatic.
  • Distribution: Forearms, penis, abdomen, chest, buttocks; palms/soles may show hyperkeratosis or purpuric papules.
  • Variants: Linear, perforating, actinic; nail pitting or ridging possible; mucosal involvement rare.
  • Associations: Crohn disease (Option B), trisomy 21, congenital megacolon, Niemann-Pick type B.
  • Differentials: Lichen planus, lichen scrofulosorum, keratosis pilaris; biopsy confirms diagnosis.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 37.10
question: Which of the following is not a feature of lichen nitidus?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lichen nitidus is characterized by pinpoint, shiny papules and histologically shows a well-circumscribed lymphohistiocytic infiltrate beneath the epidermis, with rete ridges encircling the infiltrate (ball-in-claw appearance).
  • Histology:

[[figure-1]]

  • Characteristic papule: Well-circumscribed lymphohistiocytic infiltrate immediately below the epidermis; sometimes Langhans giant cells or plasma cells.
  • The overlying epidermis may show flattening and basal cell liquefaction.
  • Rete ridges encircle infiltrate.
  • Palmar lesions: deep parakeratotic plug (distinguishes from LP).
  • Perifollicular granulomas may mimic lichen scrofulosorum.
  • Sharp infiltration with surrounding epidermal ridges produces a “ball‑in‑claw” (ball‑in‑clutch) configuration.


Saw-tooth rete ridges with band-like infiltrate (Option A): This is characteristic of lichen planus, not lichen nitidus. Lichen planus shows a dense, continuous band-like lymphocytic infiltrate with saw-tooth acanthosis.


Caseating granulomas (Option C): Seen in tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections, not in lichen nitidus.


Follicular plugging (Option D): A typical feature of discoid lupus erythematosus, not lichen nitidus.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 37.10
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK551709/

question: A patient with multiple shiny, pinhead-sized papules, as shown in the image, undergoes a skin biopsy. What is the characteristic histological feature?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows violaceous (purplish), flat-topped, polygonal papules and plaques with fine white streaks on the surface, pointing towards lichen planus.
  • Interferon is not used in the standard management of cutaneous LP.


Lichen Planus Management:

  • Treatment guided by site, severity, and symptoms.
  • Cutaneous LP: reduce itching, speed resolution; may clear spontaneously.
  • High-risk sites (nail, scalp, genital, oesophageal, ocular): early treatment to prevent scarring.
  • First line:
    • Limited: potent topical corticosteroids (clobetasol 0.05%) (Option A)
    • Widespread: oral prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day (Option B)
  • Second line:
    • Acitretin 30 mg/day
    • PUVA or narrow-band UVB ± retinoids
    • Oral steroids + phototherapy
  • Third line:
    • Methotrexate (generalised LP) (Option C)
    • Other agents are not routinely recommended


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 37.16
question: A 48-year-old patient presents with findings as shown in the image. There is no mucosal involvement. The dermatologist plans to start treatment according to standard guidelines. Which of the following medications is not routinely used in the management of the most likely condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:


Nail Involvement in Lichen Planus (LP):

  • Occurs in up to 10% of LP cases. Fingernails>toenails.
  • Pattern & Progression:
    • Initial involvement of 2-3 fingernails, progressing to other digits.
    • Often seen in severe generalised LP, skin lesions may be absent near the nail.
  • Common nail changes:

[[figure-1]]

  • Longitudinal lines and linear depressions (thinning of the nail plate). (Statement 1)
  • Elevated ridges on nails.
  • Pterygium unguis (adhesion of dorsal nail fold to nail bed → partial destruction). (Statement 2)

[[figure-2]]

  • Rare complete nail shedding, usually preceded by LP at the nail base.
  • Partial regrowth is possible; permanent loss mainly in the great toenails.
  • Other Nail Bed Changes:
    • Longitudinal melanonychia, hyperpigmentation.
    • Subungual hyperkeratosis or onycholysis. (Statement 3)
    • Changes may mimic yellow nail syndrome.
    • Ulcerative LP of the soles can lead to permanent toenail destruction.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 37.12
question:
A patient with lichen planus presents with nail involvement. Which of the following findings are typical nail changes seen in Lichen Planus?

  1. Longitudinal ridging and linear depressions
  2. Pterygium formation (adhesion of the nail fold to the nail bed)
  3. Longitudinal melanonychia and onycholysis
  4. Clubbing of all fingernails
  5. Yellow, thickened nails with slow growth

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Psoriasis vulgaris:

  • Auspitz sign is seen in Psoriasis vulgaris.
    • Auspitz sign refers to the appearance of pinpoint bleeding spots when scales are removed from the skin lesions. It is a characteristic finding in Psoriasis vulgaris
    • This phenomenon is due to the abnormal growth and turnover of skin cells in psoriasis, leading to an increased vascularity and fragility of the skin.

Incorrect Options:

Option B, C & D are incorrect

  • Pustular psoriasis, pemphigus, and bullous pemphigoid are different skin conditions with distinct clinical features and mechanisms. Auspitz sign is not typically observed in these conditions.

correctAnswer: C. Checkerboard pattern with alternate areas of hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical presentation of scaly, red follicular plaques with areas of sparing near the axilla also called islands of sparing, the diagnosis is Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris (PRP).
  • Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris is characterized by a histopathological finding known as the checkerboard pattern, which consists of alternate areas of hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum) and parakeratosis (retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum).
  • Treatment includes topical agents, the same as that used in psoriasis including topical corticosteroids and emollients.

[[figure-1]]

Hyperkeratosis

[[figure-2]]

Parakeratosis


Acanthosis and spongiosis (Option A) are histopathological findings commonly seen in conditions such as psoriasis and eczema, but they are not characteristic of PRP.

Elongation of rete ridges (Option B) is a histological feature typically associated with psoriasis rather than PRP.

Lichenoid infiltrate with Civatte bodies (Option D) is a histopathological finding seen in lichen planus, which is a different dermatological disorder unrelated to PRP.

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 36

  • Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, thereby disrupting folate metabolism and interfering with DNA synthesis, leading to decreased proliferation of skin cells.
  • It also decreases the production of inflammatory cytokines eg. TNF-alpha and ILs, thereby reducing inflammation in the joints.

[[figure-1]]

  • It is currently the most recommended single agent for managing both psoriatic arthritis and skin lesions.
  • Dosage: 7.5-25 mg/week via oral/subcutaneous route.
  • Common side effects of methotrexate include:
    • Gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
    • Hepatotoxicity necessitates regular monitoring of liver function tests.
    • Bone marrow suppression leads to anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia and requires monitoring through regular blood counts.
    • Long-term use: hepatotoxicity, pulmonary toxicity (including interstitial pneumonitis), and renal toxicity.

Oral corticosteroids (Option B):

  • They are used at times to control acute flares of psoriatic arthritis.
  • However, they are not preferred as a single agent for managing both skin disease and arthritis, considering their potential to cause instability of cutaneous psoriasis due to reactivation after stopping.

Cyclosporine (Option C):

  • It acts by inhibiting IL-2, a key cytokine involved in immune response modulation.
  • Often termed a "crisis drug," it is utilized to manage severe acute episodes of various immune-mediated disorders.
  • Due to its potential for adverse effects like hyperlipidemia and hypertension, cyclosporin is not used long-term for psoriasis with psoriatic arthritis.

Leflunomide (Option D) may be effective for arthritis, but it does not adequately address the skin disease aspect.

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Section 26

question: Which of the following medications would not be used for treating a patient with moderate to severe psoriasis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • UVB therapy, particularly narrow-band UVB, is the recommended first-line and most commonly used therapy for most patients with moderate to severe psoriasis.
  • Narrow-band UVB has a high effectiveness and tolerability compared to other UV spectra, such as broadband UVB and UVA (PUVA therapy).
  • The mechanism of NB-UVB is cutaneous immunomodulation by
    • Increasing vitamin D
    • Induction of apoptosis of T cells
    • Reduction of epidermal hyperproliferation

Wavelengths of various UV spectra are given in the image below.

[[figure-1]]

UVA (Option A):

  • While UVA therapy (PUVA) has been used in the treatment of psoriasis, narrow-band UVB is preferred now.
  • PUVA therapy is associated with concerns regarding long-term side effects, including an increased risk of skin cancer.

UVC (Option C) exposure can be harmful to the skin and is not indicated for therapeutic purposes in psoriasis management.


UVD (Option D): "UVD light" is not a recognized term in the context of ultraviolet radiation. The standard terminology for ultraviolet radiation includes UVA, UVB, and UVC.

question: A 20 year old male patient comes to your dermatology OPD complaining of non-itchy lesions on the back of his elbows, shins, and knees. On examination, you find scaly lesions that exhibit the Auspitz sign, as shown in the image below. Which of the following processes is responsible for this patient's lesions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis of the image is pustular psoriasis (a type of unstable psoriasis) characterized by the presence of multiple sterile, non-infectious pus-filled blisters on erythematous skin, forming a characteristic 'Lakes of pus' appearance.

  • This condition can occur due to the abrupt cessation of systemic corticosteroids, leading to rebound flare-ups of psoriasis.
  • Since it affects the whole body, it is also called Acute generalized pustular psoriasis or Von Zumbusch psoriasis.
  • Aggravating factors:
    • Withdrawal of steroids
    • Coal tar
    • Pregnancy
    • Stress

Classification of Unstable Psoriasis:

Erythrodermic psoriasis (Option B) is another variant of unstable psoriasis that presents with erythema and scales covering more than 90% of the body surface.

Psoriasis Vulgaris (Option C) also known as plaque psoriasis, is the most common form of psoriasis. It is characterized by raised, red patches of skin covered with silvery scales.

Rupioid psoriasis (Option D) is a severe form of psoriasis characterized by the development of large, thick, adherent, and waxy scales resembling limpet shells or oyster shells.

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Section 34
question: A patient with a fever of 103°C and pain all over his body comes to your clinic. He recently went to a high-profile medical spa, where he was treated with oral medication for his chronic psoriasis. He was elated with the complete resolution during treatment but woke up with a fever, malaise, and pain three days ago. Skin examination is given in the image below. What is your diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presentation is classical of guttate psoriasis, often seen in children and adolescents.
  • It typically occurs 1–3 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or upper respiratory tract infection.
  • The appropriate treatment includes:
    • Eradication of the triggering streptococcal infection using penicillin (or amoxicillin).
    • Topical therapies (like corticosteroids or emollients) may help skin symptoms but do not address the underlying cause.
    • Reassurance may be needed, but antibiotic therapy is essential in acute, post-streptococcal guttate psoriasis.

Clinical Features of Guttate Psoriasis

Age group

Common in children and young adults

Trigger

Post-streptococcal pharyngitis (esp. Streptococcus pyogenes)

Lesion morphology

Multiple, small (<1 cm), erythematous, scaly plaques ("drop-like")

Distribution

Trunk, proximal limbs

Course

May resolve spontaneously or evolve into chronic plaque psoriasis

Topical corticosteroids (Option A):

  • Incorrect as first-line monotherapy in acute guttate psoriasis post-infection.
  • Can be used adjunctively, but antibiotic therapy is essential to treat the underlying streptococcal cause.

Reassurance (Option B):

  • Incorrect as sole treatment. Although guttate psoriasis may be self-limited, reassurance alone is not adequate when a recent streptococcal infection is present.

Doxycycline (Option D):

  • Incorrect because it is not the first-line agent against streptococcal infection in children.
  • Penicillin or amoxicillin is preferred.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Section 16
question: A 12y/o girl comes to the OPD with her parents complaining of multiple small, erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk with a characteristic raindrop appearance 10 days after a streptococcal throat infection. An image of her lesions is given below. What is the appropriate treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pencil-in-cup deformity

  • The "pencil-in-cup" deformity is a characteristic radiographic finding in patients with psoriatic arthritis.
  • Psoriatic arthritis occurs mainly in HLA B-27 positive patients and is seronegative.
  • It results from erosive changes at the joint margins, leading to bony proliferation and destruction, causing the proximal bone to taper into the distal bone.
  • It is often seen in the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints and is indicative of severe joint damage in psoriatic arthritis.
  • The tapered phalanx is also called the ‘mouse ear deformity.’

[[figure-1]]

Ivory phalanx (Option A) occurs due to new bone formation in psoriatic arthritis; the phalanx may appear whiter due to sclerosis.

[[figure-2]]

Boutonniere deformity (Option C) is commonly seen in rheumatoid arthritis, and involves flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint with hyperextension of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint.

[[figure-3]]

Fraying (Option D): Irregularity and thinning of the cortex of long bones, particularly at the metaphyses, resulting in a fuzzy or frayed appearance seen in vitamin C deficiency/ Scurvy.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Psoriatic Arthritis, (Gladman, Rosan, and Chandran) Chapter 6
question: An orthopaedic surgeon shows you an X-ray of HLA B-27 positive female with seronegative arthritis and psoriatic skin lesions, and you observe the following deformity. What is the eponym given to this deformity?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In psoriatic arthritis (PsA), inflammation can affect the joints closest to the fingernails and toenails (DIP), resulting in swelling and inflammation. This inflammation can lead to the characteristic appearance of swollen and sausage-like fingers or toes. The image below is that of sausage toes.

[[figure-1]]


The most common type of arthritis associated with psoriasis is asymmetric oligoarthritis (50%).

Distal interphalangeal arthritis (Option B) affects 5% of patients with psoriatic arthritis. This subtype specifically targets DIP joints predominantly, often with nail involvement.


Spinal column or axial involvement (Option C) affects 40% of patients.

Arthritis mutilans (Option D) is a severe form of PsA characterized by destructive joint changes, but it is relatively rare with a prevalence of 5%.



Reference:

Psoriatic Arthritis, (Gladman, Rosan, and Chandran) Chapter 2
question: A 24 year old male patient presents to you with joint pain in his fingers. He is currently a fashion student at NIFT and shares that other students bully him for having a few ‘sausage fingers.’ There is no predominant DIP joint involvement noted. What type of arthritis would you most suspect in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Oil drop sign refers to small, yellowish-orange discolorations seen beneath the nail plate, resembling drops of oil, and is highly specific for nail psoriasis.
  • It is the most specific sign of psoriasis with a specificity of ~98%
  • It occurs due to nail bed parakeratosis and psoriasiform hyperplasia
  • It occurs just before onycholysis

[[figure-1]]

Important findings in nail psoriasis are (Mnemonic: POLISH)

  • Pits
  • Onycholysis
  • Leukonychia
  • Salmon patch
  • Subungual Hyperkeratosis

Pitting of the nails (Option A): While pitting is the most common finding in nail psoriasis, it is not as specific as the oil drop sign. Other diseases where pitting of nails is seen are : Alopecia Areata , Onychomycosis , Darier's disease , Hailey-Hailey disease etc.

[[figure-2]]

Onycholysis (Option C) or separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, can occur in various nail conditions including trauma and onychomycosis (fungal nail infection), not just nail psoriasis.

[[figure-3]]

Subungual hyperkeratosis (Option D) refers to the thickening of the skin under the nail, which can also be seen in other nail disorders including eczema and hyperkeratosis, and is not specific to nail psoriasis.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Section 14

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pityriasis amiantacea is a scalp condition characterized by the formation of thick, asbestos-like scales that adhere to the hair shafts.

[[figure-1]]

  • While the lesions are typically not itchy, they could cause hair loss if left untreated.
  • Can be secondary to an underlying inflammatory skin disorder such as:
    • Psoriasis

    • Scalp infections

Seborrheic dermatitis (Option B) is a scalp condition with red, itchy, greasy scales that affects areas rich in sebaceous glands, like the scalp, face, and upper trunk it can be caused by the fungi Malassezia furfur.

Pityriasis rosea (Option C) presents with oval-shaped, pink, or red patches on the trunk, arms, or legs. It doesn't involve the scalp, and the lesions don't cross the hairline. It is also caused by Malassezia furfur.

question: An immigrant laborer comes to your Sunday volunteer clinic complaining of thickening of the skin on his scalp. The lesions are not itchy, cross the hairline, and are not associated with loss of hair as shown in the given image. What is your diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Grattage sign, Berkeley’s Membrane, Auspitz Sign
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

While examining a patient’s psoriatic lesions during scraping with a blunt object such as the blunt edge of a glass slide, the following signs are seen.


Grattage Sign/ Candle sign: Accentuation of scaling when the lesion is scraped with the blunt edge of a glass slide.

↓

Berkeley’s membrane: Formation of a thin membrane on further scraping.

↓

Auspitz sign: Formation of pin-point bleeding on scraping the Berkeley’s membrane.

[[figure-1]]

Another sign, "Sign of the last Hauchen" or "Sign of the Last Scale," refers to the presence of small, raised, erythematous papules that become visible after the last scale is removed from a psoriatic plaque, i.e., before the formation of Berkeley’s membrane.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Section 9

Pseudo-Koebnerization: Seen in warts (verruca vulgaris) due to autoinoculation from trauma or seeding of microorgaisms
