question: As a pathologist in a prestigious private clinic, a physician contacts you for urgent feedback on a skin biopsy from a prominent politician. Suspecting psoriasis, what histopathological findings in the stratum corneum would you communicate to the attending physician?

correctAnswer: C. Spontaneous remission is commonly seen
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Plaque psoriasis is a chronic, indolent disease that rarely undergoes spontaneous remission; lesions tend to persist or slowly progress over time.


Psoriasis:

  • Epidemiology: Common immune-mediated dermatosis affecting ~2% of the global population.
  • Clinical features:
    • Erythematous, sharply demarcated papules and plaques
    • Covered with silvery micaceous scales
    • Lesions may be pruritic
  • Koebner phenomenon: Lesions develop at sites of trauma.
  • Exacerbating factors: Infections, stress, and drugs (lithium, β-blockers, antimalarials).

[[figure-1]]

Plaque-type psoriasis (most common):

  • Stable, slowly enlarging plaques
  • Chronic, indolent course (Option B); spontaneous remission is rare
  • Common sites: Elbows, knees (Option D), scalp, gluteal cleft
  • Typically symmetrical (Option A)


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 377
question: Which of the following is an incorrect feature of plaque psoriasis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lithium is one of the most strongly implicated drugs in triggering new-onset psoriasis or exacerbating existing disease.
  • Causation has been supported by rechallenge studies, making it a well-established trigger


Drug-induced/ exacerbated psoriasis:

  • Lithium salts
  • Synthetic antimalarials
  • Interferon-α
  • TNF-α inhibitors (Paradoxical psoriasis)
  • β-blockers
  • NSAIDs
  • ACE inhibitors


Corticosteroids:

  • May improve psoriasis initially
  • Risks: tachyphylaxis and rebound flares
  • Withdrawal: must be gradual; abrupt cessation can precipitate severe or unstable psoriasis


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 35.4
question: Which of the following drugs is implicated in the onset or exacerbation of psoriasis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Rupioid psoriasis shows marked hyperkeratosis with oyster-shell-like crusts, often associated with psoriatic arthritis and nail disease, and usually needs systemic/biologic therapy.

[[figure-1]]


Rupioid psoriasis:

  • A rare morphologic variant of plaque psoriasis with thick, dark, layered crusts resembling limpet or oyster shells.
  • Represents a hyperkeratotic (thick scale) presentation of psoriasis.
  • Histopathology shows psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with marked hyperkeratosis/parakeratosis, and the characteristic adherent rupioid crust may contain serosanguineous exudate.
  • Tends to affect a larger body surface area and is associated more often with psoriatic arthritis and nail disease than thin-plaque psoriasis.
  • Triggers Associated with RP Flares:
    • Certain medications (beta-blockers, lithium, antimalarials)
    • HIV infection & systemic stressors or immune dysregulation
  • Treatment:
    • Lesions are difficult to treat topically due to thickness and poor agent penetration.
    • Successful management requires good patient compliance and regular follow-up.
    • Reported systemic therapy options include:
      • Methotrexate - immunosuppressant
      • Cyclosporine - rapid immunomodulation
      • Intralesional corticosteroids - local inflammation control
      • TNF-α inhibitors (e.g., adalimumab)
    • Ustekinumab (anti-IL-12/23 p40) → effective, convenient dosing, approved for pediatric psoriasis.


Crusted scabies (Option A): Seen in immunocompromised patients with massive mite infestation, severe pruritus, and crusting, but lacks classic psoriatic plaques and nail pitting.


Pityriasis rubra pilaris (Option C): Presents with follicular hyperkeratosis, orange-red scaling, and islands of sparing rather than layered rupioid crusts.


Hypertrophic lichen planus (Option D): Produces thick verrucous plaques, usually intensely pruritic, without nail pitting or psoriatic arthritis features.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11576555/
question: A teenager with long-standing psoriasis presents with thick, dark, layered crusts resembling oyster shells over erythematous plaques, as shown in the image, with nail pitting and joint pain. Poor response to topical therapy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Flexural (inverse) psoriasis occurs in moist skin folds, leading to thin, smooth, erythematous plaques with little or no scale, unlike classic plaque psoriasis.


Flexural (inverse) psoriasis:

  • Psoriasis affecting body folds; when limited to folds, termed inverse psoriasis.
  • Common sites: Inguinal creases, axillae, submammary folds, gluteal cleft, and umbilicus.
  • Epidemiology: More common in older adults (Option B); associated with obesity.
  • Association: Often occurs with plaque psoriasis elsewhere; less commonly confined only to flexures.
  • Pathogenesis: May occur de novo or via the Koebner phenomenon over infective or seborrhoeic intertrigo.
  • Poor response to antibacterial/antifungal therapy (Option D)
  • Lesion features:
    • Thin plaques (Option A), minimal or absent scaling
    • Well-defined erythema with a smooth, glazed surface
    • Fissuring is common at the depth of folds (especially the gluteal cleft)
    • The surrounding skin may show maceration due to hyperhidrosis
  • Complications: Secondary infection and medicament dermatitis may blur lesion margins.
  • Special presentation: Psoriatic napkin eruption can be the first sign of psoriasis in infants.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 35.11
question: Which statement about flexural (inverse) psoriasis is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Goeckerman regimen is a classic, highly effective therapy specifically indicated for moderate to severe psoriasis, leveraging the synergistic effects of UVB phototherapy and coal tar to reduce epidermal hyperproliferation and inflammation.


Goeckerman regimen for moderate-severe psoriasis

  • Combination of UVB phototherapy + crude coal tar
  • Efficacy: Very high response rates; many patients achieve PASI75 or better
  • Mechanism: Coal tar has antiproliferative and anti-inflammatory effects and reduces scale, improving UVB penetration and overall efficacy.
  • Protocol: UVB exposure → topical coal tar (often with occlusion); daily monitoring
  • Safety: Minimal systemic toxicity; common effects are irritation/phototoxicity
  • Role: Effective, cost-efficient alternative or adjunct to systemic/biologic therapy


Atopic dermatitis (Option A): A chronic relapsing eczematous disorder treated primarily with emollients, topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and sometimes phototherapy


Vitiligo (Option B): A depigmenting disorder managed with narrowband UVB, topical steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, or grafting procedures


Lichen planus (Option D): An inflammatory papulosquamous disorder treated with topical/systemic corticosteroids and sometimes phototherapy



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3735239/
question: The Goeckerman regimen (UVB phototherapy combined with crude coal tar) is primarily used in the treatment of which condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Systemic corticosteroids are generally avoided in chronic psoriasis because they can cause rebound flares or exacerbation of the disease upon withdrawal.


Chronic plaque psoriasis:

  • Topical Therapies (First-line for limited disease):
    • Corticosteroids (Option A): Mild (face, flexures), potent/very potent (thick plaques, scalp, palms/soles). Can combine with vitamin D analogues.
    • Vitamin D analogues: Calcipotriol, tacalcitol; effective alone or with corticosteroids; monitor calcium if high doses.
    • Dithranol: Highly effective, mainly for plaque psoriasis; short-contact outpatient regimens
    • Coal tar: Safe, effective, often combined with UVB (Goeckerman regimen).
    • Topical retinoids (tazarotene): Effective for thick, recalcitrant plaques; combine with corticosteroids to reduce irritation.
    • Topical calcineurin inhibitors: Tacrolimus, pimecrolimus; useful for face, flexures, genitalia.
  • Phototherapy:
    • Narrow-band UVB (NB-UVB): First-line for moderate-to-severe psoriasis; 3x/week; safe and effective.
    • PUVA (psoralen + UVA): High efficacy, risk of skin cancer; mainly for severe cases; limited lifetime treatments (≤200).
  • Systemic therapy: (Moderate to severe disease)
    • Methotrexate (Option B): Immunosuppressive; effective for psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis; monitor liver (consider PIIINP or elastography).
    • Ciclosporin: Rapid induction; limited by renal toxicity, hypertension; rarely used for long-term maintenance.
    • Acitretin: Non-immunosuppressive retinoid; teratogenic; useful for pustular/erythrodermic psoriasis or in combination with phototherapy.
    • Fumaric acid esters (FAE): Immunomodulatory; used in some countries (e.g., Germany).
    • Biologics: TNF-α inhibitors (Option C), IL-17, IL-23 inhibitors; for moderate-to-severe or refractory disease.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 35.22 - 35.31
question: A 45-year-old patient presents with chronic plaque psoriasis affecting 15% of the body surface area. The dermatologist is planning long-term management. Which of the following treatments is not used in the management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pregnancy is contraindicated for 3 years after cessation of acitretin because acitretin can be converted to etretinate, a highly lipophilic, long-lasting teratogenic retinoid that persists in adipose tissue for years.


Acitretin:

  • Retinoid (metabolite of etretinate); non-immunosuppressive
  • MOA: ↓ keratinocyte proliferation; ↓ Th17, ↑ T-reg cells
  • Use: Chronic plaque, pustular, erythrodermic psoriasis; useful when immunosuppression is contraindicated
  • Dose: Escalate to 25-50 mg/day (response assessed at ~4 months); low dose has poor efficacy
  • Efficacy: Dose-dependent; modest as monotherapy
  • Adverse effects: Cheilitis, xerosis, alopecia; hyperlipidaemia, rare hepatitis
  • Pregnancy: Highly teratogenic → avoid pregnancy for 3 years after stopping
  • Best results: Combination with PUVA / NB-UVB (synergistic)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 35.28
question: A 32-year-old woman with chronic plaque psoriasis is planned to start acitretin due to poor response to topical therapy. She asks about future pregnancy planning. For how long is pregnancy contraindicated after stopping acitretin?

correctAnswer: C. Blockade of IL-17 receptor A
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Brodalumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds to IL-17 receptor A (IL-17RA) on target cells.

  • By blocking this receptor, it prevents signaling from multiple IL-17 family cytokines (including IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-17A/F, and IL-25), which play a central role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis by driving keratinocyte activation, epidermal hyperproliferation, and cutaneous inflammation.
  • Because brodalumab targets the receptor rather than a single cytokine, it produces a broad inhibition of the IL-17 pathway, leading to rapid and marked clinical improvement in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.


Inhibition of TNF-α activity (Option A): Mechanism of TNF inhibitors like etanercept and adalimumab.


Blockade of IL-12/23 (p40) pathway (Option B): Mechanism of ustekinumab.


Inhibition of IL-23 (p19) pathway (Option D): Mechanism of guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 35.46
question: A 40-year-old man with severe chronic plaque psoriasis refractory to methotrexate and phototherapy is started on brodalumab. What is the mechanism of action of brodalumab?

explanationHtml:
Grattage Test is used to diagnose psoriasis, a condition characterized by scaly plaques on the skin. In this test, gentle scraping of the lesion leads to removal of scales in a characteristic manner, revealing a shiny, thin membrane (Auspitz sign) and pinpoint bleeding.

Other Options:

Nikolsky Test (Option A): Used to diagnose conditions like pemphigus vulgaris and toxic epidermal necrolysis. It involves applying lateral pressure to the skin, which causes the epidermis to slough off.

Asboe-Hansen Test (Option B): Also known as the bulla spread sign, it helps diagnose pemphigus vulgaris by checking if pressure on a blister spreads it to adjacent skin.


Tzanck Smear( Option D): Used to diagnose herpes infections by detecting multinucleated giant cells in skin lesions.



Reference:

Neena Khanna, Textbook of Dermatology, 7th Edition, Page no: 124
question: Which of the following tests is most appropriate for diagnosing this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of a white plaque with intense pruritus in the genital region of an elderly woman, along with histopathology showing loss of rete ridges, abundant collagen, and thinning of the epithelium, is characteristic of Lichen Sclerosus.

  • It commonly affects elderly women, presenting with intense itching and white atrophic plaques in the genital region.
  • Histopathology shows loss of rete ridges, thinned epithelium, and a broad zone of dense collagen (sclerosis) in the upper dermis—classic findings described in LS.

Incorrect Options:

Lichen planus (Option A) shows saw-toothing of rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, and violaceous lesions, not white sclerotic plaques.

Candidiasis (Option C) presents with erythema, curdy white discharge, and pseudohyphae on microscopy; not sclerosis or epithelial thinning.

Vulvar leukoplakia (Option D) is a descriptive term for white patches; does not show the classic sclerosis with loss of rete ridges seen in LS.



Reference:

Lichen Sclerosus—Presentation, Diagnosis and Management - PMC
question: A 73-year-old female presents with severe pruritus and a white plaque in the genital region. Histopathological examination reveals loss of rete ridges, abundant collagen, and thinning of the epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above clinical features and HPE findings in this patient suggest the diagnosis of Pemphigus vulgaris (PV), which most commonly has antibodies against Desmoglein 3.

Pemphigus vulgaris:

  • PV is the most common chronic autoimmune blistering disease caused by antibodies against desmosomal adhesion proteins.
  • They are characterized by the presence of flaccid blisters filled with clear fluid present on normal skin or an erythematous base.
  • The blisters rupture producing painful erosion.
  • Mucosal involvement is a very important and one of the distinguishing features of PV.
  • Histopathology:
    • Intraepidermal cleavage with acantholysis (detached keratinocytes) primarily localized to the suprabasal region
    • Separation of basal keratinocytes along the basement membrane zone, resulting in an appearance that resembles a "row of tombstones"

The target antigens for PV are most commonly Desmoglein 3 and sometimes Desmoglein 1. The image below shows the common target antigen in Intraepidermal Immunobullous Disorders.

[[figure-1]]

Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option B)

  • Associated with celiac disease and characterized by intensely pruritic, grouped vesicles typically on extensor surfaces.
  • Shows granular IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, not intercellular IgG.

Bullous pemphigoid (Option C)

  • Causes subepidermal blisters and does not commonly present with oral ulcers.
  • Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermal-epidermal junction.

Linear IgA disease (Option D)

  • Characterized by linear IgA deposits at the basement membrane zone.
  • Typically causes subepidermal blistering, not intraepidermal, and oral ulcers are less common.


Reference:
  • Pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis of pemphigus - UpToDate
  • Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th ed, page no.50.1-50.4
question: A 45-year-old male comes with recurrent blisters and oral ulcers for 3 years. The histology is as shown. What is the diagnosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Bullous Pemphigoid:

  • BP is a common subepidermal immunobullous disorder mainly affecting elder people. Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal target proteins BP230(BPAG1) and BP180(BPAG2) which finally leads to bullae formation.
  • It is characterised by a prodromal non bullous stage with pruritis which is followed by a bullous stage. The later has intense pruritus with tense blisters and vesicles.
  • These blisters show a negative Nikolsky sign but a positive Bulla spread sign.
  • The rupture of blisters leads to yellow or hemorrhagic crust formation, which later heal without any scar.
  • Oral lesions can occur sometimes.
  • HPE shows a subepidermal split with inflammatory infiltrate, immunofluorescence shows a linear binding of immunoglobulin (IgG and C3) at the dermo-epidermal junction.
  • Topical and systemic steroids are the mainstay of treatment.

[[figure-1]]

Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option A)

  • DH is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy associated with deposition of IgA in the dermal papillae, not linear IgG or C3 at the basement membrane.
  • DH typically shows granular IgA deposition in immunofluorescence and not the linear patterns seen here.

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option B)

  • PV is characterized by intraepidermal blistering and acantholysis (loss of cell-to-cell adhesion between keratinocytes).
  • Immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG (not linear staining at the basement membrane zone).
  • The presence of subepidermal blisters here excludes PV.

Pemphigus foliaceous (Option C)

  • PF is another type of pemphigus that features intraepidermal blistering and acantholysis but lacks subepidermal blistering.
  • Immunofluorescence in PF typically shows intercellular IgG, not the linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane observed in this case.


Reference:
  • Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no. 50.10-50.17, 50.7, 50.53, 3.33-3.34, 50.3 , 50.7-50.8

Explanation:

The Auspitz sign, characterized by the development of pinpoint bleeding in the areas where the lesion is scraped with a glass slide, is commonly associated with psoriasis vulgaris

[[figure-1]]

While examining a patient’s psoriatic lesions during scraping with a blunt object such as the blunt edge of a glass slide, the following signs are seen:

Grattage Sign/ Cadle sign: Accentuation of scaling when the lesion is scraped with the blunt edge of a glass slide

↓

Berkeley’s membrane: Formation of a thin membrane on further scraping

↓

Auspitz sign: Formation of pin-point bleeding on scraping the Berkeley’s membrane in patients with psoriasis.

[[figure-2]]

Another sign, "Sign of the last Hautchen" or "Sign of the Last Scale," refers to the presence of small, raised, erythematous papules that become visible after the last scale is removed from a psoriatic plaque, i.e., before the formation of Berkeley’s membrane.

  • The above image depicts Pustular psoriasis, which is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered with silvery-white scales.
  • Isomorphic phenomenon: The isomorphic phenomenon is the correct finding associated with the image. In individuals with psoriasis, new psoriatic lesions can appear at sites of skin trauma, such as scratches, cuts, or other forms of injury.

Koebner's Phenomenon

  • Psoriatic lesions develop along the lines of trauma.
  • Isomorphic response
  • All or none phenomenon

[[figure-1]]

Category

Examples

Category 1 (True koebnerization)

Psoriasis, Lichen planus, Vitiligo

Category 2 (Pseudo koebnerization)

Warts, Molluscum

Category 3 (Occasional koebnerization)

Darier disease, Erythema multiforme

Category 4 (Dubious association with trauma)

Pemphigus vulgaris, Lupus erythematosus

Incorrect Options:

Meyerson phenomenon (Option B): The Meyerson phenomenon refers to the development of psoriatic lesions after light tapping or pressure on a psoriatic plaque.

Gottron's papule (Option C): Gottron's papule appear as flat-topped, violaceous eruptions overlying the joints of the fingers and elbows.

Nikolsky's sign (Option D): Nikolsky's sign refers to the ability to induce blistering or detachment of the superficial skin layers by lateral pressure or rubbing (positive Nikolsky's sign). This sign is not relevant to plaque psoriasis.

question: Identify the finding associated with the condition shown in the image below:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In the case of a patient with chronic plaque psoriasis involving more than 50% of the skin, oral steroids are generally not recommended as a long-term treatment option due to the risk of severe rebound flares and pustular psoriasis upon withdrawal.

Reasons Why Oral Steroids Are Avoided

  1. Rebound Phenomenon
    • Sudden discontinuation can cause severe exacerbation of psoriasis, leading to erythroderma or pustular psoriasis (potentially life-threatening).
  2. Risk of Pustular Psoriasis
    • Systemic steroids can trigger generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP), characterized by widespread sterile pustules, fever, and systemic illness.
  3. Limited Long-Term Efficacy
    • While steroids provide short-term relief, they do not alter disease progression and often require higher doses over time, leading to dependency.

Preferred Long-Term Treatment Options

  • Biologics (e.g., IL-17, IL-23, TNF inhibitors)
  • Methotrexate, cyclosporine, or apremilast (for systemic therapy) (Option A and C)
  • Phototherapy (NB-UVB- Narrowband ultraviolet B) (Option B)
  • Topical therapies (vitamin D analogs, corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors) for localized disease


Reference:

Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology and Sexually Transmitted Diseases, Fifth Edition – Neena Khanna Pg 55-60
question: Which of the following would you not advise for a patient who is already diagnosed with chronic plaque psoriasis and has over 50% of their skin affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The combination of lacy lesions in the mouth and genital area, along with nail changes, strongly suggests lichen planus.

Lichen Planus:

Clinical Features

  • 6 P’s → Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar Papules & Plaques
  • Mucosal involvement → Wickham striae (reticular white lines)
  • Koebner phenomenon: This phenomenon refers to the development of lesions at sites of trauma to uninvolved skin
  • Histology → Sawtooth infiltrate of lymphocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction
  • Association → Hepatitis C

Treatment

Topical (First-line for mild cases)

  • Corticosteroids (Clobetasol, Betamethasone)
  • Calcineurin Inhibitors (Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus) – for oral/genital LP
  • Antihistamines – for pruritus relief
  • Local anesthetics (Lidocaine gel) – for painful oral lesions

Intralesional (For hypertrophic LP)

  • Intralesional corticosteroids (Triamcinolone injections)

Systemic (For severe, widespread, or refractory cases)

  • Oral corticosteroids (Prednisolone)
  • Dapsone
  • Hydroxychloroquine (HCQS)
  • Azathioprine, Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF)

Phototherapy (For generalized LP, especially in children)

  • Narrow-band UVB (NBUVB) phototherapy

Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris (Option A):

  • Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris (PRP) typically presents with scaly, red follicular plaques and islands of sparing near the axilla called islands of sparing
  • It histopathologically exhibits a distinctive checkerboard pattern marked by alternating areas of hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis.

[[figure-1]]

Psoriasis (Option B):

  • Features silvery scales on erythematous plaques, commonly on extensor surfaces.
  • Nail changes include pitting, oil-drop sign, and onycholysis, but not pterygium formation.
  • Oral lesions are rare.

Pityriasis rosea (Option C):

  • Starts with a herald patch followed by oval, scaly lesions in a "Christmas tree" pattern.
  • No oral/genital lesions or nail involvement.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Section 9

  • The drug of choice used to treat Psoriatic arthritis is methotrexate
  • Methotrexate belongs to a class of drugs called disease-modifying anti-rheumatoid drugs (DMARDs). It reduces inflammation and alleviates the symptoms of arthritis.

Treatment:

Medical:

  • NSAIDs
  • Immuno suppressive agents- methotrexate and TNF inhibitors
  • Local glucocorticoid injections
  • Physiotherapy

Surgery:

  • For unstable joints.
  • Arthrodesis procedure.

Incorrect Options:

PUVA (Option A):

  • PUVA does not work effectively in reducing the arthritic condition.
  • Methotrexate is preferred over PUVA for the treatment of Psoriatic arthritis.

Steroids (Option B): Oral and topical corticosteroids can be used for short-term therapy but are not recommended for long-term use due to their many adverse effects.

Infliximab (Option D): Infliximab is preferred in moderate to severe cases of Psoriatic arthritis but is not the first drug of choice due to it being more expensive.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped papules. It frequently affects the flexor surfaces of the wrists, forearms, lower back, and mucosal surfaces.

Lichen Planus:

Clinical Features

  • 6 P’s → Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar Papules & Plaques
  • Mucosal involvement → Wickham striae (reticular white lines)
  • Koebner phenomenon: This phenomenon refers to the development of lesions at sites of trauma to uninvolved skin
  • Histology → Sawtooth infiltrate of lymphocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction
  • Association → Hepatitis C

Treatment

Topical (First-line for mild cases)

  • Corticosteroids (Clobetasol, Betamethasone)
  • Calcineurin Inhibitors (Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus) – for oral/genital LP
  • Antihistamines – for pruritus relief
  • Local anesthetics (Lidocaine gel) – for painful oral lesions

Intralesional (For hypertrophic LP)

  • Intralesional corticosteroids (Triamcinolone injections)

Systemic (For severe, widespread, or refractory cases)

  • Oral corticosteroids (Prednisolone)
  • Dapsone
  • Hydroxychloroquine (HCQS)
  • Azathioprine, Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF)

Phototherapy (For generalized LP, especially in children)

  • Narrow-band UVB (NBUVB) phototherapy

Incorrect Options:

Psoriasis (Option A):

  • Characterized by silvery-white scales on erythematous plaques, mostly on extensor surfaces.
  • Nail pitting and onycholysis are common.

Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis) (Option B):

  • Poorly demarcated, erythematous, weeping lesions with crusting and lichenification.
  • Typically affects flexural surfaces (e.g., antecubital, popliteal fossae).

Tinea Corporis (Option D):

  • Annular (ring-shaped) lesions with a central clearing and scaly border.
  • Fungal infection, confirmed by KOH preparation showing hyphae.

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Section 9
question: A 45-year-old male presents to the dermatology clinic with an itchy skin rash. Physical examination reveals flat-topped, polygonal, purplish papules with fine white lines on the surface. The lesions are primarily located on the inner wrists and forearms, as well as on the lower back. The patient reports that he has been experiencing oral discomfort and noticed white, lacy patches on the inside of his cheeks. There is no family history of similar conditions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Each type of scale is associated with a characteristic dermatological condition:

  • Collarette scales – Pityriasis rosea (1-b)
    • Fine, trailing collarette of scales surrounding oval, salmon-coloured plaques seen in pityriasis rosea.
    • Most prominent around the edges of herald patches.
  • Silvery scales – Psoriasis (2-c)
    • Thick, silvery-white scales over erythematous plaques, classically seen in psoriasis.
    • Removal may lead to Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding).
  • Mica-like scales – Pityriasis lichenoides (3-d)
    • Fine, adherent mica-like scales covering small, erythematous papules.
    • Seen in pityriasis lichenoides, a chronic inflammatory skin condition.
  • Branny scales – Pityriasis versicolour (4-a)
    • Fine, powdery, branny scales seen in pityriasis versicolour, a superficial fungal infection caused by Malassezia.
    • Often reveals yellow-green fluorescence under Wood’s lamp.

Scales in Dermatology:

Scales are abnormal accumulations of keratinized cells on the skin surface and are characteristic of various dermatological conditions. They can vary in thickness, texture, and pattern based on the underlying disease.

Type of Scale

Description

Associated Disease

Key Clinical Features

Collarette scales

Thin, peripheral scales arranged in a collarette pattern, often seen in annular lesions.

Pityriasis rosea

Herald patch followed by a "Christmas tree" distribution of lesions.

[[figure-1]]

Silvery scales

Thick, silvery-white, adherent scales that bleed upon removal (Auspitz sign).

Psoriasis

Well-demarcated erythematous plaques on extensor surfaces, scalp, and lower back.

[[figure-2]]

Mica-like scales

Fine, thin, shiny scales resembling mica.

Pityriasis lichenoides

Chronic or recurrent papulosquamous eruptions.

[[figure-3]]

Branny scales

Fine, powdery, furfuraceous (bran-like) scaling.

Pityriasis versicolor

Hypo- or hyperpigmented macules caused by Malassezia, commonly on the trunk.

[[figure-4]]

question: A 26-year-old male presented with erythematous plaques covered with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces of both arms. Punctate pitting was noted on examining the nails. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The case scenario with a 2-week history of mildly itchy, oval, pink plaques with a collarette of scale and a "Christmas tree" pattern on the trunk is suggestive of Pityriasis rosea.

  • It begins with a single, oval, pink plaque with a collarette of scale (herald patch), followed by smaller, scaly oval lesions along skin cleavage lines forming a "Christmas tree" pattern on the trunk.
  • It mainly affects young adults (15–35 years), causes mild itching, and lacks systemic symptoms.
  • The condition is self-limiting and usually resolves within weeks to months without treatment.

Psoriasis (Option B): Usually presents with thick, well-defined red plaques with silvery scales, often on extensor surfaces, and can have nail and joint involvement, unlike the milder, self-limiting rash of pityriasis rosea.

Tinea corporis (Option C): Characterized by annular, scaly plaques with central clearing, typically associated with fungal infection, and does not follow a Christmas tree pattern.

Secondary syphilis (Option D): Presents with a generalized rash including palms and soles, often with systemic symptoms and positive serology, not a solitary herald patch or Christmas tree pattern typical of pityriasis rosea.



Reference:
  • From PYQ
  • Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 35, Image 35.6

question: Diagnose the condition using the histological image provided.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Diarrhea is not a distinguishing feature of psoriatic arthritis; it is more commonly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)-related arthritis.

CASPAR Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA):

To classify a patient as having PsA, they must have inflammatory joint disease (affecting joints, spine, or entheses) plus ≥3 of the following 5 criteria:

  1. Evidence of Psoriasis (Any one of the following):
    • Current psoriasis
    • Personal history of psoriasis
    • Family history of psoriasis
  2. Psoriatic nail dystrophy (Option C ruled out)
  3. Negative Rheumatoid Factor (RF)
  4. Dactylitis (Current or past history) (Option B ruled out)
  5. Radiological evidence of juxta-articular new bone formation

Enthesitis (Option C): which is inflammation of tendons and ligaments, though not part of CASPAR criteria for PsA, is commonly found in PsA.

Note: Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative polyarthritis with erosive arthritis.

question: Which of the following does not distinguish Psoriasis from other arthropathies?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Guttate psoriasis:

  • A type of psoriasis known as guttate psoriasis is characterized by skin lesions in the shape of small drops. These sores are generally under 1 centimeter in measurement and show up on the storage compartment, appendages, and scalp.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Erythrodermic: Erythrodermic psoriasis is characterized by widespread skin scaling, inflammation, and redness, frequently accompanied by pain and itchiness.

Option C - Pustular: A form of psoriasis known as pustular psoriasis results in pus-filled blisters on plaques, which are scaly, flaky patches of skin.

Option D - Inverse: Converse psoriasis. Presents with smooth, red, and inflamed patches of skin that may be itchy, painful, and susceptible to infection are its hallmarks.

question: Identify the type of psoriasis in the given picture.

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Psoriatic Arthritis

Explanation:

The patient’s red, scaly skin lesions and painful, swollen distal finger joints are indicative of Psoriatic Arthritis

  • Swelling of the DIP joint plus skin psoriasis signs.
  • Pain, swelling, and tenderness in affected joints.
  • Nail changes like pitting or ridges support diagnosis.
  • Often involves the fingers with "sausage digits" and can cause deformities over time.

Pseudo gout (Option B) is a type of arthritis caused by the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the joints. It can also lead to joint inflammation and pain, but it typically doesn't have an association with skin lesions like psoriasis. The symptoms described in the case, including the skin lesions, make psoriatic arthritis a more likely diagnosis.

Osteoarthritis (Option C) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by the breakdown of cartilage in the joints. It is more common in older individuals and typically presents with joint pain and stiffness. However, it does not usually involve the red and scaly skin lesions mentioned in the case.

Reactive arthritis (Option D), also known as Reiter's syndrome, is an inflammatory condition that typically develops as a response to an infection in another part of the body. It often involves joint inflammation, especially in the lower limbs, and can be associated with skin lesions. However, the case description of red and scaly patches on the skin, along with finger joint DIP involvement, is more suggestive of psoriatic arthritis.

question: A 50-year-old patient presents with following skin lesions characterized by red and scaly patches. The patient also complains of a painful and swollen finger joint. On examination, the finger joint appears inflamed and tender to touch. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Severe nocturnal pruritus with interdigital involvement is highly characteristic of scabies.
  • Vesicular lesions over palms and soles are commonly seen, especially in severe infestations and children.
  • Scabies is caused by infestation with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei.

Scabies:

  • Scabies is a contagious parasitic skin infestation transmitted through prolonged skin-to-skin contact.
  • Intense itching results from a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to mites and their products.
  • Nocturnal worsening of pruritus is a classic diagnostic clue.

Clinical features:

  • Erythematous papules, vesicles, nodules, and burrows.
  • Common sites include finger web spaces, wrists, axillae, genitalia, waistline, palms, and soles.
  • Burrows appear as thin, serpiginous gray-white lines.
  • Secondary excoriations and eczematization may occur due to scratching.

Diagnosis and treatment:

  • Diagnosis is mainly clinical.
  • Skin scraping may reveal mites, eggs, or scybala.
  • First-line treatment is topical permethrin.
  • Household and close contacts should be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfestation.

[[figure-1]]

Scabies burrow

Atopic dermatitis (Option A) typically causes chronic flexural eczema with xerosis. Interdigital burrows and nocturnal itching are not characteristic.

[[figure-2]]

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (Option B) causes diffuse erythema with skin tenderness and desquamation. Usually occurs in infants with systemic symptoms.

[[figure-3]]

Psoriasis (Option D) presents with sharply demarcated scaly plaques over extensor surfaces. Vesicular interdigital lesions with nocturnal pruritus are uncommon.

[[figure-4]]

question: Which of the following correctly matches the pemphigoid disease with its primary target antigen?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical sign demonstrated is Nikolsky sign, in which gentle lateral pressure on apparently normal skin causes the superficial epidermis to shear away from the underlying layers. A positive Nikolsky sign indicates loss of cohesion between epidermal keratinocytes (acantholysis).

  • Pemphigus vulgaris is the classic disease associated with a positive Nikolsky sign.
  • It is an autoimmune intraepidermal blistering disorder caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3, and often desmoglein 1, which are components of desmosomes responsible for keratinocyte adhesion.
  • This results in the formation of flaccid bullae that rupture easily, leaving painful erosions. Oral mucosal involvement is common and often precedes the appearance of skin lesions.
  • Histopathology shows suprabasal acantholysis with a characteristic "row of tombstones" appearance, while direct immunofluorescence demonstrates intercellular IgG and C3 deposition in a fishnet or chicken-wire pattern.

Psoriasis (Option A) is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory skin disorder characterized by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales, commonly affecting the extensor surfaces and scalp. Nikolsky sign is negative because the epidermal cell adhesion remains intact, and blister formation is not a feature of the disease.

Bullous pemphigoid (Option C) is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disorder caused by antibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230 within the basement membrane. It presents with tense bullae that are less likely to rupture, and Nikolsky sign is typically negative because the epidermis remains structurally intact.

Erythema nodosum (Option D) is a septal panniculitis presenting with tender erythematous nodules, usually over the anterior aspects of the legs. It is commonly associated with infections, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and certain medications. It is not a blistering disorder and is not associated with a positive Nikolsky sign.



Reference:

Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 10th Edition, Pages 4.17, 26.28, 50.4, 50.10

correctAnswer: C. Fish net-like or honeycomb pattern in the epidermis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The characteristic immunofluorescence pattern seen in pemphigus is indeed a fish net-like or honeycomb pattern in the epidermis (Option C).

Pemphigus: It is an autoimmune blistering disease affecting the skin and mucous membranes. The two main types are pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus.

Autoantibodies: In pemphigus, autoantibodies target desmoglein proteins

Immunofluorescence pattern: When a skin biopsy from a pemphigus patient is subjected to direct immunofluorescence (DIF), it reveals a distinctive pattern:

  • The autoantibodies (usually IgG) bind to the cell surface of keratinocytes throughout the epidermis.
  • This creates a pattern that resembles a fish net or honeycomb when viewed under a fluorescence microscope.

[[figure-1]]

Linear band (Option A) is typically seen in bullous pemphigoid, not pemphigus.

Granular deposits (Option B) are more characteristic of lupus erythematosus. Pemphigus erythematosus (a/w SLE) has both intercellular IgG Deposits in epidermis and granular IgG Deposits in Dermo Epidermal Junction

Nuclear staining (Option D) is more commonly seen in SLE, Scleroderma.

Explanation:

The above clinical scenario and immunofluorescence showing granular + linear IgG and C3 deposits in the dermo-epidermal junction suggest bullous systemic lupus erythematosus(BSLE). The main antibodies in this case are directed against collagen VII.

Bullous systemic lupus erythematosus(BSLE):

  • BSLE is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease that occurs in patients with SLE. The target antigen here is type VII collagen.
  • On top of the SLE symptoms, patients with BSLE present with acute-onset vesicles and blisters, with a predilection for sun‐exposed areas like neck, upper trunk, and proximal extremities.
  • HPE would show subepidermal splitting with immunofluorescence showing granular + linear IgG and C3 deposits in the dermo-epidermal like other related bullous disorders.


Anti-CCP antibodies (Option B) are seen in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.


Ro La antibodies (Option C) are classical of SCLE. But this patient’s current condition is BSLE which mainly has antibodies against collagen VII causing the above skin lesions.


Anti-transglutaminase antibodies (Option D) are seen in dermatitis herpetiformis, which presents with pruritic vesicles and erosions involving the extensor surfaces. Patient will have a history of chronic diarrhoea

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The girl with the above lesions associated with chronic diarrhea most likely has dermatitis herpetiformis, which shows granular IgA deposition in the papillary dermis.

Dermatitis herpetiformis(DH):

  • Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is linked to celiac disease and gluten sensitivity.

  • Gluten triggers chronic diarrhea and malabsorption; gluten-free diet resolves symptoms.

  • Associated with HLA-DQ2/DQ8 and IgA autoantibodies against transglutaminase.

  • Presents as pruritic, grouped papules/vesicles on extensor surfaces; excoriations common.

  • Histology: subepidermal blisters with neutrophils at dermal papillae tips.

  • Immunofluorescence: granular/fibrillar IgA in papillary dermis (“picket fence” pattern).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

HPE with papillary abscess and infiltrate

Immunofluorescence with IgA in papillary dermis

[[figure-3]]

Management includes a gluten‐free diet that improves diarrhoea as well as skin lesions. Dapsone is given for targeting pruritis and skin lesions.

question: A 14-year-old girl presents with complaints of pruritic papules on the elbows and knees as shown below. She also gives a history of chronic diarrhea which stopped after certain dietary restrictions. What is the immunofluorescence pattern seen on the biopsy of these lesions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Among the given options, the only condition that shows antibodies on the blister floor during salt-split skin immunofluorescence is epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

Salt split technique(SST):

  • To a skin biopsy specimen, 1 molar of NaCl is added and left to sit for some time.
  • This splits the basement membrane at the level of lamina lucida, leaving 2 different targets for antibodies to be visualized on immunofluorescence microscopy.
  • This is used to differentiate and diagnose blistering disorders.
  • Immunofluorescence at the blister roof is seen in
  1. Mucous membrane pemphigoid
  2. Bullous pemphigoid
  3. Linear IgA disease

[[figure-1]]

  • Whereas immunofluorescence on the blister floor is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This clinical scenario and the presence of antibodies against collagen VII suggest a diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa aquisita (EBA).

Epidermolysis bullosa aquisita:

It is a subepidermal blistering disease defined by autoantibodies against type VII collagen. It has two forms:

  1. Mechanobullous variant: Skin fragility, erosions, blisters, crusts, and scars on trauma‐prone areas such as the hands, knuckles, elbows, knees, and toes

[[figure-1]]

  1. Inflammatory variant: present similar to bullous pemphigoid.

HPE examination will show subepidermal blistering with immunofluorescence showing linear deposition of IgG at the dermal-epidermal junction. Patients have antibodies against collagen VII.

Linear IgA disease (Option A): Characterized by linear deposition of IgA at the basement membrane zone. Common in children (chronic bullous disease of childhood) but also occurs in adults. Not associated with anti-collagen VII antibodies. Typically shows “string of pearls” arrangement of blisters.

Bullous pemphigoid (Option B): Involves IgG antibodies against BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230, not collagen VII. Causes tense subepidermal blisters, usually in the elderly. Common on trunk and extremities, less often in groin. Not associated with anti-collagen VII antibodies.

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option D): Caused by IgG antibodies against desmoglein 3 (and sometimes desmoglein 1). Leads to intraepidermal (suprabasal) blisters, which are fragile and rupture easily. Mucosal involvement is common. Not associated with collagen VII.

question: A 45-year-old patient presents with erosions, blisters, and crusts in the groin and thigh region as shown below. His blood tests reveal he has antibodies against collagen VII. What is the most probable diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Oral steroids are first-line management
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The incorrect statement about linear IgA disease is that oral steroids are the first line of management, as the first line of management includes topical steroids or Dapsone.

Linear IgA disease:

  • It is an autoimmune blistering disorder with bimodal distribution in pediatric (peak<5 years) and adult patients (60 years).
  • It is the most common autoimmune blistering disease in infants and children.
  • The antigens BP 180 and LAD are targetted by IgA antibodies.
  • Blisters and vesicles are formed in an annular pattern with blistering along the edges forming a string‐of‐pearls/crown of jewels appearance.
  • It commonly affects the trunk and limbs but starts as perioral and perennial lesions in children. Mucosal involvement may be seen.

[[figure-1]]

  • HPE will show subepidermal blistering.
  • Immunofluorescence will reveal a linear deposit of predominant or exclusive IgA at the dermo-epidermal junction.
  • Dapsone is the first line of treatment.
  • Oral steroids are used only in some cases to suppress blister formation.


Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no. 50.33-50.37

question: Which of the following statements regarding Linear IgA disease is incorrect?

correctAnswer: B. C3 deposit along the dermo-epidermal junction
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most common microscopy finding in many cases of pemphigoid gestationis is the C3 deposit along the dermo-epidermal junction.

[[figure-1]]

Pemphigoid gestationis:

  • It is a bullous disorder presenting mainly in late pregnancy or the immediate postpartum period.
  • Circulating complement‐fixing IgG antibodies bind to a BP‐180 in hemidesmosomes of the dermo-epidermal junction causing blisters. These blisters are formed in the subepidermal.
  • It presents as intense pruritis with erythematous papules and plaques starting on the abdomen which later become tense blisters.
  • The lesions show remission and exacerbation with most of them usually resolving after pregnancy
  • Immunofluorescence is the gold standard test showing linear C3 deposition along the dermo-epidermal junction in 100% of cases and additional IgG deposition in 30% of cases.
  • Management is done using topical and systemic steroids.

Intraepithelial IgG Deposition (Option A) is a feature of pemphigus vulgaris and related disorders.

Ig A deposit along the dermo-epidermal junction (Option D) is a feature of linear IgA disease.



Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no.115.13-15.14, 50.35

question: A 32 week pregnant lady presents with itching and erythematous plaques involving the periumbilical region. She is diagnosed with pemphigoid gestationis. What is the most common microscopy finding in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above clinical features and immunofluorescence pattern suggests a diagnosis of cicatricial pemphigoid.

Cicatricial pemphigoid:

  • It is a variant of pemphigoid disease in which skin lesions heal with scarring.
  • They are positive for BP180.
  • They present with blisters, erosions, haemorrhagic crusts and atrophic scars on the head, neck and upper trunk.
  • The mucous membrane may rarely be involved, but it is not predominant.

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option B): PV never heals with scarring

Mucous membrane pemphigoid (Option A) predominantly affects the mucous membranes like the oral cavity, conjunctivae, nasopharynx, skin, anogenital region, larynx and oesophagus.

Brunsting Perry pemphigoid (Option D) is a variant with lesions predominantly in head and neck with no mucosal involvement. The presence of involvement extending to upper trunk favors cicatricial pemphigoid instead.



Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no. 50.10, 50.49
question: A patient presented with blisters confined to the head, neck and upper trunk. Some of these blisters show scarring in the neck. The examination of the oral cavity is normal without any lesions. Electron microscopy shows a linear IgG deposition at the dermo-epidermal junction. What is the most probable diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. The lesions commonly heal without scarring
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

[[figure-1]]

The image showing tense bullae and the biopsy findings suggest a diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid (BP), which commonly heals without scarring.

Bullous Pemphigoid:

  • BP is a common subepidermal immunobullous disorder mainly affecting elder people.
  • Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal target proteins BP230 (BPAG1) and BP180 (BPAG2) which finally leads to bullae formation.
  • It is characterised by a prodromal non bullous stage with pruritis which is followed by a bullous stage.
  • The later has intense pruritus with tense blisters and vesicles.
  • These blisters show a negative Nikolsky sign but a positive Bulla spread sign.
  • The rupture of blisters leads to yellow or hemorrhagic crust formation, which later heal without any scar.
  • Oral lesions can occur sometimes.
  • HPE shows a subepidermal split with inflammatory infiltrate, immunofluorescence shows a linear binding of immunoglobulin (IgG and C3) at the dermo-epidermal junction.
  • Topical and systemic steroids are the mainstay of treatment.

[[figure-2]]

question: A 60-year-old male patient presented with ruptured vesicles and bullae on the skin and erosions in the mucous membrane. HPE of the skin biopsy revealed a row of tombstones. Antibodies against which of the following structures are most commonly present in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

[[figure-1]]

  • Hemidesmosomes(HD), anchoring filaments, and anchoring fibrils are present at the dermal-epidermal junction and maintain the integrity of the skin.
  • The lower end of the epidermis is made up of basal keratinocytes.
  • Hemidesmosomes are attachment complexes that connect the keratin intermediate filaments within the basal keratinocytes to the lamina lucida with the help of anchoring filaments (Option B).
  • Lamina lucida(LL) and densa(LD) are part of dermal–epidermal basement membrane forming the interface between the two (Option C).
  • The anchoring filaments are thread-like structures passing under the HD and merge with the lamina densa.
  • Whereas anchoring fibrils are U‐shaped structures extending from lamina densa to the upper reticular dermis (Option D).

A middle aged female patient presented with vesicles and blisters over the skin and oral cavity. On examination, the blisters are flaccid with an erythematous base, and a firm sliding pressure with a finger separates the Superficial epidermis layers from basal epidermis, producing a new lesion. Which of the following microscopic features is not seen in this patient?

B

correctAnswer: A. It is most commonly associated with lymphoma and leukemia
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

PNP is most frequently associated with hematologic malignancies, particularly non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other B cell lymphomas. Other associated neoplasms can include Castleman's disease, thymoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia and sarcomas.

The antigens associated include

  • Envoplakin and Periplakin (most specific)
  • Desmoglein1 and 3
  • Desmoplakin 1 and 2
  • Epiplakin and Plectin
  • Bullous pemphigoid (BP) antigen 1

Oral mucosal involvement is actually a hallmark of PNP and is often severe and resistant to treatment. It can be one of the earliest and most persistent manifestations of the disease. (Option B)

While autoantibodies against desmogleins (particularly desmoglein 3) can be present in PNP, they are not exclusive targets. PNP is characterized by autoantibodies against multiple antigens, predominantly members of the plakin family (including desmoplakin, envoplakin, and periplakin). (Option C)

PNP generally has a worse prognosis compared to other forms of pemphigus. It is often more resistant to treatment and can be associated with significant morbidity and mortality, partly due to the underlying malignancy. (Option D)

question: Which of the following statements about paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP) is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows moist, vegetative, hypertrophic plaques located in a flexural region, which is characteristic of pemphigus vegetans.
  • The patient has a history of vesicles and bullae, which later ruptured to form vegetative erosions in intertriginous areas- supporting the diagnosis.
  • This is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris, often misdiagnosed without considering the specific morphology and location of lesions.

Pemphigus Vegetans:

  • A variant of pemphigus vulgaris, characterized by vegetating plaques.
  • Flexural involvement is typical- especially in areas like groin, axillae, inframammary region.
  • Develops after bullae or pustules rupture, leading to:
    • Hypertrophic, granulating, exudative erosions.
    • Lesions may become foul-smelling and infected.
  • Oral mucosa may be involved:
    • Cerebriform tongue (called Premlata sign)

[[figure-2]]

  • Two subtypes:
    • Neumann type – more severe, vesiculobullous onset.
    • Hallopeau type – milder, pustular onset leading to vegetative growth.

Differential Diagnoses:

Diagnosis

Key Features

Pemphigus vegetans (Option D)

Vegetating erosions in flexures; post-vesicular phase; cerebriform tongue (Premlata sign); Neumann/Hallopeau types.

Pemphigus foliaceus (Option A)

Crusted erosions in seborrheic areas (face, chest, scalp); no mucosal involvement; superficial blistering.

Endemic PF (fogo selvagem) (Option B)

Seen in rural Brazil/Colombia; associated with black fly bites (Simulium); affects children/young adults.

Condyloma acuminata (Option C)

HPV-related genital warts; soft, pink, verrucous or filiform lesions; no vesicle-bullae history.

Condyloma lata (secondary syphilis)

Flat, moist, broad-based lesions in groin/perineum; painless; seen in syphilis- not relevant here.

question: A female patient came with a history of vesicles and bullae in the flexural parts one week ago. She presented to a dermatology clinic today because the lesion has changed. On examination, the following lesion is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given scenario is of pemphigus herpetiformis due to the presence of circulating IgG and C3 autoantibodies against DSG 1 or DSG 3.

Pemphigus herpetiformis is a variant of pemphigus that resembles dermatitis herpetiformis(DH) clinically

  • It is characterized by clusters of pruritic that develop on an erythematous background. Pruritis is due to eosinophils in the epidermis.
  • Pemphigus herpetiformis has acantholysis while DH is intradermal pathology with papillary dermis involvement
  • Immunofluorescence revealing intercellular staining is the key to diagnosis. Patients possess circulating IgG autoantibodies against DSG 1 or 3 and desmocollins 1 or 3 in some individuals.
  • It may progress to PV or classical PF.
  • Treatment of both PH and DH Is Dapsone

[[figure-1]]

Papules and vesicles of pemphigus herpetiformis which are similar to DH

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no. 50.7, 50.53

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with pruritic, grouped vesicles and small blisters on her trunk and upper extremities. The patient reports that new lesions appear in waves, often in a herpetiform pattern. Biopsy shows eosinophilic spongiosis and acantholysis. DIF reveals intercellular IgG and C3 deposits. ELISA is positive for anti-desmoglein 1 antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Mucosa is not affected in Pemphigus foliaceus.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pemphigus foliaceus (PF) is a blistering disorder that typically affects the skin and spares the mucosa.

Pemphigus vulgaris(PV) and foliaceus are autoimmune blistering disorders caused by antibodies against structural protein desmosomes (DSG). They affect the skin and mucosa in a unique way, which is explained by the distribution of DSG1 and 3 in the skin and mucosa.

  • In skin, DSG1 is present throughout the epidermis whereas DSG3 is found only in the basal and immediate suprabasal layers.
  • In mucosa, DSG 3 is expressed through all layers whereas DSG 1 is found only at low levels.

Because DSG1 and 3 work together, antibodies against DSG1 cannot destabilize the oral mucosa, but they can significantly affect the skin. As a result, skin blistering without mucosal involvement is seen in PF patients who only have anti-DSG 1 antibodies. As PV has both DSG 3 and DSG 1 antibodies, both skin and mucosal lesions are seen.



Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th Edition, Page 50

question: Which of the following is being demonstrated in the image given below?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The correct answer is BP180 ectodomain because Linear IgA disease is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disorder characterised by linear IgA deposition at the DEJ, most commonly directed against cleaved ectodomain fragments of BP180 (LABD97 and LAD-1).


Linear IgA Disease (LAD):

  • Autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease
  • Diagnostic hallmark: Linear IgA deposition along the dermo-epidermal junction (DEJ) on direct immunofluorescence
  • The most common autoimmune blistering disease in children
  • Synonyms:
    • Adults: Linear IgA disease, IgA bullous pemphigoid
    • Children: Chronic bullous disease of childhood
  • Main target antigen: BP180 (type XVII collagen) ectodomain
    • LABD97 (97 kDa), LAD-1 (120 kDa)
  • Triggers:
    • Vancomycin (most common)
    • NSAIDs, penicillins, infections
  • Clinical manifestations:
    • Tense vesicles/bullae
    • Annular pattern → “crown of jewels”

[[figure-1]]

  • Pruritus variable
  • Mucosal involvement
  • No scarring (usually)
  • Histology: Subepidermal blister & neutrophil-rich infiltrate
  • Direct IF: Linear IgA ± C3/IgG at DEJ

[[figure-2]]

  • Prognosis:
    • Excellent response
    • Children: remission in ≤2 years


Desmoglein 3 (Option A) is the target in Pemphigus Vulgaris. It results in intraepidermal (suprabasal) blistering rather than the subepidermal blisters seen here.


Epidermal transglutaminase (Option C) is the autoantigen for Dermatitis Herpetiformis. While that condition also involves IgA, the deposition is granular (at the dermal papillary tips) rather than linear.


Type VII collagen (Option D) is the target in Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA) and the inflammatory "bullous systemic lupus erythematosus" (BSLE).



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 50.33 - 50.38
question: A 4-year-old child develops sudden-onset tense vesicles and bullae arranged in an annular “crown of jewels” pattern with oral erosions. Biopsy shows a subepidermal blister with neutrophils. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates linear IgA deposition along the dermo-epidermal junction. What is the most common target antigen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hailey-Hailey disease, Darier disease, and epidermolysis bullosa simplex are inherited, non-autoimmune disorders and therefore do not show immunoglobulin or complement deposition on direct immunofluorescence.

  • Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita: Autoimmune disease with antibodies against type VII collagen; shows linear IgG ± C3 at the dermo-epidermal junction, hence DIF is positive.
  • Hailey-Hailey disease: ATP2C1 mutation causing acantholysis; DIF is negative as there are no autoantibodies.
  • Darier disease: ATP2A2 mutation with dyskeratosis and acantholysis; DIF is negative.
  • Epidermolysis bullosa simplex: Keratin 5/14 defect causing intraepidermal blistering; DIF is negative.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 50.43
question:
In which of the following conditions is direct immunofluorescence (DIF) absent (negative)?

  1. Hailey-Hailey disease
  2. Darier disease
  3. Epidermolysis bullosa simplex
  4. Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is IgA pemphigus, because the presence of intercellular IgA deposition on DIF, along with pruritic annular pustules in flexural areas and absent mucosal involvement, is characteristic of this condition.


IgA Pemphigus:

  • Autoimmune intraepidermal blistering disease
  • DIF: Intercellular IgA deposition
  • Types:
    • Subcorneal pustular dermatosis (SPD) type → Desmocollin-1
    • Intraepidermal neutrophilic type → target uncertain (± IgA anti-Dsg1/3)
  • Clinical: Pruritic flaccid vesicles/pustules, annular/circinate, central clearing
  • Sites: Axillae, groin > trunk, face, scalp
  • Mucosa: Rare
  • Course: Chronic, indolent
  • Associations: Monoclonal IgA gammopathy, HIV, IBD, RA, thiol drugs


Pemphigus foliaceus (Option A): Shows IgG (not IgA) intercellular deposition; pustules are uncommon.



Subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Option B): Clinically similar, but DIF is negative or nonspecific.


Pemphigus vulgaris (Option D): Shows IgG anti-desmoglein 3, painful erosions, and mucosal involvement.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 50.7
question: A 45-year-old man has chronic pruritic flaccid pustules in annular patterns over the axillae and groin. Mucosa is spared. Biopsy shows intraepidermal neutrophilic pustules. DIF: intercellular IgA deposition as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Penicillamine, Glibenclamide, and Rifampicin are well-known triggers of drug-induced pemphigus.


Drug-Induced Pemphigus:

  • Common drugs:
    • Thiol: Penicillamine (most common)
    • Non-thiol: ACE inhibitors, glibenclamide
    • Phenol: Cephalosporins, rifampicin, pyritinol, phenobarbital, aspirin
  • Penicillamine:
    • Incidence 3-10%, onset ~1 year
    • Associated with autoimmune disease (e.g. RA)
    • HLA-B15 association
  • Treatment: Drug withdrawal ± systemic steroids/immunosuppressants


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 50.4
question:
Which of the following drugs are commonly implicated in drug-induced pemphigus?

  1. Penicillamine
  2. Glibenclamide
  3. Rifampicin
  4. Metformin

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and unique immunofluorescence pattern (u-serrated pattern) point to Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA).

  • Type VII collagen is the autoantigen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA), located in the anchoring fibrils beneath the lamina densa.
  • Antibodies against it cause subepidermal blistering.


Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA):

  • Rare subepidermal autoimmune blistering disease caused by anti-type VII collagen antibodies.
  • Two forms: Mechanobullous (classical) and Inflammatory (mimics BP, LAD, MMP).
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Antibodies target the NC1 domain of type VII collagen → neutrophil recruitment → ROS & proteases → subepidermal blister
  • Clinical features:
    • Mechanobullous: Trauma-prone sites; blisters, erosions, scarring, milia
    • Inflammatory: Resembles BP/MMP/LAD; mucous membrane involvement ~50%
  • Diagnosis:
    • Direct IF: Linear IgG ± C3, u-serrated pattern

[[figure-1]]

  • Indirect IF: Binds blister floor on salt-split skin
  • Serology: Anti-type VII collagen ELISA/IF (IgG ± IgA)
  • Treatment:
    • First-line: Prednisolone + colchicine ± dapsone
    • Second-line: Ciclosporin, mycophenolate
    • Refractory: IVIG, rituximab, immunoadsorption/plasmapheresis


BP180 (Collagen XVII) (Option A): Target in bullous pemphigoid.


Laminin 332 (Option C): Target in mucous membrane pemphigoid.


Desmoglein 3 (Option D): Target in pemphigus vulgaris.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 50.41 - 50.46
question: A 52-year-old patient presents with chronic, trauma-induced blisters, erosions, and scarring on the hands and elbows. Mucous membranes are also involved. The direct immunofluorescence image is given below. What is the primary target antigen in this patient’s disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex (EBS).
  • Keratin 5/14 mutations cause basal keratinocyte fragility, leading to intraepidermal (basal) cleavage, palmo-plantar blisters worsened by heat and friction, and healing without scarring.


Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex (EBS):

  • Plane of cleavage: Intraepidermal (keratinocyte level)
  • Inheritance: Mostly autosomal dominant
  • Common genes: KRT5, KRT14 (≈⅔ cases)
  • Scarring: Usually minimal or absent (exceptions exist)


Acral peeling skin syndrome (Option D): This condition is autosomal recessive, involves TGM5 mutations, and shows cleavage above the granular layer, not basal keratinocyte fragility.


Junctional epidermolysis bullosa (Option B): Cleavage occurs at the lamina lucida, commonly involves laminin-332 or type XVII collagen, and is usually more severe with mucosal involvement.


Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (Option C): Caused by COL7A1 mutations, shows sub-lamina densa cleavage, and is associated with scarring and milia, which are absent here.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 71.6 - 71.12
question: A 25-year-old man has had recurrent findings as shown since early childhood, worse with heat and friction, healing without scarring. Biopsy shows intraepidermal basal cleavage. Genetic testing reveals a keratin 5 / keratin 14 mutation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH).
  • Intensely pruritic excoriated papules on extensor surfaces + granular IgA deposition in dermal papillae on direct immunofluorescence is classic for dermatitis herpetiformis.


Dermatitis Herpetiformis:

  • Chronic, intensely pruritic autoimmune blistering disease
  • Granular IgA anti-TG3 deposits in dermal papillae → neutrophils → subepidermal blisters
  • Associations:
    • Celiac disease (most important)
    • Autoimmune thyroid disease
    • Type 1 diabetes, Addison's disease, vitiligo
    • ↑ Risk: small bowel lymphoma
  • Clinical features:
    • Severe pruritus & grouped papules/vesicles (often excoriated)
    • Symmetrical extensor surfaces: elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp
    • Heals without scarring
  • Pathogenesis:
    • IgA autoimmunity
    • Target: Epidermal transglutaminase (TG3)
    • HLA-DQ2 (± DQ8)
  • Investigations:
    • Direct IF (gold standard): Granular IgA in papillary dermis

[[figure-1]]

  • Histology: Subepidermal blister + neutrophils in dermal papillae
  • Positive IgA anti-tTG / anti-TG3
  • Treatment:
    • Dapsone + gluten-free diet


Bullous pemphigoid (Option A): Subepidermal blistering with linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane, typically in elderly patients; pruritus may occur, but IgA is not granular in papillae.


Linear IgA bullous dermatosis (Option B): Shows linear IgA deposition along the basement membrane, not granular papillary deposits; distribution and GI association differ.


Pemphigus vulgaris (Option D): Intraepidermal acantholysis with IgG against desmogleins; mucosal involvement is common; IF shows intercellular “fish-net” IgG.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 50.52 - 50.55
question: A 40-year-old man has intense pruritus with excoriated papules over the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp. Direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA deposition as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dapsone is the treatment of choice for the acute management of Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH).


Management of DH:

  • Gluten-free diet (lifelong) (BROW)
    • Barley
    • Rye
    • Oats
    • Wheat
  • Dapsone 25-150 mg/day (rapid itch relief)
  • Topical potent steroids (adjunct)
  • Second line:
    • Sulphamethoxypyridazine 0.5-1.5 g daily (with gluten-free diet)
  • Third line:
    • Sulphapyridine 250-750 mg daily
      OR
    • Sulphasalazine 1-2 g daily (with gluten-free diet)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 50.54, 50.55
question: A patient with intensely pruritic excoriated papules as shown on the extensor surfaces and granular IgA in dermal papillae on direct IF. Which drug provides rapid symptomatic relief?

correctAnswer: C. There is no increased risk of malignancy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with celiac disease and carries an increased risk of small bowel lymphoma.


Dermatitis Herpetiformis:

  • Chronic, intensely pruritic autoimmune blistering disease
  • Granular IgA anti-TG3 deposits in dermal papillae (Option B) → neutrophils → subepidermal blisters
  • Associations:
    • Celiac disease (most important) (Option A)
    • Autoimmune thyroid disease
    • Type 1 diabetes, Addison's disease, vitiligo
    • ↑ Risk: small bowel lymphoma
  • Clinical features:
    • Severe pruritus & grouped papules/vesicles (often excoriated)
    • Symmetrical extensor surfaces (Option D): elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp
    • Heals without scarring
  • Pathogenesis:
    • IgA autoimmunity
    • Target: Epidermal transglutaminase (TG3)
    • HLA-DQ2 (± DQ8)
  • Investigations:
    • Direct IF (gold standard): Granular IgA in papillary dermis

[[figure-1]]

  • Histology: Subepidermal blister + neutrophils in dermal papillae
  • Positive IgA anti-tTG / anti-TG3

question: Which statement regarding dermatitis herpetiformis is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Recurrent flexural erosions worsened by heat/sweating with suprabasal acantholysis showing a “dilapidated brick wall” appearance is classic for Hailey-Hailey disease.


Hailey-Hailey disease: (Familial benign chronic pemphigus)

  • Autosomal dominant acantholytic dermatosis
  • Recurrent erosions/blisters in flexures & friction sites\
  • Pathogenesis:
    • ATP2C1 mutation (3q21-24) → ↓ Golgi Ca²⁺ (SPCA1)
    • Defective keratinocyte adhesion
  • Histology:
    • Suprabasal acantholysis & minimal dyskeratosis
    • “Dilapidated brick wall”

[[figure-1]]

  • Triggers: Heat, sweating, friction, infection, UV
  • Clinical:
    • Painful, pruritic, malodorous flexural erosions
    • Axillae, groin, inframammary folds

[[figure-2]]

  • Fissures, maceration, vegetations
  • Longitudinal leukonychia
  • Management:
    • Avoid heat/friction, weight loss
    • Topical potent steroids ± antimicrobials
    • Short-course oral steroids (flares)
    • Refractory: tacrolimus, doxycycline, retinoids, ciclosporin, methotrexate
    • Botulinum toxin / surgery for severe disease


Darier disease (Option A): Shows suprabasal acantholysis with prominent dyskeratosis (corps ronds and grains) and presents with greasy papules in seborrhoeic areas, not recurrent painful flexural erosions with a “dilapidated brick wall” pattern.


Pemphigus vulgaris (Option B): An autoimmune blistering disease with IgG against desmogleins, mucosal involvement, and “tombstone” basal cells on histology, not a friction-triggered flexural erosive disorder.


Bullous pemphigoid (Option D): A subepidermal blistering disease with tense bullae and linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane, not suprabasal acantholysis or a dilapidated brick wall appearance.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 66.10 - 66.13
question: A 35-year-old man presents with recurrent painful erosions and fissuring in the axillae and groin, worsened by heat and sweating. Skin biopsy shows findings as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, intensely pruritic blistering skin condition strongly associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy).
  • It presents with grouped vesicles and papules on extensor surfaces such as elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp.
  • Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae—this is diagnostic.
  • Pathogenesis involves IgA antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase, triggered by gluten exposure.
  • First-line treatment is a gluten-free diet; dapsone can provide rapid symptom relief.

[[figure-1]]

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option B): An autoimmune blistering disease with flaccid bullae, oral mucosal involvement, and IgG antibodies against desmoglein; immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG in a “fish-net” pattern, not granular IgA at dermal papillae.

Bullous pemphigoid (Option C): Presents with tense bullae in elderly patients, due to IgG antibodies against hemidesmosomes; immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane, not IgA deposits.

Psoriasis (Option D): A chronic inflammatory skin disease with erythematous plaques and silvery scales, no vesicles, and no IgA deposition on immunofluorescence.
question: A woman presents with a pruritic rash on the elbows, buttocks with recent diagnosis of gluten sensitive enteropathy. On immunofluorescence IgA deposition is seen as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Pemphigus vulgaris:

  • The fishnet pattern of immunofluorescence observed between keratinocytes in the image is diagnostic of pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune blistering disorder.

Incorrect Options:

  • Options A, C, and D do not show fishnet pattern on immunofluorescence.
question: Identify the condition based on the immunofluorescence pattern shown in the image.

correctAnswer: A. Statements 1 &amp; 2 are correct, 2 is not explaining 1
explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Statements 1 & 2 are correct, 2 Is not explaining 1:

  • In pemphigus vulgaris, both flaccid blisters and suprabasal acantholytic split, as well as rows of tombstones, are seen.
  • The row of tombstones' appearance is seen due to the detached basal cells from the basement membrane.
  • Statement 1 describes suprabasal acantholytic split (mechanism = anti-Dsg3 antibodies).
  • Statement 2 describes a morphological consequence seen on histopathology.
  • Although both occur in PV, the presence of tombstones does not explain why the split is suprabasal.
  • The pathophysiology (anti-Dsg3 antibodies) explains Statement 1, not Statement 2.

Incorrect Options:

Statement 1 Is Incorrect (Option B): this choice is incorrect as there is the presence of flaccid blisters and suprabasal acantholytic split seen in PV

Statement 1 and 2 Is Incorrect (Option C): both statements correctly describe pemphigus vulgaris.

Statement 1 and 2 are correct and 2 Is the correct explanation for 1 (Option D): Statement 2 is not the correct explanation of statement 1.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5901732/

question:
Statement 1 - A 59-year-old patient presents with flaccid bullae. Histopathology shows a suprabasal acantholytic split.

Statement 2 - The row of tombstones' appearance is diagnostic of Pemphigus vulgaris.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Bullous Pemphigoid:

  • In prodromal phase of Bullous Pemphigoid itchy eczematous lesions can be seen. The associated antibody is IgG. Direct immunofluorescence linear deposition shows IgG and C3. Hence, this option is correct.
  • BP is a common subepidermal immunobullous disorder mainly affecting elder people. Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal target proteins BP230(BPAG1) and BP180(BPAG2) which finally leads to bullae formation.
  • It is characterised by a prodromal non bullous stage with pruritis which is followed by a bullous stage. The later has intense pruritus with tense blisters and vesicles.
  • These blisters show a negative Nikolsky sign but a positive Bulla spread sign.
  • The rupture of blisters leads to yellow or hemorrhagic crust formation, which later heal without any scar.
  • Oral lesions can occur sometimes.
  • HPE shows a subepidermal split with inflammatory infiltrate, immunofluorescence shows a linear binding of immunoglobulin (IgG and C3) at the dermo-epidermal junction.
  • Topical and systemic steroids are the mainstay of treatment.

[[figure-1]]

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option A)

  • PV is characterized by intraepidermal blistering and acantholysis (loss of cell-to-cell adhesion between keratinocytes).
  • Immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG (not linear staining at the basement membrane zone).
  • The presence of subepidermal blisters here excludes PV.

Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option C)

  • DH is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy associated with deposition of IgA in the dermal papillae, not linear IgG or C3 at the basement membrane.
  • DH typically shows granular IgA deposition in immunofluorescence and not the linear patterns seen here.

Pemphigus foliaceous (Option D)

  • PF is another type of pemphigus that features intraepidermal blistering and acantholysis but lacks subepidermal blistering.
  • Immunofluorescence in PF typically shows intercellular IgG, not the linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane observed in this case.


Reference:

question: A 60-year-old female presents with eczematous itching lesions. Biopsy revealed a subepidermal cleft with direct immunofluorescence showing linear C3 & IgG deposition along the basement membrane zone. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Clinical Presentation:
