question: What is the probable diagnosis for a 30-year-old patient who has presented with flaccid bullae on her skin that are prone to easy rupture, with the biopsy showing a suprabasal split?

explanationHtml:
• Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of inherited disorders characterized by the formation of blisters and erosions on the skin and mucous membranes in response to minor trauma or friction.
  • It is caused by defects in the proteins that help anchor the layers of the skin together.
  • The fact that the baby's previous sibling had similar complaints and died at a young age further supports the diagnosis of a genetic disorder like EB, as it is an inherited condition.
  • It has four main types: EB simplex, junctional EB, dystrophic EB, and Kindler syndrome.

Pathophysiology

  • Caused by mutations in genes encoding skin structural proteins (keratins, laminins, collagen).
  • Leads to weakened dermal-epidermal adhesion, resulting in blister formation with minor friction or trauma.

Features

  • Fragile skin with fluid-filled blisters, erosions, and scarring.
  • Mucosal involvement (oral, esophageal, ocular, and genitourinary).
  • Severe forms can lead to deformities, malnutrition, and infections.
  • Dystrophic EB may cause mitten-hand deformities due to fusion of digits.

Investigations & Diagnosis

  • Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence mapping – Identifies the defective protein.
  • Genetic testing – Confirms mutation type.
  • Electron microscopy – Assesses ultrastructural defects.

Chronic bullous disorder of childhood (Option B): This condition is characterized by recurrent blistering and typically occurs in older children, not in infancy.

Congenital syphilis (Option C): While syphilis can cause skin manifestations, it typically presents with other symptoms as well and can be confirmed through specific diagnostic tests.

Neonatal pemphigus (Option D): Neonatal pemphigus is a rare autoimmune condition in which autoantibodies are transferred from the mother to the baby, resulting in blistering.

question: What is the diagnosis for a male baby, born to a non-consanguineous couple, who develops blisters on areas of friction, with a history of a previous child having similar complaints and dying at 2 weeks of age?

explanationHtml:
• Dapsone is the treatment of choice for sub-epidermal blister formation with neutrophils located at the tips of the dermal papillae.
  • This presentation is characteristic of a group of autoimmune blistering diseases known as subepidermal autoimmune bullous diseases, which include bullous pemphigoid and dermatitis herpetiformis.

Mechanism of Action of Dapsone

  • Inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, reducing blister formation.
  • Suppresses inflammatory mediators, leading to decreased skin damage.

Indications in Subepidermal Autoimmune Bullous Diseases

  • Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH) – First-line treatment
  • Linear IgA Bullous Dermatosis (LABD) – Effective in most cases
  • Bullous Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (BSLE) – Used in resistant cases
  • Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA) – Occasionally used as adjunct therapy

Incorrect Options:

Rituximab (Option A): Rituximab is not the treatment of choice for sub-epidermal blister formation with neutrophils located at the tips of the dermal papillae.

Cyclosporine (Option C): Cyclosporine can be effective in managing certain blistering diseases, it is not the treatment of choice

Azathioprine (Option D): Azathioprine may be beneficial in some cases of autoimmune blistering diseases, it is not the treatment of choice.



Reference:

Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology and Sexually Transmitted Diseases, Fifth Edition – Neena Khanna Pg 449
question: What is the preferred treatment for the condition resulting in the formation of blisters beneath the epidermis, where neutrophils are found at the tips of the dermal papillae?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the given information of a child presenting with tense bullae over the torso and a biopsy showing subepidermal blistering and neutrophil infiltration, the most likely diagnosis is Bullous Pemphigoid.
  • The primary treatment for Bullous Pemphigoid is systemic immunosuppressive therapy, and Dapsone is one of the drugs of choice for this condition.

Mechanism of Action of Dapsone

  • Inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, reducing blister formation.
  • Suppresses inflammatory mediators, leading to decreased skin damage.

Indications in Subepidermal Autoimmune Bullous Diseases

  • Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH) - First-line treatment
  • Linear IgA Bullous Dermatosis (LABD) - Effective in most cases
  • Bullous Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (BSLE) - Used in resistant cases
  • Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA) - Occasionally used as adjunct therapy


Incorrect Options:

Rituximab (Option A): Rituximab can be used in some cases of autoimmune blistering disorders, it is not typically the drug of choice for Bullous Pemphigoid.

Cyclosporine (Option C): Cyclosporine it is not the first-line drug of choice.

Azathioprine (Option D): Azathioprine is usually reserved for cases that are refractory to first-line treatments or as a steroid-sparing agent. It is not the initial drug of choice.

Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology and Sexually Transmitted Diseases, Fifth Edition – Neena Khanna Pg 449
question: A child presents to OPD with tense bullae over the torso. A biopsy of the lesion showed a subepidermal level of blistering and neutrophil infiltration. What is the drug of choice?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Positive Nikolsky sign is classically associated with Pemphigus vulgaris.
  • Pseudo-Nikolsky sign is seen in Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
  • False Nikolsky sign may occur in Bullous pemphigoid.
  • Cerebriform tongue is characteristic of Pemphigus vegetans.

Vesiculobullous disorders are classified based on the level of skin separation:

  • Intraepidermal split → flaccid bullae → pemphigus group.
  • Subepidermal split → tense bullae → bullous pemphigoid.

Nikolsky sign refers to epidermal separation induced by tangential pressure:

  • True positive Nikolsky sign:
    • Seen in pemphigus vulgaris.
    • Due to acantholysis from antibodies against desmogleins.
    • Causes superficial epidermal shearing.
  • Pseudo-Nikolsky sign:
    • Seen in Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN.
    • Occurs due to epidermal necrosis rather than acantholysis.
    • Skin peels over already damaged areas.
  • False Nikolsky sign (bulla spread sign):
    • Pressure on an existing blister extends it into adjacent skin.
    • Can be seen in bullous disorders like bullous pemphigoid.

question: A 35-year-old construction worker presents with a painless lesion on his right forearm following sustaining a minor abrasion while working with bricks a few weeks ago. Physical examination reveals a shallow ulcer with undermined edges. Acid-fast bacilli staining of a biopsy specimen from the lesion is positive. Which of the following types of cutaneous tuberculosis is most likely responsible for this presentation?

correctAnswer: B. Post-primary tuberculosis with poor immunity
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario and the image suggest the diagnosis of Tuberculosis verrucous cutis which is also known as Prosecutor's wart, Anatomist's wart (Option A), Verruca necrogenica, and Warty tuberculosis.
  • It is a form of Cutaneous tuberculosis that occurs after direct inoculation of the mycobacteria into the skin of a previously sensitized host with good immunity against the bacillus. (Option B)
  • It is a paucibacillary lesion (Option C), and inoculation typically occurs from an exogenous source.
  • In adults, TBVC most frequently develops on the acral extremities; the fingers and dorsum of the hands are commonly affected, while in children, the ankles or buttocks are frequent sites for lesion occurrence.
  • It presents as a painless, slowly progressive, red or brown warty, hyperkeratotic plaque with a verrucous or papillomatous surface and it grows via peripheral extension.
  • On histopathological examination, it is characterized by granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes, giant cells, and caseous necrosis(caseating granulomas).
  • It can be treated with Antitubercular drugs (Option D).

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27

question: A 45-year-old female presents with a slowly progressive, verrucous plaque on her left foot. She has a history of pulmonary tuberculosis treated several years ago. On examination, the lesion appears well-defined, hyperkeratotic, and verrucous, with a papillomatous surface as shown in the image. All of the following statements are true about this condition except?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario and the image suggest a diagnosis of Scrofuloderma, which is caused by the direct extension of an infection (endogenous spread) to the skin from the underlying TB focus (Lymph node, bone joint).

  • It is a multibacillary manifestation and is the most common form of cutaneous TB in children, although it can occur in any age group.
  • It often presents as painless subcutaneous swellings and ruptures into the overlying skin, resulting in discharging sinuses or undermined ulcers or fibrotic scars.
  • The most common focus of infection is the cervical lymph node.
  • The most common sites are the neck and axilla.
  • Biopsy reveals positive staining for acid-fast bacilli and characteristic caseating granulomas seen.

Actinomycosis (Option B): Chronic bacterial infection causing indurated nodules or abscesses with sinus tracts and sulfur granules.
Unlike scrofuloderma, it lacks caseating nodules.

[[figure-1]]

Sporotrichosis (Option C): Fungal infection presenting as painless papules/nodules after trauma, spreading linearly along lymphatics.
Unlike scrofuloderma, it lacks central caseation.

[[figure-2]]

Pyoderma gangrenosum (Option D) : Rare, non-infectious ulcers with undermined borders, linked to systemic diseases (IBD, RA, hematologic malignancies).
Histology shows neutrophilic infiltrate without infection, vasculitis, or granulomas

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.13
question: A 40-year-old woman presents with a slowly enlarging, painless lesion on the neck. She has a history of pulmonary tuberculosis with nodal involvement, treated 3 years ago. On examination, there is a firm, erythematous plaque with crusting and shallow ulceration. Ipsilateral, non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy is also noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario is suggestive of Lupus vulgaris which is a chronic form of cutaneous tuberculosis that occurs in previously sensitized individuals with moderate immunity to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

  • These lesions usually appear as well-defined, erythematous to reddish-brown plaques or nodules with smooth, slightly scaly, or verrucous surfaces and may have active, raised margins.
  • They may initially appear as small papules or nodules that gradually enlarge and coalesce to form larger plaques.
  • Often exhibits induration due to the underlying granulomatous inflammation and atrophy due to underlying tissue destruction by the tuberculosis infection.
  • The center of the lesion may show atrophy and scarring.
  • Diagnosis is often confirmed by histopathological examination of skin biopsy specimens, which typically show caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli.
  • Diascopy shows characteristic ‘apple jelly nodules’.
  • Treated with Antitubercular therapy.

[[figure-1]]

Fig. Apple Jelly Nodule on diascopy


Psoriasis (Option B):

  • This typically presents as well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales, most commonly on extensor surfaces and scalp.
  • It is associated with systemic manifestations such as psoriatic arthritis and does not produce apple jelly nodules on diascopy, spitz sign positive.

[[figure-2]]

Fig. Psoriasis


Lupus pernio (Option C):

  • It is a distinctive form of chronic cutaneous sarcoidosis, a multisystem inflammatory disorder characterized by the formation of non-caseating granulomas.
  • It typically presents as persistent, violaceous or dusky-red, indurated plaques or nodules, often involving the nose, cheeks, lips, and ears.
  • It can present with apple jelly nodules on diascopy, but histopathological examination reveals non-caseating granuloma.

[[figure-3]]

Fig. Lupus pernio


Granuloma Annulare (Option D):

  • It is a benign, self-limiting dermatosis characterized by the formation of dermal granulomas, which are typically devoid of necrosis.
  • Typically presents as asymptomatic or minimally pruritic, erythematous to skin-coloured papules or plaques.

[[figure-4]]

Fig. Granuloma Annulare



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.21 27.22
  2. Jean L. Bolognia, Dermatology, 4th Edition, Page 1306
question: A 20-year-old woman presents with a large erythematous, scaly plaque with deep-seated nodules on her buttock, as shown in the image. The lesion gradually progressed over 4 years, exhibiting scarring and atrophy in some areas. Diascopy of the nodules reveals an "apple jelly" nodules. She has a history of a positive tuberculin skin test but no active tuberculosis. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. It is a multibacillary lesion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Based on the history and the image provided, the diagnosis is Lupus vulgaris and it is a chronic, progressive, paucibacillary (not multibacillary) form of cutaneous tuberculosis.

  • Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous TB seen in adults (Most common in females).
  • Causative organisms: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium bovis.

Pathogenesis :

  • Route of spread: Endogenous spread or from exogenous inoculation.
  • It occurs in a previously sensitized individual with an increased cell-mediated immunity to tuberculin. (Option B)

Clinical features:

  • Presents as a single or a group of erythematous violaceous annular plaques with central scarring and atrophy with active margins. (Option C)
  • The periphery shows erythematous deep-seated nodules which on diascopy may stand out as apple jelly nodules. (Option D)
  • Most commonly seen in the buttocks, upper extremities, and face.
  • Papules may recur within scarred areas, enlarging and coalescing into large, firm, elevated plaques.

Complications:

  • Secondary scarring and squamous cell carcinoma may develop rarely.

Treatment :

  • Anti-tubercular drugs.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.21, 27.22

question: A 24-year-old man presents with an erythematous plaque over the dorsum of hand that has been there for 4 years and is slowly progressing. Examination revealed a well-demarcated, indurated, annular-shaped plaque with irregular borders that was progressing towards one side and scarring on another border. Which of the following statements is FALSE about this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Based on the clinical history and image, the diagnosis points to Lichen scrofulosorum, a rare form of tuberculid (Option C), commonly seen in children (not in adults).

[[figure-1]]

Fig. Lichen Scrofulosorum showing annular and plaque‐like lesions with strong tuberculin reaction

[[figure-2]]

Lichenoid variety of Lichen Scrofulosorum

  • Lichen scrofulosorum presents with asymptomatic, lichenoid-grouped papules, often perifollicular in distribution. (Option D)
  • The trunk is the most common site for these lesions. (Option B)
  • Healing typically occurs without scarring.
  • Positive Mantoux test indicates previous exposure to tuberculosis antigens.
  • Biopsy reveals superficial dermal granulomas surrounding hair follicles. These granulomas contain epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, and occasional giant cells, typically without caseation.
  • Treatment involves a course of antitubercular therapy: 2 months of HRZE followed by 4 months of HRE.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.26

It is not a type of lichen planus

question: An 11-year-old child presented in dermatology OPD with a micro papular rash on the trunk without any necrosis or itching. The Mantoux test is positive. Histopathology examination shows perifollicular non-caseating granulomas. Which of the following statements is false about its diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. It is commonly seen in adults
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has lichen scrofulosorum, a rare tuberculid that occurs predominantly in children and adolescents with a strong immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Characteristic features include:

  • Strongly positive Mantoux test.
  • Asymptomatic, minute, grouped perifollicular lichenoid papules (Option D).
  • Lesions are found mainly on the trunk (Option B) (abdomen, chest, and back) and proximal limbs.
  • Histopathology shows superficial dermal non-caseating granulomas surrounding hair follicles and sweat ducts.
  • It is a cutaneous marker of underlying tuberculosis, and most patients have an underlying tuberculous focus elsewhere.
  • Lesions heal without scarring and usually respond rapidly to standard antitubercular therapy.

[[figure-1]]

It is a tuberculid and not a type of lichen planus (Option C): Lichen scrofulosorum is a cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction (tuberculid) associated with tuberculosis and is unrelated to lichen planus.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 27.25-27.28

question: An 11-year-old child presents with multiple asymptomatic, grouped lichenoid papules over the trunk. The Mantoux test is strongly positive. Skin biopsy shows superficial perifollicular non-caseating granulomas. Which of the following statements regarding the diagnosis is false?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical history suggests a diagnosis of Erythema induratum of Bazin. It is a type of tuberculid whose cause is not fully understood. It is believed to be a hypersensitivity reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens.

  • It is most common in middle-aged females.
  • It presents as recurrent nodular and ulcerative lesions that are usually localized to the lower legs(posterior calves).
  • Biopsy reveals Lobular panniculitis and vasculitis.
  • Tuberculids can be considered to be cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions to hematogenous dissemination of M. tuberculosis or its antigens from a primary source in an individual with strong anti-tuberculous cell‐mediated immunity.
  • Patients with tuberculids typically have a good response to anti-tuberculous therapy.

[[figure-1]]

Lichen Scrofulosorum (Option B):A tuberculid with grouped perifollicular lichenoid papules on the trunk, common in children, healing without scars.

[[figure-2]]

Papulonecrotic tuberculid (Option C) :A tuberculid with necrotic papules on extremities, seen in adults, showing obliterative vasculitis and thrombosis on biopsy.

[[figure-3]]

Erythema nodosum(Option D): Erythema nodosum presents with tender red nodules on extensor limbs, without ulceration or scarring.

[[figure-4]]

.

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.25, 99.21
question: A 57-year-old female presented in dermatology OPD with bilateral nodular lesions and ulceration on her calf. On examination, tenderness was noticed. The Mantoux test was positive, and the culture for M. tuberculosis was negative. What is the likely diagnosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical picture shows an erythematous plaque with central scarring and an advancing edge, which suggests a clinical diagnosis of Lupus vulgaris.
  • Rifampicin is an antibiotic that is part of the standard Anti-Tuberculous Therapy (ATT), started in this patient.
  • It is used in combination with other medications, such as Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol, to treat cutaneous tuberculosis, such as lupus vulgaris.

Amphotericin B (Option A):Amphotericin B treats serious systemic fungal infections but not cutaneous tuberculosis.

Itraconazole (Option B):Itraconazole treats skin fungal infections but is ineffective against Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Minocycline (Option D) :It is a tetracycline used for acne, not effective for mycobacterial infections.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.22
question: A 14-year-old girl presents with an erythematous plaque with central scarring and an advancing edge on her face. She reports a gradual progression of lesions over several months. Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation. Which of the following drugs will be started as a part of treatment in this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Non tender, erythematous nodules along lymphatic vessels
explanationHtml:
Explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests Swimming pool granuloma or Fish tank granuloma, which is caused by Mycobacterium marinum following exposure to contaminated water sources such as swimming pools or aquariums.

  • It is characterized by erythematous, painless nodules along lymphatic vessels of the affected area.
  • Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen may reveal granulomatous inflammation.
  • Treated with clarithromycin + ethambutol.

Erythematous nodules with central clearing (Option A) present as expanding red nodules with central clearing, a bull’s-eye rash typical of Lyme disease.

[[figure-1]]

Vesicular rash with a linear distribution (Option C) is a characteristic feature of herpes zoster (shingles), a viral infection caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. It typically presents with a painful vesicular rash that follows a dermatomal distribution (i.e., along the path of a sensory nerve).

[[figure-2]]

Target-like lesions with central clearing (Option D) are a characteristic feature of erythema multiforme, which various factors, including infections, medications, and autoimmune disorders can trigger.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.33

Vesicular rash with a linear distribution

question: A 28-year-old swimming pool worker presents to the dermatology clinic with a lesion on his left hand which is mostly painless but has gradually increased in size as shown in the image. He recalls sustaining a minor cut while cleaning a pool about a month ago. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

It is caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, which is endemic to wetland areas.

  • It presents as a painless ulcer with necrosis and undermined edges.
  • Necrosis is due to a cytotoxin, Myolactone, released by the organism
  • Acid-fast bacilli in a smear from the lesion support the diagnosis.
  • The four main diagnostic laboratory tests for Buruli ulcer are direct smear (with acid‐fast stains, auramine O or Ziehl–Neelsen), culture at 32°C, histopathology (lympho-epithelioid cell proliferation and panniculitis with characteristic fat necrotic changes), PCR (highest sensitivity).

Treatment:

Small ulcers(<5cm)

Rifampicin + Clarithromycin/Streptomycin for 8 weeks

Large ulcers (>5cm)

Surgery is recommended along with antibiotic therapy.


Cutaneous Tuberculosis (Option B): Although cutaneous tuberculosis is caused by an acid-fast bacillus (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), it typically presents in areas with a high prevalence of tuberculosis.


Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (Option C): causes painful ulcers with Leishmania parasites, often after travel to endemic areas.


Diabetic Ulcer (Option D) : Diabetic ulcers are typically found on pressure points of the feet, are associated with neuropathy and vascular disease, and do not usually present with undermined edges or a necrotic base unless secondarily infected.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.38
question: A 15-year-old boy presents to the clinic with a large painless ulcer on the lower extremity with a necrotic base and undermined edges. His family reports that they live near a wetland area in a region known to have cases of similar ulcers. There has been no response to standard treatment for common bacterial skin infections. A smear from the lesion shows acid-fast bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has Buruli ulcer, a chronic necrotising skin infection caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans.

  • It is prevalent in rural tropical wetlands and commonly affects children aged 5-15 years.
  • Lesions most often involve the lower extremities.
  • The disease begins as a painless nodule, papule, plaque, or oedema that progresses to a painless necrotic ulcer with deeply undermined edges.
  • Tissue destruction is caused by mycolactone, a necrotising, immunosuppressive toxin produced by the organism.
  • Diagnosis is supported by acid-fast bacilli on direct smear.
  • The four main laboratory tests are:
    • Direct smear (Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine O stain)
    • Culture at 32°C
    • Histopathology
    • PCR, which has the highest sensitivity for confirmation.
  • Treatment:
    • Category I (<5 cm): Rifampicin + streptomycin for 8 weeks
    • Category II (5-15 cm): Antibiotics followed by surgery if required, then completion of an 8-week antibiotic course.
    • Category III (>15 cm): Antibiotics with early surgery, followed by completion of 8 weeks of therapy.

Cutaneous tuberculosis (Option B): Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It may produce chronic skin lesions but does not typically present as a painless ulcer with deeply undermined edges caused by mycolactone.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (Option C): Caused by Leishmania species. It presents with chronic ulcerative skin lesions but acid-fast bacilli are absent, and the disease is unrelated to Mycobacterium ulcerans.

Diabetic ulcer (Option D): Typically occurs over pressure points in patients with diabetes mellitus, secondary to neuropathy and peripheral vascular disease. It is not associated with acid-fast bacilli or wetland exposure.



Reference:

question: A 15-year-old boy presents with a large painless ulcer over the lower extremity with a necrotic base and deeply undermined edges, as shown in the image. His family lives near a tropical wetland where similar ulcers are common. The lesion has not responded to routine antibacterial therapy. A smear from the ulcer demonstrates acid-fast bacilli. question: A 45-year-old man from a leprosy endemic region presents with small, ill-defined, multiple symmetrically distributed skin nodules as depicted below. Additionally he also has thickened peripheral nerves. What type of T lymphocytes are predominantly involved here?

correctAnswer: B. It is a diagnostic test
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Lepromin test does not detect leprosy, because many confirmed patients especially lepromatous cases show no reaction.

  • A test that is negative in diseased individuals cannot be used for diagnosis.

  • It is primarily a measure of cell-mediated immunity, not an indicator of infection.

  • Diagnosis of leprosy depends on clinical signs and slit-skin smear, not Lepromin.

  • So, lepromin test is not a diagnostic test.

Incorrect Options:

Option A) An early reaction is called the Fernandez reaction: The initial response within 48 hours is known as the Fernandez reaction, reflecting early cellular hypersensitivity.

Option C) It is also called the Mitsuda test: The test’s delayed response at 3–4 weeks is known as the Mitsuda reaction, giving the procedure its alternative name.

Option D) It may be used to classify patients: The test assists in grading disease along the immunological spectrum, helping differentiate tuberculoid from lepromatous forms.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 28.6,11,12,13,14

question: A second-year medical student asks you to describe Lepromin Test in the dermatology ward. While reviewing the test together, she recalls several statements. Which of the following statements recalled by her is false?

explanationHtml:
Correct answer: B) Borderline tuberculoid

Explanation:

  • The image shows a single large hypopigmented patch with clear but slightly irregular margins.

  • Satellite lesions around the main patch indicate a spreading nature typical of borderline forms.

  • Pseudopodia (finger-like extensions) from the main lesion are characteristic of Borderline Tuberculoid (BT) leprosy.

  • BT usually presents with few lesions (1–5), matching the image pattern.

  • Lesions are typically dry, well-defined, and hypoesthetic, consistent with BT leprosy.

Incorrect Options:

  • Option A) Borderline Lepromatous (BL): Presents with multiple, ill-defined lesions spread across the body. The image shows only one major lesion with satellites, not widespread disease.

  • Option C)Lepromatous Leprosy (LL): Has numerous, symmetrical, poorly defined lesions with late sensory loss. The solitary large lesion with clear borders and satellites is not typical of LL.

  • Option D) Tuberculoid Leprosy (TT): Shows a single, sharply defined lesion without satellite lesions or pseudopodia. This does not match the irregular margin and spreading pattern seen in the image.



Reference:

Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9nd Edition Chapter 28 Page No 28.11
question: What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with hypoesthetic lesions as shown in the image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The multiple asymmetrically distributed hypoesthetic plaques shown in the image favor borderline tuberculoid leprosy.

  • Borderline leprosy is characterised by an asymmetrical distribution of skin lesions, which may present as macules, plaques, annular lesions, or bizarre-shaped bands.
  • Towards the tuberculoid end of the spectrum, lesions are:
    • Few in number
    • Dry
    • Associated with hair loss (alopecia)
    • Associated with anhidrosis
    • More hypoesthetic due to greater nerve involvement
    • Commonly associated with thickened peripheral nerves

Borderline lepromatous leprosy (Option A): Lies closer to the lepromatous pole and presents with more numerous lesions, less sensory impairment, less hair loss and anhidrosis, and a higher bacillary load than borderline tuberculoid leprosy.

[[figure-1]]

Lepromatous leprosy (Option C): Characterised by multiple, bilateral symmetrical macules, papules, nodules, or diffuse infiltration with poorly defined margins. Sensory loss occurs late, and hair growth over lesions is initially preserved.

[[figure-2]]

Tuberculoid leprosy (Option D): Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) usually presents with a solitary or very few sharply demarcated plaques with raised edges, a dry hairless surface, and marked sensory loss.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 28.7-28.10

question: A 6-year-old child presents with well demarcated hypopigmented lesions with fine scaling on the face and upper arms. The lesions are well-demarcated with fine scaling and have been present for several months. On examination, there is no erythema or induration. The child is otherwise healthy with no systemic symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This clinical vignette is suggestive of a patient with Leprosy

A slit skin smear is performed by taking a sample from the earlobes or lesions and staining for acid-fast bacilli is done, which is diagnostic for leprosy.

Diascopy(Option A):

  • Diascopy is used to determine the nature of erythema or lesions by applying pressure with a glass slide.
  • It helps to differentiate erythema from purpura but is not useful for diagnosing hypopigmented, anaesthetic lesions in leprosy.

Lepromin Test(Option B):

  • The Lepromin test is not a diagnostic test for leprosy.
  • It is used to determine the type of immune response (cell-mediated immunity) a person has to Mycobacterium leprae.
  • It can help classify the form of leprosy and give an estimate of the patient's prognosis, but it does not confirm the presence of the disease itself.

Wood’s Lamp Examination(Option D):

  • This examination is primarily used to assess for fluorescent pigments or substances in the skin, such as in the case of fungal infections or certain pigmentation disorders, but it may not be specific enough to confirm the diagnosis in this case.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology- 9th Edition Chapter 28 Page No 28.1, 28.3, 28.12

question: A 12-year-old child presented with skin lesions, as shown in the image. On examination, bilateral ulnar and lateral popliteal nerves were enlarged. According to the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) Guidelines, what would be the most appropriate treatment for the child on day 1?

correctAnswer: C. Rifampicin acts by inhibiting RNA-dependent DNA polymerase
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Rifampicin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, not RNA-dependent DNA polymerase.
  • This inhibition interferes with bacterial RNA synthesis, ultimately leading to bactericidal activity against Mycobacterium leprae.

  • Other adverse effects of Clofazimine are:
    • Ichthyosis of skin.
    • Skin discoloration (red to purple-black)

question: You are training a pharmacist at a local PHC to supply multi-drug therapy at regular intervals for patients with leprosy in a village. Which of the following statements would be incorrect regarding treatment of leprosy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The common peroneal nerve, located in the leg, is commonly affected in leprosy. This nerve involvement can significantly impact mobility and function in affected individuals, resulting in neurological deficits such as foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.
  • Common peroneal nerve lesions cause difficulty in dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot and anaesthesia of the outer border of the foot, a combination which predisposes to traumatic damage and plantar ulceration

[[figure-1]]

  • Motor nerve deficits in leprosy:-

[[figure-2]]

  • Surface markings of all the nerves commonly affected in Leprosy:-

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

Median nerve(Option A):Median nerve involvement causes hand weakness and sensory loss, leading to claw hand, not foot drop.

Ulnar nerve(Option B):Ulnar nerve involvement causes hand weakness and sensory loss, leading to partial claw hand; it is the most commonly affected peripheral nerve in leprosy.

Radial nerve(Option C) :Radial nerve involvement in leprosy causes wrist drop; less common than common peroneal nerve, with radial cutaneous nerve most often biopsied.

question: A 30-year-old patient from an endemic region presents with weakness and numbness in the lower leg and foot. On examination, there is evidence of foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most likely involved in a patient of leprosy, leading to these neurological deficits?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • History of a pre-existing skin lesion on the face turning red and swollen, along with significant oedema of the hands and feet, is indicative of Type 1 lepra reaction
  • Pain and tenderness over multiple nerves are other characteristic features of Type 1 lepra reaction.
  • Type 1 lepra reaction is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, that typically occurs in patients with borderline leprosy (BT, BB, or BL disease).
  • It is characterized by an inflammatory response to Mycobacterium leprae antigens usually seen on starting MDT, resulting in a sudden exacerbation of pre-existing skin lesions and nerve involvement.


Cellulitis (Option A):Acute, painful, red swelling of skin and subcutis, usually post-injury; differs from lepra reaction in presentation.

[[figure-1]]


Psoriasis (Option C):It is a chronic autoimmune skin condition characterized by red, scaly patches on the skin, over the elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back.

[[figure-2]]


Erythema multiforme (Option D): Hypersensitivity reaction with target lesions, often post-infection or drug-related; not consistent with leprosy reaction.

[[figure-3]]

Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, Pages 28.15 to 28.16
question: A 28-year-old woman presents with an erythematous, swollen patch in a skin lesion on the face, along with significant oedema of the hands and feet. She reports the patch has been present for several months now, but has only recently turned painful and red. Additionally, the patient experiences pain and tenderness along multiple nerves and reports a general feeling of fatigue and malaise. The patient has been on regular medications but is unsure about their names. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Continue MDT and add oral steroids
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Corticosteroids and thalidomide are mainstay treatments for type 2 lepra reactions
  • In patients with lepra reactions, MDT is never discontinued in order to prevent the development of drug resistance and further progression of the disease. MDT is considered safe in pregnancy.
  • A Type 2 lepra reaction, also known as Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL), is a type 3 hypersensitivity reaction that occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy, which can present with painful nodules, fever, malaise, and other systemic symptoms.
  • Corticosteroids: Treatment of choice. They help reduce inflammation and immune response.
  • Thalidomide: Only severe cases of type-2 lepra reaction or erythema nodosum leprosum are treated with Thalidomide.
  • Thalidomide is the gold standard for type II Lepra reaction, but it is NOT the drug of choice due to its cost factor & also its adverse drug reaction profile.
  • Alternative drugs: Methotrexate, clofazimine, or tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-a) inhibitors


Stop MDT and start oral steroids (Option A): Stopping MDT is not advisable because it can increase the bacterial load and risk the development of drug resistance.


Antibiotics (Option B): While antibiotics are a part of MDT to treat the bacterial infection, they alone are not sufficient to address the acute inflammatory symptoms of a Type 2 lepra reaction.


Thalidomide (Option C): Thalidomide is an effective treatment for Type 2 lepra reactions due to its potent anti-inflammatory properties. However, it is absolutely contraindicated in pregnant women due to the risk of phocomelia in the first trimester.



Reference:

Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 28, Page 28.16

question: A pregnant woman at 10 weeks of gestation, who is currently undergoing multidrug therapy (MDT) for leprosy, now presents with type 2 lepra reaction. What is the preferred treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In leprosy, sensory involvement is the earliest and most prominent neurological feature, and it precedes motor weakness.
  • The disease preferentially affects small, poorly myelinated and unmyelinated cutaneous nerve fibers due to the predilection of Mycobacterium leprae for cooler areas of the body (skin and superficial nerves).
  • Because of this selective fiber involvement, the sequence of sensory loss is:
    • Temperature (C fibers) - lost first
    • Pain (A-delta fibers) - lost next
    • Touch (larger myelinated fibers) - lost last
  • Proprioception and vibration (large fiber modalities) are usually preserved until late stages of the disease.
  • Early leprosy presents with hypopigmented or erythematous skin patches with loss of temperature and pain sensation first.
  • The sensory loss is initially intracutaneous and patchy, not strictly following a single peripheral nerve or root distribution.
  • With progression, peripheral nerves become thickened and tender, leading to more defined nerve territory sensory loss, motor weakness, and deformities (e.g., claw hand, foot drop)
  • Autonomic involvement may occur, causing dry, anhidrotic skin, which predisposes to cracks, ulcers, and secondary infections.


Reference:
  1. Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology
  2. https://ijdvl.com/content/126/1999/65/2/Images/ijdvl_1999_65_2_59_4761.pdf

question: A patient with early leprosy presents with patchy hypoesthetic skin lesions. Which of the following correctly describes the order of sensory loss seen in leprosy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is Borderline leprosy, because the patient shows asymmetrically distributed skin lesions, including “punched-out” plaques, with thickened peripheral nerves and a moderate bacillary load.
  • Neural symptoms preceding skin lesions and immunological instability are characteristic of BL.


Borderline leprosy

  • Intermediate between tuberculoid (TT) and lepromatous (LL); most common & unstable.
  • Skin Lesions: Asymmetrical; macules, plaques, annular or band-like; “punched-out” plaques mid-spectrum.

[[figure-1]]

  • Toward TT: fewer, dry, hair loss, anhidrosis, hypoesthetic, few bacilli.
  • Toward LL: more numerous, wetter, more bacilli.
  • Nerves: One or more thickened; neural symptoms may precede skin lesions by years.
  • Subpolar LL (LLs): LL lesions + asymmetrical thickened nerves + borderline lesions; differs from polar LL (LLp).
  • Other Tissue: Clinically spared; bacilli may be present.
  • Dynamics: Unstable; can downgrade to LL or upgrade to TT; clinical changes lag behind histology/immunity

question: A patient with leprosy undergoes a skin biopsy. Histological findings are given in the image below. In which type of leprosy is this histological feature absent?

correctAnswer: C. Glove and stocking anaesthesia is an early feature
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most probable condition is Lepromatous leprosy
  • Glove and stocking anaesthesia is a late feature of lepromatous leprosy due to gradual peripheral nerve fibrosis; early nerve involvement is usually asymptomatic.


Lepromatous Leprosy (LL):

  • Early: Nasal stuffiness, discharge, epistaxis; leg oedema; early nerve involvement, asymptomatic
  • Skin: Multiple, bilateral, symmetrical macules (Option A), papules, nodules, diffuse infiltration
    • Macules: small, shiny, ill-defined, erythematous/hypopigmented
    • Sensation & hair initially preserved (Option B)
    • Spares scalp, axillae, groin, perineum

[[figure-1]]

  • Mucosa: Nasal & oral involvement → epistaxis (Option D), palatal/uvular nodules
  • Nerves: Distal sensory loss → glove & stocking anaesthesia (palms/soles late)
  • Late features: Leonine facies, madarosis, thick ear lobes, nasal collapse, hoarse voice
  • Systemic: Bone resorption, dactylitis, eye disease, testicular atrophy
  • Variants:
    • Lucio leprosy: Diffuse skin thickening, alopecia, no nodules
    • Histoid leprosy: Discrete firm nodules on normal skin


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 28.8 - 28.10

question: Which of the following statements about the most probable condition shown in the image is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pure Neuritic Leprosy is characterised by the absence of any skin lesions.


Pure neuritic leprosy:

  • Presentation: Asymmetrical involvement of peripheral nerve trunks (Statement 1)
  • Skin: No visible skin lesions (Statement 2)
  • Histology: Cutaneous nerve biopsy may show any spectrum of leprosy (Statement 3)
  • Epidemiology: Seen most commonly in India and Nepal
  • Frequency: Accounts for ~5-10% of leprosy cases
  • Smears: Skin smears are negative by definition
  • Nerves: Thickened, tender nerves; mononeuritis multiplex (ulnar, common peroneal, posterior tibial common)
  • Symptoms: Sensory loss in nerve distribution, pain/neuritis; motor deficits → deformities
  • Diagnosis: Clinical ± nerve biopsy/FNAC; HRUSG helpful
  • Risk: High risk of early disability
  • Course: May later develop typical skin lesions
  • Treatment: MDT (PB/MB based on nerves involved) + steroids for neuritis


Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 28.11

question:
Which of the following statements regarding pure neuritic leprosy are true?

  1. It presents with asymmetrical involvement of the peripheral nerve trunks.
  2. Visible skin lesions are a defining feature.
  3. Cutaneous nerve biopsy may show any spectrum of leprosy.

correctAnswer: C. Neuropathy may progress even after effective MDT
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Neuropathy in leprosy results from direct invasion of peripheral nerves by Mycobacterium leprae and immune-mediated inflammation.
  • Even after completion of effective MDT, nerve damage can continue to progress due to residual inflammation or immune reactions.


Leprosy and Neuropathy:

  • Primary impairments (WHO grade 1): Anaesthesia within lesions (paucibacillary/ borderline leprosy) and progressive symmetric distal sensory neuropathy (lepromatous leprosy).
  • Secondary impairments (WHO grade 2): Visible consequences of nerve damage:
    • Skin fissures and wounds
    • Clawing, contractures, and shortening of digits
    • Blindness
    • Deformities → activity limitations and social restrictions
  • Progression:
    • Neuropathy can continue even after effective MDT
    • Secondary impairments may appear years later
    • Continuous monitoring is required despite the infection being “cured”
  • Tuberculoid leprosy → asymmetric nerve involvement, localised to skin lesions
  • Lepromatous leprosy → symmetric, diffuse nerve involvement, not restricted to individual skin lesions
  • Pure neural leprosy: nerve involvement without skin lesions, can be tuberculoid or lepromatous


Sparing of superficial nerves (Option A): Superficial nerves are commonly involved in leprosy, often leading to glove-and-stocking sensory loss.


Skin lesions may continue to spread despite effective MDT (Option B): MDT effectively stops bacterial replication, so new lesions do not typically appear after treatment.


Multidrug therapy is ineffective against Mycobacterium leprae (Option D): MDT is highly effective and remains the standard treatment for all forms of leprosy.



Reference:

Andrews Diseases of the Skin: Clinical Dermatology, 13th Edition, Page 340

question: A 42-year-old man with borderline lepromatous leprosy has completed a full course of multidrug therapy (MDT). Which of the following statements about leprosy is true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Histoid leprosy is a rare variant of lepromatous leprosy presenting as well-demarcated, shiny nodules on normal skin, usually painless, with preserved sensation and abundant bacilli.


Histoid leprosy:

  • Clinical features:
    • Occurs as multiple shiny, skin‑colored cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules and plaques.
    • Nodules are well‑demarcated with normal surrounding skin.
    • Sensation (pain, touch, temperature) is usually preserved, and peripheral nerves may not be thickened.
    • May present without prior treatment or arise de novo; sometimes seen after irregular treatment or dapsone monotherapy.
  • Histopathology:
    • Dermis shows sheets of spindle‑shaped histiocytes arranged in interlacing whorls or storiform patterns.
    • Abundant acid‑fast bacilli seen on slit‑skin smear and Fite’s stain.

[[figure-1]]

  • Diagnosis & treatment:
    • Diagnosis based on clinical appearance, smear microscopy, and biopsy.
    • Managed with multibacillary multidrug therapy
    • Good clinical response reported with proper therapy.


Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4458807/
question: A 28-year-old man presents with multiple shiny, skin-colored nodules on normal-appearing skin for 1 year. Lesions are painless, well-demarcated, and sensation is preserved. Slit-skin smear shows abundant acid-fast bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is Lepra bonita (also known as "Pretty Leprosy" or Lucio's Leprosy).
  • It presents with diffuse, shiny, smooth skin, loss of natural facial lines, and high bacillary load, typically in Mexico and Latin America.
  • Ulcerations may result from the Lucio phenomenon, a vasculonecrotic complication unique to this form.


Lucio's Leprosy:

  • A severe variant of lepromatous leprosy is characterised by diffuse, non‑nodular skin infiltration.
  • Called “pretty leprosy” because the skin appears shiny and smooth, with natural lines and wrinkles obliterated.

[[figure-1]]

  • Pathogenesis:
    • Thought to stem from uncontrolled proliferation of Mycobacterium leprae (or related strains) in the skin.
    • Vascular involvement: Infiltration of blood vessel walls and thrombosis underlies many clinical features.
  • Clinical features:
    • Diffuse, shiny, myxedematous skin without nodules.
    • Flattened facial features with loss of natural skin lines.
    • Madarosis (loss of eyebrows/eyelashes) and body hair.
    • Progressive oedema, ulcerations, and vascular necrosis (Lucio phenomenon) may develop.
  • Investigations:
    • Multibacillary infection: heavy bacillary load on skin smears.
    • Histopathology: diffuse infiltration, endothelial invasion by bacilli, thrombosis.
    • Unresponsive lepromin test.
  • No specific therapy for the “pretty leprosy” variant itself.
  • Standard multidrug therapy (MDT) for leprosy is used.


Tuberculoid leprosy (Option A): Usually shows hypopigmented anaesthetic macules, few lesions, and strong cellular immunity; skin is not diffusely shiny.


Indeterminate leprosy (Option C): Early, mild, and ill-defined lesions; does not feature diffuse shiny skin or high bacillary load.


Histoid leprosy (Option D): Characterised by firm nodules, sometimes with high bacillary load; skin is not smooth or shiny, unlike lepra bonita.



Reference:

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0422763814001034

There are no nodules, but he reports easy bruising and occasional ulcerations on his lower limbs. Skin smears reveal a high bacillary load. Which form of leprosy is most likely?

Explanation:

  • Under the current WHO guidelines, this patient is classified as Multibacillary (MB) because he has numerous acid-fast bacilli on his slit-skin smear and multiple skin lesions.
  • WHO recommends 12 months of MDT for multibacillary leprosy, using rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone. This regimen effectively clears the bacterial load and prevents relapse.

question: A 35-year-old man presents with findings as shown and erythematous skin patches, diffuse thickening of peripheral nerves, and loss of sensation in his hands and feet. Slit-skin smears show numerous AFB. What is the recommended duration of multidrug therapy (MDT) according to WHO guidelines?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The drug described is Clofazimine.
  • It is a lipophilic dye used in the Multibacillary (MB) regimen that is famous for causing reddish-brown skin pigmentation and is also used to treat Type 2 Lepra reactions (ENL).
  • Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity are not associated with clofazimine; they are classically seen with aminoglycosides.


Clofazimine:

  • Brick-red, fat-soluble crystalline dye
  • Weakly bactericidal against Mycobacterium leprae
  • Anti-inflammatory effect
    • Useful in managing erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL)
  • Accumulates in:
    • Intestinal mucosa
    • Mesenteric lymph nodes (Option D)
    • Body fat
  • Adverse effects:
    • Skin discoloration (red → purple-black)
      • Dose-dependent and related to leprous infiltration
      • Fades 6-12 months after stopping (Option A)
      • Residual pigmentation may persist up to 4 years
    • Pink discoloration of urine, sputum, and sweat
    • Ichthyosis over shins and forearms
    • GI symptoms:
      • Abdominal cramps, diarrhea, weight loss
      • Due to crystal deposition in small-bowel wall (Option B)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 28.15
question: A patient with multibacillary leprosy is receiving multidrug therapy. One of the drugs causes skin discolouration, ichthyosis, and pink discolouration of urine and sweat, and also helps control ENL reactions. Which of the following is not a feature of this drug?

correctAnswer: C. Standard antitubercular therapy for 6 months
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of a chronic, slowly progressive, reddish-brown plaque on the face with "apple-jelly" nodules on diascopy is highly characteristic for Lupus Vulgaris, the most common form of cutaneous tuberculosis in adults.

[[figure-1]]

  • The recommended treatment is standard antitubercular therapy (ATT) for 6 months.


Cutaneous Tuberculosis:

  • Forms:
    • Multibacillary (low immunity):
      • Scrofuloderma
      • Tuberculous chancre
      • Orificial TB
      • Acute miliary TB
      • Tuberculous gumma
    • Paucibacillary (high immunity):
      • Lupus vulgaris (Commonest)
      • TB verrucosa cutis
      • Tuberculids (lichen scrofulosorum, papulonecrotic tuberculid, erythema induratum)
    • Tuberculids:
      • Hypersensitivity reaction
      • Bacilli absent
      • Strong tuberculin positivity
  • Histology:
    • Tuberculoid granulomas ± caseation
    • Many bacilli in multibacillary forms
  • Treatment:
    • Standard anti-TB therapy
    • 6 months (2HRZE + 4HR)


Dapsone + rifampicin for 12 months (Option A): Regimen for leprosy, not cutaneous TB.


Short-course systemic corticosteroids (Option B): May worsen TB if used alone.


Azithromycin for 8 weeks (Option D): Used for atypical infections, not TB.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 27.5 - 27.9
question: A 32-year-old woman presents with a slowly progressive, reddish-brown plaque on the cheek for 2 years. Diascopy findings are given in the image below. There is no pain or discharge. What is the recommended treatment for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - Type 4 & greater auricular nerve

Explanation:

The image shows a patient with a visibly thickened and enlarged nerve in the neck region, which is the greater auricular nerve. The question also mentions that the patient has borderline tuberculoid leprosy and is experiencing a reaction.

  • Leprosy Reactions: Leprosy reactions are episodes of acute inflammation that occur during the course of the disease. Type 1 (reversal) reactions are a form of delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction. They are caused by a sudden increase in the cell-mediated immune response to the Mycobacterium leprae bacteria.
  • Clinical Presentation: These reactions often involve inflammation of existing skin lesions and, most importantly, acute neuritis, which is the painful inflammation and enlargement of peripheral nerves. The greater auricular nerve is a common site for this nerve enlargement.

Therefore, the correct pairing is a Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction and the greater auricular nerve.

Incorrect Options:

Type 1 & greater auricular nerve (Option A) is an immediate, IgE-mediated reaction (e.g., an allergic reaction), which is not what causes leprosy reactions.

Type 2 & greater auricular nerve (Option B) is a cytotoxic, antibody-mediated reaction. A Type 2 leprosy reaction is known as erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), which presents with painful red nodules and is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction.

Type 3 & anterior auricular nerve (Option C) is an immune complex-mediated reaction. A Type 2 leprosy reaction (ENL) is an example of this. The anterior auricular nerve is not the most commonly affected nerve.



Reference:

.
question: A patient with borderline tuberculoid leprosy presents with the following findings. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction and nerve is enlarged?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In a patient with a progressive, asymptomatic lesion over the neck, clinically suggestive of Lupus Vulgaris (a form of cutaneous tuberculosis), the most helpful investigation would be skin biopsy and TB workup.

  • It is a chronic, progressive, paucibacillary (not multibacillary) form of cutaneous tuberculosis.
  • Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous TB seen in adults (M/C in females).
  • Causative organisms: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium bovis.
  • Pathogenesis :
    • Route of spread: Endogenous spread or from exogenous inoculation.
    • It occurs in a previously sensitized individual with an increased cell-mediated immunity to tuberculin.
  • Clinical features:
    • Presents as a single or a group of erythematous violaceous annular plaques with central scarring and atrophy with active margins.
    • The periphery shows erythematous deep-seated nodules which on diascopy may stand out as apple jelly nodules.

[[figure-1]]

  • Most commonly seen in the buttocks, upper extremities, and face.
  • Papules may recur within scarred areas, enlarging and coalescing into large, firm, elevated plaques.
  • Treatment: Antitibercular therapy.
  • Complication: Secondary scarring and squamous cell carcinoma may develop rarely.

KOH preparation (Option 1) is used to detect superficial fungal infections like tinea or candidiasis by identifying fungal elements in skin scrapings. Since lupus vulgaris is a form of cutaneous tuberculosis, KOH is not helpful for its diagnosis.

HIV testing (Option 4) is useful in immunocompromised patients or atypical infections, but this patient has a localized, slow-growing lesion without systemic signs. It doesn't directly help diagnose lupus vulgaris and isn't a first-line test.



Reference:
  • Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 27.21 27.22
  • Bolognia Textbook of Dermatology, 4th Edition, Page 1306.
question:
A patient presents with a progressive and asymptomatic lesion over the neck region and no systemic symptoms. Which of the following investigations would be helpful?

  1. KOH preparation
  2. Skin biopsy
  3. Chest X-ray (TB workup)
  4. HIV testing

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous tuberculosis, often arising from hematogenous or lymphatic spread from a latent pulmonary focus.
  • Clinical clue: indurated plaque with central atrophy on the face + old TB lesion in the lung (apical calcification).
  • PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA is the most sensitive and specific test to confirm cutaneous TB.
  • PCR detects bacterial DNA even when bacillary load is low (as in lupus vulgaris, which is paucibacillary).
  • While Mantoux may support diagnosis, it is not confirmatory

[[figure-1]]

Lupus vulgaris

  • Chronic, progressive, paucibacillary (not multibacillary) form of cutaneous tuberculosis.
  • Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous TB seen in adults (M/C in females).
  • Causative organisms: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium bovis.

Pathogenesis :

  • Route of spread: Endogenous spread or from exogenous inoculation.
  • It occurs in a previously sensitized individual with an increased cell-mediated immunity to tuberculin.

Clinical features:

  • Presents as a single or a group of erythematous violaceous annular plaques with central scarring and atrophy with active margins.
  • The periphery shows erythematous deep-seated nodules which on diascopy may stand out as apple jelly nodules.
  • Most commonly seen in the buttocks, upper extremities, and face.
  • Papules may recur within scarred areas, enlarging and coalescing into large, firm, elevated plaques.
  • Diagnosis is often confirmed by histopathological examination of skin biopsy specimens, which typically show caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli.

[[figure-2]]

The above image depicts the Apple Jelly Nodule

Complication:

  • Secondary scarring and squamous cell carcinoma may develop rarely.

Treatment :

  • Anti-tubercular drugs.

Mantoux test (Option A): Indicates prior sensitization to TB but cannot confirm active disease; may be positive in BCG-vaccinated individuals and other mycobacterial infections.

Slit skin smear (Option B): Useful for detecting acid-fast bacilli in leprosy, not for cutaneous TB where bacillary load is very low.

Probe test (Option D): Used in oral submucous fibrosis to assess fibrous bands in the oral mucosa; not related to lupus vulgaris diagnosis.
question: A patient presents with an indurated plaque on the cheek with central atrophy. Chest X-ray reveals apical calcification. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Tuberculoid leprosy with a positive antigen test
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presentation of hypopigmented nodular lesions with sensory loss, ulnar nerve thickening, and biopsy showing epithelioid cell granulomas is characteristic of tuberculoid leprosy.

  • Lesions are well-defined with anesthesia due to nerve involvement.

  • Non-caseating granulomas with epithelioid cells are seen histologically.

  • The Lepromin (intradermal antigen) test is positive, indicating strong cell-mediated immunity.

Lepromatous leprosy with a positive antigen test (Option B): Lepromatous leprosy shows a negative lepromin test due to poor cell-mediated immunity.

Erythema nodosum leprosum with a negative antigen test (Option C): ENL is a Type II lepra reaction, not a primary form of leprosy.

Lepromatous leprosy with a negative antigen test (Option D): Although the test result fits, the clinical features (few anesthetic lesions, nerve thickening, granulomas) indicate tuberculoid, not lepromatous, leprosy.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559307/

question:
A 38-year-old patient presents with hypopigmented nodular skin lesions and loss of sensation over the arm. On examination, there is thickening of the ulnar nerve. A skin biopsy reveals epithelioid cell granulomas, and an intradermal lepromin (antigen) test is performed.
Which of the following statements most accurately describes this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Continue MDT and add oral steroids
explanationHtml:
Answer: D) Continue MDT and add oral steroids

Explanation:

Type 2 lepra reaction (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL) is an immune complex-mediated reaction seen in multibacillary leprosy. Pregnancy does not alter the management of leprosy itself, and stopping multidrug therapy (MDT) is not recommended. The preferred treatment for type 2 reactions includes oral corticosteroids, which are safe in pregnancy. Thalidomide is strictly contraindicated due to teratogenicity.

Leprosy and Its Management in Pregnancy

Aspect

Details

Cause of Leprosy

Mycobacterium leprae

Types of Reactions

Type 1 (Reversal), Type 2 (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum)

Type 2 Lepra Reaction

Immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity)

Common Symptoms

Painful nodules, fever, malaise, neuritis

Management of Type 2 Reaction

Corticosteroids (safe in pregnancy)

Role of MDT in Pregnancy

Must be continued to prevent relapse

Drugs to Avoid

Thalidomide (teratogenic)

Management of Type 2 Lepra Reaction in Pregnancy

Aspect

Details

Continue MDT

Essential to prevent disease relapse

Preferred drug

Oral steroids (prednisolone)

Avoid in pregnancy

Thalidomide (teratogenic, causes phocomelia)

Supportive therapy

Analgesics, wound care if ulcerated lesions present

Alternative options

Clofazimine has mild immunomodulatory effects

Stop MDT and start oral steroids (Option A) is incorrect because stopping MDT can lead to disease relapse and worsening nerve damage. MDT must be continued while managing the reaction with steroids.

Antibiotics (Option B) is incorrect because type 2 lepra reaction is an inflammatory immune response, not an infectious complication. Antibiotics have no role in managing ENL itself.

Thalidomide (Option C) is incorrect because thalidomide is highly teratogenic (causing phocomelia and limb defects) and is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Although thalidomide is an effective treatment for ENL, it should never be used in pregnant women.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s textbook of dermatology 9th edition page no.- 28.15 to 28.16
  2. Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Pages 211, 212

question: What is the preferred treatment for a pregnant woman who is 12 weeks pregnant and undergoing multidrug therapy for leprosy but is now experiencing type 2 lepra reaction?

explanationHtml:
Answer: D) Paucibacillary leprosy

Explanation:

  • Hypopigmented patches with sensory loss strongly suggest leprosy rather than other dermatological conditions.
  • Well-demarcated, slightly raised lesions are characteristic of paucibacillary leprosy, which presents with five or fewer skin lesions with nerve involvement.
  • Skin smears revealing no acid-fast bacilli indicate a low bacterial load, confirming paucibacillary leprosy rather than multibacillary leprosy.

Leprosy:

Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, primarily affecting the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucosa of the upper respiratory tract. It presents in a spectrum based on bacterial load and immune response.

Multibacillary leprosy (Option A) is incorrect because MB leprosy presents with multiple lesions, often widespread, with no sensory impairment in early stages and a positive skin smear for Mycobacterium leprae (acid-fast bacilli). This patient’s negative smear and limited lesion count favour paucibacillary leprosy.

Psoriasis (Option B) is incorrect because psoriatic plaques are erythematous with silvery scales, not hypopigmented. Sensory loss is not a feature of psoriasis, and skin smears do not play a role in its diagnosis.

Tinea versicolor (Option C) is incorrect because pityriasis (tinea) versicolor, caused by Malassezia spp., presents with hypo- or hyperpigmented macules, but there is no sensory loss. The lesions are typically scaly, and a KOH mount would reveal spaghetti and meatballs appearance (yeast and hyphae).

question: A 30-year-old patient presents to the clinic with hypopigmented patches on the skin. On examination, there are a few well-demarcated, slightly raised lesions with a loss of sensation. Skin smears reveal no acid-fast bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows multiple, irregular, erythematous plaques and lesions distributed on the trunk, which are characteristically seen in borderline lepromatous leprosy.

  • It typically presents with numerous, asymmetrical plaques and infiltrated lesions of varying sizes and shapes across the trunk and limbs.
  • In BL Leprosy, the bacilli are trying to invade the surrounding area, and there is a central invasion called an inverted saucer appearance.

Ridley-Jopling Classification of Leprosy:

  1. Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) – Few well-demarcated hypopigmented patches with complete loss of sensation. Strong cell-mediated immunity (CMI).
  2. Borderline tuberculoid (BT) – Multiple asymmetrical lesions, less well-defined than TT, with some sensory loss.
  3. Borderline leprosy (BB) – Intermediate form, variable lesions with partial sensory loss, and patchy nerve involvement.
  4. Borderline lepromatous (BL) – Numerous lesions resembling LL but with some sensory impairment.
  5. Lepromatous leprosy (LL) – Diffuse, symmetrical lesions with loss of eyebrows, leonine facies, and late nerve damage. Poor CMI response.

Lepromatous leprosy (Option B): Usually shows numerous, symmetric, small nodules, papules, or diffuse infiltration. The lesions are more uniform and widespread, commonly involving the face and earlobes.

Borderline leprosy (Option C): Fewer lesions than BL but with more defined margins.

Histoid leprosy (Option D): Characterized by firm, nodular lesions that are often shiny and dome-shaped, usually on a background of lepromatous leprosy.



Reference:

Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9nd Edition Chapter 28 Page No 28.11
question: The image given below is characteristically seen in which of the following types of leprosy?

correctAnswer: D. Indeterminate leprosy have more remission than tuberculoid
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Indeterminate leprosy is the earliest form of leprosy, presenting with a single or few ill-defined hypopigmented macules and minimal sensory loss.
  • In many cases, spontaneous remission occurs, particularly in individuals with a strong cell-mediated immune (CMI) response.
  • Tuberculoid leprosy, while having a strong immune response, tends to be chronic and persistent, with less likelihood of spontaneous remission.

Indeterminate Leprosy:

  • Early, undifferentiated form of leprosy.
  • Few hypopigmented macules with slight sensory impairment.
  • Histopathology: Mild inflammation, sparse acid-fast bacilli (AFB).
  • Fate:
    • Can resolve spontaneously (~25–75% of cases).
    • May progress to tuberculoid or lepromatous forms, depending on immune response.

Tuberculoid Leprosy:

  • Well-demarcated plaques with sensory loss, few lesions.
  • Strong CMI response, granuloma formation.
  • Less likely to remit spontaneously, tends to persist unless treated.

Outcomes if Untreated:

  • Indeterminate leprosy has a higher chance of spontaneous remission compared to tuberculoid leprosy.
  • If it does not resolve, it may progress toward the tuberculoid or lepromatous spectrum based on immune status.

No spontaneous remission is seen (Option A) is incorrect because spontaneous remission does occur, particularly in indeterminate and early tuberculoid leprosy, especially in individuals with good immunity.

Half of the cases resolve spontaneously after bacilli exposure (Option B) is incorrect because while some individuals clear the infection, the proportion is variable and not as high as 50% in all populations.

Spontaneous remission is more common in children than in adults (Option C) is incorrect because although children may have a higher rate of spontaneous resolution, the likelihood of remission is more dependent on the type of leprosy (indeterminate vs tuberculoid) rather than age alone.



Reference:

Rook's textbook of dermatology 9th edition page no.- 28.5, 28.6

question: Which of the following will be the outcome of Leprosy , if left untreated.

correctAnswer: B. Continue MDT, start systemic steroids
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Deterioration of preexisting lesions + nerve involvement in a patient on MDT suggests Type 1 Lepra Reaction (Reversal Reaction).
  • Type 1 Reaction is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction in borderline leprosy due to increased cell-mediated immunity.
  • Management:
    • Continue MDT: The reaction is due to immune response, not drug failure.
    • Start systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone) to reduce inflammation and prevent permanent nerve damage.

Lepra Reactions

Type

Mechanism

Clinical Features

Management

Type 1 (Reversal Reaction)

Increased cell-mediated immunity (CMI)

Worsening of existing lesions, erythema, edema, nerve pain

Continue MDT, start systemic steroids (prednisolone)

Type 2 (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum - ENL)

Immune complex deposition (TNF-α mediated)

Painful nodules, fever, neuritis, systemic symptoms

Continue MDT, start thalidomide or steroids

Stop MDT, start systemic corticosteroids (Option A): Incorrect because MDT should not be stopped; the reaction is due to immune response, not drug toxicity.

Stop MDT, start thalidomide (Option C): Incorrect because thalidomide is used for Type 2 reaction (ENL), not Type 1 reaction.

Continue MDT, start thalidomide (Option D): Incorrect because thalidomide is ineffective for Type 1 reactions; steroids are preferred.



Reference:

Rook’s textbook of dermatology 9th edition page no.- 28.15 to 28.16

question: What would be your next best course of action when a patient undergoing multi-drug therapy (MDT) exhibits deterioration of preexisting lesions and nerve involvement?

explanationHtml:
Answer: B) Anti-tubercular therapy

Explanation:

  • The image shows annular plaque with central scarring which is suggestive of Lupus vulgaris, a form of cutaneous tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. It presents as a chronic, slowly progressive skin lesion with an annular (ring-shaped) plaque and central scarring.
  • Anti-tubercular therapy: Anti-tubercular therapy is the treatment of choice for lupus vulgaris. It consists of a combination of drugs, including isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. These medications target Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative organism, and aim to eradicate the infection.

Cutaneous TB:

Exogenous:

Endogenous:
  • Source of MTB is from outside the body
  • First exposure to TB - new to TB infection is Naive infection
    • Called TB chance
    • No immunity
  • Once had TB but now recurred due to Exogenous causes:
    • Tuberculosis Verrucous cutis (TBVC)
    • Immunity present
  • Source is within the body
  • Transmitted to skin by:
    • Contiguous (ex: lymphatic TB breaking into skin) - Scrofuloderma
    • Hematogenous - Lupus vulgaris, TB gumma and miliary TB
    • Auto miliary TB
    • Auto inoculation - or Orificial TB

1. TB Chancre / Primary Inoculation TB

[[figure-1]]

2. TBVC or Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis

[[figure-2]]

1. Lupus Vulgaris

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

Apple jelly nodules on diascopy

2. Scrofuloderma

[[figure-5]]

3. Orificial Tuberculosis

[[figure-6]]

Management

  • All forms of cutaneous TB have the same treatment.
  • Total 6 months treatment:
    • 2 months: Intensive phase = HERZ for 2 months.
    • 4 months: Maintenance phase = HRE for 4 months.
  • HERZ = Isoniazid, ethambutol, rifampicin and pyrazinamide.
  • Doses
    • Isoniazid (H): 5mg/kg/day
    • Rifampicin = 10 mg/kg/day
    • Ethambutol (E): 15 mg/kg/day
    • Streptomycin (S): 15 mg/kg/day
    • Pyrazinamide (P): 25 mg/kg/day


Incorrect Options:

Anti-fungal therapy (Option A) is not the appropriate treatment for lupus vulgaris. While superficial fungal infections can also present as annular lesions, the clinical presentation and diagnostic criteria mentioned in the question suggest a mycobacterial infection rather than a fungal infection.

Topical steroids therapy (Option C): Topical steroid therapy is not the primary treatment for lupus vulgaris. While topical steroids may be used in some cases to alleviate inflammation and itching, they do not address the underlying mycobacterial infection and are not the mainstay of treatment.

Anti-leprosy treatment (Option D): Anti-leprosy treatment is not the correct choice for lupus vulgaris. Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, is a separate disease entity and requires specific anti-leprosy drugs for treatment. It is not indicated for the management of lupus vulgaris.



Reference:
  1. Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology and Sexually Transmitted Diseases, Fifth Edition – Neena Khanna Pg 268-271
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482220/
question: Please determine the medication utilized for the management of the presented medical condition:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Clinical Features in the question/ image:
    • The image suggests facial swelling with muscle weakness, commonly seen in leprosy (Hansen’s disease).
    • The Facial Nerve (CN VII) is commonly involved in lepromatous leprosy, leading to facial palsy and lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye).
  • Facial Nerve Involvement in Leprosy:
    • Mycobacterium leprae infiltrates Schwann cells, causing neuropathy.
    • This leads to weakness of facial muscles, particularly affecting the orbicularis oculi, resulting in lagophthalmos.
    • Loss of motor control can contribute to facial asymmetry and trophic ulcers.

Facial Nerve Involvement in Leprosy

Feature

Facial Nerve (CN VII) Involvement

Function

Motor to facial muscles, taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue

Affected Branches

Zygomatic & Buccal branches

Symptoms in Leprosy

Facial weakness, inability to close eye (lagophthalmos), drooping face

Complications

Corneal ulcers, facial deformity

Abducens nuclei (Option A): Incorrect because CN VI controls lateral eye movement, not facial sensation or motor function.

Optic nerve (Option C): Incorrect because CN II controls vision, not facial movement or sensation.

Trigeminal nerve (Option D): Incorrect because CN V mainly controls sensation, whereas the image suggests a motor deficit affecting facial expressions.



Reference:

Rook's Textbook of Dermatology 9th Edition Chapter 28 Page No. 28.1- 28.15

Erythrasma:

  • Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, obesity, immunocompromised state, hyperhidrosis, and older adults.

question: A 28-year-old man presents with asymptomatic brownish patches in the axilla. A Wood’s lamp examination image is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows Gram-positive organisms arranged in grape-like clusters, indicative of Staphylococcus aureus.

  • S. aureus causes direct skin infections, secondary infections, and toxin-mediated diseases, making all listed conditions associated with it.


Cutaneous Diseases Caused by Staphylococcus aureus:

1. Direct infection of skin & adjacent tissues

  • Impetigo
  • Ecthyma
  • Folliculitis
  • Furunculosis
  • Carbuncle
  • Sycosis
  • Occasionally cellulitis

2. Secondary infection:

  • Eczema
  • Infestations
  • Chronic ulcers, wounds

3. Toxin-mediated cutaneous disease:

  • Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)
  • Toxic shock syndrome (TSS)
  • Staphylococcal scarlatina
  • Recurrent toxin-mediated perineal erythema

correctAnswer: C. Inoculation through a skin breach from contaminated animal products
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely mode of transmission is inoculation through a skin breach from contaminated animal products.

Erysipeloid:

  • Erysipeloid (also known as "whale finger" or "seal finger" in specific industries) is an occupational zoonosis caused by the bacterium Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae.
  • Organism persists in soil for months
  • Reservoirs: pigs (most important), fish, shellfish, birds, mammals
    • Occupational disease:
      • Butchers, fishermen, cooks, farmers, veterinarians
  • Transmission:
    • Direct inoculation through skin breaks
    • More commonly from animal carcasses than live animals
  • Clinical forms:
    • Localized cutaneous (most common):
      • 3 days post-injury
      • Tender violaceous erythema, sharp border
      • Hands/fingers; minimal fever
      • Self-limiting (≈2 weeks)
    • Generalized cutaneous:
      • Multiple violaceous lesions, central clearing
      • Blood cultures negative
    • Systemic (rare):
      • Aortic valve endocarditis, joints, bone, CNS
      • Blood cultures positive
  • Treatment:
    • First line: Penicillin
    • Alternatives: Ciprofloxacin, Erythromycin
    • Second line: Tetracyclines
    • Severe/systemic → IV penicillin


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 26.46, 26.47
