question: A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a generalized vesicular rash covering the entire body. The child's parents report that the rash started as red spots and quickly developed into fluid-filled blisters. The child also has a mild fever and is feeling irritable. What is the most likely diagnosis for this child's condition?

explanationHtml:
• The development of skin lesions in areas of trauma or injury is referred to as Koebner's phenomenon, also known as the isomorphic response. It is a typical finding in a few skin conditions, including psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo, and morphea.
  • Koebner's peculiarity isn't found in all skin conditions, nonetheless, and one condition in which it is commonly not noticed is rosacea.

Incorrect choices:

  • Option a. Vitiligo: Vitiligo is an immune system sickness. When the immune system attacks melanocyte-containing cells in the body it results in vitiligo. These are pigment-making cells.
  • Option b. Psoriasis: Psoriasis is a skin condition that typically manifests as a rash with itchy, scaly patches on the scalp, trunk, knees, and elbows. Psoriasis is a prevalent, chronic, and long-term condition that has no cure.
  • Option c. Lichen planus: Lichen planus is a condition of the skin, hair, nails, mouth, and genitals. On the skin, lichen planus often appears as purple, itchy, flat bumps that develop over several weeks.
question: Which of the following does not exhibit the Koebner's phenomenon?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The condition described is Pityriasis Versicolor, also known as Tinea Versicolor. The term "tinea" is a misnomer, as this infection is caused by the Malassezia species (including M. globosa, M. sympodialis, and M. furfur), not by dermatophytes like Microsporum or Trichophyton.

Signs and Symptoms:

  • Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules: Most commonly hypopigmentation due to the fungus's production of Azelaic Acid or Carboxylic Acid, found in the trunk, back, and chest.
  • Lesions are often covered with fine “branny” scales, which are accentuated upon scraping; this sign is called the Besnier Sign or the Coup De Angle Sign.

[[figure-1]]

Examination Findings:

  • Wood's Lamp Examination: It is typically yellow or gold in color, attributed to the presence of porphyrins produced by Malassezia species.

[[figure-2]]

  • KOH Preparation: "Spaghetti and meatball" aka “Banana and Grapes” appearance.

[[figure-3]]

Treatment:

  • Topical Antifungal Agents such as ketoconazole cream or shampoo, selenium sulfide lotion, or ciclopirox olamine solution are used as first-line treatment.
  • Oral Terbinafine and Griseofulvin do not help in the treatment of Tinea.


Microsporum audouinii (Option B)

Trichophyton rubrum (Option C)

Epidermophyton floccosum (Option D)

The three fungi mentioned above are dermatophytic fungi that do not cause ptyriasis versicolor; they cause tinea in various body parts.



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: During your rural service, a patient arrives at the OPD with hypopigmented lesions on his trunk and back. A Wood’s lamp examination of the lesions shows yellow fluorescence, and scales become prominent when the lesion is scratched with nails. Which of the following organisms causes this infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features are characteristic of pityriasis (tinea) versicolor, a superficial fungal infection caused by Malassezia species.

  • Although Malassezia globosa is the most common causative species worldwide, Malassezia furfur remains the answer here.

Clinical Features

  • Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules over the trunk, back, chest, and proximal upper limbs
  • Fine furfuraceous (branny) scales
  • Hypopigmentation results from azelaic acid, which inhibits tyrosinase and reduces melanin synthesis.
  • Besnier's sign (Coup d'ongle sign): Fine scales become more prominent on scratching.

[[figure-1]]

Investigations

  • Wood's lamp: Yellow-gold (or coppery-yellow) fluorescence.

[[figure-2]]

  • KOH preparation: Short, curved hyphae with clusters of yeast cells producing the classic "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance.

[[figure-3]]

Treatment:

  • Topical antifungal agents (first-line): Ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, ciclopirox, or topical terbinafine.
  • Oral antifungals (extensive disease): Itraconazole or fluconazole.
  • Oral terbinafine and griseofulvin are ineffective for pityriasis versicolor.

Microsporum audouinii (Option B) is a dermatophyte that primarily causes tinea capitis and does not cause pityriasis versicolor.

Trichophyton rubrum (Option C) is the most common dermatophyte causing tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea pedis, and onychomycosis, but is not responsible for pityriasis versicolor.

Epidermophyton floccosum (Option D) is a dermatophyte causing tinea cruris, tinea pedis, and onychomycosis and is not a cause of pityriasis versicolor.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.10-32.13
question: During your rural service, a patient arrives at the outpatient department with hypopigmented lesions over the trunk and back. A Wood's lamp examination shows yellow-gold fluorescence, and fine scales become more prominent when the lesions are scratched with a fingernail. Which of the following organisms causes this infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dandruff, also known as seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, is commonly caused by Malassezia furfur.
  • KOH mount shows the characteristic "spaghetti and meatball" appearance, which refers to thin, branching hyphae (spaghetti) along with clusters of spores or arthroconidia (meatballs) of Malassezia yeast. The appearance is also called the banana and grapes appearance.

[[figure-1]]

Pilot wheel appearance (Option B) is typically observed in paracoccidioidomycosis (thick-walled cysts with multiple, narrow-necked buds attached circumferentially - Mickey mouse appearance).

[[figure-2]]

Conidia and conidiophores (Option C) are structures commonly seen in cultures of Aspergillus fungi.

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

Pseudohyphae (Option D) are chains of elongated yeast cells that lack septa, also commonly observed in Candida infections.

[[figure-5]]



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: What would you expect to see on KOH examination of a scalp fleck from a patient with chronic dandruff?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario describes Seborrheic Dermatitis caused by the Malessezia (globosa [Most common] and furfur species) fungus.
  • It is characterised by erythematous, greasy, and scaly lesions, often accompanied by itching and discomfort, in immunocompromised patients, as described in the image above.
  • Primarily affects areas rich in sebaceous glands, such as the scalp, face, and upper trunk.
  • Seborrheic dermatitis is also associated with other conditions, such as Parkinson's disease and immunosuppression.
  • Treatment involves topical antifungal agents, such as ketoconazole or ciclopirox.
  • Malessezia is known to cause folliculitis, Seborrheic dermatitis, dandruff, and confluent reticulate papillomatosis.

On the other hand, piedra is a fungal infection of the hair shaft caused by fungi of the genus Trichosporon (white piedra) and piedra (black piedra).


Folliculitis (Option A): Malassezia can lead to folliculitis, particularly pityrosporum folliculitis. It typically presents with erythematous papules or pustules centred around hair follicles, which may be tender or pruritic.

[[figure-1]]

Dandruff (Option B) also known as pityriasis capitis or seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, is commonly associated with Malassezia spp., the same organism implicated in the patient's symptoms.

[[figure-2]]

Confluent Reticulate Papillomatosis (CRP) (Option C), also known as Gougerot-Carteaud syndrome, is a rare dermatosis characterised by brown, reticulated papules typically affecting the neck and upper trunk. Malassezia spp is known to be the organism implicated in CRP.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: A 67-year-old actress, diagnosed with HIV 20 years ago, presents to your OPD with complaints of itching and flaking on her eyelids and scalp. The examination findings are shown in the image below. Which of the following conditions is not caused by the organism responsible for this patient's symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The condition described is most likely a kerion, a type of inflammatory tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) caused by Trichophyton verrucosum.
  • Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp that predominantly affects children.
  • Kerion presents with symptoms, including patchy hair loss, scaling, and, in some cases, a painful, boggy swelling.
  • The characteristic feature of kerion is its inflammatory nature, with erythematous, tender nodules commonly oozing pus
  • It is often encountered in agricultural settings where there is exposure to infected animals, particularly cattle.

  • KOH examination: Presence of branching hyphae.
  • Wood's lamp examination: No specific findings.
  • The inflammatory nature of kerion distinguishes it from other fungal infections.

Tinea schoenleinii (Option A), also known as favus, typically presents with thick, yellow, cup-shaped crusts known as scutula rather than painful, boggy swellings as seen in Kerion. It exhibits green fluorescence on Wood's lamp.


Microsporum canis (Option C) often presents as an itchy “grey patch” associated with hair loss. Wood's lamp examination may reveal fluorescent hairs in some cases. Exophytic growth is seen in microsporium.


Trichophyton concentricum (Option D) is associated with tinea corporis, a superficial fungal infection of the body. Endophytic growth is seen in trichophyton.



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: On your annual visit to the local orphanage in farmland to celebrate your birthday, you notice a 5-year-old boy crying due to a painful, boggy swelling on his scalp, shown in the image below. Multiple other boys in the orphanage also have areas of patchy, scaly hair loss. Which of the following is the causative organism of this patient’s findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario suggests tinea nigra. Tinea nigra is a painless, superficial fungal infection primarily affecting the palms and is characterized by darkly pigmented, flat, non-scaly patches.

Tinea nigra:

  • Superficial fungal infection of the skin caused by the fungus Hortaea werneckii (formerly known as Exophiala werneckii).
  • Pathology: Thickening of stratum corneum (in which hyphae are present) and minimal inflammation of the dermis.
  • Features:
    • Asymptomatic, macular, sharply defined and non-scaly lesions.
    • The most distinctive feature is the brown or black, resembling a silver nitrate stain.
    • Areas affected: Palms (M/C), soles, neck, and trunk.
  • Microscopy with a KOH mount shows pigmented filaments with conidia, abundant brown, branched, closely septate hyphae up to 5 μm in diameter, and elongated budding cells.

[[figure-1]]

  • Treatment: It is usually treated with topical antifungal agents. The most commonly used topical agents include azoles (clotrimazole or ketoconazole) or allylamines (terbinafine).

Melanocytic nevus (Option A): A melanocytic nevus is a benign growth of melanocytes, typically presenting as a brown or tan mole with well-defined borders, and don’t typically show the gradual increase in size described here without other features like irregular borders or color variation.

[[figure-2]]

Dermatofibroma (Option B): Dermatofibromas are usually small, firm, brown or tan nodules, not macules, and they typically occur on the limbs rather than the palms.

[[figure-3]]

Lichen planus (Option D): Lichen planus typically presents with purplish, flat-topped papules and often involves the wrists, shins, or mucous membranes.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Pages 32.14, 32.15
question: During a health check-up in a tropical coastal region, a 30-year-old patient presents with a well-demarcated, non-pruritic, dark brown macule on their palm. The lesion has gradually increased in size over the past few months. There is no associated pain or scaling. Based on the clinical findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The lesion depicted in the image shows an irregular, erythematous, scaly plaque without central clearing, lack of annularity and indistinct border of the lesions which is characteristic of tinea incognito.
  • The prolonged use of topical corticosteroids can mask typical features of tinea, resulting in misdiagnosis and worsening of the condition.
  • In this case, the patient's history of visiting multiple local "healing clinics" that probably used local steroid ointments and the lesion worsening after initial improvement suggest a diagnosis of tinea incognito.

[[figure-1]]

Causative Organisms: Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton species.

Treatment:

  • Stop corticosteroids.

  • Apply topical antifungals (azoles or allylamines).

  • Treat secondary infections if present.

  • Educate on proper steroid use.

Tinea manuum (Option A) is a dermatophyte infection of the hands, typically presenting with erythematous, scaly lesions on the palms and interdigital spaces.

[[figure-2]]

Tinea profunda (Option C) is a rare deep dermatophyte infection that involves invasion of the hair follicles and surrounding dermis, resulting in boggy nodules and abscess formation.

[[figure-3]]

Tinea corporis (Option D) is a dermatophyte infection affecting the trunk, limbs, or face, characterised by annular, erythematous lesions with central clearing and an active border.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: A 27-year-old boy comes to your OPD complaining of an itchy rash over his forearm for the past 8 months. He gives history of unsupervised use of over the counter creams ,but it has only gotten worse after short-lived improvements. An image of the lesion is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis ?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Distal Lateral Subungual Onychomycosis is the most common type of fungal infection of the toenail (Onymychosis) or Tinea Unguium.

Clinically, onychomycosis presents with nail discoloration, thickening, subungual keratin buildup, onycholysis, and nail dystrophy.

Diagnosis: Typically involves microscopic examination using KOH and fungal culture of nail clippings.

Treatment:

  • Oral antifungals such as terbinafine and itraconazole are often preferred.
  • Nail lacquers such as ciclopirox (applied daily), olamine and amirolfine (applied weekly) are also used as topical agents to treat onychomycosis.

The table below describes the types of onychomycosis

Distal lateral subungual onychomycosis
  • Most common
  • Primarily affecting the distal & lateral portions of the nail.

Proximal subungual onychomycosis
  • Seen in individuals with HIV.
  • Affects the proximal portion of the nail plate.

Superficial white onychomycosis

Characterized by the presence of white, crumbly material on the surface of the nail, which can be easily scrapped off

Total dystrophic onychomycosis

Characterized by extensive involvement of the nail plate, leading to complete destruction & deformity of the nail

[[figure-1]]

Paronychia (Option B) refers to an infection of the soft tissues surrounding the nail, often presenting with erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the nail folds.

[[figure-2]]

Nail Psoriasis (Option C) is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the nails, characterised by pitting, subungual hyperkeratosis, and oil drop discolouration.Absence of salmon pink sign and skin plaques can be used to differentiate from psoriasis

[[figure-3]]

Onychogryphosis (Option D), also known as ram's horn nails, is a condition characterised by abnormal thickening and curvature of the nails, typically affecting the toenails, most commonly caused by improper footwear, trauma, ichthyosis, psoriasis and fungal infections

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: A 62-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presents to the dermatology clinic with discoloured nails. The examination findings are shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The condition described, characterised by narrow, soft, white nodules loosely attached to the hair shafts, is consistent with a diagnosis of White Piedra caused by Trichosporon beigelii.
  • The differences between black and white piedra are given in the table below:

White Piedra

Black Piedra

Etiology

Trichosporon beigelii

Piedra horteii

Consistency

Soft

Hard, gritty

Attachment to the hair shaft

Loosely attached

Tightly attached

Location

All hair-bearing areas

Over the scalp
Images

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Piedra horteii (Option A): As described above, Piedraia hortae causes black piedra, characterised by hard, dark nodules on the hair shafts.


Trichosporon cutaneum (Option C): Associated with skin infections and other superficial infections.


Trichophyton violaceum (Option D): This dermatophyte fungus causes tinea infections of the skin and nails and may rarely affect the hair shaft.



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: A student from a hostel dormitory visits you with complaints of narrow nodules on her hair shafts. On examination, you find that these nodules are loosely attached to the surface of the hair, white in colour and soft in consistency. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of multiple erythematous, tender patches on the inferior surface of both breasts with multiple satellite lesions is highly indicative of intertrigo, a type of cutaneous candidiasis.

Candida intertrigo (Flexural candidiasis):

Candida Intertrigo:

  • Sites: Groin, buttocks, axillae, inframammary folds, umbilicus, toe/finger webs.

  • Features: Red macerated plaques with fringed edges, satellite pustules, itching, soreness.

  • Cause: Candida albicans (thrives in warm, moist areas).

  • Risk factors: Diabetes, immunosuppression, obesity, antibiotics, steroids, pregnancy.

  • Treatment: Topical clotrimazole/miconazole/nystatin; oral fluconazole or itraconazole if severe.

[[figure-1]]

.

[[figure-2]]

Trichophyton Circinata (Tinea) (Option B) causes dermatophyte infections that present as ring-shaped, circular patches on the skin. The lesions often have a clear central area with scaly, red edges.

[[figure-3]]

Streptococcus pyogenes (Erysipelas) (Option C):

  • Presents with well-demarcated, erythematous, raised lesions with a fiery red appearance.
  • It typically affects the face and extremities.

[[figure-4]]

Malassezia furfur (Pityriasis versicolor) (Option D): Pityriasis versicolor, caused by Malassezia furfur, presents with hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the skin, typically on the trunk, neck, and upper arms.

[[figure-5]]



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: A 67-year-old lady with diabetes comes to your OPD complaining of itching under her breasts. On examination, you see multiple erythematous, tender patches on the inferior surface of both breasts with multiple satellite lesions as shown in the image below. What is the causative organism and the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of a frayed appearance, superficial pustules, and the presence of pseudohyphae on KOH examination is indicative of Balanitis due to Candida infection.

Oral fluconazole is preferred for treating Candida infections involving the genital area due to its systemic action and effectiveness in eradicating the fungal infection in immunocompromised individuals.

[[figure-1]]

Diagnosis of Candidiasis:

  • KOH prep: Budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae.

  • Culture (SDA): Creamy white, smooth colonies.

  • Germ tube test: C. albicans shows germ tube formation after serum incubation at 37°C for 2–3 hrs.

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Local application of nystatin gel (Option A): Nystatin is an antifungal agent effective against Candida, commonly used to treat oral thrush and vulvovaginal candidiasis. However, its local application may not be adequate for treating balanitis, particularly if the infection is extensive or involves deeper tissue layers.


Local application of terbinafine ointment (Option C): Terbinafine is primarily used to treat dermatophyte infections, such as tinea corporis or tinea cruris, and is ineffective against Candida species.


Oral griseofulvin (Option D) – Ineffective against Candida infections as it primarily targets dermatophyte fungi by inhibiting microtubule function.



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
question: A 35-year-old uncircumcised male patient with a T-cell deficiency presents to your outpatient clinic. On examination, a frayed appearance and the presence of superficial pustules on the penis is noted. A KOH examination reveals the following findings. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image above describing a white plaque on the tongue, resembling cottage cheese in an immunocompromised patient, is suggestive of chronic plaque/ leukoplakia candidiasis
  • In individuals with untreated HIV/AIDS, oral candidiasis is a common opportunistic infection.
  • Management of HIV/AIDS involves initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) as the primary intervention.
  • Treatment with nystatin gargles, oral fluconazole, and oral ketoconazole- the various treatments for oral candidiasis can be initiated after ART has been started.

Oral Thrush can present as:

Red Lesions

White Lesions

Acute Lesions

Antibiotic sore mouth (due to usage of antibiotics)

[[figure-1]]

Pseudomembranous Thrush (can be scraped off)

[[figure-2]]

Chronic Lesions

Chronic Erythematous/ Denture Stomatitis

[[figure-3]]

Chronic Plaque/ leukoplakia (cannot be scraped off)

[[figure-4]]

Tongue biopsy (Option A): While biopsy may be considered if the diagnosis is uncertain or if premalignant lesions (submucal fibrosis, erythroleukoplakia, etc) are suspected, the priority, in this case, is to address the underlying HIV infection with ART.


Nystatin gargle and Oral Fluconazole (Option B) are antifungal agents that may be used for oral candidiasis, but it is not the first-line treatment in individuals with untreated HIV/AIDS.


Topical corticosteroid therapy (Option D): Corticosteroids are contraindicated in oral candidiasis as they can exacerbate fungal infections by suppressing the immune response.



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Chapter 216
question: A 40-year-old heroin and nicotine abuser with a 20-year history of untreated HIV comes to your community clinic complaining of a white patch on his tongue. You are unable to scrape the lesion off, and examination findings are given in the image below. What is the next best step of management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The lesion is consistent with chronic plaque-like (hyperplastic) candidosis (Candida leukoplakia).

  • It presents as a persistent, firm, irregular white plaque on the tongue or buccal mucosa that cannot be scraped off.
  • Oral candidiasis is the most common secondary infection in patients with HIV/AIDS, and recurrent or prolonged episodes are common.
  • In patients with AIDS, oral candidiasis frequently fails to respond to topical polyene therapy.
  • Oral fluconazole or itraconazole is the preferred treatment.
  • For chronic hyperplastic candidosis, topical therapy often has a poor response, making fluconazole (100-200 mg/day) or itraconazole (100-200 mg/day) more effective.
  • Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) improves therapeutic outcomes in patients with AIDS but does not replace antifungal therapy for active oral candidiasis.

Tongue biopsy (Option A): May be considered if the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude leukoplakia, but it is not the initial treatment for clinically evident chronic plaque-like candidosis.

Topical corticosteroid therapy (Option C): Topical steroids predispose to oral candidiasis and may worsen the infection. They have no role in its treatment.

Oral acyclovir (Option D): Acyclovir is an antiviral used for herpes simplex virus infections and is ineffective against Candida infections.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.61-32.70
question: A 40-year-old man with untreated HIV presents with a persistent white plaque over the tongue, as shown in the image. The lesion cannot be scraped off. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this oral lesion?

correctAnswer: B. Wedge-shaped hair perforations along the hair shaft
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The hair perforation test is used to identify species of Trichophyton mentagrophytes from other dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum. Trichophyton causes characteristic wedge-shaped perforations along the hair shaft, as shown in the image below; this is called a positive perforation test.

[[figure-1]]

Steps with hair perforation test:

  • A strand of blonde, autoclaved hair is placed in water in a vial and incubated at room temperature.
  • It is then inoculated with the test fungus.
  • Individual hair is removed at intervals of up to 4 weeks and examined microscopically in lactophenol cotton blue.
  • Isolates of T. mentagrophytes produce marked localised areas of pitting and erosion.
  • Isolates of T. rubrum (a more common cause of tinea) do not produce marked pitting or erosion.

Absence of hair perforation (Option A) – Seen in Trichophyton rubrum, which does not produce significant hair perforations, unlike T. mentagrophytes.


Circular perforations inside the hair shaft (Option C) – More characteristic of Trichophyton verrucosum, which forms internal perforations instead of wedge-shaped indentations.


Parallel perforations on either side of the hair shaft (Option D) – Not a recognized pattern in dermatophyte infections



Reference:

Ananth Narayanan and Panniker Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page 601

options.text: Wedge-shaped hair perforations along the hair shaft
Circular perforations inside the hair shaft
Parallel perforations on either side of the hair shaft

question: Which pattern is most likely to be observed in the hair perforation test result of Trichophyton mentagrophytes infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s presentation, along with the linear distribution of nodules, is suggestive of sporotrichosis/ Rose Gardner’s disease caused by Sporothrix schenckii.

Sporotrichosis (Rose Gardener’s Disease):

  • Sporotrichosis (Rose Gardener’s Disease):

  • Cause: Sporothrix schenckii from thorn/splinter injury; spreads via lymphatics.

  • Risk: Farmers, gardeners, barefoot walkers.

  • Types: Lymphocutaneous (MC), fixed cutaneous, osteoarticular, pulmonary, disseminated.

  • Diagnosis: KOH—cigar-shaped yeast; histology—asteroid bodies (Splendore-Hoeppli); culture—definitive.

  • Treatment: Itraconazole (DOC); Amphotericin B for disseminated; potassium iodide alternative.

The image below shows the culture of S. schenckii:

[[figure-1]]

The image below shows the asteroid body and Splendour Hoeppli phenomenon:

[[figure-2]]

Black Granules (Option B) Seen in mycetoma (Madura foot) caused by M. mycetomatis; Actinomycetoma shows yellow “sulphur” granules with discharging sinuses.

Madura foot:

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

Histopathology of Actinomycotic mycetoma:

[[figure-5]]

Muriform bodies (Option C) Seen in chromoblastomycosis—slow-growing, verrucous lesions in farmers after thorn injury; shows sclerotic (Medlar) cells.

[[figure-6]]

Spherules containing endospores (Option D) are characteristic of coccidioidomycosis, a systemic fungal infection.

[[figure-7]]

[[figure-8]]



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32
  2. Essentials of Medical Microbiology, Apurba Sastry, 3rd edition, page 580-1
question: At your community medicine posting, a farmer arrives complaining of multiple nodules over his right leg after being pricked by a thistle. Examination findings are given in the image below. What would you expect to find on a microscopic examination of tissue from one of his lesions?

correctAnswer: B. Fungal elements can be demonstrated in the dermatophytid lesions
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dermatophytid (id) reaction is a hypersensitivity response to dermatophyte antigens.
  • No fungus is present in the id lesions; fungal elements are found only at the distant primary site.


Dermatophytid (Id Reaction):

  • Hypersensitivity reaction to dermatophyte antigens (Option A)
  • Fungus in lesions: Absent
  • Occurs with: Inflammatory tinea capitis, tinea pedis; during griseofulvin therapy (Option C)
  • Sites: Trunk, face, ears, extremities, hands/sides of fingers
  • Lesions: Vesicular, papular, lichenoid, papulosquamous (± pustular)
  • Symptoms: Intensely pruritic
  • Histology: Spongiosis, superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate (± eosinophils)
  • Diagnosis: Fungus present at distant primary site, absent in the id lesion
  • Treatment: Treat primary fungal infection → rapid resolution (Option D)
  • Poor response to topical steroids alone

Types of Id reactions:

  • Dermatophytid → from tinea (esp. pedis/capitis)
  • Candidid → from candidiasis
  • Bacterid → from bacterial infections (e.g., stasis dermatitis)
  • Scabid → from scabies
  • Pediculid → from lice infestation


Reference:

Andrew’s Diseases of the Skin, Clinical Dermatology, 13th Edition, Page 294

options.text: Fungal elements can be demonstrated in the dermatophytid lesions
It may occur during antifungal therapy
Treating the primary infection leads to resolution

question: Which of the following statements regarding dermatophytid reactions is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis is best treated with oral miltefosine, especially in Indian patients, to eliminate the dermal reservoir.


Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL):

  • Definition: Dermal manifestation appearing during or after recovery from kala-azar due to persistence of amastigotes in the skin.
  • Timing:
    • Africa: During or soon after treatment
    • India: Delayed, up to 10 years post-treatment
  • Clinical Types:
    • Macular, depigmented lesions: face, arms, upper trunk
    • Papular/warty lesions: amastigotes demonstrable
  • Duration: May persist up to 20 years
  • Significance: Acts as a chronic reservoir of visceral leishmaniasis
  • Resembles: Hansen’s disease (leprosy)
  • Immunology: High IL-10 levels predict PKDL development
  • Treatment: Miltefosine - drug of choice


Sodium stibogluconate (Option A): Increasing resistance, no longer first-line


Amphotericin B (Option B): Effective but used for resistant/severe cases


Dapsone (Option D): Used for leprosy, not leishmaniasis



Reference:

Andrew’s Diseases of the Skin, Clinical Dermatology, 13th Edition, Page 426
question: A man develops hypopigmented macules and papules on the face and trunk years after treatment of kala-azar. Skin biopsy shows amastigotes in dermal macrophages. What is the drug of choice for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cutaneous leishmaniasis classically presents as a chronic painless ulcer evolving from a papule at the site of a sandfly bite, with raised margins and central crusting.
  • Demonstration of amastigotes in macrophages on Giemsa stain confirms the diagnosis.


Cutaneous Leishmaniasis:

  • Cause: Leishmania (protozoa)
  • Vector: Sandfly
    • Old World: Phlebotomus
    • New World: Lutzomyia
  • Clinical features:
    • Incubation: weeks to months
    • Lesions on exposed areas (face, arms, neck)
    • Progression: papule → nodule → crust → ulcer → scar
  • Important Species & Patterns:
    • L. major: Wet, rural, rapid ulceration
    • L. tropica: Dry, urban, slow healing
    • L. aethiopica: Facial nodules, chronic
    • L. mexicana: Ear lesion → Chiclero ulcer
    • L. brasiliensis: Large ulcers + mucocutaneous spread
  • Treatment:
    • Many heal spontaneously
    • Local: Cryotherapy, intralesional antimonials
    • Systemic: Pentavalent antimonials
    • Alternatives: Amphotericin B, Miltefosine (oral)


Lupus vulgaris (Option A): Tuberculous skin lesion with apple-jelly nodules on diascopy; amastigotes are not seen.


Chromoblastomycosis (Option C): Presents as verrucous plaques; shows Medlar (copper-penny) bodies on microscopy.


Buruli ulcer (Option D): Caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans; produces painless, undermined ulcers but no amastigotes.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 33.40 - 33.48
question: A 10-year-old child from an endemic area presents with a painless, non-healing ulcer on the forearm for 6 weeks. It began as a papule after an insect bite and gradually ulcerated. Giemsa stain shows intracellular amastigotes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lutzomyia sand flies transmit Leishmania mexicana, which causes Chiclero ulcer, a localised form of cutaneous leishmaniasis typically affecting the ear in endemic regions of Central America and southeastern Mexico.


Chiclero ulcer:

[[figure-1]]

  • Chiclero’s ulcer is a form of localised cutaneous leishmaniasis, typically involving the ear, caused by Leishmania mexicana.
  • Characterised by a chronic ulcerative skin lesion, most often on the pinna (outer ear) - a hallmark of Chiclero’s ulcer.
  • It occurs in endemic regions of Mexico and Central America, particularly where L. mexicana is transmitted by sand flies.
  • Diagnosis typically involves clinical recognition supported by laboratory confirmation (e.g., parasite detection/PCR).


African sleeping sickness (Option A): Caused by Trypanosoma brucei and transmitted by tsetse flies (Glossina species), not sand flies.


Malaria (Option B): Caused by Plasmodium species and transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, not sand flies.


Chagas disease (Option D): Caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by triatomine (kissing) bugs, not sand flies.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3205629/
question: Lutzomyia species is the vector of which condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is Chromoblastomycosis.
  • Chronic verrucous plaque after traumatic implantation with biopsy showing sclerotic (Medlar) bodies is diagnostic.

Chromoblastomycosis

Epidemiology
  • Common among barefoot agricultural workers and woodcutters.
  • Common in tropical and subtropical regions

Causative agents

Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common), Cladophialophora carrionii, Phialophora verrucosa, Fonsecaea compacta, Exophiala dermatitidis

Route of transmission

Infecting fungi enter the skin by traumatic implantation.

Clinical manifestation
  • Warty, cutaneous nodular lesions (resemble the florets of cauliflower).
  • Usually confined to the subcutaneous tissue of the feet and lower legs
  • Slow-developing lesions around the site of implantation.

Diagnosis

Microscopy: The lesions show the presence of the fungus as round or irregular, dark brown, yeast-like bodies with septa, called sclerotic bodies (other names: muriform bodies, copper pennies, medlar bodies).

Demonstration of these sclerotic bodies in KOH mounts or tissue sections, and by culture on Sabouraud agar.

Treatment

First line:

  • Itraconazole 100–200 mg/day until clinical cure
    or
  • Terbinafine 250 mg/day until clinical cure

Refractory / alternative:

  • Flucytosine ± amphotericin B (avoid flucytosine monotherapy due to resistance)

Second line / adjunct:

  • Local heat therapy or cryotherapy for 2–3 months (small/localized lesions)

Surgery:

  • Only for very small lesions
  • Always combine with antifungals (risk of satellite lesions if used alone)



Mycetoma (Option A): Characterised by painless swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and grain discharge, not verrucous plaques.


Sporotrichosis (Option B): Presents as nodules spreading along lymphatic channels (“rose gardener’s disease”); no Medlar bodies.


Cutaneous tuberculosis (Option D): Causes plaques or ulcers but lacks sclerotic bodies on histopathology.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.76 - 32.78
  2. Ananthanarayan & Paniker, Textbook of Microbiology, 6th Edition, Pages 604-607
  3. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470253/#:~:text=The%20disease%20is%20most%20common,.%5B8%5D%5B9%5D
question: A 50-year-old agricultural worker presents with a chronic, slowly enlarging, verrucous plaque on the leg for several years following a thorn injury. Biopsy reveals findings as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Painless swelling, multiple sinuses, grain discharge, and bone involvement are classic of mycetoma.
  • Black grains specifically indicate a fungal (eumycetoma) cause, most commonly Madurella mycetomatis.


Mycetoma:

  • Chronic localised infection by fungi (eumycetoma) or actinomycetes (actinomycetoma)
  • Triad: painless swelling + draining sinuses + grains
  • Epidemiology:
    • Tropics/subtropics; agricultural workers
    • More common in adult males; rare in children
    • Long latency (years–decades)
  • Mode of infection: Traumatic implantation (thorns/soil), not contagious
  • Causative agents:
    • Eumycetoma: Madurella mycetomatis (most common), Scedosporium apiospermum
    • Actinomycetoma: Nocardia brasiliensis, Actinomadura madurae, Streptomyces somaliensis
  • Clinical features:
    • Firm painless nodule → multiple sinuses with grainy discharge
    • Common site: foot
    • Late: osteomyelitis, deformity; minimal pain
  • Diagnosis:
    • Grain exam (microscopy/histology)
    • Black grains usually indicate eumycetoma; actinomycetoma grains are typically white/yellow/red depending on the organism.
    • MRI is best for bone involvement
  • Complication: Bone destruction, deformity
  • Treatment:
    • Actinomycetoma (1st line): dapsone + streptomycin
      or co-trimoxazole + streptomycin/rifampicin
    • Eumycetoma: ketoconazole/itraconazole/voriconazole (limited response)
    • 2nd line: radical surgery/amputation


Actinomycosis (Option A): Causes chronic sinuses with sulfur granules, usually involving the cervicofacial, thoracic, or abdominal regions & not the foot; grains are not black.



Botryomycosis (Option B): Chronic bacterial infection with granules, but lacks the classic triad of mycetoma and rarely causes extensive bone destruction with multiple sinus tracts.


Chronic bacterial osteomyelitis (Option D): May cause sinuses and bone changes, but does not produce grains and usually has pain and systemic signs, unlike mycetoma.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.73 - 32.76
question: A 38-year-old male agricultural worker from a tropical region presents with a slowly progressive, painless swelling of the foot for 5 years. Examination shows multiple draining sinus tracts discharging black granules & bony destruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Oriental sore (cutaneous leishmaniasis) shows a central ulcer with raised, indurated margins, giving the classic “volcano” appearance.

[[figure-1]]


Volcano sign:

  • Seen in Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis (Oriental sore)
  • Enlarged nodule with central ulceration and crusting
  • Surrounded by a rim of erythema
  • Appearance resembles an erupted volcano


Cutaneous anthrax (Option A): Characterized by a painless papule that progresses to a vesicle and then a black eschar with surrounding edema


Sporotrichosis (Option C): Presents with nodular lesions spreading along lymphatic channels (rose gardener’s disease)


Pyoderma gangrenosum (Option D): Causes painful, rapidly progressive ulcers with undermined violaceous edges



Reference:

https://ijdvl.com/cutaneous-signs-in-infectious-diseases/
question: The “volcano sign” is characteristically seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Redness (erythema) of the oral mucosa is the hallmark of atrophic (erythematous) candidosis, where the mucosa becomes denuded and inflamed, commonly affecting the dorsum of the tongue.

[[figure-1]]


Oral candidosis:

  • Candida: normal oral commensal → disease with local/systemic immunosuppression (steroids, HIV, neutropenia, antibiotics)


Types:

  • Acute pseudomembranous (Option A): White, curd-like, scrapable plaques
  • Acute atrophic (erythematous): Red, painful, denuded mucosa
  • Chronic pseudomembranous: Persistent thrush-like lesions
  • Chronic atrophic (denture stomatitis): Red palate under denture
  • Chronic plaque-like (hyperplastic) (Option C): White non-scrapable plaques
  • Chronic nodular (Option D): Rare, cobblestone tongue
  • Angular cheilitis (Perlèche): Fissures at the mouth angles
  • Median rhomboid glossitis: Diamond-shaped depapillated tongue


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.61 - 32.63
question: Redness of the oral mucosa is most characteristically seen in which type of oral candidosis?

correctAnswer: C. It is always associated with Candida infection
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Perlèche (angular cheilitis) is not always associated with Candida infection.


Angular Cheilitis:

[[figure-1]]

  • Definition: Soreness and fissuring at mouth angles (Option A); may occur without Candida
  • Synonyms: Angular stomatitis, Perlèche
  • Pathogenesis: Intertrigo; Candida is the most common (Option B), aided by moisture (saliva/lip licking), deep folds, poor nutrition, and denture stomatitis (Option D)
  • Source of yeast: Oral cavity
  • Clinical: Acute or chronic; recurrent cracking and soreness
  • Evaluation: Examine the oral cavity; swabs from the mouth and lesions


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 32.63

Candida is the most common organism involved
It is always associated with Candida infection
Denture stomatitis is an important associated factor

question: Which of the following statements regarding perlèche is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of an annular lesion with an active, scaly, raised border and central clearing, along with risk factors for dermatophyte exposure, is classic for tinea corporis.


Tinea Corporis:

  • Dermatophyte infection of glabrous skin (trunk & limbs); stratum corneum ± terminal hair.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Acquired from humans/animals/fomites (rarely soil)
    • Incubation 1–3 weeks
    • Centrifugal spread → often central clearing
    • Zoophilic → more inflammatory; T. rubrum → chronic
  • Common organisms: T. rubrum (most common), M. canis (zoophilic)
  • Features:
    • Annular, well-marginated plaques with raised edges
    • Scaling ± central clearing
    • Vesicles/pustules in inflammatory lesions
    • T. rubrum: extensive, psoriasiform, poor central clearing
  • The KOH mount shows branching septate hyphae
  • Treatment:
    • Localised: Topical terbinafine BD × 2 weeks
      or topical azole × 2–4 weeks
    • Widespread: Oral terbinafine 250 mg/day × 2–3 weeks
      Or itraconazole 100 mg/day × 2–4 weeks
    • Second line: Griseofulvin 1 g/day × 4 weeks


Nummular eczema (Option A): Coin-shaped plaques, but usually no raised active margin or central clearing.

[[figure-1]]


Psoriasis vulgaris (Option B): Psoriasis typically shows well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and lacks an active advancing border or central clearing

[[figure-2]]


Pityriasis rosea (Option D): Usually symmetrical, trunk-predominant, often preceded by a herald patch.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.35 - 32.38
question: A 28-year-old man presents with an itchy, slowly enlarging rash on his forearm for 3 weeks. Examination shows findings as shown. There is no history of fever. He works in a gym and shares towels with others. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Club-shaped macroconidia are characteristic of Epidermophyton floccosum, the only dermatophyte that lacks microconidia.


Dermatophytes:

  • Trichophyton:
    • Affects skin, hair, and nails
    • Examples: T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, T. tonsurans
    • Macroconidia: Pencil-shaped / cigar-shaped (Option C and D)
    • Microconidia: Abundant

[[figure-1]]

  • Microsporum:
    • Affects skin and hair
    • Does not infect nails
    • Examples: M. canis, M. audouinii
    • Macroconidia: Abundant (hallmark), Spindle-shaped (Option A)
    • Microconidia: Few

[[figure-2]]

  • Epidermophyton:
    • Affects skin and nails
    • Does not infect hair
    • Only species: Epidermophyton floccosum
    • Macroconidia: Club-shaped (clavate)
    • Microconidia: Absent

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.25 - 32.32
question: A 24-year-old man presents with pruritic, annular, scaly plaques in the groin and upper thigh. The KOH mount shows septate hyphae. Fungal culture grows a dermatophyte that produces only macroconidia and no microconidia. What is the characteristic shape of the macroconidia of this organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • KOH examination of skin scrapings is the first-line diagnostic test for tinea faciei and demonstrates branching septate hyphae, even when scaling is minimal or absent.


Tinea faciei:

  • Dermatophyte infection of glabrous facial skin (excludes beard/moustache area).
  • Predisposing factors:
    • Direct animal contact
    • Spread from tinea elsewhere
    • Steroid misuse (tinea incognito)
  • Causative organisms:
    • Common: T. mentagrophytes, T. rubrum
    • Others: T. tonsurans, M. canis, M. audouinii, T. concentricum
  • Clinical features:
    • Itching, burning, photosensitivity
    • Erythema ± scaling
    • Annular/circinate plaques
    • Raised indurated margins
    • Steroids → altered morphology
  • Diagnosis:
    • KOH scraping (even if no scale)
    • Examine whole skin + scalp
    • Stop steroids → rebound scaling
  • Treatment:
    • Localised: Topical imidazoles/tolnaftate
    • Extensive / steroid-modified: Oral terbinafine or itraconazole
    • Duration: 3–6 weeks


Skin biopsy for histopathology (Option A) is rarely required in tinea faciei and is generally avoided on the face. Most cases can be confirmed with KOH examination.


Antinuclear antibody (ANA) test (Option B) is used to support a diagnosis of discoid lupus erythematosus, a common misdiagnosis of tinea faciei, but it does not diagnose dermatophytosis.


Patch testing (Option D) is used for allergic contact dermatitis and has no role in diagnosing fungal infections.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 32.42
question: A 28-year-old woman presents with an itchy, erythematous patch on the cheek for 3 weeks, as shown. The lesion worsens after sun exposure and has shown partial improvement with topical steroids, but recurs on stopping them. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Microsporum species causing ectothrix tinea capitis respond best to griseofulvin, which remains the drug of choice, especially in children.


Tinea Capitis - Management:

  • Topical agents: Adjunct only (no monotherapy)
  • Oral antifungals:
    • Terbinafine: Best for Trichophyton
      • <10 kg: 62.5 mg | 10–20 kg: 125 mg | >20 kg: 250 mg
      • Duration: 4 weeks
    • Itraconazole: 2–4 mg/kg/day × 4–6 weeks
    • Griseofulvin: Best for Microsporum
      • 10 mg/kg/day × ≥6 weeks
      • 20 mg/kg/day for T. tonsurans / T. schoenleinii
  • Kerion:
    • Wet compresses help with crusting/oozing; secondary bacterial infection should be treated with antibiotics if present.
    • Steroids only if severe inflammation
  • Adjunct: Ketoconazole or selenium sulphide shampoo (to reduce spread)


Terbinafine (Option A): More effective for Trichophyton species; relatively less effective against Microsporum.


Itraconazole (Option B): Can be used as an alternative, but not first-line, for Microsporum tinea capitis.


Fluconazole (Option D): Has activity against Trichophyton; limited and less reliable efficacy for Microsporum infections.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 32.40
question: A 6-year-old boy presents with findings as shown in the image. Examination shows broken hairs and mild erythema. KOH mount reveals ectothrix spores surrounding the hair shaft. What is the drug of choice?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Tinea cruris involves the groin and is classically referred to as the Dhobie itch, especially in tropical climates.


Tinea Cruris: (Dhobie itch, Eczema marginatum)

  • Dermatophyte infection of the groin.
  • Epidemiology:
    • Adults > children
    • Males > females
    • Hot, humid climates
  • Causative organisms:
    • Trichophyton rubrum (most common)
    • T. interdigitale
    • Epidermophyton floccosum
  • Clinical features:
    • Intense itching
    • Well-defined erythematous plaques
    • Raised scaly margins
    • Partial central clearing
    • Chronic lesions → nodular/beaded edge

[[figure-1]]

  • Management:
    • Recent: topical terbinafine/imidazole × 2 weeks
    • Chronic/extensive:
      • Terbinafine 250 mg/day × 1–2 weeks
      • Itraconazole 100 mg/day × 2–4 weeks

Types of Tinea (Dermatophytosis):

Type

Site

Tinea capitis

Scalp, hair

Tinea barbae

Beard area

Tinea faciei

Face (non-beard)

Tinea corporis

Body (glabrous skin)

Tinea cruris

Groin

Tinea pedis

Feet (toe webs)

Tinea manuum

Hands

Tinea unguium

Nails

Tinea imbricata

Trunk/extremities


Ringworm of the scalp (Option A): Refers to tinea capitis, a dermatophyte infection of the scalp and hair, not the groin.


Athlete’s foot (Option B): Refers to tinea pedis, a dermatophyte infection of the feet and toe webs, not the groin.


Barber’s itch (Option C): Refers to tinea barbae, a dermatophyte infection of the beard area, not the groin.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 32.46
question: Tinea cruris is commonly known by which of the following names?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • T. rubrum is the most common cause of tinea pedis worldwide, especially the chronic dry (moccasin) type, and is frequently associated with onychomycosis


Tinea pedis:

  • Tinea pedis is a dermatophyte infection of the feet and toe webs.
  • Causative organism:
    • T. rubrum (most common)
    • T. interdigitale (Option A), E. floccosum (Option B)
  • Clinical types:
    • Interdigital: maceration, fissuring, scaling (commonest)
    • Dry / Moccasin: hyperkeratotic scaling of sole → T. rubrum
    • Vesiculobullous: inflammatory vesicles on sole → T. interdigitale
  • Complications: Cellulitis (esp. in lymphoedema)
  • Management:
    • Interdigital: topical azole × 4 weeks or topical terbinafine × 7 days
    • Dry type: terbinafine 250 mg/day × 2 weeks

or

  • Itraconazole 400 mg/day × 1–2 weeks


Candida albicans (Option D): A yeast causing candidiasis and intertrigo; it is not a dermatophyte and does not cause classic tinea pedis.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.43 - 32.46
question: A 35-year-old man presents with chronic itching and scaling of the soles and sides of both feet for several years. Examination shows findings as shown in the image below. Toenails are thickened and discoloured. What is the most common causative organism in this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Endothrix tinea capitis due to Trichophyton tonsurans
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Black dots result from hair shafts breaking at the scalp surface, which is classic for endothrix hair invasion, where arthroconidia are within the hair shaft.

  • T. tonsurans is the most common cause.

[[figure-1]]


Tinea capitis:

  • Dermatophyte infection of the scalp with hair shaft invasion.
  • Causative organisms:
    • Common: T. tonsurans, T. violaceum, M. canis
    • Favus: T. schoenleinii
    • Never cause: E. floccosum, T. concentricum, T. interdigitale
  • Types of Hair Invasion:
    • Ectothrix (Microsporum): outside hair, broken hairs, Wood’s lamp +ve (Option A)
    • Endothrix (T. tonsurans): inside hair, black dots, Wood’s lamp -ve
    • Favus (T. schoenleinii): scutula, scarring alopecia, faint fluorescence (Option C)
  • Clinical features:
    • Patchy alopecia + broken hairs + scaling
    • Kerion: boggy, painful, inflammatory mass, pus, lymphadenopathy
  • Management:
    • Oral therapy mandatory:
      • Terbinafine × 4 weeks
      • Itraconazole × 4-6 weeks
      • Griseofulvin × ≥6 weeks (best for Microsporum)


Alopecia areata (Option D): Smooth bald patches, no broken hairs or black dots



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.38 - 32.40

options.text: Ectothrix tinea capitis due to Microsporum canis
Endothrix tinea capitis due to Trichophyton tonsurans

question: A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple patchy areas of hair loss over the scalp for 2 months. Examination shows black dots on the scalp surface as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dermatophytes belong to three genera only: Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton.
  • Candida albicans is a yeast causing candidiasis, not dermatophytosis.


Dermatophytes:

  • Trichophyton (Option A):
    • Affects skin, hair, and nails
    • Examples: T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, T. tonsurans
  • Microsporum (Option B):
    • Affects skin and hair
    • Does not infect nails
    • Examples: M. canis, M. audouinii
  • Epidermophyton (Option C):
    • Affects skin and nails
    • Does not infect hair
    • Only species: Epidermophyton floccosum


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 32.18, 32.19
question: Which of the following organisms is not a cause of developing lesions as shown in the image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dermatophytes are keratinophilic fungi (e.g., Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) that have the unique ability to digest keratin using keratinases.
  • Because of this, they are strictly confined to keratinised, non-viable tissues - namely the stratum corneum of the epidermis, hair shafts, and nails.
  • In cutaneous infection (tinea corporis, etc.), the fungi remain limited to the stratum corneum and do not invade living epidermis or the dermis.
  • The centrifugal spread with central clearing seen clinically reflects outward growth of the fungus in the stratum corneum with relative clearing in the centre as host immunity suppresses fungal load there.


Dermis (Option A): Dermatophytes do not invade the dermis; any dermal involvement is due to secondary inflammatory reaction, not the presence of fungi.


Stratum basale (Option B): This is a living layer of the epidermis and is not invaded by dermatophytes.


Stratum spinosum (Option C): Another viable epidermal layer that dermatophytes do not penetrate.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 32.21
question: A 24-year-old man presents with an annular, scaly, mildly pruritic plaque on the trunk. KOH examination of skin scrapings shows branching septate hyphae. The inflammatory response extends into the dermis, but the fungus itself is confined to a specific layer of the skin. Which layer is directly invaded by dermatophytes?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presentation is typical of eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma).
  • Black granules indicate a dematiaceous (pigmented) fungus.
  • On KOH mount, it appears as septate, pigmented hyphae.
  • Hyphae are 4–5 µm wide, distinguishing them from bacterial filaments.
  • This is the definitive KOH finding confirming eumycetoma.

Incorrect Answers:

  • Option A) Arthrospores: Found in actinomycetoma (bacterial mycetoma), thin and non-pigmented.

  • Option B) Slender dematiaceous fungi: While the fungi are dematiaceous and slender, "septate hyphae 4–5 µm" is a more specific and accurate description of the structures observed in a KOH mount.

  • Option C) Yeast: Unicellular, lacks hyphae; inconsistent with black granules and filamentous morphology.



Reference:

question: A patient presents with irregular swelling over the foot, multiple discharging sinuses, and black granules. A KOH mount is performed on the discharge. What is the most likely observation?

explanationHtml:
• Tavaborole is a topical oxaborole antifungal specifically approved for onychomycosis of the toenails.
  • It inhibits fungal leucyl-tRNA synthetase, disrupting protein synthesis.
  • Onychomycosis is the fungal infection of the toenail (Onymychosis) or Tinea Unguium.
  • Clinically, onychomycosis presents with various manifestations, including
    • Discoloration of the nails (yellow, brown, or white),
    • Thickening of the nail plate,
    • Subungual hyperkeratosis (build-up of keratin debris under the nail),
    • Onycholysis (separation of the nail plate from the nail bed),
    • Nail dystrophy (deformation of the nail)
  • Diagnosis: typically involves microscopic examination using KOH and fungal culture of nail clippings.
  • Treatment:
    • Oral antifungals such as terbinafine and itraconazole are often preferred.
    • Nail lacquers such as ciclopirox (applied daily) olamine and amirolfine (applied weekly) are also used as topical agents to treat onychomycosis.

The table below describes the types of onychomycosis

Distal lateral subungual onychomycosis

Most common

Primarily affecting the distal & lateral portions of the nail

Proximal subungual onychomycosis

Seen in individuals with HIV

The proximal portion of the nail plate

Superficial white onychomycosis

Characterized by the presence of white, crumbly material on the surface of the nail, which can be easily scrapped off

Total dystrophic onychomycosis

Characterized by extensive involvement of the nail plate, leading to complete destruction & deformity of the nail

[[figure-1]]

Itraconazole (Option A): Oral antifungal – Used for onychomycosis but given systemically, not topically.

Griseofulvin (Option C): Oral antifungal – Primarily used for dermatophytosis; less effective for toenail infections.

Caspofungin (Option D): Echinocandin antifungal – Used for systemic fungal infections like invasive candidiasis, not for onychomycosis.

https://www.healthline.com/health/onychogryphosis
question: A 60-year-old female with a great toe infection. She had a significant discoloration with a subungual hyperkeratosis that caused surface changes. She was suspected of onychomycosis. Which is the topical drug given in toenail onychomycosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Tinea incognito is a term used to describe fungal infections, specifically tinea (ringworm), that have been modified or worsened due to the inappropriate use of topical steroids. In this case, the patient's history of prolonged steroid use has likely led to the modification of the typical clinical appearance of the fungal infection.
  • The expanding rash, reduced redness and itchiness, well-defined slightly raised plaques with central clearing, and scaly border all point to tinea incognito.
  • The use of steroids can mask the inflammatory response and alter the clinical presentation, making it challenging to recognize the underlying fungal infection.

Tinea corporis (Option B): Tinea corporis, also known as ringworm, is a fungal infection of the skin characterized by red, itchy, circular, or oval lesions with an active border and central clearing. While the patient's presentation does involve some elements seen in tinea corporis (such as well-defined plaques and central clearing), the fact that the patient has been using steroids and the alteration of the typical symptoms makes tinea incognito a more appropriate diagnosis in this case.

Tinea cruris (Option C): Tinea cruris, commonly referred to as jock itch, is a fungal infection that affects the groin and inner thighs. It typically presents as red, scaly, and sometimes itchy lesions with well-defined borders. The patient's symptoms are not limited to the groin area, and the modification of symptoms due to steroid use suggests a different diagnosis.

Tinea pedis (Option D): Tinea pedis, also known as athlete's foot, is a fungal infection affecting the feet. It can cause redness, itching, and scaling between the toes and on the soles of the feet. The patient's presentation involves lesions on various parts of the body and the modification of symptoms due to steroid use, which makes tinea incognito a more suitable diagnosis.



Reference:

.
question: A 35-year-old patient presents to the OPD with a history of prolonged use of steroids for a skin condition. The patient complains of an expanding rash that has become less red and itchy since using the steroids. On examination, there are well-defined, slightly raised, erythematous plaques with central clearing and a scaly border on various parts of the body. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Painful inflammatory swelling on the scalp.
    • Chronic duration (3 months).
    • Associated with a pet dog, suggesting a zoophilic fungal infection.
  • Classic Appearance:
    • Boggy, pustular mass with crusting and hair loss.
    • Purulent discharge.
    • Seen in tinea capitis (Trichophyton species, Microsporum canis - from pets).
  • Most Likely Diagnosis: Kerion (inflammatory tinea capitis)

[[figure-1]]

Kerion and Tinea Capitis Variants

Feature

Kerion (Inflammatory Tinea Capitis)

Non-inflammatory Tinea Capitis

Cause

Zoophilic fungi (Microsporum canis, Trichophyton mentagrophytes)

Anthropophilic fungi (Trichophyton tonsurans)

Appearance

Boggy, pustular, inflammatory swelling

Dry, scaly patches with black dots

Hair loss

Yes, scarring alopecia if untreated

Yes, but non-scarring

Pain/Discharge

Painful, pus-filled lesions

Painless, no pus

Diagnosis

KOH mount, Wood’s lamp (fluoresces with Microsporum)

KOH mount, culture

Treatment

Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine, topical antifungals

Oral antifungals, ketoconazole shampoo

Furuncle (Option A): Incorrect because it is a bacterial infection (S. aureus) and lacks hair loss.

Epidermoid cyst (Option B): Incorrect because cysts are non-inflammatory, firm, and do not drain pus.

Folliculitis (Option D): Incorrect because it presents as multiple small pustules, not a boggy mass.



Reference:

Rook’s Dermatology, 9th Edition, Volume 1, Section 32

  • Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton & Microsporum).

  • Inflammatory variants of tinea capitis include:

    • Kerion: Severe inflammatory reaction with pustules, abscesses, and hair loss.

    • Favus: Chronic infection with yellow crusts (scutula), leading to scarring alopecia.

question: Which type of alopecia is commonly associated with inflammatory alopecia in a 30-year-old male patient who presents with tinea capitis infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Madurella mycetomatis is the commonest cause of eumycetoma producing black grains.
  • Histopathology shows chronic inflammation with neutrophilic abscesses, giant cells, fibrosis, and black granules discharged through multiple sinuses.
  • It is a dark-grain fungus and the grains represent microcolonies found in pus.

Incorrect Options:

Actinomadura madurae (Option B) produces white/yellow grains, not black; it causes actinomycetoma, not eumycetoma.

Nocardia brasiliensis (Option C) is associated with pale/yellowish grains; an actinomycete, not a black-grain fungus.

Streptomyces somaliensis (Option D) causes actinomycetoma with yellow/white grains, not black granules.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition., Page 992-994
question: A farmer presents to the outpatient department with the lesion shown. Examination of the discharge reveals black granules. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In classical scabies, the female mite (Sarcoptes scabiei) creates characteristic serpiginous burrows within the Stratum corneum.

Scabies (Family Sarcoptidae):

  • Cause: Sarcoptes scabiei var. Hominis

[[figure-1]]

  • Clinical features:
    • Intense nocturnal pruritus
    • Burrows: thin, serpiginous lines
    • Sites: finger webs, wrists, axillae, buttocks, genitalia
    • Face spared in adults

[[figure-2]]

  • Variants

    • Infants: Vesicles, pustules, scalp involved
    • Elderly: Palms, soles
    • Scabies incognito: Steroid-modified
    • Crusted scabies: Hyperkeratotic, minimal itch, highly contagious

Treatment:

  • General principles
    • Treat patient + all close contacts simultaneously
    • Apply neck down (include scalp in infants/elderly/crusted)
    • Repeat after 7 days
  • Infants (<2 months)
    • Sulfur (5–10%) ointment → safe
    • Avoid permethrin
  • Children (>2 months)
    • Permethrin 5% cream (DOC)
      • Apply overnight (8–12 hrs)
    • Alternative: Benzyl benzoate (diluted)
  • Adults
    • Permethrin 5% cream (first-line)
    • Oral ivermectin (2 doses: day 1 & 7)
      • Indications:
        • Poor compliance
        • Outbreaks
        • Crusted scabies
  • Crusted scabies
    • Combination therapy:
      • Oral ivermectin (multiple doses)
      • Permethrin (repeated)
      • Keratolytics


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 34.39
question: A patient with classical scabies has thin, serpiginous burrows on the finger web spaces. Which layer of the skin does the female mite create these burrows in?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by dog and cat hookworm larvae, most commonly Ancylostoma braziliense, which migrate within the epidermis, producing creeping serpiginous lesions.


Cutaneous Larva Migrans:

  • Skin infestation caused by hookworm larvae from animals (commonly Ancylostoma braziliense and A. caninum). Larvae penetrate the skin and cause a characteristic serpiginous (snake-like) track rash.
  • Transmission:
    • Contact with contaminated soil/sand (e.g., barefoot walking on beaches, playgrounds).
    • Larvae enter through intact skin.
  • Clinical features:
    • Pruritic, erythematous serpiginous tracks that advance slowly through the skin.
    • Often on feet, legs, and buttocks.
    • May last for weeks to months if untreated
  • Treatment:
    • Oral albendazole or ivermectin is effective.
    • Topical thiabendazole may be used for limited lesions.


Ancylostoma duodenale (Option A): Human hookworm causing intestinal infection and anaemia; does not produce creeping skin lesions.

Enterobius vermicularis (Option C): Causes perianal pruritus, especially at night; no serpiginous tracks.

Sarcoptes scabiei (Option D): Causes scabies with burrows and nocturnal itching, not migrating serpiginous lesions.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507706/
question: A 24-year-old man presents with intensely pruritic, erythematous serpiginous tracks on his foot that have been slowly migrating over several days. He recently walked barefoot on a beach. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pediculosis pubis is caused by the crab louse (Pthirus pubis), named for its short, broad body and claw-like legs, which allow it to grasp coarse pubic hair.

[[figure-1]]


Pediculosis Pubis:

  • Agent: Pthirus pubis (crab louse)
  • Transmission: Sexual contact
  • Sites: Pubic hair, axillae, beard, chest; eyelashes in children
  • Features:
    • Intense pruritus
    • Excoriations
    • Maculae ceruleae (blue-grey macules)
    • Lice/nits attached to coarse hair
  • Diagnosis: Lice or nits seen on hair shafts
  • Treatment:
    • Permethrin 1% / pyrethrins (repeat after 7 days)
    • Petroleum jelly for eyelashes
    • Treat partners; wash clothes/bedding


Head louse (Option A): Causes pediculosis capitis; infests scalp hair.

Body louse (Option B): Lives in clothing seams; causes pediculosis corporis.

Scabies mite (Option D): Sarcoptes scabiei burrows in skin; not a louse.



Reference:

Andrew’s Diseases of the Skin, Clinical Dermatology, 13th Edition, Page 442
question: Pediculosis pubis is caused by which parasite?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pediculosis pubis (crab lice) presents with pubic pruritus, nits attached to hair, and characteristic maculae ceruleae due to louse feeding.


Pediculosis Pubis:

  • Agent: Pthirus pubis (crab louse)
  • Transmission: Sexual contact
  • Sites: Pubic hair, axillae, beard, chest; eyelashes in children
  • Features:
    • Intense pruritus
    • Excoriations
    • Maculae ceruleae (blue-grey macules)
    • Lice/nits attached to coarse hair
  • Diagnosis: Lice or nits seen on hair shafts
  • Treatment:
    • Permethrin 1% / pyrethrins (repeat after 7 days)
    • Petroleum jelly for eyelashes
    • Treat partners; wash clothes/bedding


Pediculosis corporis (Option A): Lice and nits are found in clothing seams, not attached to pubic hair; causes vagabond’s disease.


Scabies (Option B): Caused by mites burrowing in skin; shows burrows and nocturnal pruritus, no lice or nits on hair.


Tinea cruris (Option D): Dermatophyte infection with annular plaques and central clearing; no ectoparasites or maculae ceruleae.



Reference:

Andrew’s Diseases of the Skin, Clinical Dermatology, 13th Edition, Page 442
question: A 28-year-old man presents with intense itching in the pubic region for 2 weeks. Examination shows excoriations and multiple blue-grey macules on the lower abdomen and thighs. Close inspection reveals findings as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis for this patient is Vagabond’s disease.


Key clues:

  • Homeless man (poor hygiene, infrequent clothing change)
  • Chronic pruritus
  • Lice and nits in clothing seams (not on scalp)
  • Diffuse hyperpigmentation and excoriations


Vagabond’s disease results from chronic body lice (Pediculus corporis) infestation, seen in homeless individuals with poor hygiene. It presents with persistent pruritus, excoriations, and diffuse hyperpigmentation, and lice/nits are found in clothing seams, not on the scalp.


Body / Clothing Lice (Pediculus corporis):

  • Epidemiology: Poor hygiene, infrequent washing of clothes, is common among the homeless, refugees, and prisons
  • Habitat: Lives in clothing seams; visits skin only to feed; lays eggs on clothes
  • Transmission: Close contact, shared clothing/bedding
  • Diseases transmitted:
    • Epidemic typhus: Rickettsia prowazekii
    • Relapsing fever: Borrelia recurrentis
    • Trench fever: Bartonella quintana (± endocarditis)
  • Clinical features:
    • Pruritus, excoriations
    • Secondary infection
    • Chronic cases → hyperpigmentation (vagabond’s disease)
    • Lice/nits seen in clothes, not hair
  • Management:
    • Hot wash/iron clothes & bedding (kills lice and eggs)
    • Topical pyrethroids or malathion
    • Ivermectin for mass infestation
    • Antibiotics if louse-borne disease present


Scabies incognito (Option A): Steroid-modified scabies with atypical lesions; mites are found in skin burrows, not in clothing.

Pediculosis capitis (Option B): Head lice infestation; nits are attached to scalp hair, not clothing seams.

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (Option D): Pigmentary sequelae after inflammation; no active lice or nits present.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 34.21, 34.22
question: A 60-year-old homeless man presents with findings as shown. Lice and nits are seen in clothing seams, not on the scalp. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Massive mite burden, hyperkeratotic crusts, minimal pruritus, nail involvement, and high infectivity in an immunocompromised patient are classic for crusted (Norwegian) scabies.


Crusted (Norwegian) scabies:

  • Severe, highly contagious scabies with massive mite load and hyperkeratotic crusts

[[figure-1]]

  • Pathogenesis: Impaired host immune response → uncontrolled mite proliferation
  • Risk factors: Intellectual disability, Down syndrome, dementia, immunosuppression (HIV, HTLV-1, steroids, biologics), topical steroids; may occur in healthy individuals
  • Clinical features:
    • Thick warty crusts on hands, feet, palms, soles
    • Nail dystrophy with subungual debris
    • Erythema and scaling of scalp, face, trunk → may generalise
    • Pruritus is minimal or absent
    • Lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, ↑IgE
  • Diagnosis: Skin scrapings → numerous mites and eggs
  • Management:
    • Hospitalise and isolate; treat all contacts
    • Keratolytics + topical scabicide (repeated)
    • Oral ivermectin (3-7 doses based on severity)
    • Continue treatment until 2 negative scrapings


Nodular scabies (Option A): Presents with persistent pruritic nodules, usually genital or axillary, with low mite load.

Animal scabies (Option B): Causes transient pruritic papules; mites do not multiply on humans.

Darier disease (Option D): Genetic keratinisation disorder with greasy papules; no mites on scraping.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 34.47
question: A 58-year-old immunocompromised man has thick hyperkeratotic crusts on hands and feet, nail debris, minimal itching, and contact with pruritus. Skin scrapings show numerous mites. What is the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Nodules contain large numbers of live mites
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nodular scabies represents a hypersensitivity reaction to mite antigens; live mites are usually absent in the nodules.


Nodular scabies:

[[figure-1]]

  • Lesions: Few violaceous, intensely pruritic nodules (Option A ruled out)
  • Sites: Groin, axillae, male genitalia (Option B ruled out)
  • Pathogenesis: Hypersensitivity reaction to mite antigens
  • Course: May persist for weeks to months after successful treatment (Option D ruled out)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 34.42
