Commonly involves the groin, axillae, and male genitalia
Nodules contain large numbers of live mites
Lesions may persist for weeks or months after treatment

question: Which of the following statements regarding nodular scabies is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical presentation of nocturnal itching and involvement of the finger webs and wrists, the most likely diagnosis is Scabies. Skin scraping, dermoscopy, and adhesive tape test are useful for confirming this infestation; patch testing is not.


Scabies - Investigations:

  • Burrow identification or microscopy
  • Skin scraping + mineral oil microscopy:
    • Mites, eggs, egg shells, or scybala
    • Negative scraping does not exclude scabies
  • Mandatory in crusted scabies and healthcare settings
  • Dermoscopy:
    • Shows “jet with contrail” sign (mite in burrow)
    • Advantages: quick, painless, screens multiple sites
    • Limitations: cost, operator dependence
  • Adhesive tape test:
    • Tape applied to lesion → transferred to slide
    • Simple; useful in severe scabies, nursing homes
    • Low sensitivity
  • Skin biopsy:
    • Confirms diagnosis only if mite/parts are seen
    • Usually nonspecific: spongiosis, eosinophil-rich infiltrate
  • Confocal microscopy: promising but expensive; limited data


Patch testing is used to diagnose allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity reactions). Suspected allergens are applied to the back under occlusive patches and left for 48 hours, with readings taken at 48-96 hours to detect delayed hypersensitivity reactions.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 34.43
question:
A 22-year-old man presents with intense nocturnal itching and pruritic papules as shown. Two family members have similar symptoms. Which of the following tests are useful to confirm the diagnosis?

  1. Skin scraping with mineral oil microscopy.
  2. Dermoscopy
  3. Adhesive tape test
  4. Patch testing

correctAnswer: B. Apply permethrin only to visible lesions
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Permethrin must be applied to the entire body, not just lesions.


Scabies - Management:

  • Treat: Patient + all close contacts (even asymptomatic) (Option A ruled out)
  • Education: Avoid close contact until all are treated
  • Treatment:
    • DOC: Topical permethrin
    • Alternatives: Benzyl benzoate, lindane, crotamiton, sulphur
    • Oral ivermectin: 200 μg/kg (>2 yrs, >15 kg), repeat after 7-14 days
  • Application:
    • Apply to the entire body; include the face in infants
    • Do not wash your hands during treatment
  • Environment: Wash clothes/bedding >50°C or seal 72 h (Option C ruled out)
  • Special cases:
    • Children: No ivermectin <15 kg
    • Impetigo: Prefer ivermectin or add antibiotics
    • Pregnancy: Permethrin is safe
  • Follow-up: Itching may persist for weeks (Option D ruled out); reassess if >4 weeks


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 34.43-34.45

options.text: Apply permethrin only to visible lesions
Wash clothes and bedding in hot water or seal for 72 h

question: A patient with nocturnal pruritus and burrows is diagnosed with scabies. Which statement regarding management is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Infantile scabies characteristically involves the face, scalp, palms, and soles, with intense pruritus and household contact history, which are uncommon in classic adult scabies.


Infantile Scabies:

  • Distribution:
    • Unlike adults, the face, scalp, palms, and soles are commonly involved
    • Also affects the trunk and extremities
  • Pruritus: Severe → irritability, poor feeding
  • Lesions:
    • Papules, vesicles, pustules, nodules
    • Burrows may be difficult to identify
  • History of itching in caregivers or family members
  • Key distinction from adult scabies: Wider distribution, including head and acral areas
  • Complications: Secondary infection due to scratching

[[figure-1]]


Atopic dermatitis (Option A): Chronic, relapsing eczema; pruritus present, but no burrows and usually spares palms and soles in infants.

Impetigo (Option C): Bacterial infection with honey-colored crusts; itching and family involvement are not typical.

Papular urticaria (Option D): Hypersensitivity to insect bites; no nocturnal pruritus or household spread.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 34.40, 34.42
question: A 6-month-old infant presents with intense itching, irritability, and a generalised papulovesicular rash. Lesions involve the scalp, face, palms, and soles. The mother also complains of nocturnal itching. Examination shows excoriations and crusted papules. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Animal scabies commonly causes persistent human infestation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Animal scabies causes transient infestation in humans and does not persist, as mites cannot complete their life cycle in human skin.


Animal scabies:

  • From dogs, cats, livestock
  • Transient pruritic papules
  • No burrows (Option A ruled out)
  • Resolves after animal treatment
  • Permethrin hastens recovery

Treatment:

  • General principles
    • Treat patient + all close contacts simultaneously
    • Apply neck down (include scalp in infants/elderly/crusted)
    • Repeat after 7 days
  • Infants (<2 months)
    • Sulfur (5–10%) ointment → safe
    • Avoid permethrin
  • Children (>2 months)
    • Permethrin 5% cream (DOC)
      • Apply overnight (8–12 hrs)
    • Alternative: Benzyl benzoate (diluted)
  • Adults
    • Permethrin 5% cream (first-line)
    • Oral ivermectin (2 doses: day 1 & 7)
      • Indications:
        • Poor compliance
        • Outbreaks
        • Crusted scabies
  • Crusted scabies
    • Combination therapy:
      • Oral ivermectin (multiple doses)
      • Permethrin (repeated)
      • Keratolytics


Permethrin is the drug of choice for scabies (Option B): Correct - topical 5% permethrin is first-line treatment.

Crusted scabies is highly contagious (Option C): Correct - due to very high mite burden.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 34.40 - 34.47

options.text: Burrows are absent in animal scabies
Permethrin is the drug of choice for scabies
Animal scabies commonly causes persistent human infestation

question: Which of the following statements about scabies is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In primary scabies, symptoms appear after 3-4 weeks due to delayed hypersensitivity to mite antigens. Reinfection causes rapid symptoms within days.

In a first-time (primary) scabies infestation, symptoms are delayed because:

  • The itching is due to a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction
  • The body needs time to become sensitised to:
    • Mite proteins
    • Eggs
    • Faecal pellets (scybala)

Scabies - Clinical Features:

  • Itching: Severe, worse at night, face spared in adults
  • Onset: 3-4 weeks after first infection; immediate on reinfection
  • Sites: Finger webs, wrists, elbows, axillae, buttocks, genitalia, breasts
  • Lesions:
    • Burrows: Brownish, tortuous tracks
    • Papules/nodules: Very itchy, especially on the male genitalia
  • Post-treatment: Nodules may persist for weeks
  • Secondary lesions: Excoriations, eczema, impetigo


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 34.40
question: A patient acquires scabies for the first time. After how long do symptoms typically begin?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The likely diagnosis of this case is scabies, a parasitic infection of the skin caused by Sarcoptes scabiei (itch mite).


Mode of spread: Scabies are highly contagious, and transmission is by skin-to-skin contact and fomites. Risk factors include poor personal hygiene.


Clinical manifestation:

  • The characteristic sign of scabies is the presence of burrows, Are thin, grayish-white or skin-colored, linear or wavy lines found in areas like the webbing between fingers, wrists, elbows, armpits, waistline, buttocks, genital area, and ankles, causing intense itching, especially at night.

  • Examination typically reveals excoriated papules, typically over the web spaces of the fingers (as shown in the image).

Other areas of the body that must be examined for lesions include:

  1. The medial aspect of the wrist

  2. The medial aspect of the forearm

  3. Umbilicus (Option D)

  4. Axilla (Option B)

  5. Nipple

  6. Genitalia/ groin (Option C) - burrows (wavy, grey tunnels)

This distribution is called the circle of Hebra.


The face is typically spared, due to high amounts of sebum in the facial skin but pre pubecent children lack sebaceous glands and hence their faces can be affected


Circle of Hebra demonstrating the typical location of scabies lesions:

[[figure-1]]



Reference:
  1. Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 34.1, 34.43, 34.44
  2. www.uptodate.com/contents/scabies-epidemiology-clinical-features-and-diagnosis
question: A 25-year-old male presents with complaints of severe itching in both his hands for the last 2 weeks. He reports that the itching is significantly worse at night and disturbs his sleep. His hands show lesions characteristic of scabies. Which body site is usually not affected by this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nocturnal pruritus, involvement of the finger webs, presence of burrows, and household contact are classic findings of scabies.


Scabies (Family Sarcoptidae):

  • Cause: Sarcoptes scabiei var. Hominis

[[figure-1]]

  • Transmission: Prolonged skin-to-skin contact
  • Mite load: ~12 mites (classical); millions in crusted scabies
  • Life Cycle:
    • Eggs → larvae (3-4 days) → adults
    • Total cycle: 14-21 days
  • Clinical features:
    • Intense nocturnal pruritus
    • Burrows: thin, serpiginous lines
    • Sites: finger webs, wrists, axillae, buttocks, genitalia
    • Face spared in adults

[[figure-2]]

Scabies burrows

  • Variants

    • Infants: Vesicles, pustules, scalp involved
    • Elderly: Palms, soles
    • Scabies incognito: Steroid-modified
    • Crusted scabies: Hyperkeratotic, minimal itch, highly contagious
  • Treatment:
    • Treat patient + contacts
    • DOC: Permethrin 5% topical
    • Alternative: Benzyl benzoate
    • Oral ivermectin: Poor compliance, outbreaks, crusted scabies


Pediculosis corporis (Option A): Causes itching from body lice, but no burrows; usually affects areas in contact with clothing seams.

Atopic dermatitis (Option B): Chronic, relapsing eczema; no burrows and not contagious.

Prurigo nodularis (Option D): Firm nodules from chronic scratching; no burrows or contagious spread.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 34.39-34.47
question: A 22-year-old man presents with intense itching, worse at night, for 3 weeks. Examination shows multiple excoriated papules and thin serpiginous burrows as shown in the finger web spaces and flexor wrists. His roommate also has similar symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Strongyloides stercoralis causes larva currens, a characteristic fast-moving serpiginous rash resulting from autoinfection. The rash typically migrates at a rate of several centimeters per hour, most commonly over the trunk, buttocks, and proximal thighs, which is a key distinguishing feature.


Ancylostoma braziliense (Option B): Causes cutaneous larva migrans, but the rash progresses slowly (mm per day) and is usually confined to the feet or exposed skin, not rapidly moving.


Cutaneous larva migrans due to hookworm species (Option C): Refers broadly to hookworm infections (Ancylostoma, Necator), which again produce slowly migrating serpiginous lesions, unlike larva currens.


Sarcoptes scabiei (Option D): Causes scabies, characterized by burrows and nocturnal pruritus, not a rapidly migrating serpiginous rash.



Reference:
  1. Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 33.17
  2. https://mdsearchlight.com/infectious-disease/cutaneous-larva-migrans-creeping-eruption/
  3. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/larva-currens

options.text: Cutaneous larva migrans due to hookworm species

question: A 25-year-old man presents with an intensely pruritic, rapidly progressing, serpiginous rash over the trunk and proximal limbs. The lesion is noted to migrate quickly over hours to days. Which of the following organisms is the most likely causative agent?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient likely has post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis due to inadequately treated visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
  • VL is transmitted by sandflies and is caused by L. donovani or L. infantum.
  • Splenomegaly is characteristically massive.
  • It is characterized by multiple hypopigmented macules, typically on the trunk. These may progress to papules/ nodules.
  • Lesions may resemble those of lepromatous leprosy (Option C), but there are no associated sensorineural changes.
  • A definitive diagnosis of VL requires the demonstration of Leishmania by smear or culture, typically using a bone marrow sample. PKDL may be diagnosed via PCR of macular scrapings.
  • Treatment of VL involves liposomal Amphotericin B, while PKDL may be managed with Oral Miltefosin.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (Option B) is typically characterized by a pink papule that ultimately forms an indurated ulcer. There may be associated eschar (Old World) or yellow fibrin coverage (New World).


Pityriasis versicolor (Option D) is a cutaneous fungal infection that may also present with multiple hypopigmented macules. However, it typically lacks systemic complaints, as seen in this patient.

Condition Primary Skin Presentation Systemic Findings Key Distinguishing Features
Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL) Hypopigmented macules (trunk), papules, or nodules. Massive splenomegaly; history of Visceral Leishmaniasis. Follows inadequately treated Kala-azar; diagnosed via PCR of scrapings.
Lepromatous Leprosy Similar lesions to PKDL (macules/nodules). Often involves nerve thickening. Presence of sensorineural changes (unlike PKDL).
Cutaneous Leishmaniasis Pink papule that evolves into an indurated ulcer. Usually localized to the skin. Presence of eschar (Old World) or yellow fibrin coverage (New World).
Pityriasis Versicolor Multiple hypopigmented macules. None (purely cutaneous). Fungal infection; lacks the systemic complaints seen in Leishmaniasis.


Reference:
  1. https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-99-6999-9_6?
  2. https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(03)00517-6/abstract?
question: A 50-year-old female who recently migrated from Bihar presents for evaluation of a new rash. Her history is significant for low-grade fever and fatigue over the last few months. She reports receiving some treatment at the local government hospital, but cannot recount any more details. Examination reveals hundreds of hypopigmented macules over her back and arms. She also has palpable splenomegaly. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This case describes Old World Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (CL) in a soldier recently deployed to Iraq, a region endemic for Leishmania major. The clinical features (painless ulcerated plaque with crusting and lymphadenopathy) are classic for cutaneous leishmaniasis.

  • Leishmaniasis is a vector-borne disease caused by protozoa of the genus Leishmania, transmitted by female sand flies (Phlebotomus in the Old World).

  • The clinical spectrum ranges from cutaneous ulcers to systemic multiorgan disease (visceral leishmaniasis).

Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (CL):

Type Region Species Clinical Features
Old World CL Middle East, Africa, Asia L. major, L. tropica Painless papule → nodule/plaque → ulcer, often with crusting and raised volcano-like margins
New World CL Central and South America L. mexicana, L. braziliensis Similar lesions; L. mexicana causes Chiclero's ulcer (chronic ulcers on the ear due to multiple bites)

[[figure-1]]

New World CL: The ulcer may be covered with thick white-yellow fibrinous material. ‘Chiclero’s ulcer’ - multiple, small, chronic ulcers on the ear, due to multiple sandfly bites.

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Mucocutaneous Leishmaniasis (ML):

  • Caused by L. braziliensis (Option B).

  • Involves mucosal destruction of the nasal septum, mouth, and throat.

  • Features include nasal congestion, bleeding, pain, and eventual disfigurement.

[[figure-4]]

Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar):

  • Caused by Leishmania donovani (Option D).

  • Presents with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia.

  • No cutaneous lesions are typical.



Reference:

www.uptodate.com/contents/cutaneous-leishmaniasis-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis
question: A 30-year-old male soldier who had recently been deployed to Iraq presents with a mildly itchy, raised rash on his neck. He has no other systemic complaints. Examination revealed a painless plaque with ulceration and overlying crusting associated with tender posterior lymphadenopathy. What is the likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

American trypanosomiasis:

The given image shows Romana's sign, i.e., a swollen nodule or ‘chagoma’ at the site of infection, most commonly over the eyelids or near the mouth. This is an early sign of Trypanosoma cruzei infection, which is endemic to South America and is therefore called American trypanosomiasis.

Trypanosoma cruzei is transmitted via the bite of the Reduviid bug, or kissing bug (named so because the bite is painless).

Early symptoms are non-specific and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and the Romana sign.

If untreated, it can lead to Chaga’s disease, the manifestations of which include

  1. Dilated cardiomyopathy - heart failure (Option B), arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death.
  2. Megaesophagus and megacolon (Options C and D) - due to autonomic nerve destruction.

Diagnosis of acute disease is by demonstration of T cruzi trypomastigote on blood smears.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment of acute disease involves Nifurtimox or Benznidazole.
Chaga’s disease is incurable and requires supportive care as appropriate.

Sleeping sickness:

  • This is caused by T. brucei (rhodesiense or gambiense). It is endemic to rural Africa and is transmitted by the tse tse fly. It is also known as African trypanosomiasis.
  • Early infection is non-specific, with fever, cervical lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom’s sign: posterior cervical triangle lymphadenopathy), Kerandl sign (delayed pain after a sharp blow or squeeze to soft tissue) and arthralgia, which lasts for varying lengths of time.
  • Late infection is characterized by neuropsychiatric manifestations, with sleep-wake cycle disturbance prominent.



Reference:
  1. www.uptodate.com/contents/human-african-trypanosomiasis-epidemiology-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis
  2. www.uptodate.com/contents/chagas-disease-acute-and-congenital-trypanosoma-cruzi-infection
question: As shown in the figure, a 10-year-old boy presents with a painless swelling over his left lower eyelid. He reports visiting the Amazon forest on vacation with his family recently. If left untreated, which of the following is not a long-term risk?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given case scenario describes cutaneous larva migrans.
  • This is caused by animal hookworm larvae (Ancylostoma braziliensis/ caninum) and typically occurs due to walking barefoot on contaminated sand or soil.
  • It classically begins with a pruritic, erythematous papule at the site of penetration, followed by intensely pruritic, serpiginous, reddish-brown skin tracks, along the path of migration of the larvae. These develop slowly over days (1-2 cm/day)
  • The larvae cannot penetrate beyond the dermis, so systemic manifestations are uncommon.
  • Treatment involves oral ivermectin.

Loa loa (Option A) is the African eye worm. It causes Calabar swellings, painless, transient swellings over the eyelid.

[[figure-1]]

Strongyloides stercoralis (Option C) causes larva currens by its intradermal migration. While similar to cutaneous larva migrans, it is distinguished by more rapid migration within the skin (5-15 cm/hour), intense urticaria surrounding the path of migration, and potential perianal involvement.


Ascaris lumbricoides (Option D) causes ascariasis with larvae migrating through the bloodstream to the lungs and intestines, causing primarily gastrointestinal and respiratory symptoms. Unlike hookworms, Ascaris larvae do not migrate within the skin and thus do not cause cutaneous larva migrans.



Reference:

question: A 9-year-old girl presents with complaints of an itchy scalp for the last few days. Local inspection reveals mild crusting in areas of the scalp, with multiple white nits along the hair shafts. What is the causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario describes infantile scabies. Infantile scabies are similar to adult scabies, except that there is more extensive involvement, including the face, palms, and soles.
  • Examination reveals erythematous papules with burrows. Lesions may even be vesicular or bullous due to greater inflammatory response in children.

[[figure-1]]

  • Skin scraping and microscopic examination of the epidermis from the affected sites establish the diagnosis of scabies.
  • KOH may be used to dissolve keratin debris.
  • Microscopic evaluation will reveal mites, eggs, and feces.

[[figure-2]]

Mite with eggs

Phthirus pubis (Option A) causes pubic lice (crab louse infestation), primarily affecting pubic hair, not associated with burrows or extensive infantile involvement.


Trichophyton (Option C): A dermatophyte fungus responsible for tinea infections (e.g., ringworm), which presents with scaly patches rather than burrows or vesicles.


Staphylococcus aureus (Option D) can cause impetigo and bullous skin infections but does not produce burrows, mites, or microscopic eggs in skin scrapings.



Reference:
  1. https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2013/0415/p536.html?
  2. https://www.uptodate.com/contents/4038

question: A 6-month-old girl is brought by her parents for evaluation of a rash. On examination, she appears uncomfortable, and there are multiple small red papules on her face, palms, and soles. Multiple small burrows are also seen. Microscopy of skin scrapings is shown below. What is the causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient likely has crusted scabies or Norwegian scabies (NS).


This is a severe form of scabies due to massive infestation of the itch mite. Risk factors include:

  1. Immunocompromise (HIV, malignancy, etc)
  2. Old age
  3. Neurologic disease

NS is characterized by large, hyperkeratotic plaques that may cover up to 90% of the body's surface. Due to diminished immunity, pruritus is typically absent, contributing to the accumulation of crusts. These crusts can contain millions of mites and their eggs.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment involves both oral ivermectin and topical permethrin. Additionally, a keratolytic agent may be used to help the penetration of permethrin.


Monotherapy (Options A & B): While oral ivermectin or topical permethrin alone are used for classic scabies, they often fail when used alone for the NS due to the sheer number of mites and the protective barrier formed by the crusts.


Topical steroids (Option D): Topical steroids are the treatment of choice for nodular scabies, a special form of scabies caused by a hypersensitivity response to the mites. The lesions are typically pruritic, with firm nodules/ papules over the axilla and groin.

[[figure-2]]

Nodules in the axilla of a patient with nodular scabies



Reference:
  1. www.cdc.gov/parasites/scabies/health_professionals/
  2. www.uptodate.com/contents/scabies-epidemiology-clinical-features-and-diagnosis
question: A 30-year-old female with lymphoma on chemotherapy presents with large, crusted plaques over her entire torso, arm, and legs. She reports minimal itching. What is the optimal treatment regimen for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • 5% Permethrin is the drug of choice for scabies. It is given in addition to general measures:
    • Anti-histamines for pruritus
    • Wash clothes, and bedding with hot water
    • Examine and treat family members
  • MOA: Blocks sodium channels of the itch mite, causing paralysis.
  • Application: Apply below the neck for 8-12 hours at a time (overnight); it is typically applied twice, one week apart.
  • It is safe and can be used in all patients older than 2 months.
  • 1% Permethrinis used for pediculosis

GBHC (Option B): An older chloride-channel blocker that is rarely used. It is also not safe in pregnancy, in those with neurologic disorders, and in children.


Precipitated sulfur (Option C): While safe and effective, this is not the first choice, as its odour can make it unpleasant to use, But can be used in infants <2 months old.


Ivermectin (Option D): Given orally (200mc/kg—two doses). It is typically reserved for patients with scabies who do not respond to permethrin, atypical scabies, and those who cannot comply with or tolerate topical alternatives.


Briefly, other drugs include- Crotamiton (not safe in children), Malathion, Benzyl Benzoate, and Lindane (not safe in children, pregnancy).



Reference:
  1. Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 34.43, 34.44
  2. www.cdc.gov/parasites/scabies/health_professionals/
question: A 10-year-old boy is diagnosed with scabies after presenting with severe itching lesions, predominantly over his wrists and hands. What is the first-line treatment for his condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Ivermectin is contraindicated in children under 5 years of age; however, all the other mentioned drugs can be safely used to treat scabies in infants.

Drugs for scabies

Permethrin (1st line) (Option a)

A highly effective pyrethroid insecticide, with nearly 100% cure rates in scabies after a single application.

Lindane (2nd line)

A broad-spectrum insecticide, but less effective than permethrin and has a higher risk of systemic toxicity, particularly in children.

Benzyl Benzoate (2nd line) (Option d)

Minimally absorbed through the skin and has low systemic toxicity but can cause neurological symptoms in children.

Crotamiton (2nd line) (Option b)

Less prone to cause skin irritation and has low systemic toxicity but has produced lower cure rates in scabies.

Sulfur

The oldest scabicide but has several disadvantages, including messy application, unpleasant odour, and the need for repeated applications.

Dicophane (DDT)

Can be absorbed through the skin and cause systemic toxicity, rarely used due to potential side effects and safer alternatives.

Ivermectin

An oral medication that is highly effective in treating scabies.

Not to be given to children <5 yrs old, pregnant, or breastfeeding women. (Option c ruled out)


Reference:

K D Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th Edition, Page 961-963.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Toxoplasma IgG positivity with past infection (several years ago) indicates immunity and no active infection.
  • Once infected, the risk of congenital transmission is only present during the acute phase of maternal infection.
  • Chronic/past infection does not pose a risk to the fetus and requires no intervention.
  • Therefore, reassurance and routine antenatal care are appropriate.

Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy

Mother

Usually asymptomatic but can transmit the disease to the infant.

Infective form

Trophozoite crosses the placenta to infect the neonate.

Risk of transplacental infection based on time of infection of the mother

Transplacental infection can occur at any time during the pregnancy, but the gestational age influences the risk of transmission.

As the gestational age increases, the risk of transmission increases, but the severity of neonatal disease decreases.

Pre-pregnancy

  • Very low chance of transmission (immunocompromised mother)

First trimester

  • Minimal risk of transmission.
  • If transmitted, it results in more severe fetal complications.

Third trimester

  • Maximum risk of transmission.
  • If transmitted, it is usually asymptomatic in newborns.

Diagnosis of Toxoplasmosis

Antenatal

USG

  • Done at 20-24 weeks of gestation and repeated every 2-4 weeks
  • It helps detect lesions of congenital infection, such as
    • Hydrocephalus
    • Cerebral calcifications
    • Ascites

Serology

ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) or IFA (Immunofluorescence Assay) is done using maternal serum to detect IgM and IgG

PCR
  • Amniotic fluid can be used to detect Toxoplasma DNA, which can confirm the diagnosis.
  • It is not done routinely as it is invasive and expensive, and other safer options are available.

Postnatal diagnosis

Serology

Newborn Sera and maternal sera are both used to detect

  • IgG >= 1000: Possible infection
  • IgM >= 1:4 after 2 weeks of age: Indicates probable diagnosis
  • IgA: Disappears within 10 days of birth; thus, persistence indicates postnatal infection

Sabin-Feldman test - Complement fixation test

Other tests

  • Animal inoculation (no longer done for clinical diagnosis)
  • Skin test of Frenkel
  • Microscopy of samples to detect tachyzoites using Giemsa or PAS

[[figure-1]]

Congenital anomalies risk is high (Option A): Risk is only high with acute infection during pregnancy, not with past resolved infection.

Do amniotic sampling to find if fetus is infected or not (Option C): Unnecessary since there is no evidence of recent infection; IgM would be positive in acute infection.

Start treatment (Option D): Antiparasitic treatment is indicated only in acute infection during pregnancy to reduce fetal risk, not in past infection.

options.text: Do amniotic sampling to find if fetus is infected or not

question: A pregnant woman presents with lymph node swelling. She has a history of toxoplasmosis infection 5 years ago and is IgG positive. What should be the next step?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The child’s symptoms of severe nocturnal itching and the presence of burrows in intertriginous areas, axillae, umbilicus, and between the fingers are characteristic of scabies, which is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei (a mite).

Scabies:

  • Parasitic infection of the skin caused by Sarcoptes scabiei (itch mite).
  • Mode of spread: Scabies are highly contagious, and transmission is by skin-to-skin contact and fomites. Risk factors include poor personal hygiene.

Clinical manifestation:

  • The characteristic sign of scabies is the presence of burrows, Are thin, grayish-white or skin-colored, linear or wavy lines found in areas like the webbing between fingers, wrists, elbows, armpits, waistline, buttocks, genital area, and ankles, causing intense itching, especially at night.
  • Examination typically reveals excoriated papules, typically over the web spaces of the fingers (as shown in the image).

Other areas of the body that must be examined for lesions include:

  • The medial aspect of the wrist
  • The medial aspect of the forearm
  • Umbilicus
  • Axilla
  • Nipple
  • Genitalia/ groin- burrows (wavy, grey tunnels)

This distribution is called the circle of Hebra.

The face is typically spared, due to high amounts of sebum in the facial skin.

[[figure-1]]

Circle of Hebra demonstrating the typical location of scabies lesions

Incorrect Options:

Louse (Option A): Lice (Pediculus humanus capitis, Pediculus humanus corporis, Pthirus pubis) cause pediculosis (head/body/pubic lice), which presents with itching and nits attached to hair shafts, not burrows in the skin.

Tick (Option B): Ticks are blood-feeding arachnids that transmit diseases like Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and babesiosis. They do not burrow into the skin or cause widespread itching.

Flea (Option D): Fleas (Pulex irritans) cause pruritic papules, often in a clustered pattern ("breakfast, lunch, and dinner" sign), but they do not form burrows in the skin.

question: A young boy came to the OPD with complaints of severe itching at night. On examination, burrows are seen over intertriginous areas, axillae, umbilicus, and between digits. Which ofthe following transmits the condition described in the scenario?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:Elephantiasis is a condition characterized by massive swelling and thickening of the skin and underlying tissues, most commonly affecting the limbs and genitalia. It results from lymphatic obstruction, leading to chronic lymphedema and progressive fibrosis.

Elephantiasis:

  • Cause: Delayed sequel of repeated lymphangitis, obstruction, and lymphedema.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Persistent lymph leakage into tissues → chronic lymphedema → elephantiasis.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Nonpitting brawny edema (firm swelling).
    • Thickened skin, cracks, and fissures.
    • Growth of new adventitious tissue.
    • Increased risk of secondary bacterial and fungal infections.
  • Commonly Affected Areas:
    • Legs (most common), but other body parts can also be involved.

Causes of Elephantiasis:

  • Lymphatic Filariasis (most common cause)
    • Caused by parasitic nematodes like Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori
    • Transmitted by mosquito bites
    • Leads to chronic lymphatic obstruction and severe swelling
  • Non-Filarial Elephantiasis (Podoconiosis)
    • Caused by chronic exposure to volcanic soil with high silica content
    • Seen in tropical regions like Africa and South America
  • Other Causes:
    • Repeated bacterial infections (e.g., streptococcal cellulitis)
    • Tumors obstructing lymphatics
    • Milroy’s disease (congenital primary lymphedema)

Filariasis:

  • Agent:
    • Wucheria bancrofti: Lymphatic filariasis
    • Brugia malayi: Brugian/Malayan filariasis
  • Endemic areas: Bihar, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Gujarat
  • Host:
    • Definitive: Man
    • Secondary/ intermediate: Culex quinquefasciatus or fatigans
  • Mode of Transmission: Bite of the mosquito (vector)
    • W. bancrofti: Culex quinquefasciatus or fatigans (polluted water)
    • B. malayi: Mansonia (ponds, lakes)
  • Incubation period: 8-16 months.
  • Transmission: Cyclodevelopmental
  • Clinical features:
    • Asymptomatic amicrofilariae: No symptoms, smear-negative
    • Asymptomatic microfilariae: No symptoms, smear-positive
    • Acute stage (few months): Fever, lymphadenitis, epididymo-orchitis.
    • Chronic Obstructive stage (>10 years): Hydrocele, chyluria, elephantiasis
    • Occult stage: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (hypersensitivity reaction) with absent microfilariae

Syphilis (Option A):

  • Syphilis (Treponema pallidum infection) causes painless ulcers (chancre), maculopapular rash, and systemic involvement, but does not lead to massive lymphedema.

Leprosy (Option B):

  • Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) leads to skin lesions, nerve damage, and deformities, but does not cause gross limb swelling like elephantiasis.

Leishmaniasis (Option D):

  • Cutaneous leishmaniasis presents with ulcerative skin lesions, while visceral leishmaniasis causes hepatosplenomegaly and fever. Neither form causes lymphatic obstruction and massive swelling.


Reference:
  • https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001706X21000978#:~:tex
  • Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27th Edition Pg: 315-317
question: Identify the disease shown in the image below

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Lymphatics

  • The correct answer is lymphatics. Filariasis is a disease caused by parasitic worms, specifically Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori. These worms primarily inhabit the lymphatic system, causing inflammation and obstruction of lymphatic vessels. This leads to the clinical manifestations of filariasis, such as lymphedema (swelling), elephantiasis (severe swelling), and other related complications.

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Arteries: Arteries are blood vessels that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart to various parts of the body. They do not play a direct role in filariasis. Filariasis is a parasitic infection caused by thread-like filarial worms, typically transmitted through mosquito bites. The worms primarily affect the lymphatic system, not the arteries.

Option B - Vein: Veins are blood vessels that carry deoxygenated blood back to the heart. Similar to arteries, veins do not have a direct role in filariasis. The infection mainly targets the lymphatic system, leading to the characteristic swelling of body parts due to impaired lymph flow.

Option D - DVT (Deep Vein Thrombosis): DVT is a condition where a blood clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the legs. While DVT involves veins, it is unrelated to filariasis. DVT results from the formation of blood clots within veins, often due to factors like prolonged immobility, certain medical conditions, or genetic predisposition.
question: The involvement of which of the following results in the given condition below?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A rapidly moving, serpiginous, intensely pruritic rash is suggestive of larva currens, a characteristic feature of Strongyloides stercoralis.

  • History of pond water exposure and larvae (not eggs) in stool strongly point toward Strongyloides.

  • Other helminths either produce eggs in the stool or cause slowly migrating skin lesions.

  • Strongyloides stercoralis is an intestinal nematode.

Infective stage

  • Filariform larva (L3): Infective stage

  • Penetrates intact skin (often from soil or contaminated water)

Life cycle

  • Filariform larvae penetrate skin → bloodstream → lungs → trachea → swallowed

  • Mature into an adult parthenogenetic female in the intestinal mucosa

  • Eggs hatch inside the intestine, releasing rhabditiform larvae

  • Larvae are passed in stool or convert to filariform larvae → autoinfection

[[figure-1]]

Egg characteristics

  • Eggs are rarely seen in stool

  • Eggs hatch in the intestinal mucosa → hence, larvae are seen instead of eggs

Clinical features

  • Skin: Larva currens (rapidly migrating, serpiginous, pruritic rash)

  • GI: Abdominal pain, diarrhoea, malabsorption

  • Pulmonary: Cough, wheeze (Löffler’s syndrome)

  • Hyperinfection syndrome (immunosuppressed): Disseminated disease, sepsis

[[figure-2]]

Diagnosis

  • Stool examination: Rhabditiform larvae (diagnostic)

  • Duodenal aspirate/agar plate culture (more sensitive)

  • Eosinophilia (may be absent in hyperinfection)

[[figure-3]]

Treatment

  • Ivermectin: Drug of choice

  • Albendazole (alternative)

Incorrect Options:

  • Ancylostoma braziliense (Option B): Causes cutaneous larva migrans, but migration is slow (mm/day), not rapid. No larvae in stool; humans are accidental hosts.

  • Ascaris lumbricoides (Option C): Eggs are seen in stool, not larvae. Does not cause serpiginous pruritic skin lesions.

  • Sarcoptes scabiei (Option D): Causes scabies burrows (mite infestation), not larval migration.



Reference:
  • Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 33.16, 33.17.
question: A young man gives a history of bathing in pond water. He develops a rapidly moving, serpiginous, pruritic rash over the body. A stool examination shows no ova and no cysts, but larvae are identified. Routine bacterial culture is negative. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The organism shown is Treponema pallidum, a spirochete seen on dark-field microscopy, which causes primary syphilis. The hallmark lesion is a painless, indurated chancre with a clean base and non-tender lymphadenopathy.

Syphilis:

  • Syphilis is a chronic systemic infection caused by Treponema pallidum, transmitted primarily through sexual contact and vertically from mother to fetus.
  • It is known as the “great imitator” because of its wide range of cutaneous manifestations.

  • Primary Stage:

    • The disease begins with a painless chancre at the site of inoculation.

    • The ulcer is typically indurated with a clean base and associated with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy.

    • It heals spontaneously within a few weeks.

  • Secondary Stage:

    • Weeks later, hematogenous spread leads to widespread skin findings.

    • The hallmark is a symmetrical maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, often copper-colored.

    • Other features include condyloma lata, mucous patches, generalised lymphadenopathy, and patchy “moth-eaten” alopecia.

    • This stage is highly infectious.

  • Latent Stage:

    • An asymptomatic period follows, divided into early and late latent phases.

    • Cutaneous lesions are absent, but serology remains positive.

  • Tertiary Stage:

    • Years later, untreated patients may develop gummatous lesions of the skin and organs, along with cardiovascular or neurologic involvement.

Painful genital ulcer with ragged edges (Option A): Seen in chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi).

Beefy red ulcer with bleeding on touch (Option C): Seen in granuloma inguinale (Klebsiella granulomatis).

Vesicular lesions progressing to shallow ulcers (Option D): Seen in genital herpes (HSV).



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 29.7-29.12

Beefy red ulcer with bleeding on touch
Vesicular lesions progressing to shallow ulcers

question: Dark-field microscopy image revealing findings as shown in the image. This organism most commonly causes which of the following?.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Secondary syphilis is characterised by generalised skin and mucocutaneous lesions due to hematogenous spread of Treponema pallidum. Gumma is a manifestation of tertiary syphilis, not secondary.


Secondary Syphilis:

  • Timing: ~6-8 weeks after primary stage
  • Serology: Always positive (immunocompetent)
  • Rash: Non-itchy, coppery red & symmetrical
  • Skin & Mucosa:
    • Roseola (macular): Early, faint coppery macules, no scale (Option A ruled out)
    • Papular syphilide (commonest): Firm papules → papulosquamous; palms & soles involved

[[figure-1]]

  • Condylomata lata (Option B): Moist, hypertrophic papules (perianal, groin, genitals)
  • Annular/psoriasiform/lichenoid variants
  • Mucous patches: Grey-white oral lesions, may form snail-track ulcers
  • Other features:
    • Alopecia: Patchy “moth-eaten” (Option C ruled out)
    • Lymphadenopathy: Painless, rubbery, generalised
    • CNS: CSF abnormalities ± headache
    • Systemic: Uveitis, periostitis, hepatitis, GN


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 29.10-29.13
question: A 32-year-old man presents with generalised, non-itchy, coppery red skin lesions and painless lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is not a cutaneous manifestation of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above examination findings are the “Dory flop sign”
  • The Dory flop sign is seen in primary syphilis when a chancre is present on the undersurface of the prepuce, causing abrupt, non-smooth eversion during retraction.


Dory flop sign:

  • Seen in: Primary syphilis
  • Cause: Chancre on the undersurface of the prepuce
  • Clinical feature: The affected part of the prepuce fails to roll smoothly during retraction
  • Characteristic movement: Prepuce rolls out suddenly and all at once
  • Resembles: The abrupt flipping movement of a dory (fishing boat)
  • Significance: Suggestive of a hidden preputial chancre in primary syphilis


Fothergill sign (Option A): Used to distinguish an intra-abdominal mass from a mass in the abdominal wall. Abdominal wall mass remains palpable on muscle contraction.


Jacquet erythema sign (Option B): Severe irritant dermatitis with erosions in the diaper area


Buschke-Ollendorff sign (Option D): Also known as the "deep tenderness" sign, it refers to extreme pain elicited when a secondary syphilitic lesion is touched with a blunt probe.



Reference:

https://ijdvl.com/cutaneous-signs-in-infectious-diseases/
question: A 26-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a painless genital lesion. On retracting the prepuce, the affected part does not roll smoothly and instead rolls out suddenly all at once, resembling the movement of a fishing boat. Which clinical sign is being described?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Rashes of secondary syphilis are classically non-itchy, coppery red, and symmetrically distributed, often involving the palms and soles.

[[figure-1]]


Secondary Syphilis:

  • Timing: ~6-8 weeks after primary stage
  • Serology: Always positive (immunocompetent)
  • Rash: Non-itchy, coppery red & symmetrical (Option A ruled out)
  • Skin & Mucosa:
    • Roseola (macular): Early, faint coppery macules (Option B ruled out), no scale
    • Papular syphilide (commonest): Firm papules → papulosquamous; palms & soles involved (Option D ruled out)
    • Condylomata lata: Moist, hypertrophic papules (perianal, groin, genitals)
    • Annular/psoriasiform/lichenoid variants
    • Mucous patches: Grey-white oral lesions, may form snail-track ulcers
  • Other features:
    • Alopecia: Patchy “moth-eaten”
    • Lymphadenopathy: Painless, rubbery, generalised
    • CNS: CSF abnormalities ± headache
    • Systemic: Uveitis, periostitis, hepatitis, GN

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 29.10-29.13
question: A 30-year-old man presents with a generalised rash associated with secondary syphilis. Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of the rash in secondary syphilis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Buschke-Ollendorff sign is slight tenderness over palmar papular lesions in secondary syphilis, caused by cutaneous vasculitis.


Secondary Syphilis - Signs:

  • Buschke-Ollendorff sign: Tenderness on pressure over palmar papules due to cutaneous vasculitis
  • Crown of Venus: Scaly papules along the scalp hairline
  • Omnibus sign (Option C): Eyebrow alopecia visible at a glance
  • Elliot sign (Option B): Induration at the margin of syphilitic skin lesions


Primary syphilis:


Dory flop sign (Option D): Chancre on the undersurface of the prepuce causes sudden outward rolling of the prepuce

question: A 32-year-old man presents with multiple papular lesions on his palms. On applying pressure with a dull probe, the lesions are slightly tender. The patient also reports a history of a painless genital ulcer 3 weeks ago. What is the name of this sign?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Condyloma lata are broad-based, moist, flat, gray-white lesions seen in secondary syphilis, typically in intertriginous areas (perineum, genital folds, perianal region). They are highly infectious and usually accompany a generalised rash and lymphadenopathy.


Secondary Syphilis:

  • Timing: ~6-8 weeks after primary stage
  • Serology: Always positive (immunocompetent)
  • Rash: Non-itchy, coppery red & symmetrical

[[figure-1]]

  • Skin & Mucosa:
    • Roseola (macular): Early, faint coppery macules, no scale
    • Papular syphilide (commonest): Firm papules → papulosquamous; palms & soles involved
    • Condylomata lata: Moist, hypertrophic papules (perianal, groin, genitals)

[[figure-2]]

  • Annular/psoriasiform/lichenoid variants
  • Mucous patches: Grey-white oral lesions, may form snail-track ulcers
  • Other features:
    • Alopecia: Patchy “moth-eaten”
    • Lymphadenopathy: Painless, rubbery, generalised
    • CNS: CSF abnormalities ± headache
    • Systemic: Uveitis, periostitis, hepatitis, GN

Condyloma Lata vs Condyloma Acuminata:

Feature

Condyloma lata

Condyloma acuminata

Cause

Treponema pallidum

HPV (6, 11)

Disease

Secondary syphilis

Genital warts

Morphology

Broad, flat, moist plaques

Verrucous, cauliflower-like

Diagnosis

Syphilis serology +

HPV tests (PCR)

Treatment

Penicillin

Podophyllin, imiquimod, cryo


Primary syphilis (Option A): Presents with a single painless chancre at the site of inoculation.


Latent syphilis (Option C): Infection persists without any clinical manifestations, detectable only serologically.


Tertiary syphilis (Option D): Characterised by gummas, cardiovascular, or neurosyphilis, not condyloma lata.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 29.10 - 29.13
question: A 28-year-old man presents with findings as shown around the perianal area. He also reports generalised non-tender lymphadenopathy and a diffuse maculopapular rash on the trunk and palms. These lesions are most characteristic of which stage of syphilis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Syphilis d'emblée refers to secondary syphilis occurring without an identifiable primary chancre due to direct inoculation into the bloodstream.

  • Historically it was described following transfusion of infected blood, although this is now exceedingly rare because of routine blood screening.
  • It often presents with palmoplantar lesions and can mimic common dermatologic disorders.
  • Serological testing and high clinical suspicion help ensure accurate and early treatment.

Feature

Chancre redux

Pseudochancre redux

Definition

Reappearance of chancre at same site

Chancre-like lesion without active infection

Stage

Late syphilis (relapse)

Tertiary syphilis

Lesion

Indurated ulcer (like primary chancre)

Superficial ulcer/scar breakdown

Spirochetes

Present (infectious)

Absent (non-infectious)


Primary syphilis (Option A): Typically presents as a solitary painless chancre at the site of inoculation, not with generalised rash and mucosal plaques.

Herpes labialis (Option C): Causes painful vesicles/ulcers on the lips, not painless plaques or systemic rash.

Oral lichen planus (Option D): Usually presents as reticular white striae (Wickham striae) on the oral mucosa, without systemic rash or positive syphilis serology.



Reference:
  1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3401849/
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9051677/
question: A 28-year-old man has had a painless gray-white plaque on the lower lip and a papulosquamous rash on the trunk, extremities, and palms/soles as shown for several months. He denies sexual contact but received an unscreened blood transfusion 1 year ago. VDRL and TPHA are positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. It is a rare gummatous recurrence at the site of the primary chancre
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pseudo-chancre redux is a late (tertiary) syphilitic lesion that reappears at the site of the original primary chancre.
  • It mimics a new chancre clinically, but does not represent reinfection
  • Instead, it is a gummatous relapse occurring in late syphilis.
    • Stage: Tertiary syphilis (gummatous lesion) (Option B)
    • Site: Same location as the old primary chancre
    • Pathogenesis: Relapse/progression of syphilis, not reinfection (Option A)
    • Organism load: Treponemes are scant or absent
    • Investigation: Dark-ground microscopy is usually negative (Option D)
  • Clinical pitfall: Can be mistaken for a fresh primary chancre, hence the term pseudo-chancre


Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 111.24
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1846534/

question: Which statement regarding pseudo-chancre redux is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The commonest manifestation seen in congenital syphilis is snuffles.


Early Congenital Syphilis: (≤2 years)

  • Snuffles (infectious rhinitis)
  • Coppery papulosquamous rash, palms/soles
  • Vesiculobullous lesions (pemphigus syphiliticus)
  • Mucous patches, rhagades
  • Bone lesions: periostitis, osteochondritis, Wimberger sign, Parrot pseudoparalysis
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, anaemia, and thrombocytopenia
  • CNS involvement, chorioretinitis


Late Congenital Syphilis: (≥3 years)

  • Interstitial keratitis (Option A)
  • Clutton joints (painless knee synovitis)
  • Sabre tibia
  • Gummata
  • Eighth nerve deafness (Option D)
  • Neurosyphilis

Stigmata (residual deformities):

  • Hutchinson teeth (Option C)
  • Mulberry molars
  • Hutchinson triad:
    • Interstitial keratitis
    • Hutchinson teeth
    • Eighth nerve deafness
  • Saddle nose
  • Rhagades
  • Parrot’s nodes
  • Pepper-and-salt fundus
  • Optic atrophy

Kassowitz Law:

  • The severity of the disease decreases with successive pregnancies in untreated mothers
    • 1st child: most severe / may be stillborn
    • Later children: progressively milder disease


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 29.28 - 29.32
question: Which of the following is the commonest manifestation seen in congenital syphilis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Wimberger sign refers to bilateral metaphyseal destruction of the medial proximal tibia, characteristic of early congenital syphilis.

[[figure-1]]


Bone lesions in early congenital syphilis:

  • Osteochondritis
  • Periostitis
  • Wimberger’s sign
  • Parrot pseudoparalysis

Note:

  • Wimberger sign → metaphyseal destruction (syphilis)
  • Wimberger ring sign → Dense white epiphyseal ring due to calcification around epiphyseal cartilage, seen in scurvy


Sabre tibia (Option A): Late congenital syphilis with anterior bowing of the tibia.


Parrot pseudoparalysis (Option C): Decreased limb movement due to pain, not a radiologic sign.


Clutton joints (Option D): Painless knee synovitis in late congenital syphilis.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 29.28 - 29.30
question: A 2-month-old infant has poor limb movement, excessive crying on handling, snuffles, and a coppery rash on palms and soles. X-ray shows bilateral symmetrical destruction of the medial proximal tibial metaphyses. This radiological finding is known as which of the following signs?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image depicts gumma, which is the manifestation of tertiary syphilis.
  • Detection of maternal IgG is not done, as passively transferred maternal IgG can persist in the infant for up to 12 months, making it unreliable for diagnosis.


Evaluation of Neonates for Congenital Syphilis:

  • Indications:
    • No documented treatment ≥ 4 weeks before delivery
    • Non-penicillin treatment
    • Suspected relapse or reinfection
  • Clinical examination for stigmata of congenital syphilis
  • X-ray of long bones (Option A) → periostitis/osteochondritis
  • CSF examination (Option B)
  • Dark-field microscopy (Option C) and/or PCR from suspicious lesions or fluids
  • Clinical examination for stigmata
  • Laboratory evidence of infection:
    • Infant non-treponemal titre ≥4× maternal titre, or
    • Positive IgM treponemal antibodies
  • Maternal IgG antibodies may persist in the infant for up to 12 months, limiting interpretation of treponemal tests.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 29.33
question: A newborn is delivered to a mother who has the following findings and was inadequately treated during pregnancy. Which of the following is not done in the evaluation of this neonate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical description, the most likely diagnosis is a Chancre.
  • A chancre is the primary lesion of syphilis, classically painless, indurated, clean-based, and associated with non-tender lymphadenopathy.
  • Primary syphilis is the initial stage of syphilis infection, typically occurring about three weeks after exposure to the bacterium Treponema pallidum.
  • The hallmark of this stage is the development of a painless ulcer known as a chancre, which appears at the site where the bacteria entered the body, commonly on the genitals, anus, or mouth.
  • The chancre is usually round, firm, and painless.
  • It can vary in size, often resembling a small, raised sore.
  • It is highly infectious and typically lasts between three and six weeks.
  • Even though it heals on its own, the absence of symptoms does not mean the infection is gone; the bacteria remain in the body.

[[figure-1]]


Chancroid (Option A): Painful ulcer with ragged edges and tender nodes.

Herpes genitalis (Option C): Painful grouped vesicles/ulcers.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (Option D): Small transient ulcer with painful lymphadenopathy.



Reference:

Apurba S Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Microbiology, 3rd Edition, Pages 756 - 763
question: A 24-year-old sexually active man presents with a single, painless ulcer on the penis noticed 2 weeks after unprotected intercourse. Examination reveals findings as shown with non-tender bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. He has no fever or systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis of this lesion?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (FHCS) is perihepatitis associated with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).
  • It presents with:
    • Sharp right upper quadrant pain, often pleuritic
    • Signs of PID (lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness)
    • Normal gallbladder on imaging
    • Characteristic “violin-string” adhesions between the liver capsule and the anterior abdominal wall (on laparoscopy)

[[figure-1]]

Causative organisms:

  • Chlamydia trachomatis → Most common cause worldwide
  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae → Classic cause in PID-associated FHCS
  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis → Can cause chronic PID and perihepatic adhesions, especially in TB-endemic regions

PID Treatment

  • Syndromic (NACO - India, Kit 6)
    • Cefixime 400 mg stat
    • Azithromycin 1 g stat
    • Metronidazole 400 mg BD × 14 days
    • Covers: Gonorrhea + Chlamydia + Anaerobes
  • CDC Outpatient
    • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat
    • + Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days
    • + Metronidazole 500 mg BD × 14 days
  • CDC Inpatient / Severe
    • Ceftriaxone IV + Doxycycline + Metronidazole


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 30.4, 30.12, 30.13

correctAnswer: B. It is due to cytokine release after spirochete destruction
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction is a cytokine-mediated acute febrile reaction occurring within 24 hours of treatment, is self-limiting, and managed with antipyretics.

Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction:

  • An acute febrile inflammatory reaction occurring within 24 hours of initiating syphilis treatment, caused by cytokine release from rapid spirochete destruction.
  • Clinical features:
    • Ffever (38–40°C) rarely persists more than 8 hrs. (Option B)
    • Headache
    • Myalgia and bone pain
    • Exacerbation of skin lesions
  • Not a penicillin allergy (Option A)
  • Patients should be warned in advance
  • Symptoms controlled with antipyretics
  • Special situations:
    • Pregnancy: May cause fetal distress or precipitate preterm labour
    • Late neurosyphilis & cardiovascular syphilis:
      • Reaction may be severe or life-threatening
  • Prevention / Management in High-Risk Patients:
    • Short course of corticosteroids recommended (Option D)
    • Example regimen:
      • Prednisolone 30–60 mg/day for 3 days
      • Start steroids 24 hours before syphilis treatment


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 29.26

question: A patient with secondary syphilis develops fever, myalgia, headache, and worsening rash 6 hours after starting penicillin. Which statement about this reaction is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis. It typically presents with the frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge with a foul odor, along with vaginal itching and discomfort during urination.
  • The characteristic appearance seen is ‘Strawberry cervix,’ an erythematous and edematous cervical mucosa with characteristic punctate red papules. It is caused by microscopic punctate haemorrhages of the cervix.
  • The standard treatment is Metronidazole 2g PO single dose.

question: A 28 year old female presents with vaginal discharge that is frothy, yellow-green in colour and has a foul odour. She reports mild vaginal itching and discomfort during urination. A per speculum reveals the image shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. The presence of multinucleated giant cells on the Tzanck smear
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Multinucleated giant cells on a Tzanck smear are characteristic of herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, particularly herpes genitalis

[[figure-1]]

  • TZANCK smear

[[figure-2]]

  • The presence of painful genital lesions, along with a tingling sensation and burning pain preceding the appearance of ulcers, is highly suggestive of HSV infection.
  • The image shows multiple vesicles and pustules with a coalescing vesicles and erosions as seen in herpes genitalis

Herpes genitalis is a sexually transmitted infection caused primarily by HSV-2, although HSV-1 can also be responsible. It is characterised by the infection of genital skin or mucosa

  • Clinical features:
    • Multiple, painful, non-indurated vesicles that may rupture, forming coalescing vesicles or polycyclic erosions.
    • Bilateral tender lymphadenopathy is common.
    • Males: Painful penile ulcerations affecting the glans, prepuce and shaft of the penis
    • Females: Involves external genitalia, vulva, vagina and cervix. Accompanied by dysuria
  • Diagnosis: Tzanck smear, revealing multinucleated giant cells, a characteristic feature.
  • Serological testing, such as ELISA for HSV glycoprotein, can also aid in diagnosis.
  • Treatment typically involves antiviral medications like acyclovir (400mg TDS), administered for 7-10 days for primary infection and 5 days for secondary infection.

Presence of bacterial colonies, "school of fish" appearance on Gram stain (Option B): This finding is characteristic of chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, which leads to the formation of painful genital ulcers.

[[figure-3]]

Donovan bodies within Pund cells on Gram stain (Option C): This finding is characteristic of granuloma inguinale, also known as Donovanosis, caused by the bacterium Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies are intracellular inclusions seen within macrophages, representing aggregates of the causative organism giving safety pin appearence.

[[figure-4]]

Clue cells on saline mount (Option D): Clue cells are epithelial cells covered with bacteria, typically seen in bacterial vaginosis (BV), caused by Gardenella vaginalis.

[[figure-5]]



Reference:

Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 25.20 - 25.22

question: A 28 year old sexually active man presents with painful genital lesions. He reports a tingling sensation and burning pain in the genital area preceding the appearance of the ulcers. Which of the following is the most characteristic finding for his condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi manifests as multiple ulcers in the genital area, characterized by their non-indurated nature, undermined edges, greyish slough, and tendency to bleed on touch.
  • Individuals with chancroid may develop unilateral, painful lymphadenopathy.
  • The suppurative lymphadenopathy observed in chancroid is termed bubo.
  • Diagnosis
    • Gram staining reveals Gram-negative bacilli arranged in chains, often referred to as "railway tracks" or "school of fish" appearance.
    • Culturing specimens on Mueller Hinton Agar supplemented with chocolate horse blood aids in the identification of Haemophilus ducreyi.
  • Treatment.
    • Azithromycin is administered orally in a single dose of 1 gram
    • OR intramuscular injection of Ceftriaxone at a dosage of 250 mg (single dose)

Lymph Node

[[figure-2]]

Pseudo-bubo (enlarged and tender but occurs due to inflammation and not infection)

question: A 35 year old truck driver presents to the clinic with complaints of a painful genital lesion that has been progressively enlarging over the past few weeks. Upon examination, you note a tender ulcerative lesion with undermined edges and a base covered by a greyish exudate. Additionally, there are enlarged and tender inguinal lymph nodes palpable unilaterally. The patient reports a recent sexual encounter with another male truck driver. Which of the following sexually transmitted infections is most likely to present with this clinical manifestation

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The correct match of the clinical description with their disease is shown below.

Ulcer Description Causative Organism
1. Painful vesicular lesions c) Genital herpes
2. Painless, beefy red ulcers with rolled edges d) Granuloma inguinale
3. Painless genital ulcer with indurated base a) Syphilis
4. Soft, painful genital ulcer with irregular borders b) Chancroid

Genital herpes presents with painful vesicular lesions & blisters which can burst and cause ulcer formation. It is most commonly caused by HSV-2 > HSV-1. The given image below shows genital herpes.

[[figure-1]]

Granuloma inguinale is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. It presents with painless, beefy ulcers that may bleed on touch. Microscopically, it shows Donovan body with a safety-pin appearance. The given image shows the clinical picture of the ulcer and Donovan bodies.

[[figure-2]]

Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum. It occurs in various stages such as primary, secondary, and tertiary. The primary lesion appears as a regularly edged, regularly based, hard, painless, and button‐like ulceration measuring up to 1 cm in diameter. The ulcer is often surrounded by a narrow, red border 1–2 mm wide. The given image shows the primary ulcer.

[[figure-3]]

Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. multiple, superficial, tender, soft, ragged ulcers which bleed on manipulation.

[[figure-4]]

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 29.3-30.24
question:
Match the following description of ulcers with their causative organisms.

1.Painful vesicular lesions

a) Syphilis

2.Painless, beefy red ulcers with rolled edges.

b) Chancroid

3.Painless genital ulcer with indurated base.

c) Genital herpes
4.Soft, painful genital ulcer with irregular borders. d) Granuloma inguinale

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical presentation of a male with painless, beefy-red ulcers on his genitals with progressive enlargement is suggestive of granuloma inguinale caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. The drug of choice for this condition is oral azithromycin.

Donovanosis, also known as granuloma inguinale, is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis bacteria. The characteristic clinical presentation includes painless, beefy-red ulcers that can bleed on touch, with rolled edges and a granular base.

Prolonged antibiotic treatment is often necessary. Antibiotics must be given for 3-6 weeks till the ulcer is healed. Drugs include

First-line

Azithromycin 1g once weekly (or)

Azithromycin 500mg daily

Second-line

Doxycycline 100mg BD (or)

Erythromycin 500mg QID (or)

Cotrimoxazole 960mg BD

Intramuscular penicillin G (Option B) is used in the treatment of syphilis.

Intramuscular ceftriaxone (Option C) is used in the treatment of gonococcal infections.

Oral doxycycline (Option D) can be used in the second-line treatment of donovanosis.



Reference:
  1. Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.25
  2. https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/donovanosis.htm

question: A 32 year old male presents to a primary care clinic with complaints of urethral discharge and dysuria. He reports having unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. On examination, you note purulent discharge from the urethra. Which colour kit would be most appropriate for initial management in this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Presence of clue cells on wet mount microscopy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of clue cells on saline wet mount is the single most reliable predictor of bacterial vaginosis.

  • Indicators towards the diagnosis:
    • Presence of fishy-smelling, vaginal discharge without a history of pruritus
    • The image shows a thin, homogenous whitish discharge that coats the walls, characteristic of bacterial vaginosis
  • Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells that are studded with adherent coccobacilli. This gives the cells a stippled, fuzzy appearance. The presence of these cells indicates bacterial infection of the vagina.
  • Clue cells in bacterial vaginosis:

[[figure-1]]

Amsel's criteria for bacterial vaginosis (BV):

  1. Thin, greyish-white vaginal discharge.
  2. Vaginal pH greater than 4.5
  3. Presence of clue cells on wet mount microscopy and
  4. Positive whiff test (amine odour) with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution.

Presence of at least three of the above findings is needed to make a diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis

Nugent’s score

It is the gold standard test for bacterial vaginosis but is not used in clinical practice as it requires more expertise. This score involves a gram stain smear of vaginal discharge.

While all the other options are part of Amsel's criteria, presence of clue cells is most diagnostic, as other features may be seen with other types of vaginal discharge. Presence of clue cells >20% is diagnostic.

question: A 32 year old woman presents with complaints of vaginal discharge and a fishy odour. She denies any genital itching or irritation. On examination, you notice the discharge coats the vaginal walls as shown in the image. There is no erythema or inflammation noted. Out of the following, which is the single most reliable predictor to support the diagnosis in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Vaginal candidiasis, (yeast infection/ vaginal thrush) is caused by overgrowth of the fungus Candida albicans.
  • Women with diabetes are at higher risk of developing yeast infections due to elevated blood sugar levels, which provide a favourable environment for yeast growth.
  • The symptoms typically include vaginal itching, thick, white, curd-like discharge, and sometimes redness and swelling of the vulva.
  • The absence of inflammation or lesions on examination further supports the diagnosis of vaginal candidiasis
  • Unlike other vaginal discharges, Vaginal pH is usually acidic.
  • Treatment:
    • Topical azole antifungals: Clotrimazole, miconazole, econazole, or tioconazole creams or suppositories
    • Oral azole antifungals: Fluconazole is an effective oral antifungal medication that may be prescribed as a single-dose regimen (150 mg) or as multiple doses depending on the severity of the infection.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) (Option A):

  • It is characterized by a thin, greyish-white discharge with a characteristic fishy odour, known as "whiff test" positivity.

Trichomoniasis (Option B):

  • Trichomonal vaginitis typically presents with a frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge with a characteristic foul odour, often described as "musty."
  • Additionally, patients with trichomoniasis may experience vulvar itching, dyspareunia, and dysuria.

Chlamydia trachomatis infection (Option D):

  • Chlamydia trachomatis infection typically presents with mucopurulent cervical discharge.
  • It may lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) if left untreated.


Reference:
  1. Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 113
  2. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Chapter 216
question: A 30 year old woman with a medical history significant for diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic with complaints of vaginal itching and thick, white, curd-like discharge. Physical examination reveals no signs of inflammation or lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation :

  • Based on the clinical presentation of single painless genital ulcer with raised edges and a clean base in a sexually active individual, the most likely diagnosis is syphilis, specifically primary syphilis.
  • Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum.
  • The treatment of choice for all stages of syphilis, including primary syphilis, is penicillin. In this case, intramuscular Penicillin G Benzathine is the recommended treatment.

Syphilis treatment:

  • Counselling and Education: Very important component of treatment and should include:
    • Avoidance of sex till healing of lesions.
    • Presumptive treatment of partners.
    • Advice on safe sex including use of condoms and encouraging single-partner relationship.
    • Follow up testing for HIV, hepatitis B virus and VDRL at 3 months and further if necessary.
  • Specific Treatment:
    • Injectable penicillin is the treatment of choice, unless patient is sensitive to it when either erythromycin (in pregnant women sensitive to penicillin) or doxycycline are used.

[[figure-1]]

Doxycycline (Option A) is effective for treating genital ulcers like donovosis.


Oral Azithromycin (Option B) is not the first-line treatment for primary syphilis. Azithromycin is also used for the treatment of Chlamydia and Gonorrhoea.


Oral Acyclovir (Option D) is used to treat herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections that present with multiple painful ulcers.



Reference:

Neena Khanna’s Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology and Sexually Transmitted Diseases, 7th Edition, Page 300
question: A 28 year old sexually active male presents to the clinic with a painless single lesion on his genitals. On examination, the healthcare provider observes single small, round, painless ulcer with raised edges and a clean base as shown below. The patient denies any recent travel, but he reports having unprotected sexual contact with multiple partners in the past month. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation and absence of bacteria on Gram stain suggest Chlamydia trachomatis as the likely cause of non-gonococcal cervicitis. The first-line treatment is a single dose of Azithromycin (1g orally).
  • The diagnosis of NGU/NGC requires the exclusion of gonorrheal infection. This can be achieved with a gram stain that lacks gram-negative diplococci or by any negative gonorrhea test (culture, nucleic acid testing, among others).

Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D-K are the most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis. In females, it can cause various manifestations such as:

  • Mucopurulent cervicitis (most common).
  • It may progress to endometritis, salpingitis (fallopian tube), pelvic inflammatory disease, and finally pelvic peritonitis.
  • Perihepatitis (Fitz–Hugh–Curtis syndrome).

First-line management involves a single oral dose of azithromycin 1g stat. It is preferred due to its greater effectiveness and lower cost.

The table below shows the management of uncomplicated chlamydial infections:

Non-pregnant

First line: Azithromycin 1g single dose

Second line: Doxycycline 100mg BD x 7 days

Third line: Ofloxacin 200-300mg BD x 7 days

Pregnancy

First line: Azithromycin 1g oral single dose

Second line: Amoxicillin 500mg TDS x 7 days

Ceftriaxone (Option B) is used for the treatment of gonococcal infections.

Fluconazole (Option C) is used for the treatment of vaginal candidiasis.

Doxycycline (Option D) is also highly effective for treating uncomplicated chlamydial infections. It is used when azithromycin is not available or there is a history of allergies. The recommended dose is 100 mg BD x 7 days.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.10-15
  2. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition Page 1449-50
  3. Essentials of Medical Microbiology, Apurba Sastry, 4th Edition, Page 768, 770
  4. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535411/
question: A 24-year-old sexually active female presents with dysuria, increased urinary frequency, and mild cervical discharge on per speculum examination. She denies fever or abdominal pain. A urinalysis reveals pyuria, but no bacteria are seen on Gram staining of the discharge. Which of the following agents is the first-line drug for this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Presents with an indurated ulcer and painless lymphadenopathy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical presentation of a male with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse, swelling in the inguinal region (inguinal lymphadenopathy) and a painless ulcer that has healed without scarring is suggestive of lymphogranuloma venerum, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. The incorrect statement is that it presents with an indurated ulcer and painless lymphadenopathy.

Lymphogranuloma venerum (LGV):

  • It is a sexually transmitted disease caused by serovars L1-L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis (M/C strain causing LGV: L2). It occurs in sexually active adults of all ages. It can cause LGV-associated proctitis in homosexuals, associated with HIV and hepatitis C co-infection.
  • The incubation period of LGV is around 3-30 days, and the disease presents in three stages, described in the table below:

Primary

Secondary

Tertiary

3-30 days

Days-weeks

Years after a chronic, untreated infection

Small papule/pustule/
Non-indurated ulcer at the site of inoculation which heals spontaneously with no scarring.
  • Lymphatic involvement of nodes that drain the primary lesion.
  • Classic form: Tender unilateral or bilateral inguinal and/or femoral adenopathy (Groove sign of Greenblatt).
  • The lymph nodes may coalesce to form a bubo or abscesses that may rupture spontaneously with the development of
    Fistulae or sinus tracts.
  • There may be systemic features such as malaise and fever.

Lymphatic obstruction due to chronic inflammation leads to fistula formation, strictures, and disfiguring conditions such as genital elephantiasis and esthiomene, which refers to hypertrophic enlargement with ulceration of the external genitalia.
  • Diagnosis of LGV can be confirmed by the Nucelic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT). Antibody detection by real-time PCR can also be done. Treatment includes:
    • First line: Doxycycline 100mg BD x 21 days.
    • Second line: Erythromycin 500mg 4 times a day x 21 days.
    • Third line: Azithromycin 1g weekly once x 21 days.

Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3 (Option A): This statement is true; these specific serovars are the causative agents of LGV.

Can be associated with hepatitis C co-infection (Option B): This statement is true; co-infections with other STIs, including HCV, are possible in individuals with LGV.

Esthiomene is a complication in the tertiary stage of this disease (Option D): This statement is true; esthiomene (genital elephantiasis) is a recognized chronic complication of untreated or persistent LGV infection.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.15-30.20
