Esthiomene is a complication in the tertiary stage of this disease

question: A 28 year old male presents to the STD clinic with a history of swelling in the inguinal region as shown in the image below. He has a history of unprotected sexual intercourse in the past few months and reports a painless ulcer, which healed without scarring. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The symptoms described in the stem, along with the patient's inability to conceive despite actively trying, raise suspicion of chlamydia infection.

  • Chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease often presents asymptomatically but can cause symptoms such as lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia, and cervical motion tenderness.
  • These symptoms, along with the patient's reported inability to conceive despite actively trying for the past 18 months, raise suspicion for chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which can lead to fallopian tube damage and subsequent infertility.

Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs). It is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis

  • Clinical features in females: Although it is mostly asymptomatic, it can present in the following forms:
    • Cervicitis
    • Urethritis
    • Pelvic inflammatory disease
    • Perihepatitis
    • Pregnancy complications
  • Clinical features in males:
    • Urethritis
    • Epididymitis
    • Prostatitis
  • Common features:
    • Conjunctivitis
    • Pharyngitis
    • Proctitis
    • Genital lymphogranuloma venereum
  • Diagnosis is made through nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) of genital samples.

Genital herpes (Option A) presents with multiple, painful, non-indurated, umbilicated vesicles that rupture to form coalescing vesicles or polycyclic erosions.

[[figure-1]]

Syphilis (Option C) presents as painless genital ulcers (chancre).

[[figure-2]]

Trichomoniasis (Option D) presents with frothy discharge, vulvar itching, and strawberry cervix.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 113
question: A 28 year old female presents with lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia, and cervical motion tenderness. She also reports that she has been unable to conceive despite actively trying for the past 18 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Given the symptoms and risk factors, the most likely diagnosis is gonorrhoea. IM ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic, is the recommended treatment. Ceftriaxone is typically given as a single dose, often combined with azithromycin to cover potential co-infection with Chlamydia trachomatis.

In case of chlamydia the urethral discharge is mucoid/mucopurulent.

question: A 28 year old sexually active male presents with dysuria and urethral discharge which is purulent, profuse, thick and creamy. He reports having unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. What is the most appropriate initial management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
  • Additionally, the history of multiple sexual partners and inconsistent condom use is suggestive of a higher risk for STIs, including gonorrhoea.

[[figure-1]]

Gram stain showing Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Neisseria Gonorrhoea

Genital discharge (purulent), dysuria, pelvic pain, rectal symptoms

Complications

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), epididymitis, prostatitis, disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI)

Transmission

Primarily through sexual contact (vaginal, anal, oral) with an infected individual

Risk Factors

Unprotected sex, multiple sexual partners, history of gonorrhoea

Diagnosis

In males, by gram stain(gram negative intracellular diplococci) and culture and in females by culture.

Multiplex PCR

Treatment

SOD cefixime 400mg or intramuscular ceftriaxone 125/250mg as SD

Bacterial vaginosis (Option A) is characterized by a thin, greyish-white vaginal discharge with a fishy odour, but it does not present with purulent discharge or intracellular gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain.

[[figure-2]]

Candidiasis (Option B) is a fungal infection that causes vaginal itching and thick, white, cottage cheese-like discharge.

[[figure-3]]

Trichomoniasis (Option C) is caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis and typically presents with frothy, yellow-green, malodorous discharge.

[[figure-4]]

question: A 22 year old sexually active woman presents to the clinic with complaints of vaginal discharge and pelvic pain. She reports having multiple sexual partners and inconsistent use of condoms. On examination, the healthcare provider notices purulent vaginal discharge and tenderness on pelvic examination. A Gram stain of the discharge reveals intracellular gram-negative diplococci. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hutchinson’s Triad is a feature of the late-onset congenital syphilis.
  • Congenital syphilis occurs when a pregnant woman with untreated syphilis passes the infection to her fetus during pregnancy. The bacterium Treponema pallidum can affect various organ systems in the newborn.
  • The lesions in Congenital syphilis can be classified as Early onset (within 2 years after birth) and Late onset (after 2 years of birth).

Lesions in Early Onset Congenital Syphilis: (Options A, B, C ruled out)

  • Vesiculo Bullous rash - Over palms & soles (aka SYPHILITIC PEMPHIGUS)
  • Inflammation of oral and nasal mucosa
  • Continuous discharge from the nose is called snuffles.
  • Wimberger Sign (Bilateral Medial Tibial Erosions)
  • Osteochondritis & Peri Osteochondritis (Pseudo Paralysis of Parrot - Child not able to move)

Lesions in Late Onset Congenital Syphilis

  • Hutchison’s Triad: Peg-shaped incisors, interstitial keratitis, and deafness
  • Mulberry Molars
  • Deformed nose
  • Rhagades: Fissures around the mouth
  • Frontal bossing / Olympian bow
  • Higoumenakis Sign (Unilateral Medial Clavicle Periostitis)
  • Cluttons Joint (Painless)
  • Sabre Tibia (Anterior Tibia Periostitis)


Reference:

Neena Khanna’s Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology and Sexually Transmitted Diseases, 7th Edition, Page 300

options.text: Inflammation of oral and nasal mucosa

question: A newborn infant presents with symptoms suggestive of congenital syphilis. The mother had untreated syphilis during pregnancy. Which of the following is not a manifestation of early-onset congenital syphilis in newborns?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis for this patient's presentation is secondary syphilis.
  • Secondary syphilis occurs a few weeks to months after the initial infection (primary syphilis) and is characterized by a variety of symptoms, including a diffuse maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles.
  • Other common features of secondary syphilis include fever, sore throat, and mucous membrane involvement (such as white patches in the mouth). The presence of a painless genital ulcer (chancre) in the history supports the diagnosis.

question: A 28 year old man presents to the clinic with a diffuse, maculopapular rash on his palms and soles, as well as fever and sore throat. He reports that the rash developed a few weeks after he noticed a painless ulcer on his genital area, which resolved on its own. The rash is not itchy and does not involve the face. The patient also has white patches in his mouth and a few small, red papules on his genitals. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Intracellular bipolar “safety-pin” organisms in macrophages
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation describes Granuloma Inguinale (also known as Donovanosis), and the finding that confirms this diagnosis is intracellular bipolar “safety-pin” organisms in macrophages.

  • The causative organism of Donovanosis is Klebsiella granulomatis

[[figure-1]]

Donovanosis - Diagnosis:

  • Gold standard: Microscopic identification of Donovan bodies
  • Location: Inside monocytes/macrophages
  • Morphology: Bipolar staining → “safety-pin” appearance
  • Stains used: Giemsa, Wright, Leishman
  • Specimen: Crushed tissue from the lesion, Biopsy material

Gram-negative diplococci in neutrophils (Option B): Suggests gonorrhoea, not donovanosis.

[[figure-2]]


Spirochetes on dark-field microscopy (Option C): Seen in primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum).

[[figure-3]]


Multinucleated giant cells (Option D): Characteristic of herpes simplex infection.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.25
question: A man presents with a painless, beefy-red genital ulcer that bleeds on touch. A Giemsa-stained smear is examined. Which finding confirms the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. The incubation period is around 50 days
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical presentation, the patient has Granuloma Inguinale (Donovanosis), caused by Klebsiella granulomatis.
  • The incubation period of granuloma inguinale is variable (1-360 days), but lesions typically appear after an average of ~50 days, making this statement correct.


Granuloma Inguinale (Donovanosis):

  • Cause: Klebsiella granulomatis
  • Transmission: Mainly STI; rare non-sexual & vertical transmission
  • Clinical features:
    • Incubation: ~50 days (1-360 days)
    • Ulcer: Painless, beefy-red, friable, bleeds on touch
    • Types: Ulcerogranulomatous (common), hypertrophic, necrotic, sclerotic
    • Nodes: Absent; pseudobuboes possible
    • Sites: Coronal sulcus/prepuce, labia/introitus, anus (MSM); rare extragenital
  • Complications: Scarring (Option B), pseudo-elephantiasis, haemorrhage, squamous cell carcinoma (Option A), ↑ HIV risk
  • Diagnosis: Donovan bodies in macrophages (safety-pin) on Giemsa/Wright/Leishman

[[figure-1]]

  • Treatment (≥6 weeks or till healing)
    • Azithromycin (first line)
    • Doxycycline (alternative) (Option C)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 30.23 - 30.25

options.text: Not associated with squamous cell carcinoma
Doxycycline is the first-line drug of choice
The incubation period is around 50 days

question: A 32-year-old man from an endemic area presents with a painless, beefy-red genital ulcer as shown that bleeds on touch. There is no true inguinal lymphadenopathy. Smear from the lesion shows intracellular organisms with bipolar staining. Which of the following statements is true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pseudobuboes are subcutaneous granulomatous swellings that mimic enlarged lymph nodes but do not arise from lymph nodes.
  • They are classically seen in Granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis).
  • In granuloma inguinale:
    • The causative organism is Klebsiella granulomatis.
    • The disease causes painless, beefy-red, friable genital ulcers that bleed on touch.
    • True inguinal lymphadenopathy is usually absent.
    • Instead, pseudobuboes may appear due to subcutaneous extension of granulomatous tissue, giving the false impression of lymph node enlargement.
    • These swellings are not lymph nodes → hence the term pseudo-bubo.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (Option A): Causes true tender inguinal buboes due to lymphadenitis.

Chancroid (Option B): Characterised by painful ulcers with suppurative tender buboes.

Primary syphilis (Option D): Causes non-tender lymphadenopathy, not pseudobuboes.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.24

question: A 25-year-old man presents with recurrent genital ulcers associated with a burning sensation. He is managed under the syndromic approach (NACP 2024). The Red Kit (Kit 5) is used in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Genital herpes (HSV) differs from other causes of genital ulcer disease in partner management:
  • In HSV infection, asymptomatic partners are not given routine antiviral treatment.
  • Antivirals (acyclovir/valacyclovir/famciclovir) are used for:
    • Symptomatic episodes, or
    • Suppressive therapy in the index patient to reduce recurrences and transmission risk.
  • For asymptomatic partners, management focuses on:
    • Counselling (natural history, recurrence, transmission risk)
    • Risk reduction (condom use, avoiding sex during active lesions)
    • Testing if indicated, but no empirical treatment.
  • In contrast, bacterial STIs causing GUD require presumptive partner treatment because:
    • They are curable,
    • Untreated partners act as a reservoir of infection, and
    • Early treatment prevents complications and reinfection.

Primary syphilis (Option A): Sexual partners must be traced, evaluated, and treated presumptively, even if asymptomatic, to prevent ongoing transmission and complications.

Chancroid (Option B): Partners are treated empirically, even if asymptomatic, because chancroid is a bacterial STI with high transmissibility.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (Option D): Partners require evaluation and treatment (usually doxycycline), even if they have no symptoms, to prevent persistent infection and complications.



Reference:

https://naco.gov.in/sites/default/files/National%20Technical%20Guidelines%20on%20STI%20and%20RTI_Final.pdf

question: A 26-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a painful genital ulcer for 5 days. The ulcer is soft, non-indurated, with undermined edges and a purulent base. He also has findings as shown. The HIV test is negative. What is the most appropriate treatment?

correctAnswer: B. Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on vaginal swab
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis for this patient is acute cervicitis, typically caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis is the nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on a vaginal swab.


Genital Chlamydia:

  • Men: Urethritis, epididymo-orchitis, proctitis
  • Women: Cervicitis, PID, postcoital bleeding
  • Extragenital: Conjunctivitis, neonatal pneumonia
  • Complications: Infertility, ectopic pregnancy, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis, reactive arthritis
  • Diagnosis:
    • NAAT = test of choice
      • Men: First-void urine
      • Women: Vaginal/endocervical swab
      • MSM: Rectal & pharyngeal swab
    • Culture (Option D) & serology (Option C) → Not routine


Gram stain of endocervical smear (Option A): Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular organism and cannot be reliably visualised on Gram stain.


Urethritis Syndromes:

Feature

Gonococcal Urethritis (GU)

Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (NGU)

Causative Organism

Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Chlamydia trachomatis (most common), Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma

Onset

Acute, rapid

Subacute, gradual

Discharge

Profuse, thick, purulent, yellow-green

Scanty, mucoid or watery

Dysuria

Marked

Mild to moderate

Gram Stain

Gram-negative intracellular diplococci seen

No organisms seen

Incubation Period

2-5 days

7-21 days

Complications

Epididymitis, prostatitis, DGI

Reactive arthritis, epididymitis

Treatment

Ceftriaxone single dose + Azithromycin

Doxycycline 7 days (or Azithromycin single dose)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.13

question: A 22-year-old sexually active woman presents with postcoital bleeding and mucopurulent cervical discharge. She is otherwise asymptomatic. Speculum examination shows a friable cervix. Which of the following is the investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Doxycycline is now the preferred first-line agent for uncomplicated urogenital chlamydia in non-pregnant patients due to superior efficacy (especially for rectal/extra-genital infections) and is recommended by the 2025 European guidelines and the CDC's updated STI treatment guidelines.

Chlamydial infection – Treatment:

  • Uncomplicated Urogenital Infection (non-pregnant):

    • First line: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 7 days

    • Alternative: Azithromycin 1 g single dose (useful when compliance is uncertain; also preferred in pregnancy)

    • Pregnancy: Azithromycin 1 g single dose (preferred; doxycycline contraindicated)

  • Complicated / Extragenital Infections:

    • Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): Ceftriaxone + Doxycycline + Metronidazole (14 days)

    • Epididymo-orchitis: Ceftriaxone + Doxycycline (10–14 days)

    • Proctitis / LGV (inguinal bubo): Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 21 days (as per NACP-2024 Black Kit)

Azithromycin 1 g single dose (Option A) remains an acceptable alternative, particularly when compliance is uncertain or in pregnancy, but it is no longer the primary drug of choice in non-pregnant adults.

Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose (Option C): Drug of choice for gonorrhoea, not chlamydia.


Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days (Option D): Used for anaerobic infections and Trichomonas vaginalis, not chlamydia.




Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.15

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days

question: A 19-year-old sexually active woman presents with mucopurulent cervical discharge and dysuria. NAAT confirms Chlamydia trachomatis infection. She is not pregnant and has no drug allergies. Which of the following is the drug of choice for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Gonococcal urethritis. Acute onset, profuse purulent discharge, short incubation (1-5 days), and Gram-negative intracellular diplococci are classic for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.


Gonorrhoea:

  • Sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae → purulent inflammation of the genital mucosa.
  • Vertical transmission → ophthalmia neonatorum.
  • Organism:
    • Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus
    • Infects columnar epithelium
    • Marked antigenic variation
  • Clinical Features:
    • Men:
      • Acute urethritis: Severe dysuria & profuse purulent discharge

[[figure-1]]

  • Women:
    • Often asymptomatic
    • Cervicitis: Vaginal discharge, postcoital bleeding & risk of PID
  • Extragenital:
    • Rectal → pain, discharge
    • Pharyngeal → usually asymptomatic
    • Eye → purulent conjunctivitis
  • Diagnosis:
    • Gram stain: intracellular diplococci (male urethra highly sensitive)

[[figure-2]]

  • Culture (gold standard; sensitivity testing)
  • NAAT (more sensitive)
  • Treatment:
    • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + Azithromycin 2 g PO
      • Always cover Chlamydia
      • Test of cure at 2 weeks
      • Partner notification essential


Chlamydial urethritis (Option A): No organisms seen on Gram stain (intracellular but not visible as diplococci)


Non-specific urethritis (Option C): Diagnosis of exclusion; Gram stain would not show diplococci


Trichomoniasis (Option D): Seen as motile protozoa on wet mount, not Gram-negative diplococci



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 30.1-30.8
question: A 22-year-old man presents with 2 days of severe dysuria and profuse purulent urethral discharge. He had unprotected intercourse 4 days ago. Gram staining findings are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Pharyngeal gonorrhoea is usually symptomatic.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Infections of the pharynx are most commonly asymptomatic.


Gonorrhoea:

  • Sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae → purulent inflammation of the genital mucosa.
  • Vertical transmission → ophthalmia neonatorum.
  • Organism:
    • Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus (Option A)
    • Infects columnar epithelium
    • Marked antigenic variation
  • Clinical Features:
    • Men:
      • Acute urethritis: Severe dysuria & profuse purulent discharge

[[figure-1]]

  • Women:
    • Often asymptomatic
    • Cervicitis: Vaginal discharge, postcoital bleeding & risk of PID
  • Extragenital:
    • Rectal → pain, discharge
    • Pharyngeal → usually asymptomatic
    • Eye → purulent conjunctivitis
  • Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI):
    • Dermatitis + Arthritis syndrome: (Option D)
      • Fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular/necrotic skin lesions
  • Diagnosis:
    • Gram stain: intracellular diplococci (male urethra highly sensitive)
    • Culture (gold standard; sensitivity testing) (Option B)
    • NAAT (more sensitive)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 30.1-30.8

question: A 20-year-old man is diagnosed with gonorrhoea. Which of the following statements is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical sign described is the Groove sign (also known as Greenblatt’s sign), and it is characteristic of Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV).

[[figure-1]]


Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV):

  • LGV is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3.
  • Incubation Period: Typically 3-30 days (average ~1-2 weeks).
  • Stages of LGV:
    • Primary Stage:
      • Appears as a small, painless genital or anal ulcer, often unnoticed.
    • Secondary Stage (Inguinal Syndrome):
      • Painful inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy (“bubo”)
      • May cause the groove sign: enlarged nodes above and below the inguinal ligament.
    • Tertiary/Chronic Stage
      • Genital or rectal fibrosis, strictures, and fistulas
      • Can lead to elephantiasis of the genitalia (esthiomene).
  • Diagnosis:
    • NAAT (PCR) for C. trachomatis from lesion or lymph node aspirate
    • Serology and culture are less commonly used
  • Treatment
    • Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 21 days (first-line)
    • Alternatives: azithromycin 1 g weekly for 3 weeks


Chancroid (Option A): Painful ulcer with fluctuant buboes, but no groove sign.


Granuloma inguinale (Option C): Painless beefy-red ulcers; lymphadenopathy is uncommon.


Primary syphilis (Option D): Painless chancre with non-tender lymphadenopathy; groove sign absent.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 30.11 - 30.18
question: A 26-year-old man develops painful inguinal swelling 2 weeks after a small painless genital ulcer. Examination shows findings as shown in the image. Which of the following conditions is associated with these findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and Gram stain finding (Gram-negative intracellular diplococci) confirm a diagnosis of Gonorrhea. The drug of choice (DOC) for this condition is Ceftriaxone.

[[figure-1]]

  • Diagnosis:
    • Gram stain: intracellular diplococci (male urethra highly sensitive)
    • Culture (gold standard; sensitivity testing)
    • NAAT (more sensitive)
  • Treatment:
    • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + Azithromycin 2 g PO
      • Always cover Chlamydia
      • Test of cure at 2 weeks
      • Partner notification essential
    • Second line:
      • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM
      • Spectinomycin 2 g IM + Azithromycin 2 g PO (Not effective for pharyngeal infection)
      • Cefixime 400 mg PO + Azithromycin 2 g PO (higher failure)
    • Complicated infection:
      • Epididymo-orchitis: Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin → then Doxycycline 10-14 days
      • PID: Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin → then Doxycycline + Metronidazole 14 days
      • Conjunctivitis: Eye irrigation + Azithromycin + Ceftriaxone (3 days)


Benzathine penicillin G (Option A): Used for syphilis, not gonorrhoea due to resistance.


Doxycycline (Option B): Used for Chlamydia; not adequate monotherapy for gonorrhoea.


Ciprofloxacin (Option D): Not first-line due to high resistance rates.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.7
question: A 24-year-old sexually active man presents with purulent urethral discharge and dysuria for 3 days. Gram stain of urethral smear shows findings as given below. What is the drug of choice (DOC) for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The history of a transient primary ulcer followed by painful inguinal buboes is classic for Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV). The tertiary stage of LGV causes chronic lymphatic obstruction leading to genital elephantiasis and fibrosis (esthiomene).

[[figure-1]]


LGV-Stages:

  • Primary (3-30 days):
    • Small painless papule/ulcer
    • Heals spontaneously
  • Secondary (Days-Weeks):
    • Tender inguinal/femoral nodes
    • Groove sign
    • Bubo, sinus formation
    • Proctitis (anal exposure)
    • Fever, malaise
  • Tertiary (Years):
    • Chronic lymphatic obstruction
    • Fistulae, strictures
    • Genital elephantiasis (Esthiomene)


Primary syphilis (Option A): Causes a painless genital ulcer (chancre). No chronic vulval fibrosis or inguinal buboes in the long term

Chancroid (Option B): Causes a painful genital ulcer. May cause unilateral bubo, but rarely chronic fibrosis or massive vulval enlargement

Granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis) (Option D): Painless, beefy red ulcerative lesions, rarely involve lymph nodes. Does not cause inguinal buboes or massive vulval fibrosis



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.18
question: A 32-year-old woman presents with massive vulval enlargement and fibrosis. She gives a history of recurrent painful inguinal buboes years earlier, following a transient genital ulcer. It is seen in which condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image depicts Saxophone penis deformity.

  • Peyronie's disease causes penile curvature due to fibrous plaques of the tunica albuginea, but does not cause diffuse lymphoedematous enlargement typical of saxophone penis.


Saxophone penis results from chronic lymphatic obstruction of the penis.

  • Lymphogranuloma venereum → Chronic inguinal lymphadenitis leads to lymphatic fibrosis and genital lymphedema, producing the classic deformity.
  • Primary genital lymphoedema → Congenital lymphatic malformation causing progressive penile swelling and curvature.
  • Periurethral abscess due to gonorrhoea → Chronic inflammatory damage and lymphatic obstruction may result in saxophone deformity.


Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.4
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3841672/
  3. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2858891/
question:
Which of the following numbered conditions are known to cause deformity as shown in the image?

  1. Lymphogranuloma venereum
  2. Primary genital lymphoedema
  3. Peyronie disease
  4. Periurethral abscess due to gonorrhoea

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Vaginal pH < 4.5 is not part of the criteria; it usually indicates normal vaginal flora or Candida infection.


Amsel’s criteria for Bacterial vaginosis:

  1. Thin, greyish-white vaginal discharge.
  2. Vaginal pH greater than 4.5
  3. Presence of clue cells on wet mount microscopy and
  4. Positive whiff test (amine odour) with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution.

Presence of at least three of the above findings is needed to make a diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis.

question: Which of the following is not part of Amsel’s criteria for diagnosing bacterial vaginosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of a single painless genital ulcer with raised edges and a clean base, accompanied by painless swelling of the inguinal lymph nodes, strongly suggests Primary Syphilis.

  • Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum. Primary syphilis typically manifests as a chancre, which is a painless ulcer appearing at the site of inoculation. The associated lymphadenopathy is also painless, helping to differentiate syphilis from other sexually transmitted infections.
  • Treatment of syphilis:
    • Primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis: A single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units.
    • Late latent syphilis or tertiary syphilis (excluding neurosyphilis): Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks.
    • Neurosyphilis: Intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G at 18–24 million units daily, divided into doses every 4 hours or by continuous infusion for 10–14 days.

Chancroid (Option A) is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi and presents as a painful genital ulcer with irregular edges, often accompanied by tender, suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes).

Herpes genitalis (Option C) is caused by Herpes simplex virus (HSV), it presents with multiple painful vesicles or ulcers on the genital area, often associated with burning or itching sensations.

Granuloma inguinale (Option D) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis, it presents as beefy red ulcers that bleed easily on touch, with no associated lymphadenopathy. The ulcers are typically painless but have a different appearance than the chancre of syphilis.



Reference:
  1. Fitzpatrick Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 3160.
  2. Rook’s textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 30.7
question: What is the probable diagnosis for a young woman who presents with a painless ulcer in the genital region accompanied by pain less swelling of the lymph nodes in the groin?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Lower abdominal pain is not part of male syndrome management in STI programs.

It is a female-specific syndrome, usually related to PID (Pelvic Inflammatory Disease), and therefore not included in male STI syndromic case management algorithms.

Incorrect Options:

Urethral discharge (Option A) is included in male STI syndromic management; usually due to gonorrhea or chlamydia.

Genital ulcer (Option B) is included as a major syndrome; covers HSV, syphilis, chancroid.

Inguinal swelling (Option C) represents bubo syndrome (LGV, chancroid).

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Genital warts are caused by certain strains of the human papillomavirus (HPV), which is a sexually transmitted infection.
    • They typically appear as raised, flesh-colored or grayish growths on or around the genitals, including the penis in males.
    • In some cases, they can also be found near the anal canal, as mentioned in the scenario.

  • Benign, moist, soft, pedunculated wart found on the external genitalia and has low malignant potential.

question: A sexually active male presented with warts on his penis as shown below. Similar lesions were present near the anal canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Don’t involve in intercourse when active lesions are present
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Genital warts are caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV) and can be transmitted through sexual contact. When a female patient presents with active genital warts and a history of recurrence, it is important to provide appropriate advice to prevent transmission to her partner.
  • The most effective measure to prevent transmission of genital warts is to avoid sexual intercourse when active lesions are present. This is because the virus is most contagious and easily transmitted when the warts are actively present

Treatment for genital warts involves both individual and partner management

Individual Treatment:

  • Topical Medications: Various topical medications can be prescribed to treat genital warts. These include:
  • Imiquimod cream/Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) or bichloroacetic acid (BCA): These acids are applied directly to the warts to destroy them.
  • Surgical Procedures
  • These procedures include:
    • Cryotherapy
    • Electrocautery
    • Surgical excision

Partner Management:

  • It is important to inform the partner about the presence of genital warts so that they can also seek appropriate medical evaluation and treatment if necessary.
  • It is best to avoid sexual activity, especially during active wart outbreaks, to prevent transmission to the partner.


Incorrect Options:

Give continuous prophylaxis to the patient (Option A): Prophylactic treatments such as topical creams or vaccines are typically used for individuals who have not yet contracted the virus or to prevent future outbreaks.

Give prophylactic antivirals to the husband (Option B): Antiviral medications are primarily used for the treatment of active infections or to reduce the severity and duration of outbreaks, but they do not provide long-term protection against transmission.

Give antivirals whenever active lesions are present (Option C): While antiviral medications can be used to treat active genital warts and reduce the duration of outbreaks, using them solely when active lesions are present is not the most effective approach to prevent transmission.



Reference:

Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology and Sexually Transmitted Diseases, Fifth Edition – Neena Khanna Pg 339-341

Explanation:

  • Tzanck cells are multinucleated giant cells seen in herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infections.
  • Genital lesions caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2 typically present as painful vesicles that rupture to form ulcers.
  • Tzanck smear from lesion scrapings shows multinucleated giant cells with acantholysis, confirming HSV infection.
  • HSV-1 and HSV-2 cause genital and orolabial herpes, with HSV-2 being more commonly associated with genital lesions.

Clinical Features of Genital Herpes:

  • Painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
  • Vesicles rupture to form shallow ulcers

  • Tzanck smear: Shows multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells) but cannot differentiate between HSV-1 and HSV-2.
  • PCR: Most sensitive and specific test for HSV.
  • DFA (Direct Fluorescent Antibody test): Detects viral antigens.

Management of HSV:

  • First-line therapy: Oral antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir).
  • Supportive care: Pain relief, hydration, avoiding triggers for recurrence.

Cells with clear halo around the nucleus (Option B) is incorrect because this refers to koilocytes, which are seen in human papillomavirus (HPV) infections (genital warts).

Molluscum bodies (Option C) is incorrect because these are Henderson-Patterson bodies, seen in molluscum contagiosum. They appear as intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in affected keratinocytes.

HP bodies (Option D) is incorrect because HP (Hailey-Penrose) bodies are associated with Hailey-Hailey disease, a rare genetic blistering disorder, and are not found in genital lesions.

question: A 45-year-old truck driver with a history of multiple sex partners presented to the dermatological department, as shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The lesions depicted in the image, along with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse, suggest a diagnosis of Secondary Syphilis, which is best confirmed through serological testing.

  • It is the second stage of syphilis, which occurs if primary syphilis is left untreated.
  • It presents a few weeks to several months after the initial chancre has healed.
  • It is marked by systemic manifestations and can affect multiple organ systems.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Diffuse, non-pruritic rash, often reddish-brown macules or papules, that is polymorphous and non-vesicular.
    • Mucous membrane lesions, such as condylomata lata, appear in moist areas like the oral cavity and genitals and are highly infectious.
    • Oral signs may include mucous patches or snail track ulcers.
    • “Moth-eaten" alopecia: A patchy, non-scarring hair loss.
    • Buschke-Ollendorff sign: Deep tenderness over lesions.
    • Painless generalized lymphadenopathy (especially epitrochlear nodes)l.
    • Systemic symptoms include fever, malaise, and fatigue, with rare cases showing neurological or ocular involvement.
  • Diagnosis: By serological testing: (Option A)
    • Non-Treponemal Tests:
      • RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) and VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) are used for screening.
      • These tests detect nonspecific antibodies and can be positive in other conditions.
    • Treponemal Tests:
      • FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) confirms the diagnosis by detecting antibodies specific to Treponema pallidum.
  • Treatment:
    • Standard treatment: Benzathine penicillin G.
    • Dosage: 2.4 million units intramuscularly in a single dose.
    • For those allergic to penicillin, alternatives such as doxycycline or tetracycline can be used.
  • Complications: If left untreated, secondary syphilis can progress to the latent stage and eventually tertiary syphilis, which can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular, neurological, and systemic damage.

Incorrect Options:

Tzanck smear (Option B) is a diagnostic test primarily used for identifying infections caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus. It involves examining cells scraped from a lesion under a microscope. However, this test has no role in diagnosing syphilis, as it does not detect Treponema pallidum, the bacterium responsible for the disease.

KOH preparation (Option C) is commonly employed to diagnose superficial fungal infections such as dermatophytosis or candidiasis. A sample from the skin, hair, or nails is treated with potassium hydroxide, which dissolves keratin and allows for the visualization of fungal elements under a microscope. Since syphilis is a bacterial infection, this test is irrelevant in its diagnosis.

Biopsy (Option D) is used to evaluate suspicious skin lesions when the diagnosis is unclear, and it can sometimes reveal histopathological features suggestive of syphilis. It is invasive and nonspecific, whereas serological tests are more sensitive, specific, and the preferred method for diagnosing secondary syphilis.



Reference:

Essentials of Medical Microbiology by Apurba S. Sastry, 3rd Edition, Page 78-79

Lymphogranuloma venerum (LGV):

  • It is a sexually transmitted disease caused by serovars L1-L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis (M/C strain causing LGV: L2).
  • It occurs in sexually active adults of all ages. It can cause LGV-associated proctitis in homosexuals, associated with HIV and hepatitis C co-infection.

explanationHtml:

  • The key clinical feature is a painless, indurated ulcer with a clean base, associated with rubbery, non-tender lymph nodes. Primary syphilis commonly presents in sexually active adults, consistent with the patient’s profile.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

  • Chancroid (Option A): Presents with painful, soft genital ulcers and tender suppurative lymphadenopathy, unlike the painless ulcer described.
  • Genital herpes (Option B): Characterized by multiple painful vesicles or ulcers, often associated with burning or dysuria, not a single painless lesion.
  • Lymphogranuloma venereum (Option D): Initially causes a small, transient, painless ulcer that often goes unnoticed, followed by painful lymphadenopathy, not non-tender nodes.


Reference:
  • Andrews Diseases of the Skin, Edition 13th, Page 18.
question: A truck driver presents with a single painless genital ulcer that appeared 3 weeks after an unprotected sexual encounter. There is associated non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above clinical scenario points towards the diagnosis of C (LGV).
  • LGV is a sexually transmitted infection caused by invasive strains of Chlamydia trachomatis. It classically begins with a small, painless, transient genital ulcer that often heals spontaneously and may go unnoticed.
  • After 1-3 weeks, patients develop painful inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy (buboes) associated with systemic symptoms such as fever, which is the hallmark of LGV. This biphasic presentation is characteristic and helps distinguish it from other chlamydial infections.
  • LGV is caused specifically by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3, which have the ability to invade lymphatic tissue, leading to suppurative lymphadenitis.

Incorrect Options:

  • A-C (Option B): These serovars cause trachoma, a chronic conjunctival infection, and are not associated with genital ulcers or lymphadenopathy.
  • D-K (Option C): These serovars cause uncomplicated urogenital chlamydial infections such as urethritis and cervicitis, without invasive lymph node involvement.
  • B, Ba (Option D): These serovars are also associated with ocular infections and do not cause LGV.



Reference:
  • Andrews Diseases of the Skin, Edition 13th, Page 289.
question: A 27-year-old individual develops a transient genital lesion that resolves spontaneously. About 2 weeks later, he presents with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) and fever. Which Chlamydia trachomatis serovars are responsible for this infection?

correctAnswer: A. Granular continuous deposit of IgG and C3 in the dermo-epidermal junction
explanationHtml:
Based on the clinical presentation described, with a typical “malar rash/butterfly rash” aggravated by sunlight exposure along with systemic symptoms such as fatigue, myalgias, and arthralgias, the patient likely has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

[[figure-1]]

Malar rash with sparing of nasolabial folds.

  • The lupus band test (LBT) is a diagnostic tool where immunofluorescence reveals homogenous deposits along the dermo-epidermal junction.
  • These deposits contain
    • Predominantly IgG, but also occasionally IgM and IgA,
    • Complement components (C1q, C3)
  • Present both in lesions and normal skin.
  • Present in 80% of patients with SLE and DLE.

[[figure-2]]

Option

Direct Immunofluorescence Test - Image

Linear IgG and C3 deposits along the BMZ (Option B) :

  • Also known as shoreline fluorescence pattern
  • Seen in epidermolysis bullosa

[[figure-3]]

Granular IgA in dermal papillae (Option C):

  • Papillary tip immunofluorescence is seen in dermatitis herpetiformis

[[figure-4]]

Intercellular IgG and C3 deposits in the epidermis (Option D):

  • Characteristic fish-net pattern of immunofluorescence is seen in pemphigous vulgaris

[[figure-5]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 51.16-51.17 and 50.21-51.22.

question: A 32-year-old woman comes to the dermatology OPD with lesions on her cheeks that aggravate when exposed to sunlight, as shown in the image below. She has also had fatigue, myalgias, and arthralgias over the past four months. What would be the expected finding on direct immunofluorescence of a skin biopsy of a lesion from this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

‘Carpet tack sign,’ as shown in the image, is seen in discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE). Scales on the undersurface of the lesion appear like tin tacks penetrated on carpets.

[[figure-1]]

Discoid lupus erythematosus is the most common type of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus.

Clinical features:

[[figure-2]]

  • Localized Skin Involvement: Predominantly affects the face and scalp, presenting as circumscribed/ discoid erythematous patches on cheeks, nose bridge, ears, neck, and scalp

[[figure-3]]

  • Lesions exhibit adherent scale with underlying horny plugs (“tin-tack” sign) due to follicular plugging.
  • Characterized by three zones:
    • Central Atrophy area
    • Middle activity - perifollicular plugging, scaling, telangiectasias
    • Zone of hyperpigmentation
  • Schuster sign: Lesions over the ear conchae

[[figure-4]]

  • Cicatricial alopecia
  • Scarring and pigmentary changes: Scarring (atrophic, hypertrophic, cribriform) is common. Hyper/Hypo pigmentation is also seen, especially in dark-skinned individuals.

Psoriasis (Option A) typically presents with silvery scales and found on the extensor surface such as elbow and knees

Seborrheic dermatitis (Option B) presents with greasy scales and erythema affecting scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds.

Rosacea (Option C) is characterized by facial erythema, telangiectasia, but not with scaly plaques



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 51.2-51.9
  2. https://www.aocd.org/page/DiscoidLupusErythe
question: A 42-year-old woman presented with complaints of a circular, scaly rash on her scalp, as shown in the image. On examination, you notice multiple small spikes over the underside of the rash. This presentation is most characteristic of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
• A neonate presenting with facial rashes exacerbated by sunlight exposure, along with a maternal history of positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, is highly suggestive of neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE).
  • NLE occurs when maternal autoantibodies, particularly anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, cross the placenta and affect the fetus.

Clinical features of Neonatal Lupus Erythematosus are:

  • Cutaneous: Rash resembling subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) or discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE).
  • Owl’s eye sign or Racoon sign- Erythematous, slightly scaly eruption on the face and periorbital skin
  • Cardiac:
    • Various degrees of heart block, including first-degree, second-degree, or complete heart block.
    • A complete heart block may require pacemaker placement.
  • Hepatic involvement:
    • Hepatitis
    • cholestasis,
  • Hematological abnormalities:
    • Thrombocytopenia
    • Anemia
  • Neurological manifestations:
    • seizures
    • Developmental delay.
  • Respiratory manifestations:
    • Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)
    • Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN),

Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, also known as anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies are commonly implicated in neonatal systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and also Sjögren's syndrome.

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) (Option B) is commonly seen in premature infants and is associated with conditions such as respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD).

Coarctation of the aorta (Option C) can occur in the context of Turner syndrome.

Aortic stenosis (Option D) occurs in Williams Syndrome (Chromosome 7 defect)



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 51.37-51.39.
question: A 3-week-old neonate is brought to the dermatology OPD with facial rashes exacerbated by sunlight exposure. Examination reveals erythematous, scaly papules around the eyes as shown in the image below. Maternal history includes positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies. Which congenital cardiac anomaly is commonly associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Leflunomide is an immunomodulatory drug that can cause drug-induced lupus erythematosus, and hence, it is contraindicated in the treatment of cutaneous LE.

  • It acts via the inhibition of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
  • It is used to treat rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis.

Some of the most commonly implicated drugs in drug-induced LE (DILE) include:

  • Procainamide
  • Hydralazine
  • Isoniazid
  • Minocycline
  • Quinidine
  • Anti-TNF agents (e.g., infliximab, adalimumab)
  • Methyldopa
  • Propylthiouracil
  • TNF-α inhibitors

Usually, withdrawal of causative drug resolves the disease


Positive anti-histone antibodies are particularly specific for DILE


Corticosteroids (Option B): These are the preferred first-line drugs for cutaneous lupus erythematosus due to their potent anti-inflammatory effect.

  • They can be applied topically or administered intralesionally.
  • Cutaneous atrophy is a common side effect of this drug, and the patient should be carefully instructed to limit the application over the skin only.

Photoprotection (Option C): UV radiation is directly responsible for inducing lesions and hence, should be avoided.

  • Sunscreens and protective clothing should be worn daily.
  • Photoprotection also includes avoiding drugs that cause photosensitivity (e.g., Tetracyclines, Metformin, Hydrochlorothiazides, sulfonamides, etc.)

Chloroquine (Option D): Antimalarial agents like chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine agents for cutaneous lupus.

  • These drugs have an immune-modulating and photoprotective effect.
  • Ocular toxicity, specifically retinopathy, is a common side effect



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 51.10-51.36.
  2. https://www.uptodate.cn/contents/initial-management-of-discoid-lupus-erythematosus-and-subacute-cutaneous-lupus-erythematosus
  3. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35186126/
  4. https://www.uptodate.cn/contents/overview-of-cutaneous-lupus-erythematosus
question: A 32-year-old woman was recently diagnosed with cutaneous lupus erythematosus. During her review, she has come to you with a pamphlet and would like to discuss all her treatment options. Which of the following drugs are not used for the treatment of cutaneous LE?

explanationHtml:
• The presence of limb weakness and cutaneous manifestations in association with a malignancy indicate a diagnosis of dermatomyositis.
  • Inflammatory myopathies like dermatomyositis have an association with malignancies such as ovarian, lung, gastrointestinal, and breast cancer.

Dermatomyositis is a chronic, inflammatory myositis seen in adults around 50-60 years of age.


Clinical features

  • It presents as symmetrical muscle weakness (proximal > distal)
  • Gottron’s papules (erythematous scaly papules over knuckles) are pathognomonic of the disease.

[[figure-1]]

  • Gottron’s sign: Symmetric, confluent, violaceous macular erythema (CMVE) on the back of fingers (interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints) , on the extensor surfaces of joints of the elbows, knees, or ankles.

[[figure-2]]

  • CMVE is seen over other sites too, and is named accordingly.
    • Heliotrope rash: CMVE over the periorbital skin
    • V-Sign: CMVE over the anterior aspect of the neck
    • Shawl sign: Involvement of upper back
    • Holster sign: Rash over the lateral aspect of the thigh
    • Mechanic’s hand: Hyperkeratosis and fissuring on the edges of the fingers.

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Holtser Sign

[[figure-6]]

Mechanics Hands

[[figure-7]]

Shawl Sign

Polymyositis (Option A): Differences between dermatomyositis and polymyositis are as follows:

Dermatomyositis

Polymyositis

Skin Involvement

Present

Typically lacks characteristic skin manifestations

Associated Conditions

More frequently associated with malignancies

Less frequently associated with malignancies

Muscle Biopsy Findings

May show perifascicular atrophy pattern

Typically shows endomysial inflammation pattern

Lambert-Eaton syndrome (Option C) is a neuromuscular disorder that presents with proximal muscle weakness but no cutaneous manifestations, it is also associated with adenocarcinoma of the lung. Unlike dermatomyositis, deep tendon reflexes are lost in this syndrome.

Drug reaction (Option D): Acute presentation of generalized urticaria/ drug reaction does not present with characteristic features of Grotton’s papules and the V- Sign.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 53.2-53.10
question:
A 50-year-old man was recently diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the lung and started chemotherapy. During a follow-up visit, he complained of rashes over his face and hands, as shown in the image. He also reports fatigue and weakness in his legs while climbing stairs.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) En coup de sabre

Explanation:

  • "En coup de sabre" is a French term meaning "struck by the sword." It refers to a specific subtype of localized scleroderma called morphea, characterized by excessive collagen deposition leading to thickening and hardening of the skin and underlying tissues.
  • This linear lesion typically extends vertically from the hairline downward, resembling a stroke from a sabre or sword.
  • It may vary in width and depth and often results in a visible depression or indentation in the skin. This may resemble the appearance of the fictional character "Kakashi Hatake" from the anime series Naruto, who has a similar linear scar on his forehead.

[[figure-1]]

Scleroderma is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by excessive collagen production, leading to the thickening and hardening of the skin and other connective tissues

The types of scleroderma are described below,

  • Localized Scleroderma: This type of scleroderma primarily affects the skin and underlying tissues in specific areas of the body.
    • Morphea
    • Linear Scleroderma
    • En coup de sabre alopecia.

  • Systemic Sclerosis (Systemic Scleroderma): Systemic sclerosis is a more severe form of scleroderma that not only affects the skin but also involves internal organs such as the lungs, heart, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract.
    • Limited Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (lcSSc)
    • Diffuse Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (dcSSc)

[[figure-2]]

Atrophic scar (Option A) usually occurs following injury or surgery, which is not present in this patient.

Gottron’s papules (Option B) are raised, violaceous to erythematous lesions typically found over the extensor surfaces of the joints, such as the knuckles, elbows, and knees in dermatomyositis.

Rowell syndrome (Option D), also known as lupus erythematosus overlap syndrome, is a rare condition characterized by features of both systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and erythema multiforme



Reference:

1. Zulian F. 2023. Juvenile localized scleroderma. UpToDate

2. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology. 9th Edition, Page 57.11-57.20
question:
A 60-year-old women comes to your OPD with her mother due to depressed linear lesion associated with hair loss on scalp for the past 3 years. She also has an area of progressive hypopigmentation and hair loss in her scalp as shown in the image below.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Anti-topoisomerase I antibody, also known as anti-Scl-70 antibody, is positive in systemic sclerosis. It is part of the diagnostic criteria for systemic sclerosis.
  • The image depicts the ‘salt and pepper appearance’ of skin seen in scleroderma
  • This in combination with a history of ILD, thickened skin proximal to MCP joints or sclerodactyly (see image), and digital tip ulcers indicates a diagnosis of scleroderma.

[[figure-1]]

‘salt and pepper appearance’ of skin

[[figure-2]]

thickened skin proximal to MCP joints or sclerodactyly

[[figure-3]]

Mask-like face in scleroderma.

Other antibodies include: Anticentromere and Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies


Anti-Ro (SS-A) antibodies (Option B): Most commonly positive in discoid lupus erythematosus, especially neonatal lupus.

Antisynthetase antibodies (Option C): Seen in Dermatomyositis

Antinuclear antibodies (Option D): Positive in multiple autoimmune connective tissue diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Sjogren's syndrome, and polymyositis/dermatomyositis.



Reference:

1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 56.2-56.18.

2. Varga J. 2023. Clinical manifestations and diagnosis of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) in adults. UpToDate
question:
A 54-year-old man with interstitial lung disease presents to you with complaints of a lesion over his chest.

On examination, you notice the skin proximal to MCP joints appears thickened. There are also small ulcers over his fingertips.

Which of the following would be the most specific investigation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cold-associated colour changes in the fingers, such as bluish-red discoloration, along with dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), are classic symptoms associated with Raynaud's phenomenon and oesophagal dysfunction, respectively, which are features of scleroderma.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • CREST syndrome is a type of limited scleroderma that consists of calcinosis cutis, Raynaud phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia
  • Calcinosis cutis, the deposition of calcium in the skin and subcutaneous tissues is a common complication of systemic sclerosis.

Von Kossa stain used for calcinosis cutis:

[[figure-3]]

Pitted scar on fingertips in Raynaud's phenomenon:

[[figure-4]]

Hypercalcemia (Option A): While hypercalcemia can occur in certain conditions, such as hyperparathyroidism or malignancies, it is not a characteristic feature of systemic sclerosis.

Malar Rash (Option C): A malar rash, a rash that appears on the cheeks and resembles a butterfly shape, is characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), not systemic sclerosis.

Morphea (Option D): Morphea, a localized form of scleroderma, primarily affects the skin and does not typically involve the oesophagus or cause dysphagia (systemic sclerosis)



Reference:

https://www.verywellhealth.com/raynauds-phenomenon-8643512
question: A 32-year-old woman complains that the tips of her fingers are changing from pale white to bluish-red during winter. She states that it started five years ago but has worsened recently, along with difficulty swallowing food. Which of the following findings would you also expect to find in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Mixed connective tissue disease presents a combination of features of cutaneous LE, scleroderma, and dermatomyositis.
  • Anti-U1RNP antibody (anti-U1RNP) is a specific serological marker for mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD).
  • Mixed connective tissue disease is a type of overlap syndrome where one patient will have features of multiple connective tissue diseases.
  • Due to its non-specific presentation, autoantibody testing is fundamental.
  • Treatment:
    • First line: Corticosteroids show good response
    • Second line: Hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate

[[figure-1]]

Scleroderma (Option A): While scleroderma is associated with various autoantibodies, including anti-centromere antibodies and anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibodies, it is not typically associated with anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein antibodies. Scleroderma primarily presents with skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, and internal organ involvement.Malar rash is not a feature.


Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (LE) (Option C): Systemic lupus erythematosus is primarily associated with anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA - Most sensitive), anti-dsDNA antibodies, and anti-Smith (anti-Sm - Most specific) antibodies.


Dermatomyositis (Option D): Dermatomyositis is associated with various autoantibodies, including anti-Jo-1 antibodies and anti-Mi-2 antibodies. Dermatomyositis is characterized by muscle weakness and skin involvement, including a characteristic skin rash.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 54.1-54.3.
question: A 40-year-old woman presents with a history of Raynaud’s phenomenon, arthritis, myalgia and fatigue. On examination, she has a rash on her face that spares her nasolabial folds. Her fingers appear puffy and sausage-shaped. Positive autoantibodies to anti-U1RNP along with her history are most indicative of which of the following diseases?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given image shows a heliotrope rash, which is a characteristic feature of Dermatomyositis.

Clinical Features of Dermatomyositis

  • Weakness: Symmetric, proximal greater than distal.
  • Rash: Characteristic rashes include:
    • Heliotrope rash: Erythematous eyelid discolouration with periorbital edema.
    • Gottron sign: Erythematous rash over extensor surfaces (knuckles, elbows, knees, ankles).
    • Gottron papules: Raised erythematous rash over knuckles.
    • V-sign: Rash on sun-exposed anterior neck and chest.
    • Shawl sign: Rash over the back of the neck and shoulders.
    • Nail bed telangiectasias: Dilated capillaries at nail beds.
    • Subcutaneous calcium deposits.
  • Weakness and rash can appear together or be separated by months.
  • Some patients may present with only a rash (amyopathic DM), while others may show mainly weakness.
  • Additional Symptoms: Myalgias, arthralgias, dysphagia, and dysarthria.
  • Skin symptoms significantly affect overall life quality; pruritus can be debilitating.
  • Pulmonary Issues: Dyspnea from ventilatory muscle weakness or intrinsic lung problems (interstitial lung disease, bronchopneumonia, alveolitis).
  • Malignancy Risk: Higher risk (~15%) in adult-onset cases within the first 2–3 years.

[[figure-1]]

Heliotrope rash

[[figure-2]]

Gottron’s Papules

[[figure-3]]

Shawl sign

[[figure-4]]

V Sign

Polymyositis (Option A): Muscle involvement similar to dermatomyositis but lacks skin manifestations.

Inclusion body myositis (Option C):

  • Does not present with a heliotrope rash.
  • The feature distinguishing inclusion body myosistis from dermatomyositis and polymyositis is the lack of responsiveness to immunosuppressive treatment.

Discoid lupus erythematosus (Option D):

  • Carpet track or Tin tack sign, also called Cat's tongue is characteristic of DLE.



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2820
  • Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1039
question: What is the most probable diagnosis of the given image?

explanationHtml:
• The patient presents with proximal muscle weakness (difficulty in climbing stairs, standing from a chair, and combing hair).

  • The image shows a heliotrope rash or shawl sign, which are characteristic skin findings in dermatomyositis.

  • Dermatomyositis is often paraneoplastic, commonly associated with ovarian cancer.

Dermatomyositis

Feature

Dermatomyositis

Autoimmune inflammatory myopathy, often paraneoplastic

Symmetrical, proximal muscle weakness

Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A): Incorrect because SLE presents with malar rash, arthritis, and systemic involvement, but not prominent muscle weakness.

Systemic sclerosis (Option C): Incorrect because systemic sclerosis causes skin tightening, Raynaud's phenomenon, and esophageal dysmotility, not proximal muscle weakness.

question: A 50-year-old female patient with a known case of ovarian cancer presents with difficulty in activities like climbing stairs, getting up from a chair, combing hair, etc. The following characteristic sign was found on examination. The most probable diagnosis is:

explanationHtml:
• Gottron’s papules are erythematous to violaceous plaques over the extensor surfaces of the knuckles, elbows, and knees.
  • They are characteristic of juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM), an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy.
  • The clinical triad includes proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash (violaceous rash on eyelids), and Gottron’s papules.
  • Muscle biopsy typically shows perivascular and perimysial inflammation with CD4+ T-cell infiltration.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed with elevated muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase), electromyography, and MRI findings of myositis.
  • Treatment involves high-dose corticosteroids and immunosuppressants (methotrexate, IVIG).

[[figure-1]]

Juvenile Dermatomyositis (JDM)

Feature

Description

Definition

Autoimmune inflammatory myopathy affecting muscles and skin in children

Age Group

Common in children aged 5–15 years

Muscle Weakness

Proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, getting up from a chair)

Skin Findings

Gottron’s papules (erythematous plaques over knuckles)

Heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital rash)

Shawl/V-sign (rash over shoulders and chest)

Lab Findings

↑ CK, aldolase, ANA, anti-Mi-2, anti-Jo-1 antibodies

Diagnostic Tests

Muscle biopsy (perifascicular atrophy, inflammatory infiltrates), MRI, EMG

Treatment

Corticosteroids, methotrexate, IVIG

Mechanic Hands

[[figure-2]]

Holster sign

[[figure-3]]

Shawl sign (Option B) is incorrect because the Shawl sign is a macular erythematous rash over the shoulders, neck, and upper back, typically seen in Dermatomyositis (DM) but does not specifically describe the lesions over the hands.

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Heliotrope rash (Option C) is incorrect because a heliotrope rash refers specifically to a purplish rash on the eyelids. While present in JDM, it is not the primary observation being asked in the question.

[[figure-6]]

Scleroderma (Option D) is incorrect because scleroderma presents with skin thickening, tightness, and Raynaud’s phenomenon, not inflammatory myopathy with characteristic rashes like Gottron’s papules.
