explanationHtml:
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) is a rare, acute hypersensitivity reaction caused in approximately 90 per cent of cases by drugs, most often antibiotics, calcium channel blockers, and antimalarials.

  • AGEP is characterized by the development of numerous nonfollicular, sterile, small pustules on a background of edematous erythema with flexural accentuation.
  • Fever above 38°C (100.4°F) and leukocytosis with a neutrophil count >7000/microL are usually present.
  • The eruption usually occurs a few hours to a few days after the administration of the offending drug.
  • The eruption resolves spontaneously in one to two weeks after the discontinuation of the offending drug

[[figure-1]]

Features which distinguish acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) from psoriasis:

AGEP Psoriasis
History of psoriasis Possible Common
Distribution pattern Predominance in the folds More generalized
Duration of pustules Shorter Longer
Duration of fever Shorter Longer
History of drug reaction Usual Uncommon
Recent drug administration Very frequent Less frequent
Arthritis Rare ∼30%
Histology
  • Spongiform subcorneal and/ or intraepidermal pustules,
  • Oedema of papillary dermis,
  • Vasculitis,
  • Exocytosis of eosinophils,
  • Single‐cell necrosis of keratinocytes
  • Subcorneal and/or intraepidermal pustules,
  • Papillomatosis,
  • Acanthosis



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology 9th edition, Page 119.4

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with a sudden onset of widespread, non-follicular pustules on an erythematous base. She reports having taken medication for a urinary tract infection two days ago. On examination, she appears febrile with diffuse erythema and multiple small, sterile pustules on her trunk and extremities. There is no mucosal involvement. What is the most likely cause of her presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are severe cutaneous adverse reaction characterized by extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis.

The pathophysiology behind TEN is as follows,

  1. Genetic predisposition: HLA variants, pharmacogenetics.

  2. Drug antigen presentation: Drugs bind self-proteins/HLA, activating T cells.

  3. T cell response: CD8⁺ T cells release cytotoxic proteins; immune dysregulation.

  4. Keratinocyte death: Granulysin, perforin/granzyme, FasL induce apoptosis/necrosis.

  5. Other mediators: NK/T cells, Th17, neutrophils, cytokines (TNF-α, IL-15), alarmins.

  6. Pathologic Sequelae: Epidermal necrolysis, full-thickness detachment, mucosal involvement.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology 9th edition.
  2. https://www.uptodate.com/contents/stevens-johnson-syndrome-and-toxic-epidermal-necrolysis-pathogenesis-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis
lessonTitle: Adverse Drug Reactions, Pediatric Dermatoses, Urticaria and Angioedema
question: Which of the following factors is involved in the pathogenesis of Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis?

explanationHtml:
Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are severe cutaneous adverse reactions characterized by extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis.


Classification based on Body surface area involvement (BSA)

  • SJS: <10 % of BSA detached (Option B ruled out)
  • SJS/TEN overlap: 10 to 30 % of BSA detached
  • TEN: >30 percent of BSA detached

The term "epidermal necrolysis" collectively refers to SJS, SJS/TEN overlap, and TEN.

  • Cause: Drugs (NSAIDs, allopurinol, antiepileptics, sulfonamides, antiretrovirals); T cell-mediated, HLA-linked keratinocyte necrosis.

  • Clinical: Prodrome → atypical target lesions → diffuse erythema → bullae → sheet-like skin peeling; positive pseudo-Nikolsky; mucosal involvement common.

  • Management: stop offending drug, provide supportive care, consider cyclosporine or IV immunoglobulins.

  • Prognosis: SCORTEN predicts mortality.

[[figure-1]]

Erythema multiforme(Option A): Mild, target lesions, <10% BSA, limited mucosal involvement; unlike TEN.


Pemphigus vulgaris (Option C): Autoimmune intraepidermal blisters (anti-desmoglein 3>1); lacks widespread epidermal detachment seen in TEN.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology 9th edition.
  2. https://www.uptodate.com/contents/stevens-johnson-syndrome-and-toxic-epidermal-necrolysis-pathogenesis-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis

question: A 50-year-old patient presented to the emergency department with widespread blistering and skin detachment, along with mucosal involvement, after starting a new medication a week ago. On examination, there are large areas of epidermal detachment involving more than 30% of the body surface area. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be responsible for this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanantion:

Based on the history provided and the Target lesions seen in the image, the diagnosis is erythema multiforme.

Erythema Multiforme (EM) is an acute, immune-mediated condition characterized by distinctive target-like skin lesions accompanied by erosions or bullae involving the oral, genital, and/or ocular mucosa.

[[figure-1]]

  • Types: EM Major (severe mucosal/systemic involvement), EM Minor (mild/no mucosal/systemic symptoms).

  • Causes: Infections (HSV-1, Mycoplasma), drugs (NSAIDs, sulfonamides, antimalarials), SLE, leukemia.

  • Clinical: Target lesions on distal extremities, possible mucosal involvement; prodrome rare in mild cases.

  • Target lesion zones: central dusky/blistered area, dark red middle zone, pale outer ring, possible peripheral erythematous halo.

  • Treatment: Stop offending drug, acyclovir, short course of systemic steroids if needed.

Fixed drug eruption(Option A): Recurrent lesions at same site, acutely erythematous/bullous, later slate-brown; commonly affects mucous membranes, face, acral areas.

Nummular eczema(Option B): Coin-shaped lesions, lacks EM’s concentric rings.

Urticaria(Option C): Transient pruritic wheals with central pallor, not targetoid. Has transient wheals lasting <24 hours, not fixed target lesions. Lacks the characteristic three-zone concentric rings seen in EM



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition.

question: A 26-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset of skin lesions. Upon examination, you notice distinct lesions with concentric rings resembling a "bull's eye" appearance. The patient reports a recent malarial infection. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for these skin lesions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation: The brown-pigmented lesions shown in the image are café au lait macules, and the presence of pigmented nodules on the iris, known as Lisch nodules, suggests the diagnosis of Neurofibromatosis type-1(NF-1), also known as Von Recklinghausen's disease.

  • It is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome.
  • The gene for NF-1 is located on chromosome 17 and encodes for neurofibromin.
  • Malignancies associated with this syndrome are Optic nerve gliomas and astrocytoma.
  • In NF1, optic nerve gliomas typically present in children and are often associated with specific clinical features such as café-au-lait spots (light brown skin patches), Lisch nodules (pigmented nodules in the iris), and axillary freckling (freckling in the armpits).
  • Other characteristic features of the syndrome include
    • Buttonhole sign: Lesions invaginate when pressed with a finger.
    • Bag of worms: Plexiform neurofibroma has a lot of nerves which feels like a bag of worms.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology 9th edition, Page 80.1
lessonTitle: Genodermatoses, Vector-Borne Diseases, Bedside Tests in Dermatology
question: An 11-year-old boy presents to the clinic with asymptomatic light brown-colored lesions on his body as shown in the image. On slit lamp examination, pigmented nodules on the iris were noted. What is the most common malignancy associated with this syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation: The given clinical presentation suggests the diagnosis of Tuberous Sclerosis (TSC), an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome.

  • This syndrome is caused by mutations in the genes TSC 1(Chromosome 9) and TSC 2 (Chromosome 16), which encode the proteins hamartin and tuberin, respectively.
  • There are four pathognomic skin lesions associated with this condition:
  1. Ash-leaf macules are characterized by oval or irregularly shaped hypopigmented (lighter than surrounding skin) patches and are accentuated on Wood’s lamp examination.
  2. Angiofibroma, previously misnamed adenoma sebaceum, consists of hyperplastic blood vessels and sebaceous glands in immature hair follicles.
  3. Periungual fibroma (Koenen tumours) emerge from the nail folds.
  4. A Shagreen patch is characterized by thickened, leathery skin and typically appears as irregularly shaped plaques with a rough, raised surface, commonly located on the lower back.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Angiofibroma

Infantile spasms, also known as West syndrome, can occur in infants and young children with tuberous sclerosis complex.

question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the paediatrician with a history of developmental delay, multiple hypopigmented macules on his trunk, and a history of infantile spasms. On examination, he also has facial angiofibroma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation: The history of recurrent abdominal pain with GI bleed and multiple pigmented macules on lips with hamartomatous polyps suggests the diagnosis of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by mutations in the STK11 gene located on the short arm of chromosome 19.

Gardner Syndrome (Option A) is a phenotypic variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), an inherited condition characterized by the development of numerous adenomatous polyps in the colon, along with extracolonic manifestations such as osteomas, epidermal cysts, fibromas, and dental abnormalities.

Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (Option B) is an inherited genetic disorder characterized by the development of numerous adenomatous polyps in the colon and rectum.

Cowden Syndrome (Option C) or multiple hamartoma syndrome, is a genodermatosis linked to mutations in the PTEN gene located on the long arm of chromosome 10.

  • It manifests as multiple benign hamartomas affecting various organs, with mucocutaneous lesions and macrocephaly being characteristic features.
  • Individuals with Cowden syndrome have an elevated risk of developing malignant neoplasms, particularly thyroid, endometrial, or breast cancers.

question: A 28-year-old male presents to the gastroenterologist with a history of recurrent abdominal pain and episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding. On examination, he has multiple pigmented macules on his lips and oral mucosa. A colonoscopy reveals numerous hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation described in the question is typical of Xeroderma Pigmentosum.


Xeroderma Pigmentosum:

A rare autosomal recessive NER defect causing extreme UV sensitivity, freckling, ocular damage, neurological deficits, and early skin cancers (melanoma, SCC, BCC).

[[figure-1]]

Vitiligo (Option A) is an acquired depigmentation disorder resulting from the absence of melanocytes in the epidermis, which causes white macules and patches on the body.

[[figure-2]]

Gorlin syndrome (Option B) or nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the PTCH1 gene, which is involved in the Hedgehog signalling pathway.

  • It is characterized by multiple basal cell carcinomas, along with jaw cysts, skeletal abnormalities, facial deformities, and an increased risk of other cancers like medulloblastoma.

Bloom syndrome (Option D) is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the BLM gene.

  • It presents with short stature, photosensitivity, and characteristic facial features including a long, narrow face and prominent nose, along with other physical anomalies such as micrognathia and cafe-au-lait spots.
  • Increased risk of various cancers, particularly leukaemia and lymphoma, at an early age.


Reference:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) refers to a group of rare genetic disorders characterized by fragile skin that blisters and ulcerates easily with minor friction or trauma and is also known as mechanobullous disease.
  • Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is caused by mutations in the COL7A1 gene, which encodes type VII collagen resulting in Subepidermal bulla.
  • Depending on the specific type of DEB and the inheritance pattern of the mutated gene, it can be inherited in an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive manner.
  • A positive family history is present.
  • Common presenting complaints include blistering, skin fragility, and non-healing wounds disproportionate to mechanical trauma.
  • Diagnosis is made with transmission electron microscopy, immunofluorescence antigen mapping using biopsy specimens, and genetic sequencing to confirm the subtype.
  • Treatment mainly focuses on wound care, prevention of infection, and symptomatic management of skin and mucosal complications.

[[figure-1]]

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a newborn with a taut and glistening membrane, which suggests a diagnosis of colloidion baby, which is a feature of lamellar icthyosis.

  • Clinical features: collodion membrane, fish-like scales, ectropion, eclabium, deformed ears, palmoplantar keratoderma, and nasal blockage.

Ichthyosis vulgaris (Option A) develops later (not at birth), mostly spares flexures, and is due to filaggrin gene defect.

X-linked ichthyosis (Option B) occurs in males, presents with fine scales and a “dirty” appearance later; flexures spared.

[[figure-2]]

Harlequin ichthyosis (Option C) is more severe with thick, armor-like plates, severe ectropion/eclabium, risk of respiratory failure, and often lethal.

Explanation:

Verrucous

Mainly on the limbs

Hyperpigmentation

Hyperpigmented streaks and whorls along Blaschko’s lines

Hypopigmentation

question: A 3-month-old female infant presents with linear streaks of hyperpigmentation along Blaschko's lines on her trunk and extremities. The mother reports that the infant also experienced vesicular eruptions shortly after birth that resolved without scarring. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation given in the question suggests Darier’s disease, an autosomal dominant disorder with an ATP2A2 gene defect (chromosome 12) responsible for calcium-bound ATPase type 2.

Darier’s disease

  • Its onset is typically in childhood, exacerbated during summer and monsoon.
  • It presents as warty, dirty, foul-smelling papules in seborrheic areas like the scalp, forehead, nasolabial folds, retro auricular region, chest, middle of the back, axillae, and groins and they are covered with a crust, causing discomfort and itching (No bulla or vesicles are observed).
  • Nails exhibit alternate longitudinal white and red bands (erythro-leukonychia) with distal notching (V sign).
  • Cobblestone lesions on the palate can be seen.
  • HPE shows suprabasal acantholysis and dyskeratosis, leading to the formation of dyskeratotic cells known as Corps ronds and grains.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Based on histopathological findings showing acantholysis and dyskeratosis, what is the most likely diagnosis?

Explanation:

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (Delhi boil/Chiclero ulcer) causes annular crusted ulcers after endemic travel; Giemsa smear shows amastigotes, NNN culture promastigotes; treated with liposomal amphotericin B or miltefosine.

Lyme disease (Option A): Erythema chronicum migrans, the bull’s-eye rash of Lyme disease, is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi via Ixodid ticks and may include flu-like symptoms.

question: What is the most probable diagnosis of the given image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • FDE characteristically reappears at the same site each time the offending drug is taken, producing a well-defined dusky red/violaceous plaque → heals with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
  • Shows same-site recurrence due to persistent lesional T-cells / ICAM-1 expression.
  • Leaves slate-brown residual hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin.
  • Common triggers: tetracyclines, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, sedatives.
  • Lesions often occur on genital/perianal areas, but may occur anywhere.

Incorrect Options:

  • Cutaneous Mastocytosis (Option A): Lesions are persistent with urtication on stroking (Darier sign); they do not recur at the same site only after drug exposure.
  • HSV-1 (Herpes Simplex Virus-1) (Option C): Causes grouped painful vesicles that may recur but not exclusively at the same fixed site, and do not leave persistent slate-brown pigmentation.
  • Erythema Multiforme (Option D): Shows target lesions on multiple sites, related to infections (often HSV), and does not show same-site fixed recurrence with pigmentation.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 2233.

Explanation:

  • Herpes labialis, commonly known as cold sores or fever blisters, is a viral infection caused by the herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1).
  • The characteristic presentation of multiple vesicles and crusts clustered on an inflamed base around the lips is indicative of a herpes simplex virus infection. Occurs on the vermillion border of lips.
  • Recurrent outbreaks are common, often triggered by factors such as stress, sun exposure, or fever.

Incorrect Options:

Herpangina (Option B): It typically presents as small, painful ulcers or vesicles on the back of the throat, soft palate, or tonsillar pillars.

Molluscum contagiosum (Option C): It typically presents as small, raised, dome-shaped papules with a central indentation (umbilication). The lesions are usually flesh-colored

Impetigo (Option D): It commonly presents as honey-colored crusts or bullae on an erythematous base.

question: Identify the finding shown in the image below:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient presents with acne that is not responding to oral isotretinoin and antibiotics, which suggests that a more systemic or hormonal cause could be contributing to the acne.
  • Hyperandrogenism is commonly associated with conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), both of which can lead to increased sebum production and hormonal imbalances, exacerbating acne.
  • Evaluating for hyperandrogenism through tests like testosterone levels, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS), and other hormonal markers is crucial to rule out these underlying causes.
  • Hyperandrogenism is when the body produces too much androgen, a male hormone. This can contribute to the development of acne in women and other symptoms such as hirsutism and irregular periods.
  • Treatment may involve medications such as oral contraceptives or anti-androgen drugs.

Look for dietary triggers (Option A): Acne can be affected by diet in some people, particularly those with a high glycemic index or a diet high in dairy products. However, this is typically considered after other causes of acne have been ruled out. Additionally, dietary changes may not be sufficient to treat acne on their own, but rather they can be used in conjunction with other treatments.

Check for antibiotic resistance (Option C): Antibiotics are often used to treat acne, but over time, the bacteria that causes acne can become resistant to the antibiotics. If a patient's acne is not improving with antibiotics, checking for antibiotic resistance can help determine if a different treatment approach is needed.

Look for drug triggers (Option D): Certain medications can contribute to the development of acne. For example, corticosteroids, anticonvulsants, and some hormonal medications can cause acne as a side effect. If a patient takes any medications that may increase the risk of acne, it is important to evaluate their treatment plan and consider alternative medications if necessary.



Reference:

Rooks’s Textbook of Dermatology 9th edition, 90.1
question: A female patient presented with acne that is not resolving on oral isotretinoin and antibiotics therapy. Which of the following is the next best investigation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient is from Bihar, an endemic region for visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).

The image shows multiple hypopigmented macules over the back, characteristic of PKDL.

History of prolonged fever in childhood suggests prior kala-azar infection, which is a prerequisite for developing PKDL.

No thickened nerves rule out leprosy.

Post Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL):

  • PKDL is a chronic dermal complication of visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania donovani.
  • Endemic in India, Nepal, and Sudan, especially in Bihar, West Bengal, and Uttar Pradesh.

Clinical Features:

  • Occurs months to years after treated visceral leishmaniasis.
  • Hypopigmented macules, erythematous papules, or nodules on the face, trunk, and extremities.
  • No loss of sensation or thickened nerves (differentiating from leprosy).
  • Histopathology: Presence of Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies.

Diagnosis:

  • Slit-skin smear or skin biopsy showing Leishmania donovani bodies.
  • PCR or rK39 serology can confirm diagnosis.

Management:

  • First-line treatment: Miltefosine for 12 weeks.
  • Alternatives: Liposomal amphotericin B or paromomycin.

Tuberculoid leprosy (Option A) is incorrect because it presents with single or few hypopigmented macules with loss of sensation. Thickened peripheral nerves are a hallmark feature, which is absent in this case.

Lepromatous leprosy (Option B) is incorrect because it presents with multiple ill-defined hypopigmented macules with symmetric distribution. Thickened nerves and sensation loss are typical, but they are absent in this patient.

Mycosis fungoides (Option C) is incorrect because it presents as erythematous scaly plaques rather than hypopigmented macules. It is a form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which is not related to prior fever or endemic infections.



Reference:

Post Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis: Clinical Features and Differential Diagnosis - PMC
question: A 45 year old male patient from Bihar presented with normoanesthetic hypopigmented lesion as shown below. He had a history of fever for a long duration in his childhood. No thickened nerves were present. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Answer: A) KOH mount

Explanation:

The image depicts a scaly, inflamed, well-demarcated lesion on the scalp with hair loss, suggestive of Tinea Capitis (scalp ringworm).

KOH (potassium hydroxide) mount is the gold standard for diagnosing superficial fungal infections, including Tinea Capitis, by detecting fungal hyphae in hair shafts and skin scrapings.

Tinea Capitis:

  • Caused by: Trichophyton and Microsporum species.
  • Common in children, especially in warm, humid climates.
  • Types:
    • Non-inflammatory: Scaly patches with broken hairs.
    • Inflammatory (Kerion): Painful, boggy swelling with pustules and crusting (as seen in the image).

Diagnosis:

  • KOH Mount: Detects fungal hyphae in hair shafts and skin scrapings.
  • Fungal Culture: Confirms the fungal species.
  • Wood’s Lamp Examination: Fluorescence in Microsporum infections.

Management:

  • Systemic antifungals (Griseofulvin or Terbinafine) for 6–8 weeks (topical antifungals alone are ineffective).
  • Antifungal shampoos (ketoconazole or selenium sulfide) reduce fungal shedding.
  • Kerion cases may need corticosteroids to reduce inflammation.

Slit Skin Mount (Option B) is incorrect because it is used for leprosy diagnosis by identifying acid-fast bacilli from skin lesions, which is not relevant in this case.

Gram Staining (Option C) is incorrect because it is useful for diagnosing bacterial infections (e.g., impetigo, folliculitis) but not fungal infections like Tinea Capitis.

Biopsy (Option D) is incorrect because skin biopsy is rarely needed for diagnosing Tinea Capitis and is usually reserved for atypical or unclear cases.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology. 9th ed. Blackwell; 2016. p. 89.10 -86.47.-89.24
question: What is the appropriate next course of action for a child who exhibits itchy scalp lesions and hair loss, as depicted in the image provided?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a unilateral, dermatomal eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. The patient has painful lesions, which is a key feature of Herpes Zoster (Shingles). The lesions appear in a band-like distribution, following the sensory nerve dermatome.

Herpes Zoster (Shingles):

  • Cause: Reactivation of Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) in the dorsal root ganglion.
  • Risk Factors:
    • Immunosuppression (HIV, malignancies)
    • Elderly individuals
    • Stress and trauma
  • Clinical Features:
    • Painful, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a unilateral dermatomal pattern.
    • Pre-eruptive phase (burning, tingling pain) 48–72 hours before rash onset.
    • Thoracic dermatomes are most commonly involved.
    • Postherpetic neuralgia (persistent pain after healing) may develop in older adults.
  • Diagnosis: Clinical, confirmed by Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells) or PCR for VZV DNA.
  • Treatment:
    • Antiviral therapy (Acyclovir, Valacyclovir) within 72 hours of rash onset.
    • Analgesics for pain control.
    • Corticosteroids in severe cases.

Molluscum Contagiosum (Option B) is incorrect because Molluscum contagiosum presents as small, umbilicated, pearly white papules, not as vesicular eruptions. It is usually asymptomatic and not painful.

Herpes Simplex (Option C) is incorrect because Herpes simplex virus (HSV) causes clusters of vesicles but does not usually follow a dermatomal distribution. HSV infections typically affect the oral (HSV-1) or genital (HSV-2) regions rather than the thoracic dermatomes.

Lymphangioma Circumscriptum (Option D) is incorrect because lymphangioma circumscriptum is a benign lymphatic malformation, presenting as clusters of small, translucent vesicles ("frog spawn" appearance). It is not painful and does not appear in a dermatomal pattern.



Reference:

Ananthanarayan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Pages 478, 479.
question: What is the probable diagnosis for a young man who has presented with painful lesions depicted in the image below?

explanationHtml:
• The image shows a dermatomal distribution of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, which is characteristic of Herpes zoster (shingles).
  • The patient reports paresthesia ("spider crawling sensation"), a common prodromal symptom due to viral reactivation affecting sensory nerves.
  • The lesion pattern is unilateral, consistent with reactivation of Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) from dorsal root ganglia.

Herpes Zoster:

Feature

Details

Etiology

Reactivation of Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) from latency in sensory ganglia.

Risk Factors

Immunosuppression, aging (>50 years), stress, malignancy, chronic diseases (diabetes).

Clinical Features

Painful, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along a single dermatome (usually thoracic, lumbar, or trigeminal).

Prodromal Symptoms

Burning, tingling, paresthesia ("spider crawling sensation"), fever, malaise before rash appears.

Complications

Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), bacterial superinfection, ophthalmic zoster (if V1 of trigeminal nerve is involved).

Diagnosis

Clinical; Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells), PCR for VZV in doubtful cases.

Treatment

Antiviral therapy (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir) within 72 hours, analgesics, corticosteroids (if severe pain).

Prevention

Zoster vaccine for elderly and immunocompromised individuals.

Irritant contact dermatitis (Option B) is incorrect because it results from direct skin damage due to chemical exposure, leading to erythema, scaling, and burning, rather than a vesicular dermatomal rash with neuropathic pain.

Allergic contact dermatitis (Option C) is incorrect because it is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction (Type IV), presenting as itchy, erythematous, and vesicular plaques in areas of contact, but lacks dermatomal distribution and prodromal neuralgia.

Herpes simplex infection (Option D) is incorrect because HSV causes grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, but these typically appear around the mouth (HSV-1) or genital region (HSV-2) and do not follow a dermatomal pattern.



Reference:

question: A 60-year-old male patient presents with the lesion given in the image below. He also mentions experiencing sensations like a spider crawling in the area of the lesion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Follicular hyperkeratosis is characterized by dry, rough skin with small, keratotic papules around hair follicles, often seen in Vitamin A deficiency. This occurs due to abnormal keratinization of epithelial cells.

Vitamin A Deficiency Manifestations :

1) Ocular manifestations :

  • Vitamin A deficiency is the most significant preventable cause of blindness, especially in children below 5 in developing countries.
  • Early Signs:
    • Loss of sensitivity to green light.
    • Difficulty adapting to dim light.
    • Night blindness.
  • Prolonged Deficiency:
    • Xerophthalmia:
      1. Dry, thick, keratinized conjunctiva and cornea. If untreated, it leads to corneal ulceration and ultimately results in blindness due to the formation of opaque scar tissue.
      2. WHO grading of xerophthalmia:

XN
  • Night blindness.

X1
  • X1A: Conjunctival xerosis.
  • X1B: Bitot spots.

X2
  • Corneal xerosis.

X3
  • X3A: Corneal ulceration, less than one-third.
  • X3B: Corneal ulceration, more than one-third.

XS
  • Corneal scar.

XF
  • Xerophthalmic fundus.
  • Bitot's Spots: Grayish-white triangular plaques firmly adherent to the conjunctiva.
  • Keratomalacia: When xerophthalmia persists for a longer time, it progresses to keratomalacia (corneal softening).

2) Immune Function:

  • Deficiency increases susceptibility to infections.
  • Infection reduces retinol-binding protein synthesis, lowering vitamin A levels and impairing immune responses.

3) Skin and Mucous Membrane Lesions:

  • Follicular Hyperkeratosis (Phrynoderma): Causes rough skin due to hyperkeratinization of the follicular epithelium.
  • Keratinizing Metaplasia: Affects respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts.
  • Epithelium is atrophied.

4) Other General Manifestation :

  • Growth retardation due to defective synthesis of chondroitin sulfate.
  • Decreased protein synthesis.

Incorrect Options:

Vitamin C Deficiency (Option B): Causes scurvy, leading to corkscrew hairs, perifollicular hemorrhages, and poor wound healing, but not follicular hyperkeratosis.

Vitamin E Deficiency (Option C): Causes neurological symptoms (ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, hemolytic anemia) but does not affect keratinization.

Vitamin B6 Deficiency (Option D): Leads to cheilitis, glossitis, irritability, and neuropathy, but not follicular hyperkeratosis.



Reference:

question: What is the probable diagnosis for a cauliflower-shaped mass on the foot of a farmer that appeared after a minor injury, with microscopy revealing copper penny bodies?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The lesions described in the question, following a thorn prick, are suggestive of a condition known as sporotrichosis or rose gardener's disease.
  • The characteristic feature of sporotrichosis is the distribution of the lesions along the lymphatic vessels. The infection typically starts as a small, painless bump or nodule at the site of the inoculation, and it then spreads along the lymphatic vessels, forming a chain of nodules or ulcers.

Sporotrichosis

  • Sporotrichosis is a chronic fungal infection caused by Sporothrix schenckii, commonly known as “rose gardener’s disease.” It occurs through trauma-induced inoculation from soil, plants, or organic matter.

Pathophysiology

  • Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus that exists as a mold in the environment and yeast in human tissue.
  • The fungus spreads via lymphatics, causing characteristic nodular lymphangitis.

Features

  • Cutaneous (most common):
    • Painless nodules and ulcers along lymphatic channels (lymphocutaneous form).
  • Pulmonary:
    • Chronic cough, fever, weight loss (inhalation exposure).
  • Disseminated (rare, immunocompromised patients):
    • Systemic involvement affecting bones, joints, and CNS.

Investigations & Diagnosis

  • Culture (gold standard): Grows Sporothrix schenckii on Sabouraud’s agar.
  • Microscopy: Shows cigar-shaped yeast on tissue samples.
  • Histopathology: Granulomatous inflammation with fungal elements.

Treatment

  • First-line: Itraconazole (100-200 mg/day) for cutaneous cases.
  • Severe/disseminated cases: Amphotericin B, followed by itraconazole.
  • Potassium iodide (older treatment): Still used in some regions.

Incorrect Options:

Streptococcus pyogenes (Option A): It is not the causative agent for the described presentation of lesions following a thorn prick.

Strongyloides stercoralis (Option C): Strongyloides stercoralis does not typically present with the specific lesion distribution described in the question.

Staphylococcus aureus (Option D): Staphylococcus aureus is not the primary causative agent for the described presentation. Sporothrix schenckii is more commonly associated with the development of sporotrichosis in this context.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK532255/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The lesion described by a forest officer suggests an eschar-like lesion, which is commonly seen in scrub typhus, cutaneous anthrax, and brown recluse spider bites.
  • KFD (Kyasanur Forest Disease) is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by a Flavivirus, transmitted by ticks. It primarily affects forest workers but does not cause eschar formation. Instead, it presents with fever, myalgia, haemorrhagic manifestations, and meningoencephalitis.
  • Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) is a tick-borne viral disease (Flavivirus) endemic to forests in South India.
  • Transmission: By Haemaphysalis ticks from infected rodents, monkeys, and livestock.

Monkey fever/Kyasanur forest disease:

General features:

  • Virus Characteristics: Enveloped virus belonging to the family Flaviviridae; contains single-stranded RNA (ssRNA).
  • Vector: Hard ticks (Haemaphysalis spinigera)
  • Hosts: Monkeys, rodents, and squirrels are common hosts; monkeys act as amplifier hosts where the virus multiplies exponentially.
  • Seasonality: KFD cases peak during dry months (November to June), coinciding with increased human activity in forests.

The life cycle of Kyasanur forest disease

[[figure-1]]

Clinical features:

  • Incubation Period: 3-8 days.
  • First Stage (Hemorrhagic Fever):
    • Acute high fever with malaise and frontal headaches.
    • Hemorrhagic symptoms: bleeding from the nasal cavity, throat, gums, and gastrointestinal tract.
  • Second Stage: Meningoencephalitis may occur 7–21 days after the first stage.

Lab diagnosis:

  • Diagnosis Methods:
    • Virus isolation from blood.
    • IgM antibody detection by ELISA.
    • RT-PCR.

Vaccination:

  • Vaccine Type: Killed KFD vaccine (formalin-inactivated chick embryo) developed at Haffkine Institute, Mumbai.
  • Vaccination Schedule:
    • Initial two doses at 2-month intervals.
    • Booster doses at 6–9 months, then every 5 years.
  • Target Area: Recommended for endemic areas of Karnataka.

Cutaneous anthrax (Option C) is incorrect because Bacillus anthracis causes painless black eschars with surrounding oedema. It is common in individuals handling animal products or exposed to spores in the environment.

question: Which of the following options should be excluded as a possible cause for the lesion seen in the image, developed by a forest officer?

explanationHtml:
• The correct option is "annular." An annular skin lesion refers to a ring-shaped lesion with a clear or normal-looking center. It typically has a raised border or edge. This pattern is commonly seen in conditions such as ringworm (tinea corporis), granuloma annulare, and erythema migrans (associated with Lyme disease).

Some other types of skin lesions:

Skin Lesion

Description

Examples

Macule

Flat, discolored spot on the skin with no palpable elevation or depression.

Freckles, flat moles

Patch

Large, flat, maculopapular area of skin discoloration.

Vitiligo, café-au-lait spots

Papule

Small, solid, elevated lesion with a palpable surface.

Acne, warts

Plaque

Elevated, flat-topped lesion with a broad, flat surface.

Psoriasis plaques, seborrheic keratosis

Vesicle

Small, fluid-filled blister, usually less than 5mm in diameter.

Chickenpox blisters, herpes simplex

Bulla

Large, fluid-filled blister, typically more than 5mm in diameter.

Bullous pemphigoid, second-degree burns

Pustule

Small, elevated lesion filled with pus.

Acne pustules, impetigo

Wheal

Transient, raised, and edematous lesion with irregular borders, often associated with itching or allergic reactions.

Insect bite reactions, hives (urticaria)

Nodule

Solid, palpable lesion, often deeper in the skin layers.

Dermatofibroma, lipoma

Tumor

Solid, elevated lesion larger than a few centimeters in diameter.

Basal cell carcinoma, melanoma

Plaque

Large, flat, elevated lesion with a flat surface and a diameter greater than its height.

Psoriasis plaques, lichen planus

Burrow

Linear or serpignious tunnel in the skin caused by infestation or burrowing of parasites.

Scabies burrows

Scale

Dry, flaky, or thickened skin with shedding of dead skin cells.

Psoriasis scales, seborrheic dermatitis

Crust

Dried exudate or secretion on the skin surface.

Impetigo crusts, dried blood crusts

Erosion

Loss of the superficial epidermis, resulting in a moist, shallow depression.

Aphthous ulcers, erosion due to scratching

Ulcer

Loss of the entire epidermis and at least part of the dermis, resulting in a deep, open lesion.

Pressure ulcers, venous ulcers

Fissure

Linear crack or slit-like split in the skin.

Athlete's foot fissures, anal fissures

Scar

Fibrous tissue that replaces normal skin after injury or surgery.

Surgical scars, keloids

Atrophy

Thinning or depression of the skin with loss of normal skin markings.

Striae (stretch marks), aged skin

Incorrect Options:

Nummular lesions (Option A): These are coin-shaped or circular lesions with distinct borders and a flat or slightly elevated surface. They are usually smaller and do not have the characteristic ring shape.

Discoid lesions (Option C): These are circular or oval-shaped lesions with well-defined borders, but they do not necessarily have a ring shape or central clearing.

Target lesions (Option D): Target or "bull's eye" lesions have concentric rings or circles of different colors. They typically have three zones—an outer ring, an intermediate ring, and a central clearing. This pattern is seen in conditions such as erythema multiforme and Lyme disease.

explanationHtml:
• Dermatitis artefacta is a condition characterized by self-inflicted skin lesions, consciously or unconsciously caused by the individual. It is considered a psychiatric disorder rather than a primary skin disease.
  • The lesions in dermatitis artefacta often have unusual or bizarre patterns and may not follow the typical distribution or characteristics of known dermatological conditions.
  • These lesions may appear in unusual shapes, patterns, or locations that are not consistent with typical henna reactions or allergic contact dermatitis.
  • Treatment involves a multidisciplinary approach involving dermatologists, psychologists, and psychiatrists to address the underlying psychological issues and provide appropriate care and support to the individual.
  • In the case of henna application, if the child deliberately scratches or traumatizes the skin in the area where henna was applied, it can result in skin lesions that resemble a dermatitis reaction. The child may create patterns or designs by scratching the skin, leading to the appearance of lesions.

However, in this case, the option "dermatitis artefacta" suggests that the lesions are self-induced rather than a true allergic contact dermatitis.

explanationHtml:
Trichothiodystrophy is a rare genetic disorder that affects the structure of the hair.

One of the characteristic features of Trichothiodystrophy is the presence of "tiger tail banding" when the hair is examined under polarized light microscopy. This term refers to alternating light and dark bands along the hair shaft, resembling the pattern of a tiger's tail.

  • Trichothiodystrophy is primarily characterized by brittle hair that is prone to breakage and has a characteristic appearance under the microscope.
  • Some key features of Trichothiodystrophy include:
    • Brittle Hair
    • Tiger Tail Banding
    • Variable Hair Color
    • Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities
    • Additional features may include dry and scaly skin, brittle nails, photosensitivity (sensitivity to sunlight), and ocular abnormalities.

Incorrect Options:

Trichorhexis nodosa (Option A): Trichorhexis nodosa is a hair shaft disorder characterized by nodules or nodes along the hair shaft. It does not typically show the specific "tiger tail banding" pattern seen in Trichothiodystrophy.

Trichorexis invaginata (Option B): Trichorexis invaginata, also known as "bamboo hair," is a condition in which the hair shaft is characterized by multiple invaginations or nodules. It does not present with the specific banding pattern seen in Trichothiodystrophy.

Monilethrix (Option D): Monilethrix is a hereditary hair disorder characterized by beaded hair shafts that resemble a necklace. It does not show the specific "tiger tail banding" pattern seen in Trichothiodystrophy.

Harlequin Ichthyosis

Introduction

  • Harlequin ichthyosis is a rare, severe genetic skin disorder characterized by thick, armor-like scales covering the body at birth. It is an autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the ABCA12 gene, affecting lipid transport in the epidermis.

Pathophysiology

  • ABCA12 gene mutation leads to defective lipid transport, disrupting the skin barrier.
  • This results in thickened, hyperkeratotic plates with deep fissures, severe dehydration, and increased infection risk.

Features

  • Thick, diamond-shaped scales covering the body
  • Ectropion (everted eyelids) and eclabium (everted lips)
  • Contracted digits (hypoplastic fingers and toes)
  • Risk of severe dehydration, infections, and respiratory distress
  • Delayed skin shedding, improving with time but requiring lifelong care

Investigations & Diagnosis

  • Clinical examination based on characteristic features at birth
  • Genetic testing to confirm ABCA12 mutation
  • Skin biopsy (rarely needed) shows massive hyperkeratosis

Treatment

  • Neonatal intensive care (hydration, temperature regulation)
  • Emollients and keratolytics (e.g., petrolatum, urea, lactic acid) to soften scales
  • Oral retinoids (e.g., acitretin, isotretinoin) to reduce hyperkeratosis
  • Antibiotics for secondary infections
  • Lifelong skin care with moisturization and gentle exfoliation

Autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis:

Subtype

Clinical Features

Genetic Defect

Harlequin ichthyosis

Thick, plate-like scales covering the entire body

ABCA12 gene mutations

Lamellar ichthyosis (Option B)

Large thick scales, often present at birth

Generalized redness, fine white scales

Different genetic mutations, including PNPLA1, CYPF22, CASP14, CERS3, etc.

Incorrect Options:

Bathing suit ichthyosis (Option C): A rare variant of lamellar ichthyosis where scaling predominantly affects the trunk and proximal limbs, sparing other areas, resembling a "bathing suit" pattern.

Ichthyosis vulgaris (Option D): A common inherited skin disorder characterized by fine, dry, scaly skin, especially on the extensor surfaces, due to filaggrin gene mutations leading to impaired skin barrier function.

question: Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis for a child born with membranes around the body, ectropion, and eclabium, presenting with lesions on the face, trunk, and extremities, and brought to the OPD, what is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Harlequin ichthyosis is the most severe form of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis caused by mutations in the ABCA12 gene, leading to defective epidermal lipid transport and severe skin barrier dysfunction.

Affected neonates are born with:

  • thick armor-like or plate-like hyperkeratotic scales,
  • deep fissures,
  • severe ectropion,
  • eclabium,
  • flattened/crumpled ears,
  • and limb contractures.

The rigid skin restricts movement and chest expansion, predisposing to:

  • respiratory distress,
  • dehydration,
  • temperature instability,
  • feeding difficulties,
  • and severe infections/sepsis.

Harlequin ichthyosis is often described as an “armor-like” congenital ichthyosis with deep fissuring of the skin.

Lamellar ichthyosis (Option B): Typically presents as a collodion baby with large brown adherent scales after shedding of the membrane, but not with massive armor-like fissured plates. Ectropion and eclabium may occur but are less severe.

Bathing suit ichthyosis (Option C): Scaling is mainly limited to the trunk and proximal body in a “bathing suit” distribution.

Ichthyosis vulgaris (Option D): A milder inherited ichthyosis presenting later in childhood with fine scaling, especially over extensor surfaces.



Reference:
  1. Neena Khanna Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology and Sexually Transmitted Diseases, 5th Edition, Page 27
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562318/

Explanation:

  • Flagellate dermatitis, also known as "flagellate erythema," is a distinctive skin reaction that can occur as a side effect of certain medications. Among the given options, the most commonly associated drug with flagellate dermatitis is Bleomycin, which is an antineoplastic medication used in the treatment of various cancers.
  • Flagellate dermatitis typically appears as linear or streak-like red or brownish patches on the skin, resembling the marks left by a whip or a scratch. It usually occurs on the trunk, extremities, or face and is believed to be an idiosyncratic reaction to Bleomycin.
  • Bleomycin-induced flagellate dermatitis is thought to be related to the drug's ability to induce the release of inflammatory mediators, resulting in the characteristic skin reaction. It typically occurs within a few days to weeks after the administration of Bleomycin and tends to resolve spontaneously once the drug is discontinued.

Some common side effects associated with the use of Bleomycin:

Side Effect

Description

Pulmonary Toxicity

Bleomycin is known to cause lung damage, which can lead to pulmonary fibrosis and respiratory symptoms such as cough, shortness of breath, and decreased lung function.

Skin Toxicity

Bleomycin can cause skin reactions, including flagellate dermatitis (linear streaks on the skin), erythema (redness), and skin desquamation (peeling).

Mucosal Toxicity

Bleomycin can cause mucosal damage, resulting in mouth sores, sore throat, and inflammation of the oral and nasal mucosa.

Fever

Fever is a common side effect of Bleomycin treatment and can occur shortly after administration.

Hematologic Toxicity

Bleomycin can suppress bone marrow function, leading to decreased production of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

Nail Changes

Bleomycin can cause nail abnormalities, including nail discoloration, brittle nails, and nail bed inflammation.

Allergic Reactions

Allergic reactions to Bleomycin can occur, ranging from mild rash to severe hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis.

Incorrrect Options:

Actinomycin (Option A): Actinomycin is an antibiotic medication used in chemotherapy. While it can cause various dermatological side effects, flagellate dermatitis is not commonly associated with Actinomycin use.

Mitomycin C (Option C): Mitomycin C is an antineoplastic medication used in the treatment of certain cancers. While it can cause skin reactions, flagellate dermatitis is not a recognized side effect commonly associated with Mitomycin C use.

Doxorubicin (Option D): Doxorubicin is an anthracycline chemotherapy drug used to treat various types of cancer. While it can cause skin-related side effects, flagellate dermatitis is not a well-known or commonly reported side effect of Doxorubicin use.

question: The given condition is caused by which drug ?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The recurrent nature of the rash in the same location after taking NSAIDs strongly supports Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE).

Fixed drug eruption:

  • Fixed drug eruption is a distinctive cutaneous allergic reaction that characteristically recurs at the same sites with the same morphology on re-exposure to the medication or other chemical agent.

[[figure-1]]

  • Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction (Option B ruled out)
  • Causative drugs: Co-trimoxazole, NSAIDs, tetracyclines, sulfonamides.
  • Mediated by memory T-cells.
  • Acutely, erythematous and bullous phases of fixed eruptions, followed by well-circumscribed areas of slate-brown pigmentation
  • Site of lesions: Mucous membrane (Lips, tongues, Glans penis), face and acral areas although can occur anywhere on the skin surface.
  • Leaves residual hyperpigmentation on healing (Option A ruled out).
  • Upon reexposure, lesions develop within 30 minutes to 8 hours (Option C ruled out).
  • Treatment:
    • Stop the causative drug.
    • Topical steroids and antibiotics combinations

Incorrect Options

Drug hypersensitivity (Option A): While this is a broad term for adverse drug reactions, it doesn't specify the unique characteristic of recurrence at the same site.

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) (Option B): PIH is a result of inflammation or injury to the skin, but it wouldn't consistently reappear in the same location with each exposure to the same drug.

Drug-induced hypermelanosis (Option D): This is a general term for increased melanin production due to drugs, but it doesn't fit the specific pattern of a solitary lesion recurring at the same site with each drug exposure.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology 9th edition - page 88.28, UpToDate.

explanationHtml:
Explanation: The correct answer is Xeroderma pigmentosum, as the girl has severe sunburns with minimal exposure, freckling, and sun-induced skin damage, which are hallmark features of XP.

Xeroderma Pigmentosum:

  • It is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by extreme sensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight.
  • It arises due to genetic mutations affecting genes responsible for the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway.
  • It presents with freckle-like pigmented patches, atrophic areas, and other skin abnormalities in sun-exposed areas.
  • Additionally, patients may experience ocular manifestations such as photophobia, conjunctival injection, and corneal ulcers due to UV-induced damage.
  • Systemic manifestations can include mental retardation and low intelligence.
  • Increased risk of developing skin cancers, including melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, at a young age.

[[figure-1]]

Bloom Syndrome (Option A):

  • It is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the BLM gene.
  • It presents with short stature, photosensitivity, and characteristic facial features including a long, narrow face and prominent nose, along with other physical anomalies such as micrognathia and cafe-au-lait spots.
  • Increased risk of various cancers, particularly leukaemia and lymphoma, at an early age.

Warts (Option C):

  • Warts (caused by HPV) present as localized verrucous lesions, not widespread freckling and sun sensitivity.

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) (Option D):

  • SLE can cause photosensitivity, but it presents with a malar rash, systemic symptoms (fatigue, arthritis, renal involvement), and autoantibodies. XP causes DNA repair defects, not an autoimmune reaction.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology - page 78.1, 79.3

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The condition described in the image is Pellagra, which is caused by niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency.

Pellagra is characterized by the classic triad of symptoms:

  • Dermatitis
    • Bright red erythema- in sun-exposed areas (face, ankles, feet)
    • Casal’s necklace- ↑pigmentation around the neck
  • Diarrhoea, and
  • Dementia.

[[figure-1]]

Causes of pellagra :

  • Dietary Deficiency- Maize and Sorghum based diet
  • Impaired Tryptophan Metabolism
    • Factors Affecting Tryptophan to Niacin Conversion:
      • Vitamin B6 Deficiency
      • Medications: Isoniazid (INH), OCPs
      • Hormonal Influences: Estrogen metabolites hinder tryptophan metabolism.
      • Genetic Disorders: Inherited conditions like Hartnup disease can impede tryptophan absorption in the intestines and reabsorption in the kidneys
  • Carcinoid Syndrome
  • Other Contributing Factors:
    • Alcoholism: Interferes with nutrient absorption, including niacin and tryptophan.
    • Malabsorption Syndromes

Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) Deficiency (Option A): Causes cheilitis, glossitis, irritability, and peripheral neuropathy, but not the characteristic photosensitive rash.

Cobalamin (Vitamin B12) Deficiency (Option B): Leads to megaloblastic anemia, neuropathy, and glossitis, but not pellagra.

Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) Deficiency (Option D): Presents with angular cheilitis, glossitis.

  • Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd Edition, Pg.542,543

question: A 28-year-old woman has multiple firm, pink nodules on her scalp. Family history is positive. Histology shows lobules in a “jigsaw-puzzle” pattern with a hyaline basal membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Breslow thickness is the single most important prognostic factor in primary melanoma.
  • Thicker tumors have a higher risk of metastasis and lower overall survival.


Melanoma - Prognostic Factors:

  • Metastasis:
    • Can spread to any organ; initially, often skin/subcutaneous tissue
    • Common distant sites: lung, brain, liver, bone
    • Sentinel node positivity → worse prognosis
  • Breslow thickness (tumour depth) - High: Strongest predictor
    • Measured from the top of the granular layer (or base of ulcer) to deepest invasive cell
  • Sentinel lymph node status - High
  • Ulceration - Moderate
    • Negative marker for prognosis.
    • Indicates aggressive biological subtype.
  • Mitotic rate - Moderate
    • Particularly relevant in thin melanomas.
    • Higher mitotic activity → worse prognosis
  • Low Prognostic Factors:
    • Regression - may underestimate Breslow thickness.
    • Age - older patients have a worse prognosis.
    • Sex - males have slightly worse outcomes.
    • Tumour location - head and neck melanomas have poorer prognosis.


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 143.19, 143.20

Melanoma:

  • Origin:
    • 75-80% arise de novo (normal skin)
    • 20-25% arise from a naevus
  • Naevi & Risk:
    • Congenital Melanocytic Naevi (CMN):
      • Large (>20 cm) → lifetime risk ~2-3%
      • Higher risk: truncal, >40 cm, satellites
      • Transformation often occurs in childhood
    • Common Acquired Naevi: Risk increases with total naevus count
    • Atypical/Dysplastic Naevi: ≥5 atypical naevi → markedly ↑ melanoma risk (Option B)
  • Genetic Risk: CDKN2A (most important) → familial melanoma, pancreatic cancer
  • Phenotypic risk:
    • Fitzpatrick I > IV
    • Red hair (Option D)
    • Blue eyes
    • Freckles
    • ≥100 naevi
  • UV Radiation (Only Established Environmental Factor)
  • Intermittent sun exposure & sunburn → strongest association (Option A)


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 143.2-143.6

options.text: Intermittent sun exposure and sunburns increase melanoma risk.
Having ≥5 atypical/dysplastic naevi significantly increases melanoma risk.
Most cutaneous melanomas arise from pre-existing naevi.
