question: Which of the following statements regarding risk factors of the most probable condition depicted in the image below is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hutchinson sign is defined as true periungual spread of brown-black pigment from a longitudinal melanonychia onto the proximal and/or lateral nail fold, visible to the naked eye.
  • It represents invasion or radial spread of melanocytic tumor cells beyond the nail matrix and is highly suggestive of nail unit (subungual) melanoma.
  • Often associated with other warning features:
  • Irregular borders of the pigmented band
  • Color variegation (brown/black/gray)
  • Nail plate dystrophy or splitting
  • Should prompt urgent biopsy of the nail matrix/bed.

[[figure-1]]


Pseudo-Hutchinson sign (Option A): Pigment appears visible through a translucent cuticle due to underlying nail matrix pigmentation, but there is no true periungual skin involvement. It has no diagnostic significance.


Micro-Hutchinson sign (Option B): Pigmentation of the proximal nail fold that is visible only with dermoscopy, not to the naked eye.


Parallel ridge pattern (Option D): A dermoscopic pattern seen in acral melanoma involving pigmentation along the ridges of acral skin, not specifically referring to nail fold extension.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 144.8,144.10
question: A 50-year-old man presents with a progressively widening dark streak on his thumbnail. Examination shows longitudinal melanonychia with brown-black pigmentation extending onto the proximal nail fold, visible to the naked eye. What is this sign called?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Gorlin syndrome (Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome) is caused by germline mutations in the PTCH1, a tumour suppressor gene located on chromosome 9q22.3 that regulates the Hedgehog signalling pathway.


Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome (NBCCS):

  • Autosomal dominant disorder with multiple early-onset BCCs + characteristic skeletal, craniofacial, and neurological anomalies.
  • Mutation in PTCH1 (Chr 9q22.3)
  • Clinical features:
    • Skin:
      • Numerous BCCs (face, chest, back; sun & non-sun areas)
      • Palmoplantar pits (diagnostic clue)
      • Milia, epidermoid cysts
    • Craniofacial: Frontal bossing, hypertelorism & macrocephaly
    • Skeletal: Bifid ribs, spina bifida occulta & scoliosis
    • Odontogenic jaw cysts, calcified falx cerebri (early), & ↑ Risk of medulloblastoma
  • Management:
    • Avoid radiotherapy
    • Regular skin surveillance
    • Excision/cryotherapy / PDT
    • Hedgehog inhibitor: Vismodegib


PTEN (Option B): Causes Cowden syndrome, characterised by hamartomas, trichilemmomas, and increased risk of breast and thyroid cancers - not multiple early BCCs with jaw cysts.


MLH1 (Option C): DNA mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer), not associated with NBCCS features.


TP53 (Option D): Mutated in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which predisposes to sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumours, and adrenal carcinoma - not classic Gorlin features.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 141.18-141.21
question: Which gene mutation is most commonly associated with Gorlin syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Muir-Torre syndrome is an autosomal dominant variant of Lynch syndrome characterized by sebaceous neoplasms (adenoma, epithelioma, carcinoma) along with visceral malignancy, most commonly colorectal carcinoma.


Muir-Torre Syndrome (MTS):

  • Autosomal dominant cancer syndrome, considered a variant of Lynch syndrome (HNPCC).
  • Characterised by:
    • ≥1 sebaceous neoplasm (adenoma, epithelioma, carcinoma) ± keratoacanthoma
    • ≥1 visceral malignancy (most commonly colorectal carcinoma)
  • Genetics:
    • DNA mismatch repair (MMR) defect
    • MSH2 most common
    • MLH1, rarely MSH6, PMS2


Gardner syndrome (Option A): Associated with FAP, osteomas, epidermoid cysts, and multiple colon polyps-not sebaceous tumors.

Turcot syndrome (Option B): Colon cancer with CNS tumors (e.g., medulloblastoma, glioma), not sebaceous neoplasms.

Cowden syndrome (Option D): Associated with trichilemmomas, oral papillomas, breast and thyroid cancers (PTEN mutation).



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 142.38-142.40
question: A 48-year-old man presents with multiple yellowish papules and nodules on the face and trunk for 3 years. Histopathology of one lesion shows a sebaceous adenoma. He also has a history of right-sided colon carcinoma diagnosed at age 45. His father died of colorectal cancer. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical presentation and the image provided, the most likely diagnosis is Verrucous carcinoma (Epithelioma cuniculatum).
  • Verrucous carcinoma is a low-grade, well-differentiated variant of squamous cell carcinoma.
  • It presents as a slow-growing, exophytic, cauliflower-like mass, commonly on the plantar surface.
  • Histology shows minimal atypia with pushing borders rather than infiltrative growth.
  • Metastasis is rare.
  • May be associated with HPV, especially low-risk types (e.g., 6, 11), though the association is variable.


Keratoacanthoma (Option A): This is a rapidly growing, dome-shaped keratinising tumour that typically enlarges over weeks and may spontaneously regress.


Conventional invasive squamous cell carcinoma (Option C): This is a more aggressive malignancy with infiltrative growth, greater cytologic atypia, and a higher risk of metastasis. It often presents with ulceration, pain, or lymphadenopathy, unlike the slow-growing, exophytic, low-grade behaviour described.


Viral wart (verruca vulgaris) (Option D): This is a benign HPV-induced lesion, usually small, multiple, and stable or slowly changing, more common in younger individuals.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 142.28
question: A 58-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging lesion on the plantar surface of his foot for 2 years. It is painless but progressively increasing in size with no regional lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. There is a risk of progression to invasive SCC
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical and histopathological findings described, the diagnosis is Bowen’s disease (also known as Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) in situ).
  • It is characterised by full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without dermal invasion.
  • The lifetime risk of progression to invasive SCC is about 3-5%.


Bowen Disease (SCC in situ):

  • Intraepidermal squamous cell carcinoma presenting as a persistent, well-demarcated, erythematous scaly/crusted plaque.
  • Epidemiology:
    • Elderly (>60 yrs), peak 7th decade
    • Female predominance (Option A)
    • Fair-skinned; UV exposure
  • Risk factors:
    • Chronic UV radiation
    • Arsenic exposure
    • Immunosuppression (transplant, CLL, HIV)
    • HPV (16, 18 - genital; 16 - periungual)
    • Radiation (Option D), chronic inflammation
  • Pathology:
    • Full-thickness epidermal dysplasia
    • Loss of polarity, atypical mitoses
    • Intact basement membrane
  • Clinical features:
    • Slowly enlarging (Option B), red scaly plaque
    • Well-defined, slightly raised edge
    • Usually asymptomatic
    • Ulceration → suspect invasive SCC
  • Common sites: Lower legs, head/neck, perianal, periungual


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 142.16-142.21

options.text: It is more common in males
It is typically a rapidly enlarging lesion
There is a risk of progression to invasive SCC
It is not associated with prior radiation exposure

question: A 72-year-old woman presents with findings as shown for 10 months. It is asymptomatic. Biopsy shows atypical keratinocytes involving the entire thickness of the epidermis with an intact basement membrane. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Chronic mechanical friction is not an established risk factor for basal cell carcinoma.
  • While trauma may occasionally draw attention to lesions, it is not causative.


BCC-Risk Factors:

  • UV Exposure (Most Important)
    • UVB → pyrimidine dimers (direct DNA damage)
    • UVA → ROS-mediated damage
    • Intermittent childhood exposure more important than cumulative dose
  • Genetic Predisposition:
    • Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome)
      • Mutation in PTCH1 (Hedgehog pathway)
      • Multiple BCC, odontogenic cysts, and palmoplantar pits
    • p53 mutation (~50%)
    • MC1R variants (fair skin, red hair)
  • Fitzpatrick I-II skin (Option A)
  • Immunosuppression (transplant, HIV, CLL) (Option C)
  • Arsenic exposure (Option B)
  • Ionizing radiation
  • PUVA / UVB therapy


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 141.2
question: Which of the following is not a recognised risk factor for basal cell carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The nodular subtype is the most common form of basal cell carcinoma (BCC), accounting for the majority of cases.
  • Clinically, it typically presents as a pearly, translucent papule or nodule with surface telangiectasia and may show central ulceration (“rodent ulcer”), especially on sun-exposed areas of the face such as the nose, periocular region, and cheeks.
  • Histologically, nodular BCC shows:
    • Nests of basaloid cells
    • Peripheral palisading of nuclei
    • Retraction clefts between tumour nests and stroma
    • Mucinous stroma

[[figure-1]]


Histological Variants of BCC

  • Nodular: Most common
  • Superficial (Option A): Common, often on trunk
  • Morpheaform (sclerosing/desmoplastic) (Option B): More aggressive, ill-defined margins
  • Infiltrative (Option D): Aggressive growth pattern, higher recurrence risk
  • Micronodular: Multiple small nodules, higher risk of subclinical spread
  • Pigmented: Contains melanin, more common in darker skin types


Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 141.6, 141.8
question: A 72-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging lesion on the lateral nose. It appears as a pearly papule with surface telangiectasia and occasional central ulceration. A biopsy confirms a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma. Which of the following is the most common histological subtype of basal cell carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Basaloid tumour nests, peripheral palisading, mucinous stroma, and retraction artefact (clefting) are classic diagnostic features of Basal cell carcinoma.


Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC / Rodent ulcer):

  • Slow-growing, locally invasive, rarely metastasises; arises from basal epidermal or follicular cells.
  • Sites: Face, around eyes, nose.
  • Features: Scaly plaque → noduloulcerative lesion with rolled margin, telangiectasia, bleeds easily.
  • Histology:
    • Basaloid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei
    • Peripheral palisading
    • Retraction artefact (cleft between tumour & stroma)
    • Mucinous stroma
    • Rare keratinization
  • Treatment:
    • Surgical excision or Mohs micrographic surgery (first-line, especially for high-risk lesions), with topical agents like imiquimod or 5-FU for selected superficial lesions, and vismodegib for advanced or inoperable cases.


Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A) shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, not basaloid palisading islands with stromal retraction.


Melanoma (Option B) demonstrates atypical melanocytes, pagetoid spread, and pleomorphism, not uniform basaloid nests with clefting artifact.


Keratoacanthoma (Option D) is characterised by a central keratin-filled crater and well-differentiated squamous epithelium, lacking peripheral palisading and retraction artefact.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 141.4-141.8
question: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the histopathology slide?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Extracorporeal photopheresis (ECP) is an immunomodulatory therapy used primarily in erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), especially Sézary syndrome and erythrodermic mycosis fungoides.
  • Mechanism:
    • Leukapheresis is performed to collect the buffy coat (mononuclear cells).
    • Psoralen (8-MOP) is added to the collected cells.
    • The cells are exposed ex vivo to UVA light, which induces apoptosis of malignant T lymphocytes.
    • The treated cells are then reinfused into the patient.
  • Immunologic Effects:
    • Induces apoptosis of tumour lymphocytes
    • Enhances antigen presentation and dendritic cell activation
    • Generates an anti-tumour immune response (often described as “transimmunization”)
    • The overall effect is immunomodulatory rather than directly cytotoxic
  • Treatment Schedule:
    • Typically performed on 2 consecutive days per cycle, repeated every 2-4 weeks (monthly or fortnightly depending on protocol and response).
  • Indications:
    • FDA-approved for CTCL, especially erythrodermic MF / Sézary syndrome
    • Often used in combination therapy (e.g., ECP + Interferon-α ± bexarotene) in advanced disease, with improved responses reported in case series.


Plaque psoriasis (Option A): This is a chronic inflammatory papulosquamous disease primarily treated with topical therapy, phototherapy (UVB/PUVA), systemic agents, and biologics.


Atopic dermatitis (Option C): This is a chronic inflammatory, IgE-mediated eczematous disorder treated with topical steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, systemic immunosuppressants, and biologics.


Vitiligo (Option D): This is a depigmenting disorder due to loss of melanocytes, managed with topical agents, phototherapy, and other immunomodulators.



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 140.26
  2. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1430395/
question: Extracorporeal photopheresis is most useful in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical presentation and the histopathological findings, the correct diagnosis is Mycosis fungoides.
  • The image shows a Sézary cell (a T-lymphocyte with a characteristic cerebriform nucleus, meaning it looks folded like a brain).


Mycosis fungoides:

  • Most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL)
  • Derived from skin-resident CD4+ memory T cells
  • Immunophenotype: CD3+, CD4+, CD45RO+, CD7-
  • Clinical Progression:
    • Patches → Plaques → Tumours → Erythroderma (Common on trunk, buttocks)
  • Histological hallmarks:
    • Epidermotropism
    • Pautrier microabscesses
    • Cerebriform lymphocytes
  • Poor prognostic factors:
    • Age >60
    • Tumor stage
    • Blood involvement
    • Large-cell transformation
    • Folliculotropic variant


Sézary syndrome (Option A): This is the leukemic (systemic) phase of CTCL. While it shares the cerebriform cells, it is characterised by generalised erythroderma (total body redness) and significant blood involvement, rather than the localised patch/plaque progression described here.


Pagetoid reticulosis (Option C): A rare localised variant of MF, typically presenting as a single slow-growing plaque on an extremity, which doesn't fit the "patches over the trunk" description.


Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) (Option D): Linked to the HTLV-1 virus, this typically presents more aggressively with "flower cells" (highly lobulated nuclei) rather than cerebriform cells, and often includes hypercalcemia and bone lesions.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 140.1-140.10
question: A 60-year-old man has chronic pruritic patches over the trunk progressing to plaques. Skin biopsy shows epidermotropism and findings as shown. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:


Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most common form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), accounting for the majority of primary CTCL cases. It is a primary cutaneous lymphoma of mature CD4⁺ T cells.

  • Clinical Course:
  • Patch stage →Plaque stage → Tumour stage (slow, indolent progression over years)
  • Lesions are often erythematous to violaceous, may be pruritic, and commonly involve sun-protected areas (e.g., trunk, buttocks, thighs)

[[figure-1]]

  • Immunophenotype: CD3+, CD4+, CD45RO+, CD7-
  • Histological hallmarks:
    • Epidermotropism
    • Pautrier microabscesses
    • Cerebriform lymphocytes


Sézary syndrome (Option A): This is an aggressive leukemic variant of CTCL, characterised by erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating Sézary cells. It is far less common than mycosis fungoides and therefore not the most common CTCL.


Pagetoid reticulosis (Option C): This is a rare, localized variant of CTCL (also called Woringer-Kolopp disease), usually presenting as a solitary plaque with marked epidermotropism. It is uncommon compared to mycosis fungoides.


Follicular mucinosis (Option D): This is a reaction pattern characterised by mucin deposition in hair follicles. It may be associated with CTCL (especially folliculotropic mycosis fungoides), but it is not itself the most common CTCL.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 140.1
question: Which of the following is the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL)?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A sudden eruption of multiple seborrheic keratosis lesions is known as the sign of Leser-Trelat. It can be a symptom of paraneoplastic syndrome typically associated with gastric adenocarcinoma. However, it can also be associated with other internal malignancies.

Seborrheic Keratoses (SK):

  • Benign proliferation of keratocytes
  • Usually seen in older age groups.
  • Appearance -
    • Hyperkeratotic plaques with a stuck-on appearance.
    • Follicular plugs
  • Sign of Leser-Trelat: The sudden appearance of seborrheic keratosis on the body reveals that there is an association with underlying GI malignancy.
  • Treatment: Treatment is usually done only for cosmetic purposes.

[[figure-1]]

Intestinal cancer and Lung cancer can sometimes present with this sign, but gastric adenocarcinoma has the most common association.(Options B and C ruled out)

There is no established association between cardiac malignancies and signs of Leser-Trelat. Cardiac malignancies do not generally present with paraneoplastic syndromes.(Option D ruled out)



Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no. 133.2
question: A 50-year-old female presented with sudden eruption of asymptomatic lesions as shown in the image below. The lesions have a stuck-on appearance suggestive of a diagnosis of Seborrheic keratosis. Which of the following malignancies is commonly suspected in the given scenario?

explanationHtml:
Erythema chronicum migrans (ECM) is not typically a marker of internal malignancy. It is the characteristic rash of early Lyme disease, caused by the tick-borne spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi.

Erythema Chronicum Migrans (ECM):

  • Seen in ~90% at tick bite site, 1–36 days post-bite.

  • Expanding ring-shaped lesion with central clearing (“target” look).

  • May itch or burn; sometimes scaly.

  • Fades in weeks without treatment; may have lymphadenopathy or mild systemic symptoms.

[[figure-1]]

Necrolytic migratory erythema (Option A):Associated with: Glucagonoma (a rare pancreatic islet cell tumor).

[[figure-2]]

Acanthosis nigricans (Option B):

  • Can be a cutaneous marker of internal malignancy, most commonly gastric adenocarcinoma.

  • Also associated with insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus.

[[figure-3]]

Erythroderma (Option C):

  • Defined as inflammation affecting >90% of the body surface area.

  • Also linked to internal malignancies, especially lymphomas

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 39.31, 147.1
question: Which of the following is NOT a cutaneous marker of underlying internal malignancy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The above image shows multiple red to purple plaque-like lesions coalescing with each other, which is suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma.

[[figure-1]]

Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm. It is the most common cancer seen in HIV patients.

Kaposi sarcoma caused by HHV-8 stimulates VEGF and inhibits p53 leading to malignancy.

All forms of Kaposi sarcoma are associated with HHV-8 infection as an etiological agent.

Types of Kaposi sarcoma:

  1. Classic (Meditteranean)
  2. Endemic African ( HIV negative )
  3. Transplant associated
  4. AIDS-associated Epidemic KS

HHV8 associated diseases:

  • Kaposi’s Sarcoma:
  • Primary Effusion Lymphoma (PEL): PEL is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by the accumulation of fluid in body cavities.
  • Multicentric Castleman Disease (MCD): MCD is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder.

Kaposi's Sarcoma of mouth due to HHV8:

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 139 page no.139.1
question: A 25-year-old homosexual male presents with the following lesion on his legs which have progressed in size. Which of the following is the most common organism associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Follicular mucinosis is not a part of the clinical triad of sezary syndrome. It is a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma presenting with boggy plaques and mucinous degeneration of hair follicles.

THE TRIAD CONSISTS OF:

  1. Erythroderma: This refers to diffuse redness affecting more than 80% of the body surface area. The skin appears eczematous and may be associated with variable scaling. Sézary syndrome often presents with rapid-onset itching and erythroderma. It can occur without prior signs of another type of CTCL called mycosis fungoides. (Option A ruled out)
  2. Lymphadenopathy: Generalized enlargement of lymph nodes is a common feature. These swollen lymph nodes are often palpable and can be detected during physical examination. (Option B ruled out)
  3. Atypical Malignant (Sézary Cells): These abnormal T-cells are found in the skin, blood, and lymph nodes, comprising >20% of total lymphocyte count or total sezary count of >1000x109/L. (Option C ruled out)



Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no. 140.18

options.text: Atypical mononuclear cells &gt;20% of total lymphocytes

question: Which of the following is not included in the clinical triad of sezary syndrome?

explanationHtml:
• Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CD4+/CD45R0+); slow-growing, may metastasize.

  • Site: Girdle area (abdomen, back).

Clinical progression:
Patch → Plaque → Tumor → Erythroderma.

Histology:
Epidermotropism with Pautrier’s microabscesses (T-cell clusters).

Treatment:

  • Patch: Topical steroids, nitrogen mustard, PUVA/UVB.

  • Plaque: Total skin electron therapy, interferon-α, retinoids.

  • Advanced: CHOP regimen, extracorporeal photopheresis.

Progression of mycosis fungoides:

[[figure-1]]

Patch stage -------------->Plague stage------------------>Tumor stage

[[figure-2]]

Sézary syndrome(Option A) – aggressive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and Sézary cells; lacks macule-plaque-tumor progression.
Psoriasis (Option B) – well-defined scaly plaques on extensor surfaces; no polymorphic progression.
BCC (Option C) – pearly nodular lesion with rolled border; not progressive or erythrodermic.



Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition-chapter 140, page no. 140.1
question: A 52-year-old male has a slow-growing, scaly, reddish patch on his lower back that has become a thickened plaque over several months. He reports no itching, pain, or discomfort. Examination reveals similar plaques on his abdomen. A biopsy shows a monoclonal proliferation of CD4+/CD45R0+ helper T cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A)Tumor thickness
Explanation:
Tumor thickness or Breslow index is the best prognostic factor for melanoma.

It is the distance in millimetres (mm) between the epidermal granular layer and the primary lesion's deepest level of invasion. Thicker tumours have a higher metastatic potential.

[[figure-1]]

The prognosis of primary melanoma depends on several factors:

  1. Tumour thickness (Breslow Depth): Thicker tumours are associated with poor prognosis.
  2. Ulceration: It is another important independent poor prognostic factor. Even in locally advanced melanoma, primary tumour ulceration retains its significance.
  3. Mitotic Rate: Higher mitotic rates are associated with a worse prognosis.
  4. Sentinel Lymph Node Status: Lymph node involvement indicates a higher risk of metastasis and poorer outcome.
  5. Other Clinicopathologic Factors: LDH levels, tumor location, and genetic mutations



Reference:
  1. Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no. 143.19 and 143.20
  2. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Melanoma_Growth_over_14_Months.jpg
question: A 45-year-old male presents with a slow-growing lesion on the face as shown in the image. What is the best indicator for the prognosis of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

1. Nodular melanoma (False): Superficial spreading is the most common type.

2. CDKN2A (False): BRAF mutation is more common in sporadic melanoma.

3. Depth >6 mm (False): >6 mm size raises suspicion, but Breslow depth is for staging.

4. Clark’s classification (True): Used for assessing melanoma invasion depth.

5. Interferon-α (True): Used as adjuvant therapy to prevent metastasis in high-risk melanoma.

Types of Melanoma:

  • Superficial spreading (MC): Upper back, lower legs; multicolored with raised border.

  • Lentigo maligna: Sun-exposed face; flat brown/tan with grey or dark nodules.

  • Acral lentiginous: Palms, soles, nail bed; dark brown to black lesions.

  • Nodular: Any site; uniform or mixed dark hues, rapidly growing.

Investigations: Clinical exam, dermoscopy, biopsy, genetics (BRAF, NRAS, NF1), IHC (S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A, MITF), CT scan.

Management: Wide local excision (margin by Breslow depth), sentinel node biopsy if >1 mm; advanced cases—immunotherapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy; interferon-α as adjuvant.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, page no. 143.7-143.28
  2. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, page no. 587
question:
A 65-year-old woman with fair skin and a history of teenage sunburns presents with a mole on her upper back that has become larger and darker over the past few months. The lesion is pigmented with irregular borders, color variation, asymmetry, slight elevation, and measures 1.5 cm in diameter. She reports occasional itching and tenderness but denies bleeding or ulceration. Identify the true statements regarding this condition.

  1. The most common type is nodular melanoma.
  2. CDKN2A mutation is most commonly involved in sporadic melanoma.
  3. Depth > 6 mm is suggestive of melanoma.
  4. Clark’s classification is used in malignant melanoma.
  5. Interferon-5ü can be used for the prevention of metastasis.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the image showing a lesion with irregular borders, asymmetry, and uneven distribution of colors in the lesion is suggestive of malignant melanoma. The gold standard investigation for diagnosis of melanoma is histopathological examination by a biopsy.

Biopsy findings in malignant melanoma:

  • Melanoma cells: larger than normal melanocytes or nevus cells.

  • Nuclei: enlarged, irregular, peripheral chromatin clumping, eosinophilic nucleoli.

  • Radial phase: horizontal spread in epidermis/superficial dermis.

  • Vertical phase: deep dermal invasion as expansile mass.

The given image below shows the histology of superficial spreading melanoma (M/C type).

[[figure-1]]

Dermoscopy(.Option A): noninvasive lesion exam using polarized/nonpolarized light; initial test for suspected melanoma, confirmed by biopsy.


Clinical examination (Option B) detects melanoma in 80–90% using the ABCDE checklist but lacks specificity; biopsy confirms diagnosis.The ABCDE features include:

  • Asymmetry: Irregular shapes.
  • Border: Irregular.
  • Colour: Various colours present or uneven distribution.
  • Diameter: > 6 mm.
  • Evolution: Changes in lesion over time (size, shape, itching, or bleeding).

[[figure-2]]


CT scan (Option D) is not used for diagnosis of malignant melanoma; rather it can be used for follow-up of patients after surgical excision.



Reference:
  1. Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 143.8-143.20
  2. Fitzpatrick Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 1991, 1992
  3. Robbins and Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page 1141
question: A 50-year-old construction worker presents to the dermatology OPD with a black mole over his back as shown in the image. Which of the following investigations is the gold standard for diagnosis of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Large congenital melanocytic nevus, especially those over 20cm (giant congenital melanocytic nevus), have a much higher risk of developing melanoma over the individual's lifetime, particularly if they are larger or have a nodular component.

[[figure-1]]

question: A 65-year-old female came with complaints of a painless nodule on the right palm for the past 3 weeks. She gave a history of sustaining a thorn prick injury to the palm 4 weeks ago. On examination, the lesions appear as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. It has pearly rolled-out edges.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The description of pearly rolled-out edges typically refers to BCC and not SCC. SCC often presents as a scaly or crusted lesion with potential ulceration and an everted edge.
  • Crusting and scaling are potential signs of photodamage.

Squamous cell carcinoma:

  • SCC arises from keratinocytes or its appendages.(Option A)
  • SCC occurs in sun-exposed sites including mucosa. SCC can occur on sun-exposed skin such as the head, neck, and arms.(Option B)
  • Predisposing factors include
  • UV exposure
  • Immunocompromised individuals
  • Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)
  • Albinism, LP(Lichen Planus), DLE (Discoid lupus erythematosus)
  • SCC is most common dermatological malignancy in transplant recipients due to immunosuppression. Overall, BCC is the most common skin malignancy and SCC is the second most common.(Option C)

[[figure-1]]

Basal cell carcinoma: Aka Basilioma, rodent ulcer

  • Most common human cancer

  • Arises from basal layer of epidermis / follicular structures

  • Slow growing, locally invasive

  • Rarely metastasizes

  • Clinical features:

    • No premalignant stage

    • Slow progressive with peripheral extension

  • Site: Face (around eyes & nose)
  • Presentation:
    • Papule/ raised nodule with central ulceration
    • Thready margin and telangiectasia (periphery)
    • Bleeds to touch
  • Association:
    • Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)
    • Albinism
    • Naevoid BCC syndrome/Gorlin syndrome
  • Treatment:
    • Medical: Low‐ Risk superficial and small nodular BCC
      • Imiquimod, 5-FU
      • PDT
      • Intralesional interferon α-2b
      • Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (e.g., Vismodegib) for locally advanced/metastatic cases
    • Surgical:
      • Excision with predetermined margins → 4–5 mm surgical margin
      • Mohs micrographic surgery
    • Others: Cryotherapy, Electron beam radiotherapy

question: A 60-year-old male presents with a slowly growing lesion on his left forearm, occasionally bleeding post-trauma, and had a lot of sun exposure throughout his life. The biopsy of the lesion is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. High potential for invasive malignancy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The clinical presentation described, including the presence of a scaly, erythematous plaque confined to the epidermis and a history of chronic sun exposure, is consistent with Bowen's disease, also known as squamous cell carcinoma in situ. The incorrect statement is that it has a high potential for invasive malignancy.

Bowen's disease/Squamous cell carcinoma in situ:

  • It is an intra-epidermal squamous cell carcinoma characterized by a persistent, non-elevated, red, scaly, or crusted plaque with a low potential for invasive malignancy.(Option A)
  • Risk factors:
    • Arsenic exposure.
    • Immunosuppression (organ transplant, HIV).
    • Chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
  • Human papilloma virus- HPV16 and HPV18 are commonly found in Bowen disease lesions, especially in anogenital areas.(Option B)
  • It usually grows progressively but sometimes undergoes spontaneous partial resolution.(Option D)
  • It can occur anywhere, but more in the head and neck region.
  • Pathology:
    • Full-thickness epidermal dysplasia & disordered differentiation with loss of epithelial polarity.
    • The intraepidermal portion of cutaneous adnexae is generally affected.
    • Parakeratosis and acanthosis are usually present, and keratinocytes show variable pleomorphism, nuclear hyperchromasia, and nuclear enlargement.
    • The dermal-epidermal junction remains distinct.
    • HPV‐associated viral cytopathic changes are frequently seen particularly, but not exclusively, in lesions from genital skin.

The image shows Bowen's disease- Red, erythematous plaque:

[[figure-1]]

Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th ed, page no.142.16-142.17

question: Which carcinoma is the possible diagnosis in the image given below?

explanationHtml:
Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer and typically occurs in sun-exposed areas such as the face, particularly around the medial canthus of the eye.

The classic clinical description includes:

  • Ulceration with rolled-out, beaded margins.
  • A pearly or translucent appearance with visible telangiectasia.

Histopathology findings include:

  • Nesting of basaloid cells.
  • Peripheral palisading of nuclei.
  • Clefting artifact between tumor cells and surrounding stroma.

Other Options:

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) (Option A): Typically presents with a scaly, keratinized lesion that may ulcerate but lacks the rolled, pearly margins and palisading pattern seen in BCC.

Nevus (Option B): A benign lesion that does not typically ulcerate or have invasive histological features.


Melanoma (Option D): Usually presents with irregular pigmentation, asymmetry, and rapid growth, rather than a rolled-margin ulcer.

question: A 60-year-old person presented with an ulcer on the medial canthus. The ulcer has rolled-out, beaded margins. Histopathology shows nesting cells with peripheral palisading patterns. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC), aka rodent ulcer is a slow-growing, locally invasive tumor and it rarely metastasizes. It arises from pluripotent cells within the basal layer of the epidermis or follicular structures.

Clinical Features

  • It presents initially small, scaly plaque
  • Slow progressive course of peripheral extension
  • Develops into nodular-ulcerative lesions, it has a thread-like margin, telangiectasia and it bleeds on touch.

[[figure-1]]

Site: Face, Around eyes, Nose

Histopathology: peripheral palisading of tumour cells (shown in the image), the cells resemble cells of stratum basale that have grown into the dermis. This cluster of cells is surrounded at the periphery by perpendicularly arranged cells. It also has a well-organized stroma surrounding it.

[[figure-2]]

Treatment

  • Medical: Imiquimod, 5-FU,Intralesional interferon α-2b
  • Hedgehog pathway inhibitors:(Vismodegib)
  • Surgical:
    • Mohs micrographic surgery, Done in recurrent BCCs.

Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A):

  • Clinical Features: There is a presence of a papule, nodule, or plaque with induration, accompanied by signs of photodamage such as crusting and scaling.
  • Histopathology: Keratin pearls.

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

Melanoma (Option C): The image presented above doesn’t meet the diagnostic criteria of malignant melanoma (ABCDE)

  • Asymmetry: Irregular shapes.
  • Border: Irregular.
  • Colour: Various colours present or uneven distribution.
  • Diameter: > 6 mm.
  • Evolution: Changes in lesion over time (size, shape, itching, or bleeding).

[[figure-5]]

Discoid lupus erythematosus (Option D): This is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by red, scaly, and atrophic lesions, typically without a tendency to bleed. Discoid lupus has distinct features like a well-demarcated, scaly plaque, and it usually lacks the ulcerative appearance seen in this case.



Reference:

Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition page no.141.4-141.6
question: A 60-year-old diabetic patient presents with a lesion on the nose as shown in the image below. The lesion bleeds on the touch. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• The image showing a lesion with irregular borders, asymmetry, and uneven distribution of colors, strongly suggests malignant melanoma. This is a malignant tumor arising from melanocytes located at the epidermal-dermal junction. Though rare, melanoma is highly aggressive with a significant risk of metastasis if not diagnosed early.

Key Diagnostic Features of Malignant Melanoma

  • ABCDE criteria:
    • Asymmetry.
    • Border irregularity.
    • Color variation (brown, black, red, white, or blue).
    • Diameter >6 mm.
    • Evolving lesion (changes in size, shape, or symptoms like bleeding or itching).

Biopsy Findings:

  • Large melanoma cells with enlarged nuclei, irregular contours, and clumped chromatin.
  • Prominent eosinophilic nucleoli.
  • Similar cellular appearance in both radial and vertical growth phases:
    • Radial phase: Horizontal spread of melanoma within the epidermis and superficial dermis.
    • Vertical phase: Deep invasion into dermal layers, forming an expansile mass.

Risk Factors:

  • Fair skin and history of sunburns.
  • Family history or genetic mutations (e.g., CDKN2A mutation on chromosome 9p21).
  • UV exposure and pre-existing nevi (e.g., dysplastic or congenital nevi).

Types of Melanoma:

Type

Site

Description

Image

Superficial spreading (M/C type)

Any (more common on the upper back and, in women, lower legs)

Brown mixed with bluish-red, bluish-black, reddish brown, and often whitish pink. The lesion border is often visibly and/or palpably raised

[[figure-1]]

Lentigo maligna

Sun-exposed surfaces, particularly malar region and temple

In flat portions, brown and tan predominate, but whitish grey sometimes present; in nodules, reddish brown, bluish grey, bluish-black.

[[figure-2]]

Acral lentiginous

Palm, sole, nail bed, mucous membrane

In flat portions, dark brown; in raised lesions (plaques), brown-black or blue-black.

[[figure-3]]

Nodular

Any

Reddish blue, purple, or bluish-black; can be uniform or mixed with brown and black.

[[figure-4]]

Staging and Classification:

  • Breslow thickness: Measures depth of tumor invasion.
  • Clark level: Describes the anatomical level of invasion.

Stage

Classification

Clarke

Breslow

I

Involvement of epidermis

≤ 0.75 mm

II

Involvement of epidermis + dermis

0.76-1.5 mm

III

Involvement of dermal papillae

1.5-4 mm

IV

Involvement of reticular dermis

>4 mm

V

Involvement of subcutaneous tissue

-

Management:

  1. Early detection and histopathological confirmation via biopsy are critical for improving outcomes.
  2. Wide local excision: Margins depend on Breslow thickness.
  3. Sentinel lymph node biopsy: Indicated for lesions >1 mm in thickness.
  4. Advanced cases:
    • Immunotherapy (e.g., immune checkpoint inhibitors).
    • Targeted therapy (BRAF/MEK inhibitors for BRAF-mutant melanoma).
    • Interferon-α: Prevents metastasis in high-risk cases.

Incorrect Options:

Option A) Condylomata lata:

  • Associated with secondary syphilis, these are smooth, moist, flat-topped, and highly contagious warty lesions, typically found in the anogenital region or mucous membranes. They lack the asymmetry, irregular borders, and color variations seen in malignant melanoma.

Option B) Mole:

  • Moles (benign melanocytic nevi) are symmetric lesions with uniform color, smooth borders, and no significant changes over time. They do not exhibit the irregular and evolving features of malignant melanoma.

Option D) Basal cell carcinoma:

  • This is the most common skin cancer, presenting as a pearly or translucent papule with telangiectasias, often on sun-exposed areas. It rarely shows pigmentation or the asymmetry and color variation seen in malignant melanoma.


Reference:
  1. Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, page no. 143.7-143.28
  2. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, page no. 587

Malignant melanoma:

  • Melanoma is a malignant tumour arising from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction. Though it is a rare skin cancer, it has a high mortality rate. It presents as a pigmented lesion that enlarges, ulcerates, or bleeds.

Risk factors:

  • Positive family history.
  • Fair skin.
  • Genetics: CDKN2A (chromosome 9p21), MC1R, and TYR genes.
  • Nevus:
    • Congenital melanocytic nevi.
    • Junctional nevi.
    • Atypical nevi.
    • Dysplastic nevi.
  • Fitzpatrick Type 1 skin.
  • UV light.

Types of Melanoma:

Type

Site

Description

Image

Superficial spreading (M/C type)

Brown mixed with bluish-red, bluish-black, reddish brown, and often whitish pink. The lesion border is often visibly and/or palpably raised

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Investigations:

  • Clinical examination.
  • Dermoscopy.
  • Biopsy.
  • Immunohistochemistry: The markers are S-100, HMB-45 (the most specific), Melan-A (MART-1), and MITF.
  • CT scan.

Breslow’s and Clarke’s Classifications of Malignant Melanoma:

Stage

Classification

Clarke

Breslow

I

Involvement of epidermis

≤ 0.75 mm

II

Involvement of epidermis + dermis

0.76-1.5 mm

1.5-4 mm

>4 mm

-

Management:

  • Wide local excision (with margins measured before excision and determined by Breslow depth, sentinel lymph node biopsy indicated for tumours with a depth of >1.0 mm).
  • If the tumour is aggressive:
    • Immunotherapy.
    • Chemotherapy.
    • Targeted therapy.
  • Interferon-𝛼 is the only adjuvant treatment that has documented beneficial effects on overall survival.

Incorrect Options:

Hyperpigmentation (Option B):

  • Generalized or localized increased skin pigmentation due to conditions like melasma, Addison’s disease, or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
  • Does not present with an irregular, evolving lesion.

Basal Cell Carcinoma (Option C):

  • Pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasia.
  • Slow-growing and rarely metastasizes.
  • May have central ulceration ("rodent ulcer").

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Option D):

  • Scaly, erythematous plaque or ulcer with crusting.
  • Often seen in chronically sun-exposed areas.
  • More locally invasive, with some potential for metastasis.

question: Identify the given disorder.

explanationHtml:
Answer D - Capillary Hemangioma:

  • The images show a bright red, raised, well-demarcated lesion commonly seen in infants.

  • Capillary hemangiomas (strawberry hemangiomas) are benign vascular tumors that typically appear after birth, grow rapidly, and regress spontaneously.

  • They are superficial hemangiomas composed of proliferating endothelial cells.

  • Commonly occur on the face, scalp, trunk, or extremities.

  • Most resolve by 5–7 years of age without treatment.

Infantile Hemangioma (Capillary Hemangioma)

Feature

Capillary Hemangioma

Cause

Proliferation of immature endothelial cells

Appearance

Bright red, raised lesion with a well-demarcated border

Onset

Appears within first few weeks after birth

Growth Pattern

Rapid growth for months, then gradual involution

Resolution

90% regress by 5–7 years of age

Treatment

Observation, propranolol (if complications occur)

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Portwine stain (Option A): Incorrect because port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) are flat, non-proliferative vascular malformations that do not regress.

Cavernous hemangioma (Option B): Incorrect because cavernous hemangiomas are deeper, bluish, and less well-defined.

Naevus simplex (Option C): Incorrect because naevus simplex ("salmon patch") is a flat, pink-red blanching lesion commonly seen on the forehead and nape of the neck.

question: A baby presents to the OPD; the image below shows the findings. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A persistent painless hyperpigmented lesion over an acral site raises suspicion for a melanocytic malignancy such as acral lentiginous melanoma.
  • Skin biopsy is the gold standard investigation for confirming pigmented neoplastic lesions.
  • Histopathology establishes the diagnosis and helps determine tumour depth and prognosis.

Acral pigmented lesions involving soles, palms, and heels require careful evaluation due to the risk of melanoma.

  • Acral lentiginous melanoma commonly presents as an irregular hyperpigmented lesion over pressure-bearing areas.
  • Early lesions may mimic traumatic pigmentation, fungal infection, or benign nevi, causing diagnostic delay.

[[figure-1]]

Role of skin biopsy in pigmented lesions:

  • Confirms malignant melanocytic proliferation.
  • Assesses Breslow thickness, ulceration, and mitotic activity.
  • Excisional biopsy is preferred whenever feasible in suspected melanoma.
  • Histology remains essential for diagnosis, staging, and treatment planning.

Clinical clues suggesting melanoma:

  • Asymmetry.
  • Irregular borders.
  • Variegated pigmentation.
  • Enlargement or non-healing acral lesion.

[[figure-2]]

KOH smear (Option B) Used to identify fungal elements in superficial mycoses. Cannot diagnose melanocytic or malignant lesions.

Gram stain (Option C): Useful for identifying bacterial organisms. Has no role in evaluating pigmented tumours.

Tzanck smear (Option D) Used in herpetic and vesiculobullous disorders. Does not assess melanocyte atypia or malignancy.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 143.12
